...to be joined, for the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "Sol & Luna"; in alchemy, these represent Gold and Silver</note> are not foreign to one another. This is because they are reduced, at the beginning of the work, into their first nature—that is, into Mercury—since they took their origin from it. However, some people strive to complete their work using Mercury alone, or simple Magnesia <note>A term for the primary "mother" material of the stone, not modern magnesium</note>, washing it in the sharpest vinegar, boiling it in oil, sublimating, roasting, calcining, distilling, and even extracting the "fifth essence" <term>Quintessence: the purest, fifth element that transcends the four terrestrial elements</term>. They torment Mercury itself with the elements and other infinite "martyrizations" <note>Alchemical jargon for violent chemical processes like intense heating or acid baths</note>, believing that through these operations they will find something great. In the end, they find very little profit.

But believe me, my son, that our entire mastery consists solely in the regulation of the fire, according to one's industrious capacity. For we perform no work ourselves; rather, the power of well-directed fire works our Stone with little labor and small expense. Consider that once our Stone has been dissolved into its first nature—namely, into the "first water," or "virgin’s milk," or the "dragon’s tail" <note>Metaphorical names for the initial liquid state of the matter</note>—then the Stone itself performs its own calcining, sublimating, distilling, reducing, washing, and congealing. Under the power of properly proportioned fire, it perfects itself in a single vessel without any further manual labor from the operator.

Understand then, son, how the philosophers have spoken figuratively about manual operations. Therefore, so that you may be certain of the purification of our Mercury, I will teach the true operation by which our common Mercury is most gently prepared. Take, then, mineral Mercury—otherwise known as "Spanish Earth," "our Antimony," or the "Black Earth with eyes" <note>Names for the raw mineral or ore, likely stibnite</note>, all of which are the same and not of an inferior kind—and which has not been used in any previous work. Take twenty-five pounds at most and pass it through a thick linen cloth three times; then pass it through a hare’s skin, and finally pass it through a thick linen cloth once more. This is the "true washing." Pay close attention: if any coarse residue, thick filth, or dregs remain in the skin, then that Mercury is not fit for our work. If, however, nothing appears, it is good. Note that with this Mercury, and with nothing else added to it, both parts of the work can be perfected.

## Chapter IV: On the Method of Amalgamating

Because our work is perfected from Mercury alone with no foreign substance added, the method for composing the Amalgam has been briefly described. However, some people misunderstand the philosophers on this point, for they believe they can complete the work from this Mercury alone without its "sister" or "companion" <note>Referring to the need for a balancing principle, often represented as Sulfur or the masculine element</note>. But I tell you with certainty that...

...that you labor with Mercury <term>Mercury: the metal quicksilver, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" of all metals</term> and its companion, and that you add nothing foreign to Mercury. Know that gold and silver are not foreign to Mercury; indeed, they participate in its nature more closely than any other bodies. Therefore, when reduced to their first nature, they are called the sisters and companions of Mercury. From their composition and simultaneous fixation, the "virgin's milk" <note>original: *lac virginis*; a term for a purified mercurial substance or a white liquid intermediate in the work</note> will flow out, if you clearly understand this point. And if you have worked with Mercury with no foreign thing added, you will achieve the desired result.

*On the composition of Gold and Mercury.*

### CHAPTER V.

Take two ounces of common purified gold <note>original: *solis*, literally "of the Sun"</note>—that is, heated in the fire—which is the "ferment of redness" <note>original: *fermentum rubedinis*; a substance believed to catalyze the final red stage of the Great Work</note>, and cut it into small pieces with shears. Add fourteen ounces of Mercury, and make the Mercury smoke on a tile, and dissolve my Gold <note>original: *Solem*</note> and stir it with a wooden rod until the Gold is well dissolved and mixed. Then pour the whole thing into clear water in a glass or stone bowl, and wash it often by wiping and changing the water until all the blackness departs. Then, if you wish to pay attention, the "voice of the turtle-dove" <note>original: *vox turturis*; a biblical metaphor often used in alchemy to signify a successful chemical reaction or the beginning of a new phase</note> is heard in our land. Once it is cleansed, make the amalgam <term>amalgam: a mixture of mercury with another metal, in this case gold</term> pass through a piece of leather tied well at the top, squeezing out the whole amalgam except for two ounces. Fourteen ounces will remain in the leather, and those fourteen ounces are the things suitable for our operation; yet note that there must be neither more nor less than two ounces of the total matter remaining in the leather <note>The text contains a numerical inconsistency here, oscillating between 14 and 2 ounces remaining in the leather; typically, the solid gold-rich amalgam stays in the leather while excess liquid mercury is squeezed out.</note>. 

If there is more, decrease it; if less, add more. And those two ounces squeezed out, which are called "virgin’s milk," save for the second operation. Then place the matter from the leather into glass, and put the glass into the furnace described above, with a lamp lit beneath it, burning continuously night and day so that it is never extinguished. Let the flame strike the vessel directly once it is enclosed, yet it should not touch the pot, and all parts of the furnace must be well-sealed with lute <term>lute: a clay-based paste used to airtight-seal alchemical vessels</term> in a similar fashion. 

If, however, after a month or two you wish to look upon the "living flowers" and the principal colors—namely black, white, yellow, and red—then without any work of your hands, and by the governance of the fire alone, the manifest shall be hidden, and the hidden shall be made manifest. Thus our matter leads itself to the perfect elixir <term>elixir: the goal of the alchemist, a substance that perfects metals or grants health</term>, turning itself into a most subtle powder, which is called the "dead earth," or "the dead man in the tomb," or the "magnesia of the end" <note>original: *magnesia finis*; a term for the base material at the conclusion of a specific stage of the work</note>, because the spirit is hidden in him in the tomb, and the soul...

...remained as if it had receded. Allow it then to stand from the beginning for twenty-six weeks, and what was thick is then made thin, the light becomes heavy, the rough soft, and the sweet bitter, by the conversion of natures, completed by the power of hidden fire. When you see your powders dried, and if you desire a trial and proof of value, they will tint <note>The alchemical term "tinging" refers to the process of a small amount of "medicine" or elixir transforming a larger body of base metal into silver or gold</note>; afterwards I will teach how to use one or two parts, since one part of our work will tint only seven parts of well-purified Mercury.

->*On amalgamation for the white.*<-

### CHAPTER VI.

In the same way, the process should be directed toward the white, that is, Silver <note>original: *luna* (the Moon)</note>; this is the ferment of whiteness mixed with seven parts of purified Mercury. Proceed in the same manner as you did for the red. For in every white work, nothing enters but the white, and in every red work, nothing but the red should enter: for from the same "water" of ours, both red and white are made, though with a different ferment added. Once the aforementioned time has elapsed, it can tint Mercury toward the white, just as you did for the red. Note, however, that "soldered silver" <term>Argentum solitatum: silver used in soldering, often alloyed with other metals to lower its melting point</term> is more useful in this material than bulk silver <note>original: *argentum massale*</note>, because it contains a mixture of certain dross from Mercury, and it must be amalgamated with cold Mercury, not hot. Otherwise, they err greatly in this operation by dissolving the amalgam in strong water <term>aqua fortis: nitric acid, a powerful solvent used to separate metals</term> to purify it; if they would consider the nature of the composition of strong water, the matter is actually more destroyed by this. Some also wish to work with mineral Sun <note>Gold</note> or Moon <note>Silver</note> according to the rules of this book, and they err, saying that the Sun has no humidity and is manifest heat, and is therefore the best; indeed the quintessence is extracted by the subtle skill of fire in the circulation vessel, which is called the Pelican <note>A specialized alchemical flask with return tubes, named for the bird that was mythically thought to feed its young with its own blood</note> from its shape. However, mineral Sun and Moon have such an impurity of dross mixed in with them that their purification for our purposes would not be "women's work and child's play" <note>A common alchemical proverb for a simple process; here, the author warns that purifying raw minerals is the exact opposite—arduous and difficult</note>, but rather the labors of a very strong old man, requiring dissolving, calcining, and other operations of the great art.

->*On the second and third operation.*<-

### CHAPTER VII.

Having finished this first work, I shall proceed to the second practice. Here, the "body" of our first work is combined with the "dragon's tail" <term>cauda draconis: a symbolic term often referring to the dregs or a specific chemical state of mercury</term>, that is, "virgin’s milk" <term>lacte virginis: a white, milky distillate or solvent</term>, adding seven parts of new Mercury to the remaining matter, according to the weight of the powders—Mercury, I say, puri[fied]...

...purified and cleansed, pass it through leather, and retain seven parts of the whole. Wash it and place it in the glass vessel and the small furnace, as you did in the first operation, governing the whole for such a period or thereabouts, until you see powders formed again. Then take them out or extract them, and if you wish, tinge <note>In alchemy, "tinging" refers to the process of transforming a base metal into gold or silver by "coloring" its essence with the Medicine.</note> with them. These powders are much finer than the first ones, because they are more fully digested <note>Digestion is a process of slow, constant heating used to mature a substance.</note>, so that one part tinges seven times seven in the Elixir. 

Then you proceed to the third practice, just as you did in the first and second operations, and place seven parts of the powder from the second operation of purified <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver</term> upon the weight, and put it in leather, so that seven parts remain in total as before. And cook it again, and make powders, which indeed are the finest powders; one ounce of these tinges seven times forty-nine parts—which are three hundred and forty-three parts—and this is done upon the Mercury. The reason is that the more our medicine is digested, the finer it becomes; and the finer it is, the more penetrative it will be; and the more penetrative it is, the more it transforms by entering into the metal. 

As a final note for this: if you do not have mineral quicksilver, you can safely work with common Mercury, because although it is not as valuable as the former, it nevertheless covers its own generous expenses.

->On the manner of operating on the matter or Mercury.<-

### CHAPTER VIII.

When you wish to <term>tinge</term> <note>Transform or transmute.</note> Mercury: Take a goldsmith's tile and smear the inside with a little suet, and place it upon a very slow fire according to the proportion of the Medicine. When the Mercury begins to smoke, throw your medicine inside, enclosed in clean wax or in paper. Have a strong and wide burning coal ready for this, and place it over the mouth of the tile, and apply a strong fire. When everything has been melted, pour it into a tube smeared with suet, and you will have the finest Sun <note>original: "solem" — Gold</note> or Moon <note>original: "lunam" — Silver</note>, depending on the addition of the ferment. 

If, however, you wish to multiply your medicine, do this in horse manure <note>Decomposing horse manure was frequently used by alchemists as a natural "heat bath" to provide a gentle, steady temperature over long periods.</note>, just as I have taught you by word of mouth. As you know, I do not write this down for you, because it would be a sin to reveal this secret to secular men, who seek this science more for vanity than for the proper end and the honor of God, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. 

Truly, that work which I have written for the common people in a sufficiently physical <note>meaning "plain" or "naturalistic" style</note> style, I saw Lord Albert <note>Likely Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and theologian often credited with alchemical discoveries.</note> perform once and for all using <term>Antimony</term> <note>A brittle, silvery-gray metalloid.</note> and the "Spanish earth" known to you. But because of the greater profit and the undue expense of time, I have advised you to work more easily...

<meta>This page concludes a short alchemical treatise attributed to Thomas Aquinas and begins the 'Book of Light' by the Franciscan friar John of Rupescissa. ### OF SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS.

...I have written this brief work, in which there is no error; it requires little expense, is easy to perform, takes little time, and achieves the truly desired end. From this, you and all your followers will perceive the truth without falsehood. Do not, therefore, my dearest friend, occupy yourself with a greater work, because for the sake of the duty of salvation and the preaching of Christ, and to save time, you ought to attend more to spiritual riches than to gape after temporal gains.

The treatise of Saint Thomas Aquinas on the **multiplication of the art** <note>original: "multiplicatione artis" — in alchemy, 'multiplication' is the process of increasing the quantity or the transmuting power of the Philosopher's Stone</note> ends here; it was published and given to his brother and companion, Brother Reginald, as a most secret treasure.

---

## THE BOOK OF LIGHT BY JOHN OF RUPESCISSA <note>John of Rupescissa (c. 1310–1362) was a French Franciscan friar who wrote extensively on prophecy and alchemy while imprisoned.</note>, a brother of the Order of Friars Minor.

### CHAPTER ONE.
First, I considered the times to come, which were predicted by Christ in the Gospel: specifically, the tribulations in the time of the Antichrist, under whom the Roman Church will be scourged and stripped of all its wealth by tyrants. And although the Church of God will then be so desolate and confused, it shall nevertheless be delivered from such great tribulations by Christ. Therefore, to liberate the chosen people of God, to whom it is given to know the ministry of God and the mastery of truth, I wish to describe—without wordiness—the work of the great **Philosopher’s Stone**, for both the **white** and the **red** <note>The 'white' stone was said to transmute base metals into silver, while the 'red' stone turned them into gold.</note>. This is contrary to the custom of the philosophers who came before us, who, out of malice and envy, hid this art even from their own sons. My intention is to benefit the good people of the Holy Roman Church, and to narrate the whole truth of it openly and briefly.

### Concerning the material of our stone. CHAPTER II.
The material of the stone is one and the same thing, of low price, which is found everywhere in "viscous water" called **Mercury**. Because they say it is found in "vile places," many brutish men who do not understand the true intention of the Philosophers have sought this stone in dung. Know then, my son, that the material is prepared by removing the "earthiness" that Mercury possesses, and adding to it the **Sulphur of the Philosophers**. This is not common sulphur; rather, our sulphur is invisible, and I shall call it by its proper name: it is the **Vitriol of Rome** <note>Likely referring to a purified form of copper or iron sulfate, used as a reagent in alchemical processes.</note>.

<summary>This page marks the transition from a short work on alchemy attributed to Thomas Aquinas to the 'Book of Light' by John of Rupescissa, who frames alchemical knowledge as a necessary tool for the Church to survive the coming of the Antichrist.</summary>

# JOHN OF RUPESCISSA

...Roman [vitriol], which some of the philosophers call magnesia, and these two operations are performed in this way.

->*Regarding the aforementioned operation.* CHAPTER III.<-

Take one pound each of Saltpeter and Roman vitriol <note>Roman vitriol is a historical term for iron(II) sulfate or copper(II) sulfate, used as a powerful reagent</note>, that is, one pound of each, ground and mixed. Dry them in a golden dish over a slow fire, stirring constantly so that the moisture evaporates. Then take one pound of quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, obtained from the mine and not extracted from lead, and having wrapped it in a soft leather cloth, squeeze it out over the mixture of vitriol and saltpeter while it is still somewhat warm. It will be sown through the pores of the mixture; move the material with a stick so that it is well mixed, until no trace of the Mercury appears. 

Place this in a vessel for sublimation <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface, used here to purify the substance</term> over a slow fire. If the material has been well dried, keep the mouth of the vessel closed; however, let it remain open until all moisture has departed. You will know the moisture is gone by placing a metal plate or a sword blade over the opening [and seeing no condensation]. Afterward, increase the fire for twelve hours, and at the end, make it even stronger so that the work is thoroughly sublimated. 

Once the vessel has cooled, remove the contents. You will find the sublimated Mercury as white as snow. Sublime this Mercury three times with its own dregs <term>Fæces: the solid, impure residue left at the bottom of the vessel after sublimation</term>, and then once more without the dregs. Through this operation, you have achieved two things: you have purged the Mercury of its earthiness, its blackness, and its inherent moisture; and you have congealed it, making it white as snow. You have made it fit for grinding and mixing, fit for digesting in a dry stove, and fit for converting into "water," as we shall describe below. 

You have placed within it an "invisible sulfur," which is the tincture <note>In alchemy, a tincture is a substance capable of changing the color or quality of another</note> of redness, and is the spirit of the Roman vitriol. This spirit provides great assistance, for it possesses the nature to stain things red and to congeal Mercury in its substance, even while making it white as snow. This is what the great philosophers wrote: that our Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is made from Mercury and sulfur that have been prepared and separated. 

Concerning this work and substance, Master Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> speaks parabolically in his treatise: "unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, etc." <note>Original Latin: "nisi granum frumenti in terram cadens mortuum fuerit, & cętera." A reference to John 12:24</note>. He understands the "grain dead in the earth" to mean Mercury "killed" <note>Mortification: the process of chemically changing a metal to strip it of its external properties</note> with saltpeter, Roman vitriol, and sulfur. There it is mortified, and there it is sublimated with fire, and thus it brings forth much fruit. This is the "Stone" greater than all others, which the philosophers sought and, having found it, kept hidden. The sign [of success] is that the spirit of the vitriol is incorporated into the Mercury, and that the sublimated Mercury leaves many dregs at the bottom of the vessel, while the spirit of the vitriol ascends because of the ascen- <meta>Catchword: afcen- (ascensionis)</meta>

*Concerning the second operation, which is: The reduction of sublimated Mercury into the quintessence.*

### CHAPTER IV.
The second operation is truly of the sublimated Mercury itself, which is as white as snow. Extract from it its spirit, which by some is more often called the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence," the purest, most medicinal, and most powerful core of a substance.</note>, or the "earth of leaves" <note>original: "terra foliorum"</note>, and "foliated earth." This spirit is incorruptible and somewhat less disturbed, and although the spirit is not fixed—rather, it is volatile—this is as it must be. Let the quintessence, namely the spirit of Mercury, be extracted and separated in this manner:

Take one pound of saltpeter and an equal amount of Roman vitriol, and make "strong water" <note>original: "aqua fortis"; nitric acid, used for dissolving metals.</note> as you know how. Grind the aforementioned Mercury very finely and dissolve it in the said strong water over hot ashes in a well-closed glass vial for twelve hours. And if our Mercury is dissolved, put into the said water with the said undissolved Mercury a seventh part of the weight of the aforesaid water of ground sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, a salt used to make acids more reactive.</note>. And this is a certain great secret in this art; set your heart upon it. Place a "blind" alembic <note>An "alembicum coecum" is a still-head without a discharge spout, used for refluxing or circulating vapors back into the liquid.</note> over the flask and distill it, and you will see the spirit of Mercury, or the soul, whiter than snow, ascend through the sides of the flask. Secondly, intensify the fire until the Mercury is fully ignited; afterwards, break the vessel and extract the quintessence or spirit of Mercury. You will find black, burnt remnants <note>original: "species nigras combustas"</note> at the bottom of the vessel, separated from the spirit of Mercury. In this operation, you have done two things: first, you have separated the white spirit of Mercury, which was earthy and corruptible, and imper-

# JOHN OF RUPESCISSA

...imperfect. And all that earthy material was burned by the **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fortis"; this refers to nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used by alchemists to dissolve metals.</note>, and it is nearly impossible that from a thing as white as snow such an earthy and black substance could be extracted and separated. Secondly, it absorbs the said **spirit of Mercury** from the spirit of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid or sulfate salts.</note> which is within the said strong water. And this is what <term>Master Arnold</term> <note>Refers to Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist whose works were foundational to this era.</note> says: let it drink as much as it can drink for twelve hours, because the Mercury dissolved in the water of vitriol drinks more of the spirit of vitriol (the invisible sulfur), and the dissolution is completed in twelve hours. 

Secondly, make new strong water as before, and in it once again dissolve the aforementioned **quintessence** <note>The "fifth essence," a purified substance thought to be the core of all matter.</note>, and sublimate it as you did the last time. Black dregs will remain at the bottom of the vessel, but not as many as before. Then, for a third time, make strong water as before and dissolve what was sublimated; and on this third occasion after distillation and sublimation, you will find only a few, slightly black dregs. At that point, you will have the perfect quintessence, which is called the "joined fifth humidity." It cannot be altered, nor consumed by perpetual fire; it will melt in fire like wax, and it never produces dregs, nor can it be consumed by any calcining water. From one pound you will have one ounce—no more, no less—and then you have the entire matter of the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> separated for the second time: incorruptible, volatile, white, whiter than snow; and this is the second operation.

->**Concerning the third operation, in which the said quintessence is prepared and dissolved into water.**<-

->### CHAPTER V.###<-

The third operation is this. Take the said spirit of Mercury, or perfectly separated quintessence, and grind it very finely upon a glass stone. Mix with one part of it two parts of <term>invisible living sulfur</term> <note>A pure, volatile form of sulfur used in the "Great Work."</note> and place it in a glass cup in a <term>philosophical furnace</term> <note>An oven designed to maintain a steady, specific temperature for long periods.</note> or in a <term>dry stove</term> to digest—that is, to be calcined <note>Reduced to powder through heat.</note>—within the ashes by the heat of coals for eight or twelve days, or more. There it is "cooked" so that it may be dissolved into water by itself, for otherwise it would not dissolve, nor could the work be brought to perfection.

->**Concerning the fourth operation, in which the quintessence, having been reduced to water, is distilled.**<-

->### CHAPTER VI.###<-

The fourth operation is to take the Mercury, or the said quintessence, with its vessel immediately after the digestion in the dry philosophical stove, and place it in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>original: "balneo Mariae"; a water bath used for gentle, even heating.</note>. Let it remain there until the whole is dissolved into water, and let it stand with the "white head" <note>An alchemical stage marked by the appearance of white vapors or residue at the top of the vessel.</note> and...

This was known by Phoebus <note>Phoebus is a name for the Sun, representing Gold or the solar principle in alchemy</note>, and Hermes—the father of the sons of wisdom—discovered it; the *Rosarius* <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical manuscript</note> understood it; it was not unknown to Avicenna; Master Arnold of Villanova dictated it, and Master Raymond Lull likewise.

Indeed, this Arnold says that it is necessary for the "son of man" to ascend from the earth into the air, and to ascend upon the "cross" of the alembic like crystal. For this reason, Arnold says he wishes to ascend onto the cross when he says: *it is necessary for the son of man to be lifted up onto the cross* <note>original: "oportet filium hominis exaltari in crucem" — a bold alchemical appropriation of the Gospel of John 3:14, equating the purification of the chemical substance with the Crucifixion</note>, that is, into the air, which is into the alembic <note>A vessel used for distillation</note>. When this dissolution is complete, then you have your perfected material; if you cast one drop of it upon a glowing hot metal plate, it will whiten it inside and out.

Thus you have seen that the material of the [Philosophers'] Stone is a single thing—not simple, but composite—made specifically from the spirit of Mercury and the spirit of Roman vitriol. For the spirit is called "invisible sulfur"—not the sulfur of the common people, but that of the philosophers. This is the internal "tincture" of redness; although it appears white, it is proven red by experiment. Because of this, Mercury requires the white sulfur of vitriol.

Therefore, when the distillation or dissolution itself is complete, you will find two elements mixed together in the bottom of the vessel: namely, the elements of air and fire, which are incombustible. What remains is the coarse, combustible matter, for you have extracted from it the element of water, animated by a spiritual soul. At that point, the material is sufficient for the "White Work" <term>The Albedo: the second stage of alchemy aimed at creating silver</term> specifically, and suitable for the "Red Work" <term>The Rubedo: the final stage aimed at creating gold</term>.

If you wish to separate the other three elements from one another, you shall work in this manner: Take those dregs, grind them, and place them to digest in a dry stove as you did before. Afterward, place them in a water bath to dissolve and distill as before with a very strong fire. That which ascends by the heat of the bath is the element of Air in its color—that is, it has the consistency of a very white oil. Take this and save it. Afterward, transfer the vessel to the fire of sublimation in an ash-bed; give it a good fire so that a "ruddy fire" may ascend through the alembic, having the quality of a red oil. Take this and save it aside.

In this way, you have the four elements separated from one another from the sublimated Mercury:
1. **First:** The element of Water, namely the "virgin's milk," distilled in the water bath during the fourth operation before the final dissolution of the material.
2. **Second:** The element of Air, namely the most white, shining oil, distilled in the bath once the final dissolution was made.

### CHAPTER VII

### This operation describes how the matter is prepared for the White, and how the **Virgin’s Milk** is digested and reduced by the power of fire into a powder so subtle that it cannot be felt by the touch. Take up, therefore, with the blessing of Jesus Christ—and some philosophers have said that "one should take the animal with all its blood" <note>The 'animal' is the alchemical matter; its 'blood' is the vital mineral spirit or liquid required for the transformation</note>. It is called an "animal" because it grows when it is sublimated, and because it has a soul of blood—namely, the aforementioned invisible **spirit of vitriol** <term>Vitriol: a sulfate mineral; its 'spirit' refers to the acidic vapor or liquid distilled from it</term>. Place it in a flask <note>original: "ampulla"</note> with a round bottom; heat its neck and "strangle" it—that is, squeeze the glass shut with forceps while hot so that nothing can escape. Place a metal plate between the fire and the flask, which should be well-prepared (that is, perforated) so that the Virgin's Milk is not destroyed by the direct heat of the fire. Place it in the **furnace of the philosophers** <note>A specialized kiln designed for slow, constant heating</note> so that it receives equal heat from every side, lest the Milk fly away <note>i.e., evaporate or explode the vessel</note> due to uneven fire. It is a great service to apply the fire temperately so the work is not destroyed; let enough coals burn so that a man's hand can still be held inside the walls of the furnace near the vessel containing the material of the shining Virgin’s Milk. You shall continue the fire until you see the matter turn black—and rejoice, for then you have the beginning of "digestion." Continue the fire until all the colors have passed through, and you will see the matter begin to whiten; and when you see the matter perfectly whitened, you have the **Stone perfected for the White**.

Concerning the sixth operation, namely the **reddening** <term>Rubification: the final stage (Rubedo) which produces the Stone capable of creating gold</term> of the White Stone.

### CHAPTER VIII

### The sixth operation of the Stone: perfecting the already completed Stone from the White into the **Red**, with absolutely nothing added or removed. Thus, extract it from the aforementioned vessel, which is called the **Philosophers' Egg** <note>An oval, hermetically sealed glass vessel used for long-term heating</note>. **Master Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist often cited by Rupescissa</note> says that our Stone is enclosed within that vessel just as Christ was in the tomb. Take then one part of this powder and keep it aside; with it, you will be able to convert all imperfect metals into true **Moon** <note>Moon (Luna) is the alchemical name for Silver</note>, and to—

And close the other part in the aforementioned vessel as before and strengthen the fire, as **Master Arnold** <note>original: "Magister Arnoldus"; likely referring to Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says; he states that after the **stone** has reached perfect whiteness, it does not fear the pains of fire, because there is no danger to it if you apply a strong fire, since it is necessary for it. The reason for this is that if it is digested by a slow fire, the invisible sulfur hidden within the **vitriol** <note>vitriol: a sulfate mineral. In alchemy, "invisible sulfur" refers to the active, combustible principle hidden within the metallic salts</note>—namely, the spirit lurking beneath the whiteness of the stone—cannot be boiled down. Instead, the spirit of **Mercury** is digested in that fire toward the white stage. Therefore, it is necessary for the fire to be increased so that it may reach deeper and digest the tincture of redness from the hidden sulfur of the vitriol, and bring it to the surface through the strengthening of the fire. Thus, by the power of the fire, it is turned into red without adding anything else to it. In this way, the **greatest king** rises from the closed tomb and has resurrected from the dead, with a most brilliant crown upon his head, as Master Arnold says.

But note that in two vessels, such a work of the stone can be performed and operated toward the white and toward the red with one fire and one furnace—except that you withdraw the vessel for the white stage when it is "clothed in whiteness," and for the vessel for the red stage, the fire is notably increased as I have said. 

And note that some perform this work only using **virgin's milk** <note>virgin's milk: an alchemical term for a specific white solvent or purified mercurial water</note> and the element of fire, and they do not care for other methods; their work is done solely through the most noble virgin’s milk. Others mix three elements together: one part weight of fire, four parts weight of air, and eight parts weight of virgin’s milk. This method is stronger for achieving the red stage but weaker for the white. In these three ways, it can be made simultaneously in one vessel from only virgin's milk for the red stage, and in another vessel from three elements, using one furnace and one fire. 

And you will see, if you test it in these various ways, the great miracles which have been bestowed by God Most High. Concerning this work, there was never anyone before me who spoke the truth so clearly. For indeed, the great **Philosophers** <note>Philosophers: the traditional term for alchemists and natural scientists of the medieval period</note> to whom this secret and mastery were revealed were bound by a horrible curse from God that they should not declare this divine work to any man in any way, lest this secret fall into the hands of wicked men. But I do not care for such a curse: therefore, I do not reveal this secret to wicked men, but I reveal it to the Church of God, and to perfect Christians, and those who fear God, so that they may aid the poor—especially those of the Gospel—and the churches, and so that they may visit widows, wards, and orphans in their needs and tribulations. 

And this is the **sixth operation**.

*Concerning the seventh operation, which is about projection.*
<note>In alchemy, "projection" is the final step where a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone or "Medicine" is thrown onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note>

### CHAPTER IX.

The seventh part of this work concerns the practice of the power of the elixir, namely the perfect medicine. The power of this elixir for the **white** <note>The "white work" or *albedo* aims to produce silver.</note> is that it converts Mercury, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Mars <note>Iron</note>, and Venus <note>Copper</note> into true Moon <note>Silver</note>. And the power of the perfect medicine for the **red** <note>The "red work" or *rubedo* aims to produce gold.</note> is that it converts the aforementioned bodies and the "moon" into the Sun <note>Gold</note>, and it is done thus: Place Mercury in a crucible and heat it for so long that the Mercury almost boils and smokes; afterward, sprinkle upon it while it is boiling the white or red Medicine as you desire, and give them a strong fire, just as if you wished to melt silver. Having obtained a suitable decoction <note>A thorough heating or "cooking" of the substance</note>, draw it out; if it should have much color, or if it should be brittle, then it is a perfect medicine. Then project it upon other Mercury until the color and the malleability please you. Experience will teach you how many weights it may fall upon, for sometimes it will fall upon many weights, and sometimes upon few, just as one method of operation will surpass another, and according to the skill of the Master of the art. 

Upon lead and tin, the fused medicine is projected, and the fire is increased as above. Upon brass <note>original: "lationem"</note>, iron, and steel, it is projected in this way: first, the powder is sprinkled upon fiery plates and weighed for re-heating, or those bodies are melted and the medicine is projected into them while they are fused. These bodies do not require a preceding purification because the medicine is like the fire of hell <note>original: "ignis inferni"</note>, virtually consuming every imperfection of all bodies and converting them into its own nature, which is their good and ultimate end. And some Philosophers, when they wish to work for silver, project the medicine upon copper or iron; and when it is for gold, they project the medicine upon the purest melted gold, and this "medicated gold" is then a medicine for converting copper or silver into gold. Furthermore, the medicine can be dissolved in a bath <note>A "balneo" or water-bath/bain-marie</note> and congealed by fire repeatedly, and thus its power is increased unto infinity.

## THE DESCRIPTION AND DESIGN OF THE PHYSICAL FURNACE FOLLOWS.

*This furnace shall be three and a half feet high in total, and one and a half feet wide overall, and divided as follows.*
*The first part of the furnace shall be so composed that a space of four or five [inches?] allows things to flow down through an iron grate <note>The ash pit area.</note>; it shall be one foot high. From the iron grate to the middle stand and the space where the hearth is built, the height shall be nine inches. With the height thus being two feet minus three inches, a clay or iron plate is to be placed in the middle, in the center of which there is a round hole having a diameter of four inches, through which the heat of the fire can ascend into the upper part where the operation takes place. Then above that hole, for example, there shall be three lids slightly wider than the hole in the intermediate plate, as marked with the letter A. Every lid will also have a different round hole. In the first, the hole will be three inches; in the second, two; and in the third, finally, one. Thus one may be used in place of another as the heat of the fire requires the changing of the lids.* <note>This allows the alchemist to precisely control the temperature by restricting airflow and heat transfer.</note>
*The space where the operation happens, namely from the intermediate plate to the top and the roof, shall be one foot and three inches high. In this space, a clay or iron tripod is placed directly over the hole of the intermediate plate, as marked by the letter B. This tripod shall be three and a half inches wide at the top, and six inches high; upon it you place the glass <note>original: "vitru" (vitrum); the chemical flask or vessel containing the "medicine".</note>, so that the material intended for the operation stands above everything.*

# JOHN OF RUPESCISSA
<note>original: "Ioannis de Rupescissa." A significant figure in medieval science, he combined chemical experimentation with apocalyptic prophecy.</note>

->[Illustration: The Complex Distillation Furnace]<-

This page features a detailed technical drawing of a <term>distillation apparatus|A set of tools used to heat a liquid until it turns to vapor, then cool it back into a liquid to purify it</term>. The illustration uses a "cutaway" view to show the internal components of the machinery.

**Components of the Apparatus:**

The central structure is a tall, cylindrical furnace or <term>retort|A vessel, usually glass or ceramic, with a long neck used for distilling liquids</term>. At the very top is a domed lid equipped with handles and a central opening. The cutaway reveals an internal conical vessel, labeled **B**, resting on a platform. Beneath this platform is a grate where a fire would be maintained to provide heat.

To the left of the furnace is an elongated, flat component with two circular holes, labeled **A**. This was likely used as a support or a specialized lid for holding multiple flasks during a simultaneous distillation.

To the right, two spherical glass vessels are shown, both labeled **B**. The upper sphere is shown split horizontally into two hemispheres to display its interior, while the lower sphere is shown in its complete form with a reinforcing band. These vessels would collect the condensed "spirits" or essences produced during the heating process.

### THE LITTLE KEY
<note>original: "Clavicula"</note>

Above that space in which the operation is performed, an earthenware lid or furnace-cover shall be placed, fashioned in the shape of a half-sphere or turned on a lathe, with a depth of six fingers, which should be fitted to the width of the furnace. Furthermore, this cover shall have a round hole of one finger’s width in the middle of the top, through which the heat of the fire—whether it be too intense or too weak—is to be investigated.

Some people use a split globe on a tripod marked with the letter B, the halves of which correspond to one another. If the letter B is noted in the margin: this globe will be seven fingers wide in the middle, where a certain earthenware instrument or vessel is enclosed, which the Chemists call the **Egg**. <note>original: "Ouum"; the 'Philosopher's Egg' was a common term for a sealed glass or ceramic vessel where the transmutation was thought to occur.</note> You have, therefore, a clear description and a precise image of the construction of this Chemical furnace.

We have called this work of ours the **Little Key**, <note>original: "Clauiculam"</note> because without this present book, no one can understand what we have written in our other books, in which we have completed the entire art, albeit in words that are quite obscure for the ignorant. I have written many lengthy books under various sections and obscure terms, <note>original: "dijs obscuris"; likely referring to the use of planetary or mythological names to hide chemical meanings.</note> as appears in our *Testament*, where we treated the natural principles, and where all things are placed that pertain to the art—yet these were placed "under the hammer" <note>an alchemical idiom for a process that is still being tested or refined</note> in the first text of Philosophy. Likewise in our chapter on the **Living Silver** <note>original: "arg. viuo" (Argentum Vivum), the technical term for Mercury</note> of the Philosophers, and in the second part of the *Testament* concerning the overflowing of physical minerals; and in our book on the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>the "Quinta Essentia" was the purest, most refined part of a substance, believed to be the medicinal or transformative core.</note> regarding the Fifth Essence of gold and silver; and finally in other books made by me, where the entire art is completed. 

But we have hidden the secret as much as possible. Furthermore, because without this secret no one can enter the "mines of the philosophers," <note>a metaphor for the foundational principles of alchemy</note> nor do anything that could be of use to them, therefore—with the help of the Most High, who was pleased to reveal this secret to us—I shall declare the entire art without any deception. 

And for that reason, beware of revealing this secret to the wicked; rather, give it only to your closest friends, although you ought to give it to no one [lightly], since it is a gift of God, who will give it to whom He wills. Whoever possesses it shall have an eternal treasure. Know, therefore, how to correct the imperfect by means of the perfect. The **Sun** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold.</note> is the father of all metals, and the **Moon** <note>The Moon represents Silver.</note> is the mother, although the Moon receives her brightness from the Sun. From these two...

But since metals cannot be transmuted <note>changed from one element into another</note>—according to the witness of Avicenna <note>original: "testè Auicenna"; Ibn Sina or Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose views on the impossibility of transmuting metals were frequently debated by later alchemists</note>—into minerals unless they are reduced to their primary matter, which is true. Common mercury is volatile and flat with a phlegmatic coldness <note>original: "frigiditate phlegmatica"; in the theory of the four humors, phlegm was cold and moist, implying the mercury is inactive and "dull"</note>, and therefore it needs to be reduced by fixed mercury, which is hotter and drier—qualities opposite to those of common mercury. Therefore, sons, I ask that you walk in the light with open eyes, and not like the blind fall into the pit of destruction.

*Concerning the difference between Common Mercury and Philosophical Mercury.*

### CHAPTER ONE

We say that common mercury cannot be the mercury of the philosophers, no matter how it is prepared by artifice, because the common kind cannot be held in the fire except by another corporeal <note>having a physical body or substance</note> mercury that is hot, dry, and more digested <note>original: "digeftum"; in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the refinement of a substance through steady, gentle heat</note>. Therefore, I say our physical mercury is of a more fixed and hotter nature than the common kind. And thus, because our corporeal mercury is converted into a running mercury that does not wet the fingers <note>this refers to "mercurius currens," a substance that flows like a liquid but behaves like a solid, a key goal in alchemical preparation</note>, and when it is mixed with the common kind they are joined, and they embrace one another in a bond of love <note>original: "vinculo amoris"</note> so that they are never separated from each other, just like water mixed with water, for so it pleases nature. Our mercury enters and is actually mixed with the other common mercury, drying up its phlegmatic moisture and removing the coldness from the body, turning it as black as coal <note>this refers to the *nigredo* or "blackening" stage, the first essential step in the Great Work of alchemy</note>, which it afterwards converts into powder. Note, therefore, that common mercury cannot perform such operations as our physical mercury can, which in all its qualities possesses the heat of nature’s true temperament; therefore, it turns common mercury into its own tempered nature. Indeed, it does something else: for after its transformation, it converts it into pure metal—that is, into Gold or Silver...

### CHAPTER IX.
Place that material of yours in a strong vessel <note>original: "metrereto" – likely a glass vessel or a specific liquid measure</note>, upon which you shall place an amalgam made of our <term>living lime</term> <note>In alchemy, "living lime" refers to a caustic, purified metallic base, not necessarily common quicklime</note>, which was prepared in our first practice, where we reduced it into silver. When it has been fixed, it will coagulate and fix all quicksilver—one ounce onto 100—into a true medicine, and again onto a thousand, and so on infinitely.

*Fixation of the aforementioned multiplied sulfur.*
### CHAPTER X.
Take the sulfur which has now been multiplied and place it in a vessel. Pour over it the oil that was saved during the "separation of the elements," and let it sit until it becomes soft. Afterward, place it upon the ashes to melt, applying heat of the first, second, and third degrees until it reaches a state of whiteness. Then break the vessel, and you will find a white crystalline plate. Place a piece of this upon a hot metal plate, and if it flows without smoking, project one weight of the aforementioned substance onto 1,000 weights of Mercury, and the whole will be converted into silver. And if the medicine is not yet flowing and fusible, place it in a <term>crucible</term> <note>a ceramic or graphite container used for melting metals at high temperatures</note>, adding the oil drop by drop until it flows like wax. Then your medicine will be perfected at a ratio of 1 to 1,000, and can thus be multiplied infinitely.

*Reduction of the white medicine into the Red Elixir:*
### CHAPTER XI.
Take, therefore, in the Name [of God], four ounces of the aforementioned plate and dissolve it in the water saved from the stone. When it has been dissolved, place it in a <term>bath</term> <note>a "balneum" or water bath, used for gentle, consistent heat</note> to ferment for 9 days. Then take two weights of our <term>red lime</term> and cast them into the aforementioned vessel. Let it ferment for 9 days, then distill it in an <term>alembic</term> <note>a classic alchemical still with a gourd-shaped base and a "beak" for condensation</note> in a bath. Afterward, place it over the ashes, applying heat of the first degree until the matter turns black. This is our second dissolution and our second "Eclipse," which the Sun <note>symbolizing Gold</note> made with the Moon <note>symbolizing Silver</note>, which is the sign of true dissolution and the conjunction of the male...

### CHAPTER XII.

Everything we have discussed in this book, we have learned to be true, and we testify to it; we have seen it with our own eyes, felt it with our hands, touched it, and performed it. This recapitulation embraces our entire mastery with a brief discourse and without deception. We therefore command the <term>stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmutation</note>, which we name, that you refine it as much by the ingenuity of nature as by art, and return it into <term>mercury</term> <note>Latin: *arg. viuum* / *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver"</note>, and to this <term>mercury</term> let there be added a white body, which is of the same nature. Let it be cooked until it reaches the true preparation of the mineral. And let that mineral be multiplied according to your will. And again, let the aforementioned material be returned into <term>mercury</term>, and dissolve it in our menstruum <note>A solvent used in alchemy to dissolve solids</note>, until the stone becomes volatile, divided from all its elements. And finally, let it be perfectly purged, until the final perfection—both the body and the soul—so that a good union of the body with the spirit can be made, by a temperate natural heat. And let the stone be made into a mineral, and let the fire be continued until it is reduced into a white powder, which we call <term>sulfur and mercury of the philosophers</term>. Then, by the power of the fire, it is made fixed or volatile—to the extent that the volatile part flies away from its coarse earths and ascends on high, whiter than snow, and the dregs should be thrown away, because they are worth nothing. Then take our sulfur, the aforementioned oil, and you shall multiply it with its stated alembic <note>A laboratory tool consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling</note>, until it is once again reduced into a white powder whiter than snow. Let the powders be fixed, multiplied by the ingenuity of both nature and practice, by cooking them with water, until everything remains in the trial of the fire, flowing like wax without smoke. And the water of the first solution must be added; when the solution is made, let something yellow be added, which is gold, by means of conjunction, with the distillation of the entire soul. Afterward, let the fire be given in the first, second, third, and fourth...

### Calcination of Silver for the Work.

## CHAPTER XIII.

Take <note>The symbol "Rc." stands for the Latin 'Recipe', the standard opening for a formula</note> one ounce of fine Silver <note>original: "Luna", the alchemical name for silver</note> purified by cupellation <note>original: "copella"; a process of refining precious metals in a shallow vat</note> and three ounces of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury</note>, and let an amalgam be made. First, heat the silver leaf in a crucible, then throw in the quicksilver, stirring it with a rod, and let both be well heated. Then place it in vinegar with salt, grinding them together in a wooden mortar with a pestle, washing and removing the impurities; continue doing this until it is finally amalgamated. Then let it be washed with clean, warm common water. Afterward, pass it through a clean linen cloth. That which remains in the cloth—having the nature of the "body" <note>the solid metallic part</note>—should be added again to three parts of salt and one part of the body, grinding and washing well; let it be strained and calcined <note>term: calcined: reduced to a powder through prolonged heating</note> for 12 hours. Grind it again with salt, repeating the process three times and adding new salt each time. Then, let it be pulverized until it is an impalpable powder, and wash it with warm water until all the saltiness has vanished. Then let it be filtered through a cotton filter and your lime <note>term: lime: 'calx', the powdery residue remaining after a metal has been calcined</note> dried; it will be a white lime. Store it until the hour of necessity, ensuring that no dampness <note>original: "frigiditas", literally 'coldness' but often implying damp or degrading air in this context</note> touches it.

### To make Oil of Tartar.

Take good tartar <note>a salt found in wine barrels</note> that is shiny when broken; let it be calcined in a reverberatory furnace <note>original: "reuerbero"; a furnace that reflects heat onto the substance</note> for ten hours. Afterward, let it be powdered and placed upon a marble slab to dissolve in a cold place; there it will dissolve into a liquid oil. When it is entirely dissolved, let it be filtered through a cotton filter and kept clean for the soaking <note>term: imbibitione: the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note> of your lime.

### CHAPTER II.

### CHAPTER IV.

Then you shall sublimate again that which has been sublimated once, using fresh material, doing everything in the same manner as above. You shall repeat this sublimation a third time, always with fresh material. Finally, you shall sublimate it by itself—that is, without any other material—until nothing further remains; then the stone is pure. For first, it has been purged of all its combustible <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represented the principle of combustion and soul; "combustible sulfur" was considered an impurity that caused metals to char or burn away.</note>, so that it can no longer be consumed by fire. It is also thoroughly purged of its <term>earthiness</term> <note>original: "terrestritate"; the heavy, impure, or non-spiritual part of a substance.</note> which prevented its entry. For that earthiness and the combustible sulfur were both left behind with the dross. The combustible sulfur previously burned its body when it was moved to the fire, and the earthiness prohibited its entry, so that it could not enter into metals. It is now separated and free from these two, as has been said.

### C H A P T E R V.

<margin>Certain subtle spirits are present in the stone.</margin>
<margin>The stone is partly fixed and partly non-fixed.</margin>
<margin>The stone must be cleansed of three superfluities: namely, from combustible sulfur, from the earthiness that prevents penetration, and from the subtle spirit that hinders fixation. The superfluous things are to be removed from the stone; the tempered parts are to be preserved within it.</margin>
Now my son shall also know that this stone still contains matter within itself which takes away its <term>fixation</term><note>In alchemy, fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable in heat so that it no longer evaporates or escapes when placed in fire.</note>: for as long as it contains that matter, this stone can never be fixed. Many are deceived in this, for they do not know this matter. But my son may ask, what is this matter? Let my son hold this as a great secret: there is present in this stone—both the white and the red—a certain most subtle spirit, so fleeting and subtle that the stone could never be fixed, even if it were in the fire for a thousand years. For when it is to be fixed, whether with a <term>ferment</term><note>A substance (often gold or silver) added to the alchemical stone to "leaven" it and direct its transformation toward a specific metal.</note> or with any other "body," such a tiny fire must be applied that nothing at all is <term>sublimed</term><note>Sublimation is the process where a solid turns into vapor and hardens again at the top of a vessel; here, the author warns against letting the spirit escape upward.</note> upward. Otherwise, it will not become fixed with the ferment or the body, and thus it would have to be joined together again and again; how then could it ever be fixed? Indeed, that stone possesses those subtle spirits, none of which can be allowed to ascend. Therefore, the subtle spirit must be separated from the stone, just like that coarse earthiness or earthy matter that prevents its <term>penetration</term><note>The ability of the alchemical medicine to "sink into" and transform base metals.</note>. Thus, these two matters must be separated from the stone before the stone can be fixed with any ferment or body.

<margin>How the most subtle spirit is separated from the middle [matter].</margin>
The "middle spirit" or matter is to be taken, which is always found in the middle place; it is this spirit that we seek, which exists between the fixed and the non-fixed. For if you place that matter in a glass crucible, it will melt before it begins to fly away; nor will it fly quickly, but like pure wax, it will ascend from the fire gradually. Thus the matter of the stone is <term>tempered</term><note>Balanced or moderated.</note> between the fixed and the non-fixed once its superfluity has been taken away—that is, first the <term>combustible sulfur</term><note>original: "Sulphur combustibile"; an alchemical term for an impure, oily substance that causes metals to be "burnt" or corrupted.</note>, then its earthiness which prevents or takes away its penetration, and finally its subtle combustible spirits which take away the stone's fixation. All alchemists err in this because they do not know the stone, nor its nature, and they do not remove its superfluity. That is to say, they do not take away its superfluous parts, nor can they preserve the tempered state between the fixed and the non-fixed. This is the greatest secret in this art. Therefore, learn to know the stone and its nature, and you shall not err.

### C H A P T E R V I.

Now my son shall take the stone, when it has all risen together <note>Referring to the result of a previous distillation or sublimation.</note> so that nothing remains behind, and he shall put it into glass or stone pots. Having placed an <term>alembic</term><note>A lid or apparatus used for distillation.</note> on top, he shall place it upon the furnace for sublimation...

...mation <note>original: "mationis," likely the conclusion of the word "sublimationis" (sublimation)</note>, with the receiver properly sealed with clay to the beak, you shall apply a very small fire, a little warmer than the Sun in mid-summer, and maintain that heat for 10 hours. And the **matter of the stone**, which adapts itself to all natures, is found in the middle, sublimated to the neck of the pot; it does not rise as high as those subtle, combustible spirits. For the matter of the stone cannot, nor is it able to, rise to that height which the subtle spirit reaches; for the matter of the stone has certain **fixed parts** in its nature which restrain those **volatile parts**, so that they cannot rise as high as those subtle, intemperate spirits, which have no fixed parts mixed within them.

Indeed, take out and preserve this noble matter of the stone, for it is that true stone which Almighty God has given us freely, and it is prepared for our work: for it is equal in all its parts for operating, and that in all the works of the *Philosophers* <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists or natural scientists of the past</note>. For if you place this stone in a **glass crucible** to the fire, it will melt like wax before it begins to rise, and then it ascends gradually, like wax or anything else that rises by fire. This is caused by the fixed parts it contains; these hold the volatile parts to themselves, so that they must melt with it before they ascend. And thus, those fixed parts sometimes rise together with them; for the volatile parts of the stone are greater than the fixed ones, and therefore the volatile parts partly lift the fixed parts with them by the power of the fire. Know this, my son: the knowledge of this stone will bring your work to a happy conclusion, by the help of God, the Best and Greatest; whereas ignorance of the stone brings forth many errors.

Then you shall take 12 [parts] of your prepared spirit, and mix them well together. Then grind them upon a stone with common water, so that a painter might be able to paint with that material using a brush. Then evaporate the

When these have passed, increase the fire gradually until it can endure a great fire. ### [Of the Fixation]

...apply such heat from above that the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in alchemy, the volatile essence of a substance that easily evaporates</note> exits through the <term>ferment</term> <note>original: "fermentum"; a substance that acts like yeast to "leaven" or transform the base material</note> and settles itself below at the bottom of the glass. Therefore, the <term>fire</term> <note>heat management was the most critical skill for an alchemist</note> must be managed in this way, so that there is equal heat in the upper and lower parts of the <term>furnace</term>. You would be greatly mistaken if you stirred up a greater heat in the upper part than in the lower part of the <term>furnace</term>, such that the <term>spirit</term> would sink below through the <term>ferment</term>, and you then took some of it from there to test it. Therefore, do as you were taught above, namely that you test and weigh: for if you took it out and tested it, but did not weigh it; when you took from your <term>ferment</term>—from which the <term>spirit</term> had been sublimated <note>turned into vapor and then solidified elsewhere</note> either below or above—you would find it at full weight. Then you would judge it to be "fixed" <note>stable and no longer volatile</note>, but you would be wrong. For the spirit would be lying at the bottom, and the <term>ferment</term> above the spirit, and you would have tested nothing other than the <term>ferment</term> alone. 

<margin>It is better to err in having too little fire than in having too much.</margin>

Therefore, watch carefully that you manage the <term>fire</term> so that the heat below, above, and at the sides is equally great. Whatever you do, apply a smaller <term>fire</term> rather than a greater one; in this way you cannot be deceived. Although it will require a much longer time before it is fixed, it is much more certain. And so, my son, be wise and take care in building your <term>fire</term>, lest you have to begin everything all over again, just as if it had never been placed in the <term>fire</term> at all. In the whole of this art, nothing requires more care than this <term>fixation</term>. For the <term>spirit</term> and the <term>ferment</term> must remain joined and united if they are to eventually be fixed. For how could two become one when one withdraws itself from the other, and when they are separated from each other? 

Therefore, my son, see prudently that you moderate your <term>fire</term> so that you do not drive the <term>spirit</term>, <term>soul</term>, and <term>body</term> <note>the three primary components of matter in alchemical theory</note> away from each other with a more violent <term>fire</term>. Instead, always build a small <term>fire</term> so that they remain joined, so that the <term>soul</term> and <term>body</term> may both be able to be one. 

<margin>Note: in the time it takes to say the Lord’s Prayer, the fire may be neglected, so that one must begin again from the start; therefore these things should be reread and remembered often.</margin>

Read this lesson often and impress it upon your mind, for many works are lost through the negligence of the <term>fire</term>. For in the time it takes to say the <term>Lord’s Prayer</term> <note>original: "orationis dominicae"; the "Pater Noster" was frequently used as a standard unit of time in a world without precision clocks</note>, it can happen that the <term>fire</term> is neglected, so that one must begin again from the very start. 

Also now, my son, you shall occasionally take some out, as was said before, and observe what heat it can bear. Increase such heat by degrees until it is fixed and can bear a flame for the length of time that the <term>Lord’s Prayer</term> could be recited ten or twelve times. If it then loses nothing in <term>weight</term>, it is fixed. Then, add to it another fifth part of <term>spirits</term>; that is, empty the glass, weigh your material, and for every four parts of matter take one part of <term>spirit</term>, which together makes five parts. Then...

When the hours have passed, and you lose nothing in your weight, and you are certain that your <term>spirit</term> <note>The volatile, "living" essence of the substance</note> is fixed with the ferment, remove the <term>matter</term> <note>The physical substance being worked upon</note> from the glass. Place it to be calcined <note>Reduced to powder through heat</note> in the <term>furnace</term> of the wise, in which it is calcined in an open vessel; or use a furnace in which spirits are calcined, which, when they cannot be dissolved, must be calcined in a furnace constructed for that purpose, where there is more heat in the upper part than in the lower. For the spirits which we wish to dissolve must be calcined in an open vessel, and in such a furnace this matter must be calcined. 

Then, indeed, you shall take this matter from the glass vessel and put it into a glass vessel that is wide and flat, made in the manner of a flat clay pan without a handle and with a flat bottom. Into this, place your matter to the thickness of a thumb, or a little more, and place it in the furnace. First add a small fire, and gradually a greater one, so that the matter is between glowing and not glowing. Leave it at the fire in this way for four days and nights. When these are finished, take it out and set it to be dissolved with <term>distilled vinegar</term> <note>A common alchemical solvent used to extract the "salt" or "tincture" from the calcined remains</note> in a <term>bath</term> <note>Usually a "Balneum Mariae" or water bath for gentle, even heating</note>. Every three days, pour off the vinegar and always pour in fresh vinegar again, mixing it three or four times each day. 

If there should be anything that refuses to be dissolved in the vinegar, you shall calcine that same part again, as described above, continuously for 24 hours. Then you shall take it out and again set it to be dissolved in distilled vinegar, as above; and do this until everything has been dissolved. When this is done, you shall congeal it again until it becomes a powder, and again set it to be calcined for 24 hours to drive off the spirit of the vinegar. 

Then, having removed your matter, you shall weigh it to see how heavy it is. Things being thus, you shall take a fifth part of the spirit to your fixed matter—namely, four parts of fixed matter and one of spirit. Mix them and grind them thoroughly together, as is handed down in the work of the second order. You shall dry it over a bath and put it in again, so that one may become fixed with the other, as is taught in the work of the second order. 

And when it is fixed again, set it once more to be calcined, then once more to be dissolved and congealed, and then again to be calcined to extract the spirit of the vinegar. Then mix it again with the spirit, and then fix it once more until your matter no longer allows itself to be calcined, but melts like wax. Then your <term>medicine</term> <note>The perfected Alchemical Stone or Elixir</note> of the third order will be perfected. Give thanks to God and perform your <term>projection</term> <note>The final act of casting the Alchemical Stone onto base metals to transform them into gold or silver</note> upon <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>Base metals like lead or tin</note> possessing a soul.

### On preparing the Stone from Silver alone.

<margin>The nature of all things that exist beneath the lunar circle must be understood.</margin>
Next, my son, I wish to teach you the composition of the **Stone of the Ancients** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver.</note>, and first how you shall arrive at it: You shall study, my son, diligently in this art, and with a sharp mind you shall grasp the sayings of the ancients; you must also learn the nature of all things, and how nature operates in all things, and especially whatever lies beneath the **lunar circle** <note>In the geocentric cosmology of the time, the "sublunary" sphere referred to the Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to change and decay.</note>, and its course: and when the Moon first began its course in the Sphere, and from where. Furthermore, you must keep in mind from where metals in the mines draw their origin, how they first grow and increase, and in what way, and to what state the nature of metals loves to be reduced—and would have reduced itself, had nature not been hindered by other things, so that it could not accomplish its perfection. You must know these things of hindrance, and also know (if you wish to be a worker in this art) in which operations you shall not imitate nature, or in which you ought to imitate it. And I tell you this must be known, or I do not advise you to undertake the work. Those who are ignorant of this are far from the art; they are without foundation or root upon which their thoughts or mental perceptions can lean: and because of this, they do not know whether they act rightly or wrongly. Unless you know the essence and nature of these things—their beginning, their growth, and their defects—and why nature cannot reach its goal there, and if you do not know their inner workings, you will accomplish nothing in our art. Therefore study diligently before you approach the work; and if you are sick or in weak health, do not begin, for the work, once it has been started, can by no means be interrupted. Also, you must excel in sharpness of wit, for here one must work with **subtlety**.

<margin>The chemical art is an enemy to the poor.</margin>
Furthermore, he who wishes to set his hands to this work can practice nothing else: likewise, this must by no means be undertaken out of greed, for you would not be able to wait for the end, as the greedy always think only of profit. And if you are poor, you will not be able to pursue it, for this art is an enemy to the poor; the expense is great, the work cannot be done with little material, and the time required is long. Unless you know yourself to be furnished with such great wealth that you can provide for two years of expenses, vessels, glasses, and other utensils for yourself and your companions, do not begin, for you cannot execute the work alone. And likewise, you must have much material from which you may fashion your work: for to accomplish it, you must have at least 3 pounds <note>original: ℔. (libra)</note> of material, and have it prepared from the start, so that if anything [should happen]

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>The error of wicked Sophists <note>In alchemical literature, "sophists" refers to fraudulent practitioners or those who follow the "letter" of recipes without understanding the "spirit" of nature.</note> who desire to extract the Stone from other things.</margin>
Furthermore, you know that all metals grow from the mixture of Mercury <term>Mercury: Often representing the "feminine," fluid principle of matter; also called quicksilver.</term> and sulfur <term>Sulfur: Representing the "masculine," active, and combustible principle.</term>, both the pure and the impure; it is also established that metals can be produced from nothing else in nature except these two. Therefore, it is clear that no foreign things enter into our Stone which did not take their first origin from these two. All those are mistaken who presume to extract the Stone from hair, eggs, blood, living creatures, or from any of the four spirits, and those who seek it from urine, or from Mercury or Sulfur that have not been bodies <note>meaning they haven't been processed or "thickened" into a metallic state</note>; all these things are the delusions and dreams of men ignorant of nature. Others amalgamate the Sun <term>Sun: The alchemical name for Gold (Sol).</term>, the Moon <term>Moon: The alchemical name for Silver (Luna).</term>, and purified Mercury, and set them to be cooked; and when they have cooked them for a long time, they obtain a red powder, like brick-dust. When they then wish to test whether the Mercury is fixed <term>Fixed: A substance is "fixed" when it can endure the heat of a fire without evaporating or "flying away."</term>, it goes up in smoke and carries away the best part of the body with it, and that which is fixed remains as a dry material that cannot be melted, so dried out is it by the fire.

There are others who wish to elicit the Stone from the Sun and Moon, as if they thought they could extract the Red or White Stone from these perfected bodies, which are hard and solid; therefore, this is also impossible for us. For our natural fire harms these bodies very little and can do nothing against them, even if the Stone could be led out from them: they are hard and fixed, and nothing foreign can be added to our Stone. Only those things which are superfluous in it must be removed, and it must be made subtle, even more than subtle. Those hard and fixed bodies—if they were to be reduced so that the Stone could be elicited from them—would have to be "un-fixed" <note>original: "defixanda"; the process of making a solid or "fixed" substance volatile or liquid again</note>, and spirits would have to be made from them, if anything is to be produced from them. Thus it is clear that our Stone cannot be extracted from hard, fixed bodies.

Now my son may ask, from where then must our Stone be extracted? Let my son know, however, that the Sages <note>original: "Sapientes"; the "Wise" or the true alchemical masters of history</note> have sought something...

He explains that while Gold and Silver are "perfect" metals, their solid state makes them unsuitable for the initial stages of the Great Work unless they are completely broken down.</summary>

...certain [substances] among minerals, in which there was Mercury, pure and unadulterated, and an incombustible sulfur <note>original: "sulphur incombustibile"; in alchemy, this refers to a stable, fixed sulfur that resists the fire</note> that was also pure and clean. And where those two were so thoroughly mixed, each according to its proportion, and thus frozen together so that they could not be separated—and because both were volatile and spiritual—from these they extracted their "Stone." And now I tell you openly, using no riddles: if indeed you are endowed with mind and reason so that you can grasp and understand my words and arguments, you will recognize the matter from which you shall build and complete the stone. You will know all our metals that grow in the mines and their nature; you will know our matter from which you will draw the stone. I have already clearly demonstrated and named this matter to you here, though using other words.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>There is only one method for both the red and the white stone.</margin>
<margin>* In other words, there is but one matter.</margin>My son shall know for certain that there are not several methods, but only one, for the <term>Red Stone</term> <note>The "Red Stone" was believed to transmute base metals into gold</note> and the <term>White Stone</term> <note>The "White Stone" was believed to transmute base metals into silver</note>. Long ago, however, there were those who could only extract this stone from the "two luminaries"—that is, from the aforementioned matter. When they had finally produced the stone, they first completed the Stone for the White without adding any "white ferment," and they produced that stone with great labor. Then, they further completed the same for the Red, with no "red ferment" <note>ferment: a substance added to the alchemical mix to "leaven" or trigger the final transformation, much like yeast in bread</note> added, and they produced it with great labor over a long time and with great subtlety. For the stone produced in this way performed a marvelous and infinite <term>projection</term> <note>projection: the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon molten base metal to transform it</note>. They did not know how to make the stone any other way than from both matters for the red and the white without any ferment. Therefore, they wrote in their secret books that the stone cannot be made except from both those matters, for both the red and the white. In this, they wrote the truth: but the stone for the Red cannot be made unless you add ferment, and the matter for the White must be present. Similarly, the stone for the White cannot be extracted unless ferment is used, and the matter for the Red must be present. These were the first who discovered the matter for making the stone.

The Moon shines by night as the Sun does by day; one without the [mixture] of the other... <note>original: "admi-", likely "admixtione"</note>
