### MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC ###

Take a sturdy and wide glass jar <term>jar<note>original: *olla*</note></term> which has a broad base at the bottom, and place your material into it—as I shall easily explain to you in person—and place upon the jar a large alembic <note>the "head" or cap of a still</note> with a wide beak, and a receiver <note>the vessel that catches the distillate</note> attached to it with lute <term>lute<note>a paste or cement used to seal alchemical vessels against leaks</note></term>.

->[A woodcut illustration of an alchemical apparatus. It consists of a conical base (the "glass jar") with a wide mouth, upon which rests a spherical alembic head with a long, downward-sloping beak or spout. The alembic and receiver appear to be sealed together at their junction.]<-

Furthermore, the lower glass jar should be quite low, flat, and very wide at the bottom, just as this figure shows you. Place your prepared materials into this, and once the alembic is placed on top, seal it well with lute. Place it in the sublimation furnace with a tray of ashes <note>used to distribute heat evenly, like a modern sand bath</note>. Join the receiver to the beak with lute, and once the lute is dry, you are ready for sublimating <term>sublimation<note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note></term>. Regarding this, a certain Philosopher says: Earth is the lowest world, and water, which ascends upward, has a soul within it. Nor are there more than two things known and two in the open, and two in secret. Just as is evident in the elements: earth and water are known, and they can be seen and touched; but fire and air are in hiding. So it is also in our Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>: three are seen clearly, and two more certain ones are obscured. How then can they be seen? Just as it appears to the sight that whiteness lies hidden under blackness <note>The alchemical stages of *nigredo* (black) and *albedo* (white)</note>, and later redness <note>the *rubedo* stage</note> which was hidden under the whiteness. Those two were first in the intellect, but now they are in the sight.

<margin>First operation.</margin> My son, how are the hidden sayings of the Philosophers to be understood? They said, in the first reduction—that is what they called the "solution"—which is the foundation of the art. Regarding this, Rhazes <note>original: *Rafis*; a 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: Unless you dissolve the body <note>original: *Nisi corpus resoluas*</note>, you labor in vain <note>original: *frustra laboras*</note>. For bodies must be reduced back to such waters as those from which they first took their origin, that is, into common water. However, the common people do not understand this solution. This is its first reduction into its essence, etc.

<margin>2. Operation.</margin> Another Philosopher says: Unless earth is produced from the thickness of the water, you are playing at work in our art, etc.

<margin>3. Operation.</margin> The third work is purification or cleansing. Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> says: When this earth putrefies with earth, and is thinned...

**Geber** <note>original: "Geber". ## CHAPTER 23.

<margin>Return to the work.</margin>
<margin>Sublimation of the stone through its stages of fire, until whatever is volatile is sublimated from the dregs.</margin>
Now, my son, let us return to our work: you shall place fire under the furnace, first a little and gradually greater by degrees, until you see your matter sublimate <note>To transform a solid into vapor by heat, which then collects again as a purified solid in the upper part of the vessel.</note>: then keep the fire at that heat as long as it ascends, but rather increase the fire a little than let it cool; and as long as you see it ascending, leave it thus with the aforementioned moderate fire. And when the ascent itself begins to diminish, increase the fire as you see necessary: You will be able to see this through the glass <term>alembic</term> <note>The upper part of a distilling apparatus, often shaped like a helmet or beak.</note>. Leave it thus night and day, always increasing the fire as you see necessary.

<margin>The dregs are to be dissolved in vinegar, so that what is not sublimated may be drawn out from the dregs of sublimation, which is the earth of the stone.</margin>
And when you see it no longer sublimating, increase your fire gradually until your glass pot glows white-hot below; keep it in that glowing state for two hours, or until you see that nothing more ascends. Then let it cool of its own accord, and after removing the alembic, empty it and store the contents in a glass jar. Take out the dregs from the glass pot and put them into a large glass vessel, and pour over it strong distilled vinegar made from wine. Place it in a warm bath <note>Likely a water bath or "Bain-marie" for gentle, steady heat.</note> and leave it to dissolve for eight days. Then pour the vinegar into a glass vessel and set it to coagulate upon the bath in a basin with sand <note>A sand bath provided even, high heat without breaking the glass.</note> until it is dry.

<margin>The sublimate, its spirit or element of water.</margin>
Know also, my son, when you place the materials to be sublimated, they must be mixed with the kind of matter that is of such a nature that it preserves your prepared matter from melting.

<margin>Both are to be kept separate until they are to be joined anew.</margin>
For you have rendered your matter so subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to a substance that has been refined into a very fine, pure, or volatile state.</note> that it would melt like butter even at a small fire. Therefore, the matter through which you sublimate the matter of the stone must be so prepared that it does not pollute your matter at all, and so that none of this matter ascends, and so that it cannot be destroyed by any fire, however great the heat placed under...

<margin>The earth of the stone must be weighed, as well as its spirit or what has been sublimated from the earth.</margin>
...you should subject it [to the fire]: it must furthermore be so prepared that glass cannot be made from the material, nor can salt be extracted from it; it must also be prepared in such a way that it cannot be dissolved by anything, and that it casts off no dregs <note>original: "fæces"; the solid, impure residue left after a chemical process</note> from itself. Prepare it also so that it is intangible: and if, my son, you do not have such a material, you will not be able to sublime <note>Sublimation is an alchemical process where a solid is heated until it turns into a vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify the "spirit" of the substance</note> your prepared material. Therefore, prepare a material of this kind, otherwise you will achieve nothing in this art. I will tell you personally how you shall prepare it: and when you set your material to be sublimated, first you shall weigh the material through which you wish to sublime, and you shall commit your weight to memory; you shall also weigh the material from which you wish to extract your stone, and you shall write down the weight, so that you are not deceived.

Therefore, my son, when you have led the spirit out from the matter, you shall put everything you find in the pot to be dissolved, and you shall dissolve the body from the matter out of which you sublimated the spirit. This you will be able to do with confidence: for your material through which you sublimated will not be dissolved. Therefore, you will dissolve nothing more than that body or earth, along with the dregs, from which you led out your spirit by dissolving. For this reason, when it is dry, weigh what you have led out from the dregs by dissolving: and then also weigh your spirit which you sublimated: in this way you will be able to know whether you have all your material. Afterward, also remove all the dregs and weigh them as well; thus you will be able to know clearly how the matter stands, and what you might be lacking, whether everything has been led out or not. Pay diligent attention, and let it not bother you to write anything down, so that it may always be clear to you what you have done; and if you should doubt anything regarding the work, you can imagine from a failed outcome how it happened, and correct it wherever you can.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

<insert>Y</insert>ou should also know, my son, that you can make the material from which you extract your spirit so subtle and so spiritual—first in its "white water" <note>original: "aqua alba"; a specific alchemical solvent or purified mercury</note> in which it is placed during putrefaction <note>The stage where the matter is broken down, often associated with the color black</note>, and afterward in solution in vinegar—that in sublimation it all ascends, so that it leaves nothing behind except the dregs. For this reason, you shall dissolve the material in vinegar after the sublimation is performed, and you shall dissolve the earth or dregs from the material through which you sublimated; thus you will easily see whether all the material of the stone has sublimated upward or not. For in the material through which you sublimated, nothing else is dissolved except what remained in it from the material of the stone which was sublimated from it: and see that you do as was said before.

## CHAPTER XXV.

<margin>Sublimation of the stone by itself without added dregs, and that with a slower fire.</margin>
You shall also keep, my son, in a glass vessel that which you have dissolved from that material through which you sublimated <term>sublimated|A process where a solid is heated until it turns into a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the substance</term>: then take that which you have raised upward through sublimation, and place it again to be sublimated, first with a small fire, increasing it gradually until everything that can be sublimated has been raised.

<margin>The dregs left behind in this sublimation are to be joined to the "earth of the stone" mentioned above.</margin>
Furthermore, my son, you shall sublimate it alone so that nothing else is present or mixed in; but add the remaining dregs <note>original: "fæces"</note> to that which I ordered you to keep, which you drew out with vinegar. Repeat the sublimation as many times as needed until everything ascends, so that nothing remains: then it is enough: then you have that Mercury from which the Philosophers <note>Referring to the great alchemists of the past</note> extract their stone; then you have the incombustible sulfur; then you have the stone for the white work <note>original: "lapidem ad album," the stage of alchemy aimed at creating silver or the White Elixir</note>. And the Sages have called this spirit "water," and the "white thing," and "arsenic," and have given it many names, such as "sulfur" and "virgin's milk."

<margin>This sublimation must be repeated as many times as necessary until the stone leaves no dregs behind.</margin>
And that pure sublimated material shall take the place of the Philosophers' Mercury: and it is also the incombustible sulfur.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

<margin>All the "earth" from the aforementioned sublimations must be reverberated until it reaches the whiteness of snow.</margin>
Also now, take [F. M. <note>likely an abbreviation for "Fili Mi," or "My Son"</note>] all that earth and the dregs which you kept from the first sublimation, drawn out with vinegar, together with all the other dregs which you left in the other sublimations; take them all together and place them to be reverberated <term>reverberated|A process of heating material in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the substance</term> until they become as white as snow. Then let them cool: take them out of the furnace, replace them in glass, place them in a bath <term>bath|Usually a "Bain-marie" or water bath for gentle, even heating</term>, and pour over them sharp distilled vinegar that has been properly rectified <note>purified through repeated distillation</note>.

<margin>The dissolution of the reverberated earth in the bath by means of vinegar.</margin>
Heat the bath moderately, and your vinegar will become reddish. Let it cool, and pour it out by inclination <note>carefully tilting the vessel to pour off the liquid while leaving the sediment</note> into another glass; seal it and set it aside. Then pour in more vinegar and place it in the bath again as before, and when the vinegar has again absorbed the color, pour it out again by decanting, add it to the previous vinegar, and repeat this as many times as necessary until your vinegar is no longer stained with color from the materials.

<margin>The dissolved earth, after evaporation, is to be reverberated again for a period of 24 hours, and then dissolved again as above.</margin>
Then dry the dregs and place them again to be calcined <term>calcined|Reduced to a powder or ash by high heat</term> for 24 hours. Let them cool, take them from the furnace, place them again in glass, place them once more in the bath, pour vinegar over them again, and set them to dissolve as before, doing everything in the same manner as before. You must continue pouring in and pouring out, and calcining the dregs, until your vinegar is no longer stained with color—

## CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>To one part of earth, 3 parts of the spirit mentioned above are to be joined.</margin>
Now you should know, my son, a great secret: namely, that you shall take 3 parts of "water," as the Philosophers say—for they call the "Spirit" water—and one part of your prepared "earth" or "body." That is to say, you shall weigh all your earth or body to see what its weight is, then you shall take three times as much of your spirit as the weight of your earth.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

Likewise, you will not retain much earth or body from the 4 pounds of material that you put in; however, even if it is a small amount, you will have enough to complete your work, no matter how little it is. For the "Earth" is of such great virtue <note>virtue: in an alchemical sense, this means "potency" or "power"</note>, however small its amount may be.

<margin>The <term>sublimate<note>The solid product gathered after heating a substance into vapor and letting it settle again.</note></term> must be kept separately.</margin>
Empty that which has been sublimated into a glass jar and keep it carefully. Then, take out what remained below in the pot and let it cool again. ### CHAPTER XXX.

<margin>This sublimation must be repeated until all the earth has been sublimated by its spirit.</margin>
A large quantity of material must be held and prepared from the beginning for this reason: because this work must be done together with the spirit, and at the very least, all the earth must be drawn up together with the spirit. Afterwards, it must be processed with the spirit frequently and many times before the <term>Stone<note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the alchemical process.</note></term> is willing to become liquid and subtle, for which a large supply of spirit is needed.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

<margin>The fermentation of the Stone joined with its earth.</margin>
Now, however, it is time that the "soul" or spirit be placed into the body that was prepared along with its spirit—and this is the <term>ferment<note>A substance added to "ripen" or complete the alchemical transformation, similar to how yeast works in bread.</note></term>. <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist.</note> **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** says regarding this matter: "When the spirit has been prepared together with the body, put the soul into it, so that it may afterwards rise from death into one body, that it may live for eternity; then all its enemies will enter into peace with it."

### CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>Silver is to be taken for the ferment.</margin>
Likewise, when you have now sublimated the body or earth upward and are keeping it in a glass jar, you must prepare the ferment which you will add to it in this manner: Take pure <term>Luna<note>The alchemical name for Silver.</note></term> that has been <term>cupelled<note>Refined in a shallow porous cup (a cupel) to remove base metals like lead.</note></term> and thoroughly purified of lead in a crucible. Then beat it into thin sheets and place them layer upon layer in a crucible with well-prepared common salt. Set it to be <term>calcined<note>Heated to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder without melting it.</note></term> moderately for 3 continuous days, so that it does not melt. Then take it out and wash away the salt with warm water; if any remains uncalcined, put it back in as before. Then dry your powder over a small fire. Next, take twice as much prepared salt and mix it with your powder, and put it in the crucible to be calcined again.

Every eight days the fire shall be increased, and when the <term>sublimated material</term> has risen to the top, you shall place the lower part of the glass (where the matter remains) at the top. You must allow it to sublimate again, and thus you must invert it until everything is <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "fixum"; rendered solid and resistant to evaporation by heat</note> together.

### CHAPTER XXXV.

And when, my son, you wish to see the <term>colors</term> <note>original: "colores"; alchemists tracked progress through specific color sequences like the black "nigredo" or white "albedo"</note> manifesting themselves in the work, remove the <term>lid of the furnace</term> <note>original: "operculum fornacis"</note> and then place it back on. Every time the <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapis"</note> changes color, you shall increase the fire a little, until everything remains at the bottom and all is <term>fixed</term> together. You must truly write down all the changes and colors, and you shall note the time passing between each one, and the time of the <term>fixation</term>. Whatever you do, do not build a great fire until everything is <term>fixed</term> and brought to a white color.

<margin>Observation of the colors.</margin>

<margin>The exact regulation of the fire.</margin>

And if you wish to work in a "blind furnace" <note>a furnace designed without windows or openings for direct observation</note>, as was said before, add fire to it day and night, so that you are able to keep your hand between the vessel and the walls of the furnace without removing it. In the space of one day and night, the glass must be inverted as many as twenty times; and this must be managed until everything is <term>fixed</term> together. Alternatively, you may place your <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"</note> in a glass egg and suspend it in the "secret furnace" for forty days at the aforementioned heat. When these have passed, break it and see if your <term>matter</term> is <term>fixed</term>; if not, place it again in the secret furnace for twenty days, and then it will be properly <term>fixed</term>. Thus you will be able to <term>fix</term> your <term>stone</term> in three ways. But I advise you to place it in the furnace with a lid, so that you may see the changes of the <term>stone</term>, its colors, and its entire <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regimen"; the systematic method of governing the heat over time</note>, because this is your first time working, so that you may see and write down everything.

<margin>The span of time in which the stone is to be fixed, namely 40 days, or at most 60.</margin>

Likewise, when your <term>stone</term> is already <term>fixed</term>, then it is ready. And know, my son, that many have taken up great labor in this art who have indeed progressed this far—that they understood what <term>matter</term> they should take for this <term>stone</term>, and they drew it out from that, and made it subtle as was said before, and purified their <term>ferment</term> <note>original: "fermentum"; an additive used to "leaven" or catalyze the transformation of the base matter into the Stone</note> properly...

...well purified and prepared: and they bound together and fixed the work; all saw the tinctures <note>original: "tincturas"; these are the color changes—black, white, yellow, and red—that signal progress in the alchemical process.</note> which it is fitting for the Stone to show, and they wisely fixed them: which being done they thought they had done enough, according to the doctrine of the Philosophers: and then they wished to make the projection <note>The final stage of alchemy, where the "Stone" is cast onto base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note>, but in vain: for the Stone made no projection: and they abandoned the work, repeatedly saying the art was impossible: and truly so as far as they were concerned; for they did not understand nature; they did not recognize that the ferment was not yet volatile, nor had it ever been: they do not understand the words of the ancients when they ask: Our stone consists of body, soul, and spirit, and these are and shall be one essence, and something inseparable. 

<margin>The fixed stone must now be made volatile again so that it is of the same quality as the ferment.</margin> Therefore the ferment also must be volatile and fleeting just as the body and spirit were. And they abandon the work when it is fixed, for they are unable to notice that the fixed matter or stone ought to be made fleeting again, for the sake of the ferment which will be placed in it. Although the spirit is fixed with the body, they are not yet gathered with the ferment: for the ferment is not yet made volatile, and for so long they are not truly gathered: believe no writings or words: for he who says otherwise to you will deceive you: the ferment with the spirit and body, or earth, must perish together <note>In this context, to "perish" means to lose its individual form to be reborn as a new, unified substance.</note>: otherwise you lose your labor, so that in its ascent it may be subtle and of great power, and is united to its body. 

<margin>The Sages called the ferment the soul.</margin> Wherefore the Sages called the ferment the soul, when they say, let the spirit draw the soul into the higher regions, and it descends again into the lower regions. Nature must be followed; will the glorified body endure until the last day into eternity, unless it be altogether subtle, and so that it may never die? And will the soul remain so crude in its first state, as it was in the body on earth? It cannot be; it must be as volatile and spiritual as the spirit. And if we seek something other than what Almighty God <note>original: "Deus Omnipotens"</note> made in his ordination, or if we seek something other than what nature teaches us, we are deceived. But the Ancients followed nature as much as they could: wherefore they arrived at a good end of the work, and their desires were fulfilled.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>Nature must be imitated so that the stone may become volatile.</margin> Now, my son, also follow nature as much as you can; so that you may likewise be able to arrive at the desired end; thus it will be that you shall regret no labor, that you may render the fixed stone volatile once more:

Likewise, when you wish to make your **earth**, or **body**, or **ferment** <note>A substance added to the alchemical base to trigger the transformation into gold or silver.</note>, or any other **fixed** <note>A substance that remains solid and does not evaporate when heated.</note> thing **volatile** <note>A substance that easily turns into vapor when heated.</note>, you shall take 3 parts of the volatile and one of the fixed, mix them together, and place them for **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid on a cooler surface.</note> over a moderate fire, just as I taught you before, when you carried the earth upward with the **spirit** <note>The volatile essence or vaporous part of a substance.</note> through sublimation. And when the spirits or volatile parts are more numerous than the fixed parts, the volatile parts pull the fixed parts upward with them; and since both the fixed parts are pure and clean, and the volatile parts are also pure and clean, and since they are of **one nature**, these two desire to remain together. Thus, the volatile more easily draws that fixed thing to itself and converts it into its own nature. But when you have sublimated it upward, you should weigh whatever remains behind and does not ascend; then you can easily take three times as much spirit as there is fixed matter remaining, and set it to be sublimated again as before. Repeat this until everything has been sublimated together. Do this with your fixed matter or **Stone**, and draw its ferment up with it, so they become of one nature; for if the ferment had not been sublimated entirely together with the spirit and body, they would not be of one nature, even if they were fixed together. And when these have been entirely sublimated together, they can never at any time be separated. And during the ascent, they are rendered a thousand times more subtle than they were before.

<margin>3 parts of spirit are to be added as mentioned above, until the whole becomes volatile; add it after sublimation to the remaining fixed part.</margin>

<margin>3 parts of volatile spirit, and in this way the ferment will also become volatile.</margin>

<margin>The **Body** <note>The physical matter of the experiment.</note> must be sublimated upward together with the **spirit** and the **soul**, so that it becomes of one nature.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXVII.
And when, my son, you have sublimated one thing with the other, then you shall again place all those materials in the **fixing glass** <note>A specialized laboratory vessel designed to withstand long periods of heat to "fix" or solidify the substance.</note> to be fixed, as was taught before, and then the **rectification** <note>The process of refining and purifying a substance.</note> shall occur. Then, indeed, all the colors will show themselves which can be imagined in the nature of things; these will be followed by the **Peacock’s Tail** <note>A famous alchemical stage (cauda pavonis) where a shimmering variety of colors appears in the flask.</note>, and then the colors will begin to diminish little by little, and they will eventually arrive at a white color. Then you may rejoice, for your **Stone** is now fixed.

<margin>Sublimated and united together, they are rendered 1,000 times more subtle than before.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.
You should know, my son, that there have been many others who attempted this work, who were even sharper than the first, and they brought their stone to the point mentioned before and rejoiced, thinking they truly possessed the Stone. They projected <note>The act of "projection," casting a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone onto molten base metals to transform them.</note> it upon **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver.</note> and upon **Jupiter** <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note>, but they achieved nothing. For their Stone would neither dissolve nor penetrate <note>The ability of the Stone to "enter" and transform the internal structure of a metal.</note>, and they looked upon the art with contempt, saying it was impossible. But if they had understood the words of the Ancients, where they say: *Moisten the lowest world with dew* <note>original: "Humecta mundum infimum rore." An allegorical instruction to soften the "fixed" matter with "volatile" liquid.</note>, the stone would be fixed. Here are the obstacles of **inceration** <note>The process of making a hard substance soft and waxy so it can melt and mix with metals.</note> along with the remedy.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

<margin>From this whole process, one can determine the quantity of material to be set out for the preparation and completion.</margin> Now, my son, you can observe for yourself how much material must be set out at the beginning to complete the entire work; see how much spirit is required. For first, a great part must be fixed with the earth; then the spirits which are fixed in the earth must be drawn up with the spirit, always taking 3 parts of spirit for one fixed part; and then the ferment <note>the "yeast" of the work, often gold or silver, used to direct the transformation</note> with the whole material, when the fixed parts are fixed together. All these things must also be made subtle again, and 3 parts of spirit must always be taken for one fixed part, until all your fixed matter is made volatile, and so on in turn. But when everything is finally volatile, then all of it is fixed; and when all is fixed, it must be "waxed" <note>softened to a melting state</note> with the spirit so many times and so often, until your stone flows like wax or butter. And all those works must be performed by the spirit.

And although I spoke of 4 pounds of matter, perhaps 7 or 8 pounds might be needed before the work is brought to its end. For if we were in the middle of the work and the spirits <note>Volatile substances, often referring to mercury or ammonia in this context.</note> were to fail, then the work would have to be interrupted until fresh matter was prepared and made ready as before, and that would be a long process. Therefore, take as much matter at the beginning as may be sufficient for you.

### CHAPTER XL.

<margin>The Stone must be made fusible <note>original: *fusibilis*, meaning capable of being melted or dissolved into liquid.</note> so that it can be projected upon Jove <note>The alchemical name for the metal Tin.</note>.</margin>
You shall also know, my son, that your matter must not be made too fusible. For you shall perform your projection <note>The final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon a base metal to transmute it.</note> upon Jove; for this is the body closest to Luna <note>The alchemical name for Silver.</note>, and it is the purest body of all the imperfect metals. It is raw and poorly "cooked" in the mine, which is why it screeches <note>Refers to the "tin cry," a distinct crackling sound made when bending a bar of pure tin.</note> when it is bitten into, and it is full of whiteness. Therefore, perform the projection upon Jove, for in it this medicine has nothing else to do but to thoroughly cook it and bring it to its own nature; then it is much better and whiter than the silver that comes from the mines. Therefore, always perform the projection upon Jove for the "white" work <note>Transmutation into silver.</note>, and upon Venus <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note> for the "red" work <note>Transmutation into gold.</note>. For if you were to perform the projection for the "white" upon Venus, it would cost much medicine—much more than upon Jove, since Jove is white of its own accord.

### CHAPTER XLI.

<margin>The stone used for Venus <note>Copper.</note> ought to be less fusible than the stone which is used upon Saturn <note>Lead.</note> or Mercury <note>Quicksilver.</note>.</margin>
Furthermore, you shall know, my son, that you must prepare the stone according to the metal upon which you wish to project it. For the medicine that you wish to cast upon Venus <note>Copper.</note> should not be made as fusible as if you wished to cast it upon Saturn <note>Lead.</note>, Mercury <note>Quicksilver.</note>, or Jove <note>Tin.</note>. You can make your medicine as fusible as you wish, for the more spirits you have fixed <note><term>Fixation</term>: the process of turning a volatile substance into a solid that can withstand heat.</note> with it, the more fusible it becomes. You could easily fix so many spirits with it that in the end you would retain a muddy powder that would melt more easily than butter in the sun. Therefore, be careful, my son, that you do not make it so liquid. For if you wished to perform a projection upon Mercury, you would make your projection more fusible than when you wish to do it upon Jove; for the matter ought to melt before your Mercury begins to "ascend" <note>Evaporate or sublime due to heat.</note>. That, however, is not necessary upon Jove. And whatever you do, see that you first <term>vivify</term> <note>To "bring to life" or chemically activate.</note> your dead body and instill a soul into it before you cast the medicine upon it; otherwise, your medicine would perform no projection at all, even if you had the most excellent medicine that ever existed in the world.

### CAP. XLII.

<margin>The body must necessarily be brought to life before projection can be performed upon it.</margin>
You shall know, my son, that it is just as necessary for life to be infused into a dead body before projection can be made upon it, as it is necessary for ferment to be placed in the medicine; keep this as a secret. <term>Morienus</term> <note>A legendary 12th-century alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the King of the Arabs.</note> says: Our <term>orichalcum</term> <note>A golden-colored alloy; in alchemy, it often refers to a purified base metal ready for transformation.</note> is not common orichalcum, for it lives and possesses a soul.

### CAP. XLIII.

Furthermore, you shall know, my son, that if you wish to perform projection for the red work <note>The final stage of alchemy, aimed at producing gold.</note> upon <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note>, you must always sublimate and fix the matter with a small fire, however long that time may be: for when one works with a small fire, the matter better retains its moisture. And because <term>Venus</term> is quite dry, the medicine must be more moist than if you were projecting it upon <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note>; moreover, <term>Venus</term> flows with difficulty due to its dryness. When, however, you wish to perform projection upon bodies that melt easily and quickly, such as <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for tin.</note> and <term>Saturn</term>: the matter of your stone must be strongly sublimated by fire, for then the moisture within it is consumed. And when you wish to perform your projection upon <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver.</note> or <term>Luna</term> <note>The alchemical name for silver.</note>, sublimate your matter over a moderate fire: for these two endure with the medicine until all their moisture is converted into redness; then they set themselves into a metallic button <note>original: "regulum"</note>, just as <term>Sol</term> <note>The alchemical name for gold.</note> or <term>Luna</term> do upon the cupel <note>original: "testa"; a shallow vessel used to refine precious metals.</note>. Thus, my son, you shall prepare your Medicine according to the metals upon which you wish to perform projection.

### CAP. XLIV.

Furthermore, if you wish to perform projection upon <term>Venus</term> and impure metal: take 50 or 60 pounds <note>original: "fo. aut 60. fb"; archaic units of weight.</note> of <term>Saturn</term> or <term>Venus</term>, and calcine <note>To heat a substance to a high temperature to remove impurities or reduce it to powder.</note> them, and wash them of all impurity. Then, dissolve them again once they are joined into one body, put in the soul, and bring it to life. Once this is done, project the Medicine upon them—not because it is strictly necessary to purge impure metals before you project upon them (for indeed your medicine has the power to transform all impure metals into <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>), but because once they are purged by <term>calcination</term> and <term>washing</term> <note>original: "ablutione"</note>, they lose their impurity and dryness, and melt gradually. They are cleansed of <term>combustible sulfur</term> <note>In alchemical theory, "unclean sulfur" was the cause of corruption and rust in base metals.</note>, so that your medicine extends much further than if the metals were in their state of impurity. For example: your medicine may be worth 1,000 when the metals are unpurged; but with metals already purged, it will easily proceed to 10,000. Thus, the labor is well compensated.

## MASTER JOHANN ISAAC
### CHAPTER XLV.

<image-desc>A technical drawing of a cylindrical earthenware vessel with a matching, snug-fitting lid shown in profile.</image-desc>

<margin>How Venus <note>the alchemical name for copper</note> is to be calcined.</margin> Likewise, to calcine Venus, take a large, square earthenware vessel made of firm clay that does not crack. It shall be made in this manner: there shall be a lid fitted to it that fits squarely and shuts it tight. Then, taking red copper <note>Latin: *aere rubro*</note>, cut it into square pieces of such a size that they can lie inside the vessel. Then, make all those pieces glow red-hot in the fire and quench them again in old urine <note>The original text "vriua" is a misspelling of "urina" (urine), which was used in early chemistry for its ammonia and salt content.</note>. Repeat this four times, heating them to a glow and always quenching them in fresh "old urine." Then wash them in clean water and wipe them clean with a linen cloth in the sun; then your Venus <note>copper</note> is ready for calcining. 

Then take white arsenic, sublimated <note>purified by heating into a vapor and cooling back into a solid</note> two or three times, and grind it on a stone with sharp distilled wine vinegar until it reaches the consistency of a thick paste—or as if you wished to paint with it. Smear your metal plates with this paste and set them to dry in the sun or in a "dry bath" <note>an oven or sand bath</note>. Then smear them again, dry them again, and repeat this a third time, smearing them everywhere. When they have dried for the last time, take common salt that has been dissolved once and crystallized again, and spread it over the bottom of the vessel until it is a finger's-breadth deep. Place a layer of the plates upon this, then another layer of salt, and continue in this order until your vessel is full. 

Then place it in the furnace and apply a gentle heat, like the heat of the sun in March. Let the moisture evaporate thoroughly for two or three continuous days. Then seal the lid onto the earthenware vessel with firm lute <note>a clay-based sealant used to make vessels airtight</note> so that nothing can escape. Once this is done, let it dry well so it does not crack. Then place the vessel in the calcining furnace; first, apply a small fire for 12 hours so the vessel does not glow red. Then you shall gradually increase the fire by degrees, so that 6 or 8 hours later the vessel glows completely. Keep it in that hot flame for 12 hours, then let it cool. 

Soon after, break the vessel and remove all the salt by dissolving it in hot water. If the metal has not been entirely calcined <note>reduced to a fine powder through heat</note>, do as before and set it to be calcined again, though you will not need to heat it to a glow or quench it in urine this time. When it is all calcined, and the salt has been thoroughly washed away, pound those calxes <note>the resulting metallic powders</note> in an iron mortar and pass them through a sieve. When this is done, wash them again with fresh water until the water runs clear, then dry them in a pan over the furnace, and pound them again...

<summary>This page describes the meticulous process of calcining copper (referred to as Venus) using white arsenic, vinegar, and salt. The process involves multiple stages of heating, quenching in urine, and gradual firing in a sealed vessel to reduce the metal to a fine powder.</summary>

Crush <note>original: "tunde"</note> it in an iron mortar, and sift it with a sieve. Afterward, grind the **calx** <note>The 'calx' is the powdery residue or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or "burned."</note> upon a stone with honey, mixing in a little water until the particles are so fine that one could paint with them, as painters do. have a linen bag made in this manner. Fill it with the aforementioned material as tightly as you can, packed down with a wooden tool, and once it is well sealed, tie its end strongly. Then **lute** <note>term: <term>Lute</term> (luto) is a specialized alchemical paste or cement used to seal vessels and protect them from high heat.</note> the bag with a mixture of clay and hair so that it does not crack; lute it all around, let it dry, lute it again, and let it dry again, repeating this until the coating is **three fingers** <note>A traditional measurement of thickness, roughly 2.25 inches.</note> thick. 

And when the material is thoroughly dry, drill a hole in one side, and place it in a wind furnace <note>A furnace designed to create a strong draft for high temperatures.</note> so that the perforated end lies half a foot lower than the other. Beneath the hole, place a large **crucible**, and build a fire under the luted bag with oak coals. Melt the contents so that everything flows down into the crucible, then let it cool. Afterward, melt it again, and then it is ready. To 10 pounds of that prepared Copper, add 1 pound of **cupelled Luna** <note>original: "Lunae cupellatae"; Silver that has been purified in a cupel (a shallow porous bowl).</note>; melt them together, and it is ready to receive your **White Medicine** <note>term: <term>Medicine</term> (medicina) refers to the alchemical agent, such as a tincture or the Philosopher's Stone, used to trigger transmutation.</note>. 

And if you wish to prepare Copper for the **Red Medicine** <note>The Red Medicine was used for making Gold (Sol), while the White was for Silver (Luna).</note>, take in place of white arsenic good **red** or **yellow arsenic** <note>original: "arsenicum rubrum aut croceum"</note> sublimated two or three times, and smear your plates with it, and proceed as described above with half **vitriol** <note>term: <term>Vitriol</term> refers to sulfate minerals, often used for their acidic properties.</note> and half salt, layer upon layer, and so on as before.

Know, my son, that this **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its chemical properties.</note> is not strictly necessary in the sense that the Medicine for Silver or Gold in Copper would otherwise have no power to transform it. For you indeed have those powers even if the metal is not calcined in this way. Truly, however, the Medicine does not "tinge" <note>To "tinge" or "color" was the alchemist's term for the inner transformation of the metal's essence.</note> as deeply as when the Copper is prepared in this manner. With this preparation, your Medicine will easily achieve a **projection** <note>term: <term>Projection</term> is the final stage of the Great Work, where the 'Medicine' is cast onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note> ten thousand times higher than if you were to cast it onto unprepared Copper, which still contains **combustible sulfur** <note>Alchemists believed that base metals were "sick" because they contained an impure, flammable sulfur that caused them to tarnish or burn.</note> along with many other dregs. It is also much more pleasant to perform the projection upon a pure metal than an impure one; for upon the impure, the Medicine must first purge the metal itself before it can [perform] the transmutation...

### CHAPTER XLVI.

Now I wish to teach the way to the Red Stone, and it is a greater secret, and requires more time and labor. It must be more subtle than the Stone for the White <note>The White Stone transforms metals into Silver; the Red Stone transforms them into Gold</note>. The Red must be rectified better and longer, for it has a firm and compact body and is more fixed. Therefore, a longer time is needed before its parts can be separated from one another, in order to open it and to extract the subtle spirits from it, or at least the more subtle part.

### CHAPTER XLVII.

<margin>How the Red Stone is to be prepared.</margin>Therefore, my son, you shall take the red stone and dissolve it in its red water, and you shall precipitate it, and wash its red water with the water of clouds <note>Rainwater, considered by alchemists to be a pure, celestial source of water</note>, and dry it in the Sun or a small fire. Then you shall place it in a <term>reverberatory furnace|A furnace that reflects heat from the roof onto the material, rather than applying flame directly</term> to be <term>calcined|Reduced to a powder through prolonged heating</term> for 12 or 16 days. However, you must take care that you do not cause the stone to melt. Therefore, give it only a moderate flame. Then take it out and dissolve it again in water. Having done this, place it in putrefaction <note>A stage of "rotting" or breaking down the substance, usually through gentle heat</note>, that is, a warm bath, and leave it there for eight days. Then distill that water again in a lukewarm bath. When these things are finished, take out the Gold <note>original: "Solem"</note>...

### CHAPTER 49.

Know, my son, that the Sun <note>original: *Solem*; refers to Gold</note> is also dissolved in the same way as was taught in the work of the white stone, but it requires more time, and must be drawn off more often, and fresh water must be poured over it again and again, more than in the white work. <margin>How to use the aforementioned things.</margin>
Likewise, after you have drawn the tincture out of the Sun, as shown in the work, and have perfected the white stone, you can sublime all the tincture, as taught in the work, and then take 3 parts of the white stone and one part of this tincture—which the philosophers called "red sulfur" <note>original: *sulphur rubrum*</note>—and mix them together, and set them to be fixed; until you have fixed as much weight of the red sulfur as your white stone weighed previously. Then you should significantly increase the fire in the manner taught above until you reach perfect redness.

And know, my son, that this is the best method of working to be found in the world: that the white stone be made first and extracted from the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; refers to Silver</note>, and then the white stone be waxed <note>original: *inceretur*; the process of "ceration," making a substance soft and flowable like wax</note> with red sulfur until it equals the weight the white stone had before it began to be waxed with red sulfur. And if the white or red stone should sometimes be unwilling to become so fusible that they could be cast upon Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*; Quicksilver</note>—for that stone which is cast upon Mercury must be as fusible as butter, otherwise the Mercury would fly away <note>evaporate</note> before the stone was dissolved. Truly, the white stone cannot be made so fusible, no matter what is done. But the medicine that transforms Mercury into the Sun <note>Gold</note> or Moon <note>Silver</note> must melt like butter, and the white cannot be made so fusible, and the red much less so, for it requires far greater heat if the redness is to be brought forth at all.

### CHAPTER 50.

You may ask now, my son, by what means the medicine is acquired which may transform <term>Mercury<note>original: "Mercurium," referring to quicksilver</note></term> into true <term>Gold<note>original: "Solem," literally "the Sun"</note></term> or <term>Silver<note>original: "Lunam," literally "the Moon"</note></term>, for it seems impossible according to the reasons previously stated. Know, my son, as a great secret in the art, that the medicine for the <term>Great Work<note>original: "Magnum," referring to the Opus Magnum or Great Work of alchemy</note></term>, whether white or red, was in the beginning distinguished and dissolved in vinegar or common water; after its perfection, it is always dissolved in the vinegar of the chemical art, or in common water, or in wine. For when the <term>White Stone<note>original: "lapis albus," used for making silver</note></term> or the <term>Red Stone<note>original: "rubus," used for making gold</note></term> is perfected, it is easily a thousand times more subtle than it was before its perfection, when it was first dissolved in vinegar. For the more noble a thing is, and the more subtle by nature, the more easily it is dissolved. Indeed, no coarse parts are present, nor any dregs <note>original: "fæces"</note>, nor dryness, which are typically separated through dissolution in vinegar. For the coarse parts, the dregs, and the superfluous dry parts—which are all one and the same—are the things that prevent a substance from being brought to dissolution. But the White and Red Stone have none of these things within them; rather, they are soluble above all things that exist in the nature of things, in both: that is, in burning dryness and in cold humidity. For in them, there are no parts that can hinder liquefaction; and in the whole world, there is no nature so perfect as our White and Red Stone. Therefore, there is nothing in the nature of things that can be dissolved in both—that is, in burning dryness and cold humidity—as our Stone can.

### CHAPTER 51.

Therefore, my son, hold this as a great secret in the art: to know our Stone in its interior nature. Know that no medicine, neither for the white nor for the red, can be prepared for the work that is so <term>fusible<note>Capable of being melted easily</note></term> that it can retain Mercury over the fire, for the Mercury would fly away <note>evaporate</note> before the medicine could melt. 
Furthermore, know that when you have prepared the medicine for the white or the red, so that you may perform a <term>projection<note>original: "proiectionem," the act of casting the alchemical powder onto base metal to transmute it</note></term> upon hard metals and upon soft bodies, and you then desire to perform a projection upon Mercury to prove your art: take a portion of your medicine for the white or the red which you have prepared, and dissolve it in sharp distilled vinegar, so rectified <note>purified by repeated distillation</note> that it leaves absolutely nothing behind it. Congeal it again, and dissolve it repeatedly in fresh vinegar until it becomes as fusible as butter. Then cease the dissolving, and cast it upon the Mercury, and perform the projection according to the art. You should dissolve and congeal it so many times that it thickens into an oil which refuses to congeal any further. For in all vegetable or animal things, there is no substance so soluble as that which is in wine.

### CHAPTER 53.

<margin>Everything that God created contains the four elements within it.</margin>
<margin>Knowing that it contains the four elements.</margin>
Know, my son, that everything God created contains the four <term>elements</term><note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water; the fundamental building blocks of matter in pre-modern science</note> within itself, as is well taught in the *Book of Vegetables*. And although the material may appear white on the outside, on the contrary, that same material is red on the inside. Furthermore, the <term>Red Stone</term><note>A reference to the Philosopher's Stone in its final, most potent state</note> possesses such a nature that it brings everything it is mixed with to its own nature. For this reason, the Red Stone moves the whiteness of the <term>Moon</term><note>original: "Lunae"; alchemical code for Silver</note> internally toward the redness of the <term>Sun</term><note>original: "Solis"; alchemical code for Gold</note>, and restores the Moon to its very own nature. Just as can be seen daily in all things growing from the earth—such as apples, pears, plums, cherries, flowers, and many other fruits—when they hang upon the trees and are ripe, see what a remarkable red color they acquire from the brilliance of the Sun shining directly upon them. Observe how an apple grows red on the side where the Sun shone upon it, and how the heat of the Sun has drawn the redness of the apple outward. Therefore, my son, do not wonder that one part of the Stone can restore 1,000 parts of the Moon to its own nature. And even when the Sun is led outside of its own nature, so that it is stripped of its body—to such an extent that it can no longer become a body—it is as red as dark blood, or like the dried <term>blood of a Dragon</term><note>original: "sanguis Draconis"; a bright red resin used as a pigment and in alchemy</note> or a goat, and it is so full of color that it cannot be described. For when it is dissolved and again coagulated, the weight of a grain of wheat would easily imbue ten *lora* <note>A Roman unit of measurement, here referring to large containers or measures</note> of white wine with its color; such abundant color resides within the Sun. Therefore, do not wonder.

### CHAPTER 54.

### CHAPTER 56.

<margin>The preparation of the Philosophers' Stone from two lights.</margin>
Likewise, I now wish to teach you how to make the Philosophers’ Stone from two lights, just as the ancient philosophers and those who followed them made with their own hands. I shall do so without obscure words, explaining its preparation and powers, and its transformation from its own nature into the "first essence." For nothing can be changed from its own nature once Nature has completed its final work upon it, as it has done in these two lights. For even if these two lights <note>Gold and Silver</note> had remained in the mines from which they came until Judgment Day, Nature would have worked nothing more in them. For Nature had already exerted its ultimate power in them. And if we wish to bring these two together, changing them from their current nature into something better or worse, we must go backward again and "unweave" <note>original: *retexendum*; the idea that the alchemist must reverse the natural process of mineralization to reach the "prime matter"</note> what Nature has worked. We must bring it back into the same form it was in when Nature first began to work upon it. Once it has been brought back to that form, we must follow Nature's path as closely as we can—and sometimes even surpass Nature itself. 
<margin>Nature must be followed, and also sometimes surpassed.</margin>
This is done through separating and rectifying, dissolving and coagulating, calcining and cleansing, as well as joining, waxing <note>original: *inceratione*, the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, and various refinements, and other works that Nature cannot perform. For Nature is not moved to do such works. Therefore, we transform metals into another form, better than what Nature made or is able to make. In this way, the combustible sulfur can be removed as is taught here, though it is not as easily removed from the other four metals as it is from Silver. The other disease by which Silver is held back is **coldness** and **immoderate moisture**, which likewise only adhere to the outside of the Silver and do not penetrate the innermost root of the Silver. ## OF MINERAL WORKS

...of **Silver** <note>original: "Lunae," the Moon, the alchemical symbol for silver</note>, namely, the combustible sulfur is removed by the calcination of **arsenic** and by washing, as described above. You should also know that arsenic, when it exists in its raw thickness, burns and consumes all bodies, just as **orpiment** <note>a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> and **sulfur** do; all three are of the same nature, such that they burn, calcine, and destroy the bodies with which they are mixed. 

However, when arsenic and orpiment are freed and cleansed of their impurity and earthiness, and of their crude spirits and non-fixed parts—leaving only the middle spirit in the fumes—you can then drive out all combustible sulfur from metals using that spirit. You do this by frequently calcining, washing, grinding, cleansing, and melting the metals with it, and then calcining them again. This process is repeated as often as necessary until they are liberated from their combustible sulfur. For **Silver**, however, this should only be done once, because the sulfur only adheres to the outside of the Silver. 

In this way, arsenic or orpiment is similar to **Theriac** <note>a famous ancient "universal antidote" made of many ingredients, including poisons like viper flesh</note>: for the material from which it is made can poison and kill men, as it is a poison; yet when that poison is prepared into Theriac, it repels all other poisons from poisoned men. Prepared arsenic and orpiment perform the same function.

<margin>Another disease of Silver: superfluous coldness and humidity.</margin>
The other disease of Silver is a superfluous coldness and humidity, which likewise adhere to the outside of the Silver and are removed by calcining it in a furnace in which spirits are calcined. Once this is prepared and reduced to the proper temperature, it is ready for the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> to be extracted from it; but even then, it still consists of thick and fixed parts, and is of a feminine nature. Therefore, **Mortienus** <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist</note> says: 

> Unless you cleanse the imperfect body, you waste your labor in our art and mastery.

## CHAPTER 59.

<margin>The material from which the Stone is to be extracted is now prepared.</margin> Likewise, the material for extracting the Stone is now ready. You shall know, therefore, that almost all the material of the Sun will ascend at once, and it will seize and carry up with it all the subtle parts of the Moon: yet of the Moon, nothing or very little ascends except its subtle parts. The greatest part of the Moon is crude, cold, and feminine, and it remains at the bottom. Truly, the Sun alone in its parts is subtle and masculine: and when the Sun is separated, it all ascends together because of its great subtlety <note>refinement or thinness of substance</note>: just as the Moon remains below at the bottom and does not wish to ascend because of its thickness. Thus, a contrary nature exists in these two bodies; the destruction of one is the nourishment of the other. Therefore, both are necessary together in the work, as you well know. 

<margin>This material must be sublimated.</margin> Furthermore, set this material to be sublimated <term>sublimation; the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the spirit</term> in every way as has been taught for the White and Red work <note>referring to the 'albedo' and 'rubedo', the final stages of the alchemical process</note>. And you must beware of the air <note>referring to the escaping vapors</note> when you open your vessels and take out the spirit, for the air would kill you. Therefore, let your vessels cool thoroughly before you break them open. And if it should happen that the spirits penetrate your lute <term>lute; a specialized airtight clay or paste used to seal laboratory glass</term> during sublimation, or if the alembic <term>alembic; the top part of a distilling apparatus</term> should crack or develop fissures, or the glass jar, beware of that air, for it would kill you instantly. For its air ascends invisibly because of its great subtlety, and the more refined you make it, the more burning and poisonous it becomes. 

For God has created no spirit among all mineral things more burning or more subtle than the spirit of the Sun, nor any spirit more subtle or more fleeting than the Sun. If the Sun were "opened" in its parts, as the Moon is, or other metals, or if the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> which are in the Sun were contrary to one another, the Sun would ascend from the fire more easily than any mineral spirit. But the elements are so equally tempered in the Sun, and so clean and pure, that they cannot be separated now, nor at any time. Therefore, when the Sun is unlocked, it all flies upward together, so that it leaves nothing behind, unless perhaps some other thing of different metallic nature was mixed with it. For with the Sun, any other metallic body or metallic thing is easily melted. Everything coming from the mines gladly joins itself with the Sun and is friendly with it. For the Sun is the King and Lord.

dissolve it once more in common water: distilled so many times that nothing remains. You shall repeat this dissolving so many times until you leave no more dregs, but the water flows away from it so clear that nothing more can be seen in it, just as if nothing had been dissolved in it at all. Then

<margin>To be congealed again.</margin>
congeal it once more until almost all the moisture has been distilled away; then let it cool. Once cooled, it will form itself into large stony pieces, the length and thickness of fingers, shining like transparent crystal, and white in the manner of snow. Then evaporate the small pieces until they become a tiny powder, white as snow. This entire work must be managed in glass bowls prepared for that purpose, standing over a boiling bath <term>Bain-marie: a vessel of boiling water used to provide gentle, even heat</term>, and with the vessels covered by a double linen cloth, so that no dust or filth may fly in. For our work must be clean and extremely pure. And then the precious earth, both the body and the ferment, is prepared to receive the soul and spirit into them, and to embrace them with great friendship and great desire, so that they may remain together forever in great harmony and peace: so that after this they may never be separated at any time; and they shall reign forever with great subtlety and power. For the body desires to receive its own soul and spirit; and the soul with the spirit desires to descend and rest in its own body. For one cannot exist without the other. And when they have been joined together as is fitting, there is so firm a bond of love between them that they unite entirely, and one is mixed with the other so that they become of the same nature, and one single thing. And it is then a simple thing like the invincible heaven; and thus it is the quintessence <term>Quintessence: the "fifth essence," a substance of extreme purity and medicinal power</term> for healing all diseases in a moment.

### CHAPTER LXII.

### CHAPTER LXVI.

<margin>That all those err who make amalgamations with the Sun and Mercury, or with the Moon and Mercury, and fix them.</margin>
Therefore, all those err who make any amalgamations with the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Mercury, or with the Moon <note>Silver</note> and Mercury, and set them to be fixed, wishing to fix one with the other. They shall by no means fix them, neither now nor ever. For that salt lies in the deepest part of the Sun and Moon: and it has with it the soul of the Sun and Moon: nor can any matter that exists in the nature of things be drawn out from the interiors of the Sun and Moon, except by its own spirit, and not by foreign spirits. And that cannot happen in the Sun and Moon either now, nor at any time. For the Sun and Moon must be so opened and unlocked, that they emit their spirit from themselves, and the spirit will attract the salt into itself, carrying the soul, from the interiors of the Sun and Moon, and will carry it up with it into the heaven <note>The upper part of the vessel or a state of sublimation</note>, and become one nature with it. When, therefore, the body is now clean and pure, and the spirit with the salt carrying the soul within it—the soul likewise being clean and pure: and then they are melted together again beside their own proper body, and that a clean one, a true conjunction occurs, and it turns black. And where this matter is not, there no blackness will show itself: and where there is no true conjunction, there blackness does not appear. Thus it is plain that all amalgamations, all fixations of cinnabar <term>Cinnabar: a bright red mineral (mercury sulfide) often used as a source of mercury</term>, or all other foolish fabricated works are false and fraudulent, however beautiful they may seem, through the reasons previously taught by me. Therefore, avoid all false opinions, and weigh carefully what I have taught you: so that you may be enlightened in philosophy: and understand the speech which the ancients always use in their books.

### CHAPTER 67.

<margin>The management of the fire is to be pursued from one color to another.</margin>
Therefore, when the blackness is observed, be certain that a true union has been achieved: and pursue the fire from one color to another, whatever color it may finally be, as was taught in the "white work" <note>original: "opere albo," the *albedo* stage of alchemy where the matter is purified to a white state</note>. When you see this, take some out, weigh it, and test on a glowing hot plate whether it is fixed <note>stable and no longer vaporizing when heated</note> and can withstand the fire. Therefore, take it out and set it to be calcined <note>reduced to powder through heat</note> with moderate heat for 24 hours in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" onto the material</note> or in a vaulted furnace. Then let it cool. Once cooled, weigh how much it weighs; then set it to be dissolved by all the methods previously mentioned. When both parts have been dissolved into clear water, mix both waters together, as taught before. Distill the moisture using a water bath <note>original: "balneo," referring to a bain-marie</note> as predicted, and place it again to be fixed in the secret furnace, in all the ways taught above, etc.

### CHAPTER 68.

<margin>By the already mentioned solution of the spirit and the body, the work becomes much more subtle and powerful.</margin>

I say that the Stone, after its perfection, gains a hundredfold in its power of projection <note>the final act of transforming base metals into gold or silver</note> with every single dissolution and solidification. And it is even more certain that the ferment and the spirit should both be dissolved into a clear water than if they were mixed together dry. For what mixing is better and more certain than that of water with water? As was said before.

### CHAPTER 69.

<margin>No mixture is better or more certain than water with water.</margin>
You shall know, furthermore, that once the spirit is fixed with the ferment, it is not strictly necessary to then calcine and dissolve it; however, with every calcination and dissolution, you will gain a thousandfold in the projection. For the work becomes so subtle through frequent calcination and dissolution that it is incredible. <margin>Through frequent calcination, the work becomes extremely subtle.</margin> For this reason, I teach you to take 8 parts of ferment and 1 part of spirit, because you will often fix the work, and often calcine, dissolve, and solidify it; the work will become as subtle as possible at the bottom, so that it may later reach a higher power of projection. One could take 4 parts of ferment and a fifth part of spirit and mix them together. But then you would not be able to calcine, dissolve, or solidify it so many times. For the work would become too "fusible" <note>melting too easily</note>. Thus, you would not be able to frequently calcine, dissolve, and <margin>Why 8 parts of ferment and 1 of spirit should be taken.</margin> coagulate it, because it would become too easily meltable in your hands, such that it could withstand no flame. Therefore, if you wish to achieve a high and subtle work, take many parts of ferment and few of spirit; in this way, you can frequently calcine, dissolve, and coagulate your work—

## CHAPTER 70.

<margin>How the stone is to be multiplied.</margin>

Likewise, regarding the <term>multiplication</term> <note>the process of increasing the power and quantity of the Philosopher's Stone</note> of your stone: this is done in its virtue and its powers, and not in its physical size. Instead, it will exalt itself in its nobility and <term>subtlety</term> <note>a state of extreme refinement and purity</note>, so that it may now achieve a ratio of 1 to 10,000 in its <term>projection</term> <note>the act of casting the Stone upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver</note>.

And when it has been thus multiplied and made subtle, and is exalted to great strength and power, it easily achieves 1 to 100,000 in projection. And if you were to multiply this stone three times and make it subtle in virtue and power, its projection would be infinite, because of the great subtlety which the stone would then possess. Indeed, you could multiply the stone so many times that you would never reach the end of its projection power, due to the great subtlety and virtue it would obtain. 

In fact, you could easily multiply it so often that you could not contain it in any glass vessels; it would withdraw and pass away, becoming so subtle a stone that when you wished to dissolve it, it would penetrate the glass invisibly while the glass remained whole. Furthermore, the stone would convert the glass into the appearance and color of a **Ruby**. To do this, place glass in a state of melting along with the completed stone, and cast as much weight of the stone upon the glass as you would take if you wished to convert Jupiter <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note> into the Sun <note>the alchemical name for Gold</note>. I say the stone will convert the melted glass into its own color—into the appearance and color of a precious **Ruby**. 

And keep it thus melted in that <term>crucible</term> <note>a heat-resistant container used for melting metals</note> for half an hour; the material will then harden so that it will never melt again, neither now nor at any time. It will be of the same hardness and the same color as a precious Ruby without flaws. ### CHAPTER LXXI.

<margin>How such Rubies are to be melted together.</margin>
Now, if by chance you wish to fuse such **Rubies**, do as has been said: when they have cooled, take them out, dry them, and sharpen them upon the grinding stone on which precious stones are sharpened—making them large or small as you please—and polish them beautifully. Thus you will have excellent Rubies without flaws, which **gladden the hearts of men** and grant victory to their master. They receive this power from the virtue of the Stone working within them. Therefore I say: you should multiply the Stone so often that it becomes incredibly "subtle" <note>In alchemy, "subtlety" refers to the fineness and penetrating power of a substance</note>. When you dissolve it again in that **red burning water** <note>original: "aqua ardente"; likely a strong acid or distilled spirit used in the process</note>, it would penetrate glass invisibly, and you would lose it, though the glass would remain whole; it would simply become red and transparent in the manner of a ruby, and hard and incombustible, as was said. You would be deprived of your noble Stone because it would become so spiritual that, in the end, it could not be contained in any glass vessels whatsoever, even if they were 10 feet thick. It would penetrate them because of the great subtlety of its multiplication and its great power. Therefore, take the Stone and multiply it in this manner.

### CHAPTER LXXII.

In the same way, prepare <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aquam fortem"; Nitric acid, used for dissolving metals</note> from clarified <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfuric acid or a metal sulfate</note>, prepared and separated from its dregs, and <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "falnitro"; Potassium nitrate</note> in equal parts. From these, distill the strong water according to the art. Then take the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>The "dead head" or solid residue left over after distillation</note> from the glass jar and grind it into a fine powder; then rub it upon the stone; then in the water...

### OF MINERAL WORKS

<margin>An excellent red water, glowing by night.</margin> ...place it in common distilled water, and let all the salt be extracted. Then, draw it off through a filter so that you have it clean and free from dregs. Congeal <note>original: "congela"; to solidify a liquid into a salt or solid form</note> it again, and once it is congealed, make an impalpable powder <note>a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers</note> from it. Put that powder into a glass jar, and then pour that same strong water <note>original: "aquam illam fortem"; likely referring to *aqua fortis* or nitric acid</note> back over the powder—the same water you previously distilled from it. Set it to be distilled again, and distill whatever is willing to come over. Then, remove the dead head <term>caput mortuum: the useless solid residue remaining in a flask after all volatile components have been distilled off</term> once more, and grind it into a powder as before; perform the process in all ways as described above. Repeat this work until you have distilled all the salt along with the strong water. Then, you will have an excellent red water that glows at night like a bright fire.

Next, take that water and rectify it in a bath <note>likely a *balneum Mariae* or warm water bath</note> by distilling it repeatedly and pouring it back over, so that in the end you have all the distillate from the bath. Then your precious water is prepared, in which you shall multiply and "open" your stone <note>the "Stone" refers to the alchemical goal, such as the Philosopher's Stone or a specific metallic tincture</note>. Likewise, take your stone and dissolve it in that water; it will dissolve immediately. Place it in a lukewarm bath with an alembic <term>alembic: the upper part of a still, used to condense vapors</term> placed on top, and with the receiver at the spout thoroughly sealed everywhere with luting <term>luting: a clay or paste used to create an airtight seal between glass vessels</term>. Keep the bath warm, and when the strong water has passed over, test the powder by placing it on a glowing-hot metal plate to see if it flies away <note>original: "ſubuolę"; refers to the substance volatilizing or turning into vapor</note>, as has been said in other places. 

Then pour that water back over it again, seal it carefully as before, and distill it once more until it no longer drips. Then test a small amount of the powder again to see if it flies away a little more. If it flies away no more than before, pour the strong water over it again, put the alembic on top, seal the receiver nearby thoroughly everywhere, and distill again in a lukewarm bath. Do this in all ways as previously taught. Repeat this craftsmanship until the entire substance flies away together from the glowing-hot plate. Then it is sufficiently "opened." Now, set it to be sublimated <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface</term> in all ways as before. You shall repeat this sublimation three or four times, always without adding any dregs; then it is enough. 

Then take a small portion of that which has been sublimated upward and set it to be fixed <note>original: "fixandum"; making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> in the furnace where the spirit is calcined <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a friable powder</term>, using a glass vessel such as the one shown here. With a small, smooth glass placed over the mouth, first apply a little heat, and then increase the fire by degrees several times, as is taught in the work. And when it is fixed, weigh how much the fixed portion weighs. Then, for every three parts of the fixed substance, take one part of the spirit, and set it to be fixed again as before...

<margin>In multiplication, no other colors reveal themselves.</margin>

And in the process of multiplication <note>The stage where the power and quantity of the Stone are increased</note>, no blackness intervenes: nor do any "colors of the world" <note>original: "colores orbis," likely referring to the "Peacock's Tail," the shifting iridescent colors seen in earlier alchemical stages</note> show themselves; nor any whiteness. Nor in sublimation does anything show itself except for redness: nor in fixation <note>The process of making a substance stable and resistant to heat</note> does any other color manifest itself except its own, which is an excellent redness <note>original: "rubedo," the final color indicating the perfection of the Stone</note>. For the Stone has no other color except redness. For it is only one substance, a simple matter, like the invincible heavens. Know also that even though it might be sublimated, it would not be deprived of its fixity; and when the Stone is finished and prepared in its extreme virtue, then the Stone cannot be changed again in any other way from its essence into another form. For if the Stone could be extracted from its essence into another essence or nature, or if it could be changed: it would not be the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance sought by alchemists to transform base metals into gold and achieve spiritual perfection</note>, nor would it be simple: nor a glorified body. No, no. Understand my speech correctly. The Stone can be changed into no other nature or essence after it is perfected. For it is only one thing: and understand this according to its own degree.

## CHAPTER LXXIII.

<margin>The solution.</margin>

Lest someone should ask: can the Stone be changed by no means? The question is: it was previously fixed and endured the fire: and yet you teach me to make it volatile again, so that I may sublimate it. Has it not therefore been led back from its fixed corporeal nature into a purely spiritual nature? You speak rightly that it first endured the fire: and afterwards was made volatile: both are true. Therefore, it has not been led back from its nature into another nature: it must be so: and unless it were so, it could perform no <term>projection</term> <note>The final act of the alchemical process, where the Stone is cast upon a base metal to transform it into gold</note>. For that which performs the projection must be <term>spirit</term>, <term>soul</term>, and <term>body</term> equally strong and powerful: and if it were not such—but the body were stronger than the spirit, or the spirit more powerful than the body—then there would be a contrary nature in it: then it would not be one thing. Our Stone is body, soul, and spirit, and these three are one in a simple essence inseparably: equal in magnitude, strength, and power: one is not separated from the other: for there is one essence, one simple nature, the one being exactly as the other. Yet there are three—spirit, soul, and body—they are in one as we understand. Understand my words thoroughly, and learn to know the Stone, and of what kind of nature it must be.
