### CHAPTER LXX.

<margin>Our stone is neither fixed nor volatile.</margin>
<margin>Why it appears fixed and bears the fire.</margin>
You shall also know, as a great secret, that our stone is neither fixed nor volatile. It is at once spirit and body; both must have spirit and body in their nature, and both must be equally strong, as we have previously demonstrated to you through reasoning. 

And as for why it appears to be fixed and to endure the fire, that happens because of its solidity. The parts of the stone are so compacted into one that no other thing in the nature of things is so tightly compressed as our stone is. For in the world, there is no thing so subtle <term>subtle: in alchemy, "subtlety" refers to a substance being refined, pure, and capable of penetrating other matter</term> and pure as our stone. And the more subtle and pure a thing is, the more firmly its subtle and pure parts come together and are compressed into one, and the heavier they are in weight. For they "love" one another, so much so that they are compressed into one, so that they can only be separated with difficulty. See how its excellence waits for the fire: the fire cannot separate its parts because it is so firmly compacted into one. And yet it is pure spirit: for it flies <note>original: "volat," meaning to vaporize or sublime</note> much more easily after it has been "opened" than any of the spirits. This is because of the great subtlety and purity it has in its nature. 

Our stone will therefore not resist the fire better and more strongly than a substance made of body and spirit together; and the body is so subtle—indeed, it was subtler than the spirit. And now body and spirit are one in one essence and one nature. How much more strongly will our stone be able to resist the fire than gold? Gold is still as it was formed by nature, and it is "pure spirit" <note>In alchemical theory, metals were often viewed as "spirit" that had been solidified by nature</note> and resists the fire; therefore, the stone ought to resist the fire ten thousand times more strongly than gold. 

And when our stone has been opened and unlocked by our "burning water" <term>burning water: often refers to strong acids (aqua fortis) or highly rectified alcohol used as a solvent</term>, which separates its compacted parts, it causes them to be lifted up and puffed out in the manner of a sponge. If gold rises in a small fire more easily than any spirit because of the subtlety that nature granted it, how much more easily and swiftly will our stone rise from a fire of small heat than gold? For our stone possesses all the extreme subtlety that nature can possibly give it. Moreover, the craftsman has infused it with extreme power and subtlety, to the highest degree that can be given to it, so that it is a hundred thousand times more subtle than gold. Therefore, our stone must ascend more easily than gold because it is much more subtle. 

And when its parts are joined to it again in a smaller proportion, so that the parts are compressed together and again driven into one—which we call fixation <term>fixation: the process of stabilizing a volatile substance so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term>—the stone will once more endure the fire as it did before, and a thousand times more strongly than fire...

### CHAPTER 75.

<margin>The Stone is not changed, but remains in its own essence, and why.</margin>
You shall also know that when you multiply <note>Multiplication: an alchemical process that increases the quantity and power of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> the Stone and raise it in height and power, it does not change in its nature; it does not become black, nor does it cast off any various colors; but it remains in its own essence and in the very nature in which it was before. For it has been brought to the ultimate point, so that it has become a simple essence <note>original: "simplex essentia"; refers to a substance that is perfectly pure and no longer a mixture of competing elements.</note> and a simple nature. And Nature cannot change it by any means, nor by any art that exists in the world. Truly, you can make it more refined than it is, but it remains in its own essence and in the own nature in which it exists, etc.

### CHAPTER 76.

<margin>The condensation of the Stone, which is improperly called fixation.</margin>
And so you can open and unlock the Stone as often as was said before, and afterward sublimate it, and after that, press it together again with its small parts so that its parts cling together into one once more—which we call fixation. We do indeed call it "to fix," but to fix is nothing other than condensation <note>The author clarifies that this type of "fixation" is specifically the physical densification of the refined material.</note>, so that all its subtle parts are driven together into one again, tightly joined as they were before, so that it may once again endure the fire. In this way, we can perform a projection <note>Projection: the final step of the Great Work, where the Stone is cast onto base metals to transmute them into gold or silver.</note> with it as we did before. Thus, you can easily multiply your Stone three or four times, but no more. For it would become too subtle, so much so that it would slip away from you invisibly when it is brought into water, because of its great refinement, as I taught you above. Therefore, you can raise your Stone to its highest degree, so much so that here below the circle of the Moon <note>original: "infra circulum Lunae"; a traditional way of describing the Earthly realm, as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</note>, a matter so noble and subtle as the Stone is not to be found. For when it is already so elevated that it cannot be raised further nor made more subtle, no earthly matter can surpass the Stone, neither in nobility, nor subtlety, nor beauty, nor potency, nor strength, nor in the wondrous influences and virtues which are enclosed within it when it is brought to its highest degree, just as shall be demonstrated in the projection, etc.

### CHAPTER 77.

<margin>How the ancients made their <term>Stone</term><note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> before the invention of <term>strong waters</term><note>Aqua fortis, or nitric acid.</note>.</margin>
You should know hereafter that the ancient <term>Philosophers</term><note>The term "Philosopher" here refers specifically to alchemists.</note> were accustomed to making their stone in that manner, as was taught before, before the art of strong waters was discovered. For until that time, <term>bodies</term><note>Metallic elements or solid substances.</note> had to be opened slowly, namely by calcining, reverberating, dissolving in our sharp <term>vinegar</term><note>Alchemical "vinegar" was often a specialized acidic solvent, not merely household vinegar.</note>, and congealing, until our stone was made spiritual; and then they worked further, as was taught before. And when the stone was already completely perfect, they did not yet have the true art of multiplying their stone in its own power; but little by little, in order to try to make it subtle for its perfection, they would dissolve it in our sharpest vinegar and congeal it, until it remained as a clear <term>oil</term>. When they desired to make that oil back into a hard mass, they took prepared <term>Sun</term><note>original: "Solem" — Alchemical code for Gold.</note>, namely stripped of its body and red in the manner of blood, and they mixed their oil with it, dissolving and congealing it once; then they placed it in a secret furnace with tempered heat until it turned into a dark red mass like <term>dragon's blood</term><note>A deep red resin, used here to describe the specific color of the alchemical state.</note>, which, through frequent dissolution and congelation, was now much more subtle than it was before. 

<margin>Posterity invented strong waters.</margin>
Posterity, noticing this, sharpened the edge of their minds and invented <term>strong water</term>, which shortened the path for them considerably. For they made strong water, as was said before, in which they could grind and mill both bodies, taking one part of each after they had been cleansed, and then they mixed the waters, and so directed it that the mixture was transparent and clear, without dregs. And they then easily made their stone spiritual; and then they further brought their stone to extreme perfection: which they could then make subtle and multiply in its own power as they pleased using the same aforementioned well-rectified strong water; and this in all ways, as was correctly taught before. Thus strong water is a great aid for shortening the work and for leading the stone to a higher perfection.

### CHAPTER 78.

And it is a noble and delightful work, or way in the art, as you shall hear. Take therefore first <term>Moon</term><note>original: "Lunam" — Alchemical code for Silver.</note> purified dry upon a hearth or <term>cupel</term><note>A small, shallow dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead.</note>, and well-refined from lead: dissolve in it...

## MASTER JOHN ISAAC
### *On the projection of the stone.* CHAPTER LXXX.

<margin>How the projection is to be performed. Metal must be prepared before the projection can be made upon it. The white stone is only to be projected onto silver, and why.</margin>
Next I will teach you who you are and in what manner you shall use your stone and join it to metals for transmuting them into Gold <note>original: "Solem," literally the Sun</note> or into Silver <note>original: "Lunam," literally the Moon</note>. You shall know this as a great secret: that you can make no projection onto any metal unless it has first been prepared for it in this manner. If you wish to make a projection onto Jupiter <note>alchemical symbol for Tin</note>, you shall melt it in a crucible and place upon an ounce of Jupiter an ounce of pure Silver, and melt them together; then you shall cast your white stone upon it. Then the Tin <note>Jupiter</note> will be transmuted into true Silver, more or less according to how subtle your stone has been made, as will now be better explained. And if you wish to work with your red stone, you shall project it onto Silver; you need do nothing other than melt the Silver and then cast your red stone upon it. Then your Silver shall become true Gold, better than that which is brought out of the mines. And above all, you shall know that when you wish to make a projection, you should project your white stone only onto Tin <note>Jupiter</note>, and onto no other metal. For Tin is the metal closest to Silver. Tin is a raw and "undercooked" body, and the stone has no other work to do than to thoroughly cook the Tin, as has been taught elsewhere. It would also easily transmute other metals into Silver, but they are more "unclean" than Tin, and the projection would then not be as high in quality. Also, the stone would have to flow in the fire longer with the impure metals before they could establish themselves as a <term>Regulus</term> <note>A "regulus" is the pure metallic heart or button that forms at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note> than would be the case with Tin, etc.

### CHAPTER LXXXI.

<margin>The projection with the red stone must be made upon silver, and why.</margin>
Furthermore, you shall make your projection with the red stone upon Silver <note>Luna</note>, which is the purest of all metals upon which a projection can be made. Moreover, no projection can be made with the red stone except upon silver. For if you were to project it upon Saturn <note>alchemical symbol for Lead</note> or other metals, it would make no projection upon them. For the red stone effects nothing except Gold <note>Solem</note>. And you shall know that one cannot arrive from the first step to the third unless the second has been passed. Thus, the imperfect metals would first have to be reduced to Silver, and only then to Gold. For no metal can reach the state of Gold unless it is first Silver. Indeed, Gold was Silver before it became Gold. Nature had to generate Silver from that point first before it could lead it through to Gold. Just as one cannot arrive at a place 100 miles distant from here unless you cross the intermediate path; from one extreme to the other <meta>catchword: extreme-</meta>

MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC
bb 4 CHAPTER

<margin>A question and its solution.</margin>
You may ask why oil does not mix with water and always floats on top? For oil is heavier than water: <note>In the Aristotelian physics used by alchemists, oil was often theorized to be "heavier" in its elemental composition or "parts" even though it sits above water; modern science defines this as being less dense.</note> how then does it float? For we see every day that it is the light thing that always floats.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII.

<margin>Why oil floats, even though it is heavier than water.</margin>
First and before all things, you shall know that oil shares no common part with water, even though they may have once been one body. This is because the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The "quinta essentia" or quintessence; the purest, celestial element that binds the four physical elements together.</note>—which the oil retains in the seed or in the other thing from which the oil is pressed or distilled—has departed. For when the fifth essence has withdrawn from any substance in which water, fire, air, earth, oil, and salt are held together, then all those parts must necessarily be separated from one another. Nor will they ever again wish to come together until they have been "glorified." <note>In alchemy, "glorification" refers to the process of purifying and refining matter to its highest, most spiritual state.</note> Therefore, oil refuses to mix with water, even though they were once bound as one body by the fifth essence. And oil always floats, yet it is heavier than water. Do you know how this happens? Oil is much more <term>subtle</term> <note>Meaning refined, thin, or spiritually elevated.</note> than water, even though oil contains many thick parts within itself, and even <term>sal ammoniac</term>; <note>original: "sal armoniacum." A volatile salt used in alchemical cooling and cleaning processes.</note> and the parts of the oil are firmly compressed into one, so that it refuses to be separated. Water is a solid element and very "open" because of the thickness within it. Oil, however, is subtle and fiery, and is firmly compressed into one. All heat tends upward, and all subtlety tends upward; furthermore, its firm parts do not wish to be separated from one another, so the oil refuses to penetrate the thick waters in order to sink. Thus, the oil must necessarily float.

It is the same with our <term>Stone</term>; <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> it also floats upon metals just as oil floats upon water. For the Stone does not yet share a part with the metals, even though it was once a metal itself. It is heavier than the metal, and this is because it is more subtle and more firmly compacted. The metal stands liquefied and is very solid, like water; but the Stone is not of the nature of metal, for it is now the fifth essence. Therefore, it does not wish to mix with the metal, nor to enter it. And so it floats because of those firm parts which refuse to be separated. Thus the Stone does not want to enter the metal, and so it must necessarily float. Know that <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> says: *Our Stone must share a part with the body, the spirit, and the soul, before it can perform <term>projection</term>.* <note>The final alchemical act of casting the Stone onto base metals to transmute them into gold.</note>

<summary>This page explains why oil floats on water despite its perceived "heaviness" by citing the absence of the fifth essence and its "fiery" subtlety. This physical observation is used as an analogy for why the Philosopher's Stone floats on molten metal until it is properly prepared for projection.</summary>

### CHAPTER LXXXIV.

<margin>No union of contrary things can occur except through a medium.</margin>
You should know, furthermore, that our stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemist’s work.</note> possesses a share of body, soul, and spirit. But these parts are united within the stone with such perfection and such spiritual substance, and driven into one, that they refuse to mix themselves with any coarse, imperfect, or impure parts, except through a **medium** <note>A "medium" or "middle" is a substance that shares characteristics with two opposites, allowing them to join.</note>. This medium must be joined to the spiritual substance, whether the stone is white <note>The "White Stone" was used to create silver.</note> or red <note>The "Red Stone" was used to create gold.</note>. For no gathering can occur in any things that are mutually contrary to one another, except through an intermediary that causes the contrary things to enter one into the other; it makes them embrace one another and remain together, a matter about which I have taught you in many places.

So also is the case here in **projection** <note>The final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transform it.</note>. The Stone does not wish to enter into black, filthy, foul, and imperfect metals without a medium. For black, impure metals are especially contrary to the stone. How, therefore, could those two contrary things come together, one into the other, without a medium? Truly not at all, neither now nor at any time. A medium must be present, through which one shall penetrate the other. 

Now, what shall be that medium through which those two dissimilar things come together? That medium must be a <term>living body</term> <note>original: "corpus vivum." In alchemy, this often refers to "living" mercury or a substance that has not been "killed" by chemical processing.</note> and must be one with the dead, impure, and stinking body. And that same living body must be one in a single body with the white and red stone. And since these two dead, stinking metals already contain within themselves that pure living body which is one with them—as are the soul and the body—the stone (whether white or red) is then projected into them, also containing within itself that same living body. Then they meet, and each draws its own into its own nature, so that a union takes place there, and one enters into the other. Thus, the stone gathered in this manner expels all corruption from itself and creates a perfect **living body**, even better and more perfect than that which comes out of the mines.

### CHAPTER LXXXV.

Alchemists used "Sun" as the symbol and name for gold.</note>. Beat this into thin plates. Then take <term>living sulfur</term> <note>original: "vivum sulphur." Native or "virgin" sulfur that has not been treated with heat.</note>, and grind it upon a stone into a thick paste with oil, and smear your plates with it, and let them dry. Then smear them again, and a third time, letting them dry again in the same way. Then, with live coals—

# MASTER JOHN ISAAC

Place [it] upon the coals and allow it to be calcined <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a brittle powder.</note>. Then grind it into a powder, and wash the powder with common distilled water until your water flows clear from the powder. Then grind the powder upon a stone with honey from the comb or gum-water, and grind it as finely as if it were to be used for painting. Then place it again into glass vessels: and wash it with warm common distilled water; let the powder settle: pour off the water from the top: stir and let it settle, pour off again: and repeat this until the water flows as clear from the powder as it was when you poured it on. Then dry your powder over a small fire or in the sun.

Then your **Gold** <note>original: *Sol*, literally "the Sun," the alchemical name for gold.</note> is prepared, etc. Then you shall take a thousand parts of this powder of Gold, and one part of its **first stone** <note>original: *primi lapidis*, referring to the Philosopher's Stone in an early stage of preparation.</note>, and pulverize the stone finely, and mix it with your prepared powder of Gold: and then have a **crucible** <note>original: *crucibulum*, a vessel made of ceramic or graphite that can withstand extreme heat.</note> that can endure a great and vehement fire: and fit another crucible to this one, and smooth it upon a stone so that one matches the other, or one is enclosed within the other as if it were a lid. Then place your powder into this, and seal <note>original: *luta*, the process of "luting" or sealing a vessel airtight with a specialized clay called "lute."</note> the crucibles one upon the other firmly, and surround the outside with strong lute to the thickness of three or four fingers: and let the clay dry thoroughly.

Then place the crucible in a wind-furnace, and first apply a small fire: several times make it hotter and hotter, until your crucible glows thoroughly red. Then you shall increase your fire significantly until you are certain your material has melted in the crucible. Then keep the crucible for three days in one constant heat: so that your material remains melted: and afterward allow it to cool of its own accord: and break open your crucible: and you will find a remarkable hard mass: and it is breakable as if it were glass, so that you can pulverize it.

And when you now wish to perform the **projection** <note>The final stage of the alchemical work where the transmuting agent is "thrown" onto base metal to change it into gold or silver.</note>, cast 1 part of this finely pulverized mass into a thousand parts of the nearest metal having a soul and being alive <note>This likely refers to purified Mercury or "living" lead or silver used as a base for the transformation.</note>: and it shall transform it into true **Gold** or **Silver** <note>original: *Solem aut Lunam*, literally "the Sun or the Moon."</note> better than that which comes from the mines. And this is that **Work of Three Days** of which the **Ancients** <note>original: *Veteres*, the classical alchemical authorities like Hermes or Geber.</note> made mention in their books: and it is a great work, rendering the body of Gold so subtle in the space of three days while it stands melted with the stone: so that the Gold becomes more medicinal than it was before: indeed, more than can be believed. And hold this as a great secret, etc.

### CHAPTER 86.

<margin>The stone just prepared can make no projection onto Mercury.</margin>
Furthermore, you shall now know that the stone prepared in this way cannot make any projection <note>The act of casting the alchemical substance onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note> onto Mercury, because of its very difficult fusion <note>meaning it has an extremely high melting point and will not melt easily into the liquid mercury</note>. Therefore, there is no need to make the stone itself so fusible; concerning this, I have taught you abundantly in the section on multiplication: how you shall make an oil from this stone. 

Thus, there is no need to treat Mercury here. But you shall remember when you wish to work with the oil and project upon Mercury: take 1 ounce <term>uncia: a unit of weight, roughly 28 grams</term> of Mercury and a half-mark <note>approximately 4 ounces</note> of pure Moon <note>Silver</note> purified by cupellation <note>a refining process where ores are treated under high heat to separate noble metals from base metals</note>. Set it upon the fire; and when it begins to smoke, cast your stone's oil upon it, which was prepared with the "body" <note>the metallic base or substance</note>, as I taught you in multiplication, and as I will now teach in other ways. 

Take the oil of the white or red stone: and take Sun <note>original: "Solem"; alchemical code for Gold</note> for the oil of the red stone. Then add ten parts of calcined <note>reduced to a powder by heat</note> and prepared Sun to one part of oil, as was taught above: and saturate the lime <note>the powder resulting from calcination</note> of the Sun with this oil, and place it in a glass flask on a tripod. 

First apply a small fire: and gradually increase it more and more, until you can hardly keep your hand inside the furnace: and in this manner let it stand for five or six days. Afterward increase the fire until the stone of the inner furnace hisses when you touch it with a wet finger: and keep it in that heat for three days. Then let it cool of its own accord: take it out, and having broken the glass, you will find a hard, solid mass. 

Therefore, wishing to make the projection upon Mercury, put Mercury into the crucible as said before: and take a portion of this mass and powder it, and cast it upon the Mercury when it begins to smoke. Then increase the fire until it begins to flow. Let it flow until it settles into a Regulus <note>original: "Regulum"; the metallic button or mass that forms at the bottom of a crucible</note>. Then extinguish the fire and let it cool: take it out and strike it with a hammer upon the anvil, and see if it is soft: if it is soft, you have good Sun <note>Gold</note>. 

And as long as it is breakable or brittle like glass, it is still the medicine <note>the transformative substance, not yet the perfected metal</note>. Then cast molten Moon <note>Silver</note> upon it until it remains soft under the hammer. Then you have good Sun <note>Gold</note>. And as long as it is brittle, you have not yet reached the end of your projection, whether of the red or white stone, or the red or white oil. Then you must continue to project onto other metals until it remains soft, with an excellent color, and passes every test <note>original: "examen"; the various metallurgical trials for purity</note>: then you have the end of your projection, etc. I say to you, my son,

### CHAPTER 87

<margin>Where each stone is first coagulated.</margin>
<margin>The purer and more subtle the poison, the more poisonous it is.</margin>
Understand my words well, which I am about to say. The white and red stone first arose and was coagulated <note>Hardened from a liquid or vaporous state into a solid.</note> from **Mercury** and from white **sulfur**: thus coagulated, they are a poison. For the stone coagulated from pure and white sulfur and from pure Mercury is white <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: "arsenicum album"</note>, pure and subtle, and it is a poison. For the purer and more subtle a poison is, the more poisonous it is. And when pure red sulfur falls into pure Mercury, it coagulates the Mercury: and that becomes a shining yellow arsenic, and it is also pure and subtle—indeed, much more subtle than white arsenic.

And if an ounce of arsenic were given to a large horse, it would undoubtedly die. For that poison would seek the heart and furthermore would pervade all the limbs, so that all the flesh and whatever is in the horse would be infected by the poison, such that it must die. And if dogs, or cats, or all birds were to eat of this horse, they would all die together from it. 

Now, if an ounce of our poison can kill such a large horse, which weighs so many hundreds of pounds, and furthermore kills whatever eats of it—if, therefore, one poison in such a small quantity can exert such great power over such a large quantity of weight, then our stone is composed of that same white or red arsenic. And out of the red, **Sol** <note>The Sun, representing Gold.</note> was produced over a long time, and thus it cooked with the heat of the sun by continuous cooking in the earth: and it brought the poison into its interior, and brought the interior outwards. And from the material which previously had been poisonous, Nature produced a great medicine. For **Sol** <note>Gold</note> is compatible with all medicines for all diseases. Our stone is composed of those two aforementioned metals, namely from the Sun and the Moon <note>Gold and Silver</note>, as appears in the work, etc.

### CHAPTER 90.

<margin>Everything created by God has redness either on the outside or on the inside.</margin>
Now you may ask how one part of the stone could tinge ten thousand, or a hundred thousand, or even more parts than the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; in alchemy, the Moon represents the metal Silver.</note>: it seems difficult to understand. Know that under every greenness hides blackness, and under every blackness, whiteness. And under every whiteness, redness is hidden. And whatever God created has perfect redness either on the outside or on the inside. For everything that is red inside is white outside; the intermediate colors are varied. And whatever is white inside is red outside; and between whiteness and redness are colors of every kind, as was said before. And the closer a thing approaches to perfection, the fewer colors it has within itself: it is simpler the closer it touches the final state. And when it has reached the supreme and final end for which God ordained it, it has only one color in itself, neither on the inside nor on the outside: but it holds within itself the power of all the colors that previously manifested in it. For a thing in which there are many colors, and many distinct, varied colors: just as many diverse complexions <note>The "complexion" refers to the balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—within a substance.</note> and virtues are present in that thing. But when that thing is perfected into a simple, perfect essence, reaching its supreme power to which God ordained it: all the virtues work together in that work, in a short time, miraculously: and yet there is only one simple essence in this thing. Its color is red both inside and outside: and between its interior and exterior—that is, in its middle—there is no difference: just as it is on the outside, so it is on the inside and in the middle. And it performs its work simultaneously without delay, in a moment or the blink of an eye: for no contrary nature remains within it to oppose itself; therefore they work as one.

### CHAPTER 91.

<margin>He applies the preceding arguments to his own stone.</margin>
So it is with our Stone: into whatever it is cast, it performs a perfect work there: it turns that very thing inside out, putting the interior on the outside, and the exterior on the inside. And the Moon <note>Silver</note> is, on the inside, a good Sun <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note>, bright and red. And the white stone, when cast into Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, draws its interior to the outside: and it becomes a white and clear Moon, and places its redness on the inside. Thus every thing holds its own tincture <note>The "tincture" is the transformative soul or coloring essence of the metal.</note> within itself, whether in white or red, even if the white and red Stone had no tincture of its own to emit, as it indeed does emit. Metals [by] the tincture of the stone...

They have no need for anything, whether in the white or in the red <note>These colors refer to the two stages of the Philosopher’s Stone: the "White Work" for making silver and the "Red Work" for making gold</note>. For every thing has within itself what it requires: and every thing contains enough <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tincturæ"; in alchemy, the "tincture" is the essential spiritual essence or "dye" that can transform the nature of a substance</note> in itself, without the support of any other thing. Every thing created by God possesses its own medicine, without the addition of any foreign medicine—whether in the vegetable, animal, or mineral kingdoms—to heal all the diseases that come upon it. If it were not so, the works of God would not be perfect. For whatever God ever made, it was all without flaw, and required no help from other foreign things; it has everything within it that it needs, even if we do not fundamentally understand it. God did nothing in vain, not even the smallest leaf growing from the earth, as shall be taught in the section on vegetables. Although we do not perceive perfection in all things, they nevertheless have it enclosed within themselves. For through the art of medicine, we are able to extract the hidden nature from all things: to make its secret manifest, and its manifest nature secret.

This is exactly what our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> achieves in metals. You should know that the White and Red Stone do not emit any tincture from themselves into the metals during <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectione"; the act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note>. For the tincture which is in the Stone is so unified with the elements and with the living spirits—forming one body and one substance—that they cannot be separated. For its nature is celestial, just as the heaven is invincible, from which the Sun, Moon, Planets, Stars, and whatever exists and stands in the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the stars</note> take their influence, which they display toward these lower things, as we see daily before our eyes.

<margin>That flowers of various colors are born through the power and heat of the sun, and by what reasoning that happens.</margin>

Through the power and heat of the Sun, flowers of various colors and various scents are born here. And all of that is done by the heat of the Sun. Do you think the Sun pours colors and scents from its own body into the flowers or herbs? Not at all. Rather, the celestial nature possesses such power and influence that it draws out <note>original: "eliciat"</note> the colors, scents, and tastes from the seed from which the herbs or flowers are born. Even if the Sun shone for a thousand years, it would not "infuse" color, scent, or taste. Instead, GOD infused them, and all of that is enclosed within the seed. But unless the Sun radiated upon them, the colors, tastes, scents, or fruits would never be born, nor would they arise from the seed. The Sun is a celestial body, and it possesses an influence such that by its heat it draws out everything internal that is in the seed, and leads the scent, taste, and color out into the open; it does this from the seed, so that through the Sun, the seed grows to its own perfection. And it ensures that, thereafter, other seeds...

...seeds grow abundantly and perpetually until the end of the world: but it does not distribute from its own proper body. I wrote to you regarding <term>multiplication</term><note>An alchemical process intended to increase the quantity or potency of the transmuting agent.</note> that the stone makes a crystal glass into the likeness of a Ruby; nevertheless, it is not a Ruby. And if the stone could be separated from the glass by art, the glass would once again be glass, just as it was before. Thus, the stone cannot confer what it does not have. Truly, it transfers from bad to good, from the impure to the pure, whatever is similar to itself—and not in all things, but specifically in metals.

### CHAPTER XCII.

Likewise, to cleanse <term>Venus</term><note>original: "Veneris." In alchemy, Venus is the traditional name for Copper.</note>, beginning with all its impurity: take 20 or 30 pounds of Venus and hammer it into thin plates like small stones. Heat the plates five or six times and quench them in urine, so that the Venus becomes clean and bright, and so that no dross or impurity remains on the plates; let them be clean, red, and bright. Then dry the plates in a clean linen cloth; then dry them even better in the sun or by the fire. Then have some very white and clear arsenic; grind it into a powder. Then grind it upon a stone with <term>oil of tartar</term><note>original: "oleo tartari." A concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used as a powerful alkaline cleaning agent.</note> as finely as soap, and smear the plates of Venus with it, and then rouse the fire again. When the plates are thoroughly dry, smear them again, and dry them once more; repeat this four or five times. Then take common salt, such as comes from the sea (common salt), and grind it finely. Then have two crucibles prepared; place a layer of your salt upon the bottom of the crucibles, and place your plates of Venus upon it...

...continue until your <term>crucible<gloss>a ceramic or graphite container used for melting metals at very high temperatures</gloss></term> is full. Then, place all your crucibles into the furnace for <term>calcining<gloss>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state</gloss></term>. Then remove it, and once the vessels are broken, place that copper into boiling water, wash it, and dissolve the salt. Pour off the salty water from the top, and wash it repeatedly with hot water until your copper no longer has a salty taste. 

Then dry your copper and pound it in a <term>mortar<gloss>a bowl-shaped vessel used with a pestle for grinding substances</gloss></term>, and sift it through a sieve. Next, grind it upon a stone as finely as if it were to be used for painting. Then take 2 or 3 large earthenware vessels and put a portion of this ground powder into each. Pour clean water over it, stir it well, and let it settle. The noblest and best part of the metal will sink to the bottom. Pour off that upper water into a large vat, or two; then pour fresh water over the powder again, stir well, and let it settle. Pour off the upper water again, adding it to the first. This process of pouring off and pouring on is to be repeated until the water runs out as clear as when you poured it in.

Then dry your powder and mix it with <term>alkali salt<gloss>likely potassium carbonate or a similar alkaline substance</gloss></term>, **borax**, and **saltpeter** <note>original: "sale nitri"</note>. Place this mixture into a linen bag, such as the one shown in this figure: and when the bag is full, sew it up and insert a small wooden quill <note>original: "pennam," likely a hollow tube or spout</note> at the end of the bag. 

Then coat the bag everywhere with good <term>lute<gloss>clay sealant</gloss></term> that can withstand fire, to a thickness of two fingers. Allow it to dry. Once it is dry, place the bag upon one or two iron bars, and place a crucible beneath the end of the bag where the wooden quill is located. 

Then build a fierce fire around it, and the metal will easily melt and flow into the crucible. Keep it there until you have gathered all your powder into a single body. When you have it all together as one body, weigh it to see how heavy it is, and for every <term>mark<gloss>a traditional unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 8 ounces</gloss></term>, you shall add one <term>drachm<gloss>symbol: ʒ; a small unit of weight</gloss></term> of pure, <term>cupelled<gloss>refined in a shallow vessel to remove impurities</gloss></term> **Moon** <note>original: "Lunae," the alchemical name for silver</note>. Melt them together in a large crucible and pour them into rods. In this way, your "body" is prepared and <term>vivified<gloss>brought to a state of alchemical "life" or high purity</gloss></term> for the application of a "medicine of the second order" <note>This refers to a stage in the alchemical process where the material is prepared for further transformation</note> upon it, according to the teachings of **Hermes** and **Geber** <note>Hermes Trismegistus and Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) were legendary foundational figures in alchemy</note>.

### CHAPTER XCIII.

<margin>How Silver is to be prepared for this medicine of the 2nd order.</margin>
I wish to teach you in what manner you shall prepare your <term>Moon</term> <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for Silver</note>. Take <term>Roman vitriol</term> <note>blue copper sulfate</note> and <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate</note> in equal parts, and from these make <term>strong water</term> <note>original: *aqua fortis*; nitric acid</note> by distillations with an <term>alembic</term> <note>a pear-shaped chemical still used to refine liquids</note> according to the art, etc.

### CHAPTER XCIV.

<margin>Dissolved Silver must be precipitated.</margin>
**L**ikewise, dissolve the Silver in that white water; namely, for every <term>mark</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 8 ounces</note> of Silver, take 2 marks of strong water, and in it dissolve your Silver, as is usually done; then when it is fully dissolved, precipitate your Silver; pour off that water from the <term>calx</term> <note>the powdery residue left after a substance is dissolved or burned</note>, and clean the calx of your Silver with common water, washing away the saltiness four or five times. <margin>The saltiness must be washed away, four or five times.</margin> Then dry the calx by a small fire: and then place the calx of your Silver in 5 or 6 earthen dishes in a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat onto the material from the roof rather than through direct contact with flames</note>: and roast your Silver with such heat that it does not melt, until your Silver swells up like an open sponge. <margin>Silver is roasted until it swells in the manner of a sponge.</margin> And this shall happen at most within eight days, or sooner. Let it cool on its own. Then take it out, and grind it upon a stone with distilled vinegar to dissolve it in a <term>Mary’s bath</term> <note>original: *balneum Mariae*; a water bath used for gentle heating, similar to a double boiler</note>. Fill two parts of the vessel and leave a third part empty: and cover it with a small smooth shingle or a small glass, and let it stand thus for one night in moderate heat: so that you can scarcely hold your hand in the water of your bath: and during the day and night take the upper glass: and stir it a little, so that the calx mixes with the vinegar: or have a long rod, and put it into the vessel from above: and raise it and lower it, as women make butter: and thus mix the calx of the Silver thoroughly with the vinegar. And do this five or six times during the day and night. Finally, let it stand undisturbed for one day, so that the calx can settle well. Then the vinegar will be a greenish-blue color. Let it cool on its own: then take it out, and pour your colored vinegar from the top into another glass: and pour fresh distilled vinegar again over the calx, as before. Place it again to dissolve in the bath in every way as was taught before. And do this until all the calx of your Silver has been dissolved. And some <term>dregs</term> <note>original: *faeces*; the insoluble waste material remaining after a process</note> may remain at the bottom; think nothing of them, for they remain from the Silver and its <term>combustible sulfur</term> <note>the impurities believed by alchemists to cause a metal to tarnish or "burn"</note>, and its blackness, and the ash collected in the roasting. You may again pour some vinegar over the dregs: and see if the vinegar is no longer colored:

### CHAPTER XCV.

<margin>Preparation of the spirit for the same medicine.</margin>
Now I will teach you to prepare your spirit for making your medicine of the second order. You shall take, therefore, <term>clean, white, transparent arsenic</term> <note>original: "arsenicum mundum album pellucidum"</note> in which there are no sulfurous fibers. Grind it into a powder, and grind it together with salt and with what is called rock alum <note>original: "alumine rupeo"</note>, which has been calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note>. Use two parts of alum to one part of salt.

<margin>Commonly called rock alum <note>original: "a lumen de focca"</note>.</margin>
Grind it with vinegar upon a stone: and shield yourself against the air <note>A vital safety warning, as grinding arsenic produces toxic dust and fumes.</note>. When it is enough, put the material of this kind into a pot, and smooth the mouth of it upon a flat stone. Then take a large glass alembic <note>A vessel used for distillation, consisting of a gourd-like body and a cap with a long beak.</note>, and likewise smooth it so that the alembic fits the pot perfectly, as this figure demonstrates to you:

And place it upon the sublimation furnace.
<margin>A small fire must be applied first, so that the moisture flies into the receiver.</margin>
Apply a small fire at first, so that the moisture flies into the receiving vessel. And when you have drawn all the moisture out of the material, so that you see no more vapor in the alembic: then increase the fire a little. At this small fire, a certain more subtle spirit will ascend, which is called the "wild spirit" <note>original: "spiritus sylvestris." In early chemistry, this refers to non-condensable gases that were often considered a nuisance or a hindrance to the "fixation" of the metal.</note>. It is so volatile and subtle that wherever it remains, the material can never at any time be fixed <note>To "fix" a substance was to make it resistant to heat and no longer volatile.</note>. Therefore, in our art, it is entirely useless. And when you see that no more of that subtle spirit ascends, increase the fire, and sublimate with a moderately strong fire for twelve continuous hours. Then let it cool of its own accord. Once cooled, take it out, and you will find the sublimated arsenic separately in the pot, with the part that sits above the dregs clearly sublimated.

## CHAPTER 96.

### CHAPTER 97.

<margin>How the same medicine can be made more refined.</margin> Likewise, if you then wish to make your medicine more refined, *so that* its power of transformation <note>original: protectio (likely a typo for *proiectio* or projection)</note> becomes higher: take very strong distilled vinegar. Then congeal it over hot ashes: then dissolve it again as before. And in each solution and coagulation, your medicine will be made so much more refined that it will gain tenfold in its power of projection, according to <term>Geber the Philosopher<note>original: Geber Philosophus; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy</note></term>. And if you were to dissolve and congeal that medicine so many times, it would take on the consistency of oil; and that oil, then distilled over warmed <term>Mercury<note>original: Mercurium</note></term> in a crucible, would convert the <term>Mercury</term> into pure <term>Silver<note>original: Lunam</note></term>, better than that sought from the mines. And when the medicine had been brought thus far, it would no longer be a medicine of the second order, but of the third order, and a perfect medicine for transmuting metals into true <term>Silver</term>. And if you then wished to fashion a perfect <term>Elixir</term> from the oil, you would take from its "middle spirit" or the matter which I taught you to sublimate before from pure <term>arsenic<note>original: arsenico</note></term>. You shall weigh the oil and take twice as much of its middle spirit, and you will grind the oil upon a stone, and put it into a glass of this kind, and place it in a secret furnace for 10 days with heat but without glowing. Take out your matter, and it is changed and congealed into a stone; it is the perfect <term>Elixir</term>, transforming all metals into true <term>Silver</term>, better than that sought from the mines.

### CHAPTER XCIX.

You shall know and understand each individual work along with that which must be done within that work, as well as the other subsequent works: the second, third, fourth, and fifth work, until the work reaches its completion—that work which is carried out in the whole of Alchemy. And whichever Alchemist does not understand all these things before he begins to operate, he will produce nothing in the entire art of Alchemy, neither now nor at any time, even if he were to work forever. By chance <note>original: *Forte fortuna*</note> he might arrive at some result, just as a blind man hits a sparrow with an arrow; but otherwise he could not reach it. This is what often happens to the ignorant, who by pure luck arrived at some result in the art; but when they tried to set it up again, they could not perform it a second time. Thus they wasted their labor and fell into despair. For what they should have done first, they frequently do last; and they even leave off the work where it should have begun. They reach such a state of delusion that they become absolute fools in the art.

### CHAPTER C.

Therefore, to avoid this wandering in error, I will teach you what **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again, used for purification.</note> is, and why it was invented, and how one must sublimate in each work; and then how one must **calcinate** <note>Reducing a metal or mineral to powder by roasting or burning.</note>, and why calcination is performed; and concerning **distillation**, and why it should be employed; and so on with many other methods regarding what must be done in each task that occurs in the art. And you shall read this lesson again and again, and impress it upon your memory, lest you fall into error.

### CHAPTER CI.

<margin>What the ancients did regarding the understanding of the generation and growth of metals, and also...</margin>Likewise, you shall know that since the Ancients knew and understood the generation and growth of metals, and understood the diseases of metals—whence those diseases arose which prevented them from becoming either Gold <note>original: *Sol*, literally "the Sun."</note> or Silver <note>original: *Luna*, literally "the Moon."</note>—so the Ancients saw by what means they could remove those flaws and diseases from them and restore them to the state of Gold and Silver. And they could find no more convenient way than to destroy the bodies with fire and calcinate them. And they discovered the matter which would preserve them...

<margin>Regarding the diseases of the bodies: why calcination and sublimation were also discovered.</margin>...so that they would not be reduced to nothing by burning, away from their combustible sulfur <note>original: "sulphure combustibili"; the alchemical principle of inflammability and impurity</note>, which they contain in great abundance, nor would they be consumed by the burning of the fire. That material was the **key** <term>clavis: a specialized chemical agent, often a salt or solvent, used to "unlock" or dissolve metals</term>: they took two or three parts of this to one part of the body [the metal]. 

The hard bodies of **Mars** <note>Iron</note> and **Venus** <note>Copper</note> they filed into fine filings; but **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> and **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note> they reduced to ashes. They then maintained the fire at this gentle glow for 24 hours, ensuring the "key" did not melt. 

Then they allowed it to cool of its own accord. Having broken the vessel, they took out the contents and poured boiling common water over it so that the "key" would dissolve. They then washed the "key" away with common water. Taking the **calcinated bodies** <note>the metallic powders</note>, they ground them on a stone until they were imperceptible to the touch, and then washed away all the filth and blackness with common water. In this way, they purified the imperfect metals from their impurity, from their combustible sulfur, from their blackness, and from the foul smell they had contracted in the mines. Thus they cleansed the imperfect metals of their filth.

But when they reduced these back into a single metal body, they were neither **Gold** <note>Latin: Sol</note> nor **Silver** <note>Latin: Luna</note>. Although they investigated every salt of alum and every other species, they found nothing that could tint the metals or enter them so that they might be turned into Gold and Silver. 

Then they thought further that nothing would be found in the world—except for **spirits** <note>volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic</note>—that would want to enter the metals and mix with them. Thus, recognizing the nature of the spirits and the "diseases" they had contracted in the mines, they saw that the spirits had as many diseases as the metals: such as many earthy and foul dregs, and combustible sulfur which would burn the metals, and stinking earthy dregs which would make the metals even more impure than they were before. ## CHAPTER 103.

Then, when the Ancients <note>original: *Veteres* — the master alchemists of previous eras</note> had purified both the body <note>the solid, fixed matter</note> and the spirit <note>the volatile essence or vapor</note>, and had freed them from all defects so that they were clean and pure, they then considered once more how they might bring it about that these two should enter into one another. They could find no other way except to reduce either the body or the spirit to water, and then submerge that body in the spirit; or to dissolve the body and let it drink in the spirit; or they had to dissolve both the body and the spirit and join both waters together—and this last method is the best. Understanding all these things fundamentally, they saw that if they were to couple and join the spirit and body, no other way could be found except those just mentioned. Then they considered even more closely in their minds that the spirits and bodies must first be dissolved and reduced to water. At that time, they held no better method for reducing spirits and bodies to water than first holding the "key of nature" <note>a metaphorical key, often referring to a specific solvent or process like salt-making</note> by which they might be brought back to water. Thus, they easily understood that they should be reduced so as to have the nature of salt; this must be done by the power of fire and by calcination <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often turning it into a fine powder</note>. Then they thought further and discovered a furnace that would be suitable, in which they could calcine the spirits <margin>The Furnace of the Wise.</margin> so that the spirits could not slip away from them. They called that the **Furnace of the Wise**; then they found vessels in which the spirits might be conveniently calcined so they would not fly away. And the spirits are to be calcined in an open vessel and with a naked fire <note>direct exposure to the flame</note>, otherwise they would not acquire the nature of salt for the purpose of dissolving. If they were placed in a closed vessel with a confined fire or heat, they would refuse to dissolve even if they stayed there <margin>The control of the fire.</margin> forever. Thirdly, they discovered a type of fire and heat that could be so regulated that the spirits would not fly away.

When all these things had been discovered, they placed the spirits in the furnace in a vessel suitable for that purpose; and they moderated their fire day and night for 40 natural days and nights. Then they allowed it to cool down on its own; they took it out and ground the dry material upon a stone until it was impalpable <note>ground so fine it cannot be felt as individual grains</note>. Then they spread it upon the stone and placed the stone in a cold and damp cellar. They placed the stone at a slight tilt and <margin>The Ancients dissolved the spirits into clear water.</margin> placed a glass vessel underneath it. There, the spirits were dissolved and gradually dripped into that glass as an exceptionally clear and bright water, without the addition of any other thing. And so, by this aforementioned method, they dissolved the spirits into an exceptionally clear, transparent, and shining water; which water they kept in a strong glass vessel.

<margin>The reverberatory furnace.</margin>
Now that the calcination, sublimation, and the solution of spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" refer to volatile or gaseous substances, such as sulfur or mercury, while "bodies" refer to solid metals.</note> have been discussed, I am now going to teach you about the calcination and reverberation of bodies. ### CHAPTER CV.

Likewise, they consulted together to investigate whether another path could be found—a method of preparing the Work so that it would not be necessary to mix "bodies" <note>original: "corpora"; the solid, physical metals like lead or copper</note> with "spirits" <note>original: "spiritibus"; volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or ammonia that "flee" the fire</note>, nor to set them aside for fixation. For it was a long labor before they could sublimate the spirits, calcine <note>reduce to powder through heat</note> and dissolve the bodies, and then purify them; only then could they join the bodies and fix them together. Much time was required for these tasks. And even when everything was finally "fixed" <note>rendered stable so it no longer evaporates or changes under intense heat</note>, they possessed nothing but a perfect metal—either **Gold** or **Silver** <note>original: "Solem aut Lunam" (the Sun or the Moon)</note>—depending on how they had directed their work.

But when the Sages saw and understood that "dead" metal could be "vivified" <note>brought to life, meaning given the properties of growth and transformation</note> by spirits, as their logic demanded, and brought to such a state that it could withstand all tests and examinations, they thought further. They believed it might be possible to find another way that was easier, more useful, and did not require so much time in the Art.

Thus they reasoned: "If we have vivified dead bodies by the application of spirits, what if we take a **living body**, calcine it, reduce it to a simple water, immerse the sublimated spirits into it, fix them together, and then **project** <note>the act of casting the alchemical "tincture" or "stone" onto a base metal to transform it</note> that mixture upon a purified dead body? We could let them melt together and see how they combine, to discover what might result."

And so they did. They took that living body, which had been mixed and fixed with the spirits, let it melt, and cast it into a mass; but they found the resulting mass to be brittle and fragile. They then deliberated on why this happened. They soon realized that the substance of the spirits combined with the living bodies was so potent that the purified dead body could not withstand it.

Therefore, they decided to melt that dead body again, adding a significant amount of purified "dead" metal to it. They did this and cast it into a mass once more. It was still brittle, but not as brittle as before. They clearly saw then that they needed to add and incorporate even more of the purified dead body. By repeatedly adding metal and re-melting it, the material finally became soft and malleable. It was perfect **Gold** or **Silver**, at which they rejoiced exceedingly.

### CHAPTER 107.

<margin>The method for reducing spirits to the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold and the Moon represents Silver.</note> as discovered by the Ancients.</margin> When the wise men had tested all these aforementioned things, and saw that they could lead all dead and unclean bodies <note>Base metals, such as lead or copper, which were considered "dead" compared to the "living" perfection of gold.</note> to the Sun and Moon, and moreover achieve a profound projection, they then sought further through reason whether it might be possible to reduce "spirits" <term>spiritus: volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or ammonia that vaporize or "fly" when heated.</term> by art and medicine even to the Sun and Moon. They consulted on this matter, and as they examined the whole nature of the medicine, they understood that the medicine was composed and united by the art of spirits and bodies, and fixed together into one. Then they also easily understood in their wisdom that if they were to reduce spirits to the Sun and Moon, those spirits must also possess the nature of the medicine; otherwise, the medicine would refuse to mix with them, nor would it enter into them, for spirits alone cannot create bodies: they have no proportion between them. The medicine consists of spirits and bodies; and these are so fixed by the fire that the fire cannot separate them; whereas the other is a pure spirit that ascends from the fire. Thus, from this reasoning, they easily grasped two things. One was that if they were to achieve this, they must first prepare the spirits so that they were of the same nature as the medicine, if the medicine were to contract a friendship <note>An alchemical term for the chemical affinity or the ability of two substances to bond.</note> with them or wish to enter into them; for "like loves its like." Thus, if they were to achieve the art, they had to make the spirits into bodies <note>Meaning to "fix" them so they no longer vaporize under heat.</note> first and foremost, so that they might be of the same nature as the medicine. Furthermore, they easily understood that if they were to lead these corporeal <note>Solidified or fixed.</note> spirits to the Sun and Moon, they must create a medicine so liquid, so subtle, and so penetrating that when they cast it upon the corporeal spirits, it would immediately liquefy and penetrate them before the fire became so hot that the spirits would fly away <note>original: "vola-" (from volare, to fly/evaporate)</note> from the body—

### CHAPTER CXI.

<margin>That the knowledge of sublimation is necessary, and why.</margin>
Now I wish to teach you the method of **sublimation** <term>sublimation: heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify chemical substances</term>, how and by what reasoning each "spirit" <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to volatile substances like sulfur, mercury, or arsenic that evaporate easily.</note> must be sublimated, and why, and by what means each thing is to be sublimated. For sublimation is performed in many different ways. Sublimation must be established according to the specific work in which the sublimated spirit is to be used, whether for the three orders, or the Elixir, or in all other works—which are many—and for the "red" and the "white" <note>The two main goals of alchemy: the "White Work" (creating silver) and the "Red Work" (creating gold).</note>, and most importantly in the stone. For according to each work we wish to perform, the sublimations must be altered in various ways. <margin>of Arsenic and Orpiment</margin>

### CHAPTER 113.

<margin>Thick dregs and dry earthiness of the stones, and how [to remove them].</margin>
Furthermore, these two stones <note>original: "lapides"; refers to the mineral ores of arsenic/orpiment</note> still contain matter that must likewise be taken away from them, for it would also corrupt the work: this consists of their thick dregs <note>original: "faeces"</note> and earthiness. For if any of these remained in these stones—either the dregs or the dry earthiness—it would prevent the <term>medicine|the transformative alchemical agent or elixir</term> from being able to enter. Therefore, to take all these things away, it is necessary that these two stones be mixed with a "fixed" dreg <note>a stable, non-reactive base</note> which attracts and which does not itself become a spirit. Why must it be fixed? Because a fixed thing only with difficulty lets go of a volatile thing once it has been mixed with it. Because the fixed dregs can hold onto the "middle spirit"—which is necessary for us in the work—until the subtle spirit has departed, and before the middle spirit separates itself from the dregs. For this reason, the fixed dregs must also be attractive or <term>styptic|binding or contracting</term>, because they will not allow the spirit to rise too high in the vessel, but will keep it just above the dregs, or allow it to remain upon the dregs, etc. And why must the fixed dregs give off nothing of themselves? Because they must not rise up with the middle spirit, so that the spirit remains pure and clean, and so that they bring nothing foreign into the work. For in the "Great Work," nothing foreign can be present. Furthermore, the dregs must be cold and dry in nature, through which these two stones are to be <term>sublimated|purified by heating until they turn to vapor and then solidify again</term>. Why cold? To restrain the heat which the combustible sulfur has within it, so that it does not destroy the spirit during sublimation, and so that the sulfur separates itself from the spirit. Why dry? So that the dregs, by their dryness, may temper the heat of the combustible sulfur and keep it held back, so that it does not separate itself along with the middle spirit, nor rise up from the dregs. For this, one needs a tall and long-necked vessel in which these two stones may be sublimated. Why a tall vessel? So that the subtle, volatile spirit—which can endure no heat—may rise into the upper part of that long vessel...

### CHAPTER CXIV.
<margin>The subtle spirit must be removed before you increase the fire in sublimation, and why.</margin>
Now you shall know that before you increase the fire in the sublimation, you ought to remove the alembic <term>Alembic (the top cap of a still used for collecting vapors)</term> and take out the subtle spirit. This is done for this reason: lest when you apply a more violent fire, the subtle spirit should fall back down; or when everything has been sublimed, the subtle volatile spirit might fall back again upon the dross, rather than onto the middle spirit, and thus they might mix together again. Once the spirit is taken from the alembic, put the alembic back on again; and then increase the fire, so that the middle spirit can come out of the dross. And when it has been sublimed from the dross, remove it and mix it again with your dross, and proceed in all ways as was taught before. Repeat this sublimation so long and so many times until nothing more of the subtle spirit ascends. Then you shall set the middle spirit to be sublimed by itself, so that you may see whether any volatile spirit remains joined to it. And if any is still joined, you shall remove it just as before, and you shall also observe whether any combustible sulfur and dross remains, etc. And you shall repeat the sublimation until you find that nothing more of the subtle volatile spirit ascends, and it leaves nothing in the bottom of the vessel. Then you are certain that you have the middle spirit clean and pure, and it is ready to be placed into the work.

### CHAPTER CXVI.

<margin>The Stone from the Sun alone surpasses all others.</margin> Now I wish to describe to you the stone which is made from the Sun alone: which stone surpasses all other stones that can be made by the hands of men. It is simple and pure; yet a dregs <note>original: 'faex'</note> of a single kind is within it, and that is hidden in it. For nature has so worked in it that nature has shown its extreme powers in it. Indeed, nature has so worked in the Sun that in the whole world nothing is more excellent than the Sun. For the Sun is clean and pure, and nature has brought it as close to a simple nature as it could. So that in the whole world, nothing approaches so closely to the simple as the Sun. For the Sun cannot be destroyed by fire, nor rot in the earth, nor become foul, nor be corrupted in the air.

### CHAPTER 119.

<margin>Two works to be done contrary to one another.</margin>
Now you must perform two works that will be the opposite of each other: one part of the powder you shall make spiritual and volatile; the other part of that powder you shall make bodily and fixed. And you shall make both parts of the powder as subtle in their degree as possible, so that nothing more subtle can be made. You must bring the interior of both parts of the powder to the outside before it becomes subtle. Its interior must be brought out so that the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary goal of alchemy</note> can be made from it. For in its interior part there is a certain kind of thick dreg <note>original: "fæcis crassæ"; impurities or "grossness" inherent in the metal</note>, and that cannot be drawn out unless the interior is brought to the outside. And then the subtle stone can be made, etc.

### CHAPTER 120.

<margin>The first powder is to be made spiritual, and how.</margin>
That work by which the spiritual powder is to be made will be the first work we undertake. Opening what <term>Nature</term> <note>Alchemists viewed Nature as the primary force that creates metals in the earth; the alchemist seeks to either reverse or accelerate these natural processes</note> has closed, and unweaving <note>original: "retexendum"; to undo or reverse a process</note> everything that Nature has made or worked; and the powder must be made in that state in which it was when Nature began to work in it. Then first the powder or matter is ready for making the Stone.

### CHAPTER 121.

For in that [first] one, everything worked by Nature must be unmapped at once; and in this work, one must begin where Nature left off. What Nature was not able to achieve, that must henceforth be perfected by <term>Art</term> <note>In alchemy, "Art" refers to the skill and laboratory operations of the alchemist</note>.

For <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "Natura"; the personified force of the natural world</note> does not move further to operate, except until it has brought a thing into that state to which God, according to His will, has ordained it, etc. And so we must begin where <term>Nature</term> left off, and lead the matter toward perfection and supreme virtue; that is, we shall lead its exterior inward, and place its interior outward <note>This refers to the alchemical concept of "inverting" a substance to reveal its hidden "soul" or essence</note>, and then we shall strip it of its exterior and interior dross, and make it subtle and fixed; thus it is prepared for the <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapidem"; the Philosophers' Stone</note> to be fashioned from it. You must pour, boil, and pour off, repeating this four or five times with fresh distilled water, until you are certain the powder is thoroughly cleansed of the "spirits" of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>literally "strong water," a term for nitric acid used to dissolve metals</note>. 

Then dry the powder in a clean glass dish over warm ashes, or in the Sun, and dry it so thoroughly that it can be reduced to a fine dust. Then your powder is ready for sublimation, and it has been made "open" and "spiritual." And it is now in such a state as it was when Nature first began to work within it—but not at the same degree. For although we might have the raw material from the mines at the moment Nature first began to work on it, we would not be able to produce the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> from it. Even though the material is now in the state it was when Nature began her work, it is not at the same level the material was then. Although the material is now "opened" and made "spiritual," it is at a better degree than it was when Nature first began her work. 

For in this material, there was once a "perfect body" <note>likely referring to a noble metal like silver</note> which was fully cooked and perfected to its ultimate limit, so that Nature had no further power to work upon it. And although we have now dissolved it again and made "spiritual" that which Nature had closed—and Nature had closed it so tightly that it resisted all fire, even resisting all the trials and examinations <note>tests for purity</note> that could be performed on it—yet even though it is now dissolved, it still holds within itself all the perfection and power it had before it was dissolved and made spiritual. For it has lost nothing, but has actually acquired more strength, even though it is now in a spiritual state. And if it had not been a perfect body in which there was no defect, how could we draw the Stone out of it? For the Stone must have such power that all...

It is impossible to draw out a good and perfect thing from a thing which is itself bad and imperfect; although many men think they can extract the stone from things that are themselves impure and imperfect. Therefore, take good care that when you make the Stone with Gold, you separate from it all the things with which you dissolve and close the Stone, so that you are certain nothing foreign remains with the Stone; otherwise you will err and lose your labor, etc.

### CHAPTER 125.

<margin>Method of calcining the matter already mentioned.</margin> You shall take the <term>sublimated</term> <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material.</note> matter, and you shall pulverize it until it is <term>impalpable</term> <note>So finely ground that no individual grains can be felt between the fingers.</note> upon a marble slab. Then, take a glass vessel with a flat bottom, made of good glass that is able to withstand the fire: put your matter into it, and spread it out widely over the bottom of the glass, and smooth it over with a feather or a rabbit’s foot. Place the vessel containing the matter of the stone into a <term>secret furnace</term> <note>original: "fornace secreta"; a specialized furnace designed for precise heat control in chemical operations.</note> in which <term>spirits</term> <note>Volatile substances like sulfur or mercury.</note> are <term>calcined</term> <note>Reduced to a powder by means of high heat.</note>. Place an inner lid made of square tile over it, and seal it firmly with <term>good lute</term> <note>A clay-based sealant used to make alchemical vessels airtight.</note> so that it is not split or broken by the fire, and let it dry well. You shall then place that other lid, which fits the furnace, over this one, and seal that itself firmly as well, and let it dry. And when it is dry, put on the lid that fits the rim of the furnace, which covers all the other lids; seal that too firmly and let it dry. 

When it is dry enough, apply fire to the furnace: first a lukewarm fire for 6 continuous hours. When those are finished, increase your fire for another 6 hours. When those are finished, increase your fire even further for 6 hours. When those are finished, increase your fire so strongly that you can put your hand through that square hole which is in the side of the furnace and moisten the tip of your finger and touch the vessel hanging in the furnace [to see] if it <term>hisses</term> <note>original: "strideat"; to make a sharp, whistling or sizzling sound.</note> and makes a sound: just as if a stone were very hot and you threw spit upon it and it hissed. So this vessel hanging in the furnace ought to hiss when moisture is sprinkled on it; it must be kept in such heat for a day and a night. 

Indeed, you shall prepare a thin rod for yourself, and to the end of it you shall tie a linen cloth six or sevenfold, and sew it firmly around. Dip the end in water to moisten it, and you shall remove the stone from the square hole in the middle of the furnace, and through it insert that rod up to the vessel with the moist end. Carefully observe whether the vessel hisses, and if it emits a hissing sound when the rod touches the vessel, then it is right enough. If it does not hiss clearly or strongly—just as if you were dripping cold water upon a hot stone—increase the fire until it hisses in that manner. And so you must keep it in that heat day and night. You can often test it by day and night with that moist rod through that hole in the middle of the furnace to see if your fire is suitably hot; but whenever you have tested it, always put the stone back into the square hole in the middle of the furnace. You must keep it in such heat for 40 continuous days and nights. When these are finished, let it cool naturally for 3 or 4 days. Then take it out, and you will find the matter of the stone properly calcined and prepared for <term>dissolving</term> <note>original: "soluendum"; the next stage in the Great Work, where the calcined powder is turned into a liquid state.</note>.

### CHAPTER CXXVI.

<margin>The calcined material is to be dissolved in common distilled water, or spread upon a table, etc.</margin>
Now take the calcined material of the stone, and dissolve it in
common distilled water: or if you were to spread the material
upon a glass table, or marble: and place it in a cold
and humid cellar, and place a glass vessel under the stone: and
tilt the stone a very little bit, so that the dissolved substance could
drip into the vessel: the material of the stone would easily be
dissolved into clear water in 8 or 10 days,
so that nothing would remain. But this method is not to be approved,
on account of the dust and other filth rising in it, and also
coming from the air: and also the humidity which is attracted
from the cellar into the material of the stone, which causes it to dissolve,
is likewise not clean, etc. Therefore, to keep the material
of the stone pure and clean, put the material of the stone into a 
receptacle constructed in this manner, and smooth the mouth 
of the receptacle upon a stone, and also smooth a small piece 
of glass above it which fits the mouth of the receptacle, which 
you can firmly seal <note>original: "lutare"; to seal with "lute," a specialized alchemical cement or clay used to make vessels airtight.</note> over the mouth of the receptacle when 
it pleases you. And while the material of the stone is in the glass, 
have common water distilled again and again so many times that 
nothing remains after distillation: and occasionally pour a very 
little bit of that water over the material of the stone, and it will 
be dissolved by a very little water on account of its subtlety. For a 
subtle material is dissolved much more easily and with a smaller 
quantity of humidity.
