->*The third exceeds the rest, yet harms only through endurance.*<-
<note>original: "Tertius excedit, sed cum tolerantia lædit." This suggests the heat is much more intense but manageable if the operator is patient.</note>

You shall continue this fire of the third degree to incinerate the little stones for one hundred days, because within the said span of one hundred days the stones will be incinerated and fixed by a true and perfect fixation <note>Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable so it does not evaporate when heated.</note>. But if our matter is not incinerated within that time, then continue the same fire of the third degree until our matter is incinerated, and then our matter will be whitened. This white thing is called the "permanent white" and the "soul." Regarding this white, Morienus says: "Whiten the laton <term>laton: a base metal alloy, often likened to brass, representing the 'unrefined' state of the matter</term>, which is the earth, and add the children <note>original: "liberos"; this likely refers to the "offspring" of the chemical marriage or perhaps a corruption of "libros" (books), but "children" is the standard allegorical term.</note>, lest your hearts be broken."

And Hermes says: "Whiten it, and sublimate it with its own fire, until the spirit goes forth, which you will find within it, which is called the Bird of Hermes." <note>The Bird of Hermes is a famous alchemical symbol for the volatile spirit that rises during sublimation.</note> And this incineration and whitening reveals, as it were, the resolution of the thirsty earth and the water of the clouds. You should know that within those one hundred days our matter, or our ash, ought to take on the color of pearls or of shining marble. Regarding this white, Algazel says: "Sublimate it quickly with fire once whitened," which is to say, dissolve it again. Know that you must continue this fire of the third degree until the "second white" appears in the aforementioned color.

Now follows the fourth part of the work, which is called the "reddening" <note>original: "rubificatio"; the final stage of the alchemical process, known as the Rubedo.</note> of our stone. We then convert the whole soul into the body when we redden our matter, which was previously white. This reddening must necessarily be performed by a fire of the fourth degree, which is described in this verse:

->*Thus the fourth, the destroyer of the senses, knows not how to proceed.*<-
<note>original: "Sic destructor sensus nescit procedere quartus." This indicates an extremely intense heat that overpowers the physical senses.</note>

The fire of the fourth degree will be a fire of flame and of wood, which is prepared as described above. Continue this fire for 47 or 50 days; for within that time the Tyrian color <note>A deep purple-red, famously associated with the highest quality ancient dyes and the final "Perfection" of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> should appear. Indeed, let the Mercury be governed by its own fire; cooked by a fire of the first degree, in 50 days it is converted into a true Raven <note>The "black" stage or Nigredo.</note>; then in 77 days it is turned into a Dove <note>The "white" stage or Albedo.</note>; then the Dove in 47 or 70 days is turned into the marine Alkasel <term>Alkasel: a rare alchemical term, here synonymous with the final deep red or purple state</term>, which is the Tyrian color. In this color, the spirit and the soul are united with the body, and they become one; the corporeal has been made incorporeal, and the Blessed Stone is made. Know that by the aforementioned fire of flame, which is the fire of the fourth degree, our completed white is melted, and through this kind of melting...

The element of water flows and runs through the body and washes it. The element of earth remains still and is the body of the Mercury, or its thickness and density. The element of air is that tempered heat and moisture which is in the Mercury: and such tempered heat is called "spirit," and it creates harmony between the combustible oiliness of the Mercury and its "muddiness"—that is, between the oily moisture and the earthy, dreg-filled substance. The element of fire is that combustible oiliness which is in the Mercury, hence the verse:

->*The earth stands, the wave washes, the fire purges, the spirit enters.*<-

Now therefore, let us repeat the intention of our whole work in brief. First, our stone **liquefies** in the operation; second, it **turns black**; third, it **turns citron-yellow**; fourth, it **turns red** with a red that is not true, nor does it last long; fifth, it **is whitened**; sixth, it **is coagulated**. And it is necessary that all these things be done with a slow fire—that is, with a fire of the first and second degree, which is a fire with coals and without flame. Seventh, our stone **is reduced to ash** with a fire of the third degree, which is a fire of the flame of three or four logs. Eighth, our stone **is liquefied**...

# ON THE STONE

...metallic and red <term>putrefaction</term><note>The OCR begins mid-word with "factione," likely completing "putrefactione." Putrefaction is the stage where the matter decomposes and turns black before further transformation.</note>, and this is done with the same fire of the **third degree**. For a bath is a temperate thing, not intense in its heat, nor yet cold, but of a diminished heat. For this reason, we see that a human being, through temperate heat, undergoes "putrefaction" and sweats out their superfluities; but if the heat were intense, they would not sweat, but would be burned. If indeed the bath were cold, then the viscosity and oiliness existing within the person would not exit. Therefore, it is necessary for us to have a "bath"—that is, a temperate heat—which is neither exceeding nor falling short of its proper degree. And this is a beautiful concept for those who understand.

There are two principles of this art. Therefore, he rightly says: that which *makes* the Sun, *is* the Sun; but the philosophical medicine does this, therefore, etc. 

And it should be known that the principles of this thing are two primarily: namely, the **matter** and the **agent**. The matter, as a certain philosopher says, is **quicksilver** and **sulfur** or **arsenic**, which are the same thing. Yet you should take notice, Holy Father, that as the philosophers say, it is not quicksilver in its raw state—nor in the state to which its mines reduced it—that is the principle of this thing, but rather that state to which their **artifice** leads it. # CONCERNING THE STONE

<header>CONCERNING THE STONE</header>
<sig>r</sig>

...ksilver and sulfur <note>original: "argentum viuum & sulphur"</note> which I have shown to you. But it might be asked: Why, then, if this matter is but one, have the philosophers named it with all possible names and compared it to all things? To this, they assign several reasons: For Diomedes says that they did this so that the foolish and ignorant might not recognize the matter. Likewise, Morienes says: "The Envious <note>In alchemical literature, "The Envious" refers to master alchemists who intentionally used obscure language to prevent the "unworthy" or "greedy" from discovering the secret of gold-making.</note> have multiplied the names and led posterity astray." They call themselves "The Envious" because they begrudge that this science should come to any others besides themselves. Likewise, Pythagoras says: "They have called this thing by many names because of the excellence of its nature." 

But Bonellus says that they multiply the names because, in the operation of this work, all colors that can be imagined in the world appear; and thus they have diversified its names according to the different colors. In the work, all elements are contained; therefore, they have named the matter by the name of any elemental thing. Regarding the fact that there are four elements in this matter, Orpholeus <note>Likely a corruption of a name like Orpheus or an Arabic authority.</note> said: "Know that in our mastery, it is necessary to mix pure, raw, sincere, and upright elements over the fire, and to beware the intensity of the fire until the elements are joined and are embracing one another." The elements, therefore, cooked by a gentle fire, are loved, they rejoice, and are converted into other natures; these are the words of Orpholeus. 

The philosopher also says: "Convert the elements, and you will find what you seek." To convert the elements, according to another, is to make the moist dry, and the dry moist, and the fleeing <note>original: "fugiens"; refers to volatile substances that evaporate easily.</note> fixed. Therefore, it is evident <note>original: "p. f.", likely an abbreviation for "patet" or "probatum fuit".</note> that in this one thing, there are four elements, which are visibly seen and naturally extracted; and for this reason, the philosophers call this water "four bodies" and "four natures." For Hermes says: "That water is a heavenly nature which, in bodily things, separates the elements existing in its region, and again composing them, reduces them into one." For Nimidus says: "This compound becomes perfect in all four elements." 

Now, this multiplication of names was the cause of error for those who work in improper matter—such as in salts, alums, urines, dungs, human blood, natural sulfur and quicksilver, in marcasites <note>Iron pyrites or other metallic ores.</note>, and in many other things—ignorant of the fact that in a thing, there cannot be found what is not already in it, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note> says; nor understanding that the philosophers have spoken metaphorically and figuratively in their sayings regarding this most precious art and...

<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>PHILOSOPHY</header>

...thinking it most secret, to be revealed to absolutely no one. Concerning this water, or rather this matter, the philosophers have said many and infinite things which would be tedious to recount. You have, therefore, dear sons, <note>The abbreviation "p. f." likely stands for "patres filii" (fathers to sons) or a similar address to the "Sons of Art" or students of alchemy.</note> what the material principles of this thing are—the material cause which is called the "medicine of the philosophers"—because it consists of quicksilver and sulfur.

It remains, consequently, to determine the "agent cause." The agent or mover that brings the matter itself toward corruption is heat, which is the instrument that drives the process toward putrefaction <note>In alchemy, "putrefaction" is a necessary stage of breakdown where the matter turns black (the *nigredo*) before it can be purified.</note>; there is no other agent in the world. And this is what the philosopher Alphidius <note>Alphidius was a legendary alchemical authority, often cited in medieval treatises, believed to be of Arabic origin.</note> said: 

> Know, sons, that the active substance in this whole world is one: namely, heat. When heat is removed, there is no motion or action; for the very root of the arrangement of matter is heat.

But there are many degrees of heat or fire. It must be seen what this fire is, and at what degree it stays. Certainly, this fire is the heat of horse dung <note>original: "fimi equini." Rotting horse manure was used as a natural, low-temperature incubator in early chemistry to provide a steady, gentle "digestive" heat.</note>. Thus Alphidius says: "It is cooked by the fire which I shall show you: it is hidden in moist horse dung, which is the 'fire of the wise' <note>original: "ignis sapientum"</note>—that is, moist and dark. This fire is hot in the first degree and moist in the second." All philosophers have spoken of this heat using deceptive and metaphorical words; they compared it to the heat of the Sun and the natural heat of a healthy man. For Mefig <note>Likely an Arabic authority or a corruption of a name like Mesue.</note> says: "By the heat of the Sun, the matter is congealed." Thus the foolish are deceived when they use different [stronger] fires, not understanding the words of the philosophers—namely, being ignorant that the generation and procreation of natural things can only happen through a most temperate and equal heat, and not one that exceeds it.

### *The Method of Mixing.*

Having seen the natural principles of this thing, we must next look at the method of mixing or their "conception" with one another. It must be known that the material principles upon which nature builds its action in its miraculous operation are sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, as has been said. Each of these is of the strongest composition and uniform substance. This is because they are united at the most minute level <note>original: "per minima," a scholastic term meaning the smallest possible particles of matter</note>, so that none of their parts can leave the other during dissolution. Rather, each runs and each is dissolved because of the union of form which they have with one another at the smallest level, brought about by an equal active heat according to the requirements of their nature.

of their essences. It must, however, be noted that the aforementioned sulfur and quicksilver are converted into an earthy nature, and from both of these earthy natures, a very thin smoke is released, increased by the heat within the vessel. And this double smoke is the immediate matter of metals, or of medicines, or of the <term>philosopher’s stone</term> <note>original: "lapidis philosophorum"</note>. From the smoke and by the tempered heat in the vessel of its cooking—or having been cooked—it is converted into the nature of that same earth. And thus it undergoes a certain fixation, by which the water flowing down through the vessel dissolves its sponginess and becomes uniformly bound to it. Through this union, all the elements come together according to the proper natural proportion, and they are mixed "through the smallest parts" <note>The Latin term "per minima" refers to an Aristotelian concept where substances are mixed at the level of their smallest possible particles, rather than just being a pile of different components.</note>, until they create a uniform mixture through successive, long-lasting, and very temperate cooking in its vessel, until it thickens and hardens; and so it becomes the medicine, or the metal, or the philosopher’s stone. Therefore Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have lived in the 7th century, often cited as a teacher of alchemical secrets.</note> says: "The arrangement of the wise and the transformation of natures is the wondrous mixing of those natures—hot, cold, moist, and dry—through a subtle arrangement; and it is the sole proof of the wise." Note, however, that entry, submersion, fixation, connection, thickening, conjunction, complexion, composition, and mixing—since these things are gathered together—all others are mixed through division. And all these things are one and the same according to Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher. In alchemical literature, "Democritus" often refers to "Pseudo-Democritus," the author of early Greek alchemical texts like *Physica et Mystica*.</note>. Mixing is the union of things that can be mixed, that is, of the elements; for these are the first principles of every mixture. Nor can we know the manifest and hidden nature of the mixture itself unless we know how to mix or compose the elements themselves. Wherefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition and alchemy.</note> says: "Understand, sons of the wise, the science of the four elements, which are passive according to their own principles in their hidden opening." For their hidden opening is in no way indicated unless it is composed, because it is not perfected until its colors are fully realized. Also note: "through the smallest parts" <note>original: "per minima"</note> means through indivisible particles. For the "minimum" is that which is indivisible; for if it could be divided, it would not be the minimum. It appears, moreover, that the mixing of the elements occurs through the smallest particles of the body itself—that is, through indivisibles; for an element is the simple and smallest particle of the body itself.

These stages, however, are determined according to the various proportions of the mixable elements that occur during its operation. And every operation in its own stage—following the order that nature maintains in the path and pursuit of its own generation—they have called by the name of some metal.

For the first stage of their operation they called **iron** or **Mars**; the second stage they called **copper** or **Venus**; the third, **lead** or **Saturn**; the fourth, **tin** or **Jupiter**; the fifth, **silver** or the **Moon**; the sixth stage, the **Sun** or **gold**. And they named these metals of theirs metaphorically with infinite other names, and all of this for the purpose of hiding the science. These things, however, insofar as they are generated from the same first principles—namely, from one primary matter which is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and **sulfur**—are said to be and are the effects of said principles: sulfur and quicksilver.

And the philosophers have treated each of the aforementioned specifically, defining them according to their various properties individually, because they had a different composition or generation in their creation or production. It must be noted, however, that the philosophers sometimes name what they call their "gold" as "iron" or "lead," and so forth; and likewise, conversely, they call "iron" or "lead" (and so forth) "gold." And this is for various reasons: because insofar as the breakdown and corruption of one is the generation or cause of another, the effect exists within its cause. Hence they said that gold is iron, and so on for the rest.

Note the cause of the error of those who work with natural [physical] metals—namely by <term>calcining</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>, dissolving, and congealing them—believing that the philosophers create their medicine from these, because the philosophers say that gold is generated from iron, lead, and the rest. This is because that thing which they call gold, or the "medicine of gold," is generated from the breakdown or corruption of the other "metals" <note>The author clarifies that the "metals" being corrupted are not physical iron or lead, but stages of the alchemical matter inside the vessel.</note>. For in the same operation, all said metals are generated and corrupted, and from these same things their gold is generated. Hence they also said that iron, and so on for the rest, is gold, because the cause is in some way its own effect. Through these same considerations, the names of the other metals are also shared with one another, insofar...

...then the destruction of one is the generation of another. It must be noted, however, that the philosophers call all these metals **quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> and **sulfur**, because the metals themselves are made and generated from them. The philosophers called the aforementioned generations of metals **complexions** <note>A term from medieval science referring to the specific balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>; but all were considered unequal except for those of gold and silver. And for this reason, they even said that silver is "unequal" in respect to gold. 

They said that only the complexion or perfection of gold is "equal," and the philosophers sought no other of the said complexions or generations except only that which they call equal—namely, that of gold—concerning which **Johanninus** <note>Likely referring to Johannes Damascenus (John of Damascus), a figure frequently cited in medieval medical and alchemical texts.</note> says: "An elemental mixture is that which, with moderation, is called a healthy body." And note that he says "with moderation," meaning the moderation of the four natures: namely, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. For when none of these natures exceeds another, then the body is said to be "equal," because there is as much of one as there is of another. 

Likewise, it is called "healthy"—that is, sound or clean from every cause of corruption. And note that it is gold itself, or the **medicine of gold** <note>The "Elixir" or "Stone" which was believed to have the power to "heal" base metals by perfecting their elemental balance.</note>, that performs this for **tin** or **lead**. Therefore **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic and European alchemy.</note> says: "Tin is the purest lead, and within it is the quality of **fixation** <note>The process by which a volatile substance is made stable and resistant to fire.</note> or thickness of the two components—namely, quicksilver and sulfur—not a quality of quantity, since the quicksilver prevails in the mixture."

Likewise, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> and the **Sons of the Philosophers** <note>A traditional name for students and practitioners of the alchemical arts.</note> say: "There are seven bodies [metals]." Regarding these, note that gold is not the first by way of its physical generation, but by the "intention of nature." This is because nature always desires that which is better, nobler, and more perfect, and it intends toward this goal. Alternatively, it is called "first" in nobility and dignity. 

Their first is gold, their best head and king, which is not corrupted by the earth, nor burned by a burning thing, nor altered by water, because its complexion is tempered and its nature is balanced in heat and cold, dryness and moisture; in it there is nothing superfluous nor anything lacking. And therefore the Philosophers preferred it, and magnified it, and said: "For gold holds the same place among metallic bodies as the Sun does among the stars." 

There remain to be determined the **artificial principles** <note>Laboratory operations or techniques performed by the alchemist that mimic or accelerate the natural processes of the earth.</note> of this thing we seek. Note that these modes are called "artificial principles," even though they are natural, because nature works through their service and craftsmanship. And these are the modes of its operation, by means of which this thing we seek is generated and brought into actual be-

For at times the philosophers, considering their matter—which, when it is in its vessel and feels the heat of the Sun, is immediately exhaled or evaporated into the appearance of a very subtle smoke and ascends on high into the head of the vessel—called such an ascent **sublimation**. Seeing afterwards such matter, which had ascended, descend back to the bottom of the vessel, they called it **distillation** or **descent**.

Furthermore, seeing this matter of theirs thicken, turn black, and give off a foul stench, they called it **putrefaction** <note>The "nigredo" stage, where the matter dies and decays before it can be reborn.</note>. And this earth putrefies with the water, and when it has been purified by the help of Him who rules all things, the whole Mastery is perfected."

Again, seeing the earth mixed with its water, and the water gradually diminishing because of a temperate boiling and the earth increasing, they all said that this was perfect **waxing** <note>original: "ceratio"; the process of softening a hard substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency.</note>. Whence the philosopher says: "Because the earth is waxed with water, it is soaked, and by the temperate cooking of the heat of the Sun it is dried out, and the whole matter is turned into earth." Whence the same says: "This is complete, if it shall have been turned into earth."

Likewise, seeing that the whole matter arrived at a certain dissipation, and in a way reduced itself to a solid substance—and because it did not flow, but rather stood firm—they said that it was perfect **congelation**.

The general rule of the philosophers is this: for they say that no thickening <note>original: "inspissatio."</note> of any liquid occurs unless there is first an exhalation of the most refined parts from the liquid: and unless there is first, likewise, a refining of the thicker parts from the liquid. If, however, the liquid in the composition or mixture overcomes the dry, and a true mixing of dry and liquid occurs, so that the liquid is tempered by the dry, and the dry by the liquid: and this does not happen except through the long-lasting mixing of the viscous liquid and the refined earth, bit by bit <note>original: "per minima"; down to the smallest possible particles.</note>, until that same liquid becomes one with the dry, and the dry becomes one with the liquid. And of this refined vapor or smoke, no resolution or exhalation happens suddenly; rather, it happens gradually and over a great and long time. And the cause or reason is this: because the substance of the principles and of nature is uniform. Therefore, if the resolution of the superfluous liquid were to happen suddenly—since the liquid does not differ there from the dry because of their strong mixing together—the liquid would surely take the dry with it in that resolution...

## THE TREASURY OF PHILOSOPHY.

May He grant us His salvation—He to whom all things belong: the heaven, the earth, and the sea; He who was able to create all things from nothing, and willed to bind dissonant things into harmony, and who ordained to cure the sick with medicines out of His goodness. The ancient wise men, understanding this fully, set down a twofold way in their books: one true, and the other leading astray.

Indeed, they presented the true way in obscure words, so that it might be understood fully by none except their "sons" <note>original: "filijs"; a traditional term for the initiated students or spiritual heirs of an alchemical master.</note>. They concealed this so that the wicked, seizing upon this science, would not be more prone to commit profane acts, for which the wise would have to give an account of their sins. Therefore, take care, most beloved, not to share this science with anyone unworthy, but conceal it in the philosophical manner; when you have known it through true experiment, your love and affection for it will increase.

They set down the false way in clear words; I will omit speaking of this way and its errors along with their causes. But, most beloved, listen and understand, and may God illuminate your intellect. Know that our science is the science of the **four elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, viewed here as the fundamental building blocks of all matter.</note>, and of times, and of qualities, and their conversion into one another; in this, all philosophers agree. And know that in every thing under heaven there are four elements—not by sight, but by effect. 

Hence the Philosophers, under the veil of the science of the elements, handed down this science and worked it. But those not understanding the letter of the work have tried all these things in blood, hair, and eggs, as well as many other trifles <note>original: "truffis"; a derogatory term for the common, useless materials used by "puffers" or amateur alchemists who lacked philosophical understanding.</note>; and I too tried them, and I was reduced to a state of amazement. And so, as if despairing of the science, I put the **Mastery** <note>original: "Magisterium"; the grand work of creating the Stone.</note> aside; others I rejected due to the weakness of my own intellect. 

Returning to myself later, however, I finally began to think along with **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose views on the formation of metals were highly influential in Western alchemy.</note>: "If this thing exists, how does it exist? And if it does not exist, how does it not exist?" I knew then that the matter and "seed" <note>original: "sperma"; the generative, essential substance from which metals grow.</note> of all metals is **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity and metallic nature, not necessarily the common liquid metal.</note> cooked and thickened in the womb of the earth by a sulfurous heat, by cooking it; and according to the variety and multiplicity of the **sulfur** <note>Sulfur represents the active, combustible, and "fixing" principle that acts upon Mercury to create different metals.</note> and its various...

PHILOSOPHY.

[...quali]ty, various metals are procreated in the earth. For their primary matter is one and the same; however, they differ only by accidental action, and by a greater or lesser cooking <term>decoction: the process of heating a substance to refine it or extract its essence</term>, whether temperate or intemperate, scorching or not scorching: thus all philosophers harmoniously assert. Indeed, it is certain that every thing is made from or out of that into which it is resolved: for ice is converted into water by means of heat. It is clear, therefore, that it was water first; so too all metals are converted into **Mercury** <term>Mercurius: here referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the fluid, foundational substance of all metals</term>; therefore, they were previously made from **Mercury**. I will show the method of converting them into **Mercury** below. 

This being assumed, the saying of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle's "Meteorologica" was a foundational text for medieval science, though the specific quote about alchemy was often drawn from a later Arabic addition known as the "Avicenna gloss."</note> is resolved, where he says in the fourth book of *Meteorologica*: "Let the practitioners of **Alchemy** <term>Alchimia</term> know, therefore, that the species of metals cannot be changed." And this is true, unless they (as follows) are reduced into their primary matter. Indeed, the reduction of these into one another is easy and possible, for everything that grows and is born is multiplied, as is evident in all plants, trees, and animals: for from one grain a thousand grains are procreated; from one tree a thousand branches proceed, and from one man the entire race of men is procreated. Just as each thing is increased from its own species, so consequently a metal can increase its own metal from itself. And there is no difference, as Aristotle says, whether these things happen in natural or artificial organs <note>vessels or environments where transformation occurs</note>. 

Indeed, all metals are born and grow in the earth; it is therefore possible for augmentation and multiplication to occur in them, and so on unto infinity. But this cannot be done except through that which is more perfect in the lineage of metals: the complete medicine of those metals is of a more perfect generation, which is the **Philosophers' Elixir** <term>elixir Philosophorum: the legendary substance capable of perfecting base metals into gold</term>. However, it is not possible to arrive at this **elixir** except through its own medium. Observe the nature of the medium, in which there is always the containment of extremes. The extremes are **sulphur** <term>sulphur: the active, masculine, and combustible principle in alchemy</term> and **Mercury**, and the completed **elixir**. From those things which are more purified, cooked, and digested, those are better and more perfect, and even more closely related. 

O most beloved, do not go astray, for "whatever a man sows, this he shall also reap" <note>original: "quæ enim seminauerit homo, hæc & metet"; a reference to the biblical Book of Galatians 6:7, used here to mean you must start with the right "seed" to get the right metal.</note>. Now it is sufficiently clear what the **stone** <term>lapis: the Philosophers' Stone</term> is, and what its medicine is, to which nothing foreign is added, except that superfluous things are removed: because nothing is suitable to a thing except what is closer to it by nature. Now, therefore, most beloved, I will explain the sayings of the Philosophers and the obscure words of the wise hidden in parables, so that you may judge my [words as the words of the philosophers...]

Therefore, the first thing is what the Philosophers called **solution** <term>solutio: the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</term>, which is the foundation of the art. Whence **Maria** <note>Maria the Jewess, a legendary early alchemical author and supposed inventor of the bain-marie</note> says: "Couple the gum with the gum in a true marriage, and make them like a flowing stream of water." **Rosinus** the Philosopher <note>likely Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note> says: "Unless you turn bodies into incorporeal things, you labor in vain." Likewise, **Parmenides** treats this solution, saying in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <term>Turba Philosophorum: a famous medieval text portraying a debate among ancient thinkers</term>: "Certain people hearing of this solution think it happens without its own body when it is joined, and made into one permanent thing." For the solution of the philosophers is not the "rejoicing of water" <note>original: "aquae iubilatio"; likely a poetic or technical term for a superficial dilution</note>, but the solution—or conversion—of bodies into the water from which they were first created, namely into **Mercury**, just as ice is converted into the liquid water from which it previously was. Behold, by the grace of God, one element which is water, and the reduction of the body itself into liquid water.

The second word <note>In this context, "word" refers to a stage of instruction or a specific operation</note> is that from water, earth is made by a gentle cooking <term>decoctio: a process of heating a substance to refine or concentrate it</term> repeated so many times until blackness appears on the surface. For as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose medical and scientific works were foundational to European alchemy</note> says in the chapter on *Humors*: "Heat acting upon a moist body first generates blackness, as can be seen in the lime <note>original: "calce"; referring to quicklime or burnt minerals</note> made by common folk." Therefore **Menabdes** <note>a figure in the "Assembly of Philosophers"</note> says: "I command those who come after to make bodies into non-bodies through dissolution, and incorporeal things into bodies through sweet cooking; in which one must be extremely careful lest the spirit be converted into smoke and vanish through excessive fire." Whence Maria says: "Guard it, and beware lest anything escapes into smoke." And let the measure of the fire be the heat of the sun in the month of July, so that from the sweet and long cooking the water may be thickened and become black earth. Thus you have the other element, which is earth.

The third word that preceded is the purification of the earth. Whence **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the art to King Khalid</note> says: "This earth putrefies and is purified with its own water; when it has been cleansed, by the help of God, the entire mastery <term>magisterium: the completion of the alchemical work</term> will be directed." **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of alchemy</note> also says: "**Azoth** <term>a universal solvent or the essential mercurial principle</term> and fire wash the **latten** <term>laton: an impure metallic alloy, often representing the "body" of the metal before it is purified</term> and take away the blackness from it." Therefore the philosopher says: "**Whiten the latten**, and put away your books <note>original: "liberos"; likely a scribal variant for "libros" (books), suggesting that once the practitioner sees the result, they no longer need written instruction</note>, lest your hearts be broken." For this is the composition of all the wise, and also the third part of the entire work. Therefore join, as it is said in the *Assembly*, the dry with the moist—that is, the black earth with its own water—and cook it until it is whitened. Thus you have water and earth by themselves, and earth whitened with water.

The fourth word is that the water, which has been thickened and coagulated with the earth, should ascend by **sublimation** <term>sublimatio: the process of turning a solid into vapor through heat, then back into solid form to achieve high purity</term>. Thus you have earth, water, and [air...]

<summary>This page outlines the first three stages of the alchemical Great Work: the solution of solids into "Philosophical Mercury," the cooking of that water into a black "earth," and the subsequent whitening and purification of that earth. It cites numerous authorities to emphasize that the process mimics natural cycles, such as ice melting into water.</summary>

# PHILOSOPHY
<note>The header "PHILOSOPH." likely refers to the "Philosophy of the Stone" or a section dedicated to the sayings of the Philosophers.</note>

...air. And this is what the Philosopher says:
> Whiten it, and quickly sublimate it <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again</term> with fire, until the spirit goes out from it, which you will find within it, and which is called the "bird," or the "ash of Hermes."

Whence also **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says:
> Do not despise the ash: for it is the crown of your heart, and the ash of permanent things.

And in the book of the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," a seminal medieval alchemical text</note> it is said:
> Increase the governance of the fire: and through whiteness, one arrives at ash-making <term>cineratio: reduction to ash</term>, which is called calcined earth, and is of a fiery nature:

And you have in the aforementioned proportions the four elements, namely dissolved water, whitened earth, sublimated air, and calcined fire. Concerning these four elements, **Aristotle** also says in the book *On the Government of Princes* <note>the "Secretum Secretorum," a text attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages</note> to Alexander:
> When you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then you will have the full art of philosophy.

And here is the end of the first composition, as **Morienus** says. Now let us pass to the second composition, which must breathe life into, tinge, and vivify the first composition. Whence **Khalid** the philosopher <note>original: "Calidus," referring to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says:
> No one ever could, or later will be able to, tinge the "foliated earth" <term>terra foliata: a purified, layered state of alchemical matter</term> except with gold.

Therefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> commands, saying:
> Sow your gold in the white foliated earth, which through calcination has been made fiery, subtle, and airy:

Into this earth, therefore, we sow gold when we apply the tincture of gold to it. But gold can never perfectly tinge another body than itself; certainly this cannot happen unless it is perfected by art. Whence **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull, a famous Catalan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> says:
> Although this stone of ours already naturally contains the tincture within itself—for it was created as perfectly as the body of "magnesia" <term>magnesia: in alchemy, a term for the primal matter of the stone, not the modern mineral</term>—it does not, however, possess it by itself unless it is perfected by art and operation.

**Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry"</note> says in his *Operation of Roots*:
> The operation is done for this purpose: so that the tincture of gold in gold may be improved more than it is in its own nature; and also so that it may become the **Elixir** according to the allegory of the wise—that is, a clear condiment composed of species, an antidote and medicine for all bodies to be cured, purged, and transformed into true Silver-making <note>original: "Lunificum"</note> and Gold-making <note>original: "Solificum"</note>.

But lest we should think we need only gold and no other body, hear **Hermes** saying:
> Its father—that is, the father of the first composition—is the Sun <term>Sol: alchemical gold</term>, its mother is the Moon <term>Luna: alchemical silver</term>. The Father is hot and dry, generating the tincture; its Mother is cold and moist, nourishing that which is born.

Therefore the Sun by itself, and the Moon by itself, are very difficult to melt. But when they are joined in the manner of a solder for gold, they melt very quickly. Therefore **Maria** says:

# OF THE TREASURY

When they are truly cleansed, the body and spirit soon embrace each other, and one perfect operation comes from them, because they are altered from their nature; the thick things are made thin. And the spirit is joined with the body through the mediation of the soul, and together with it, it is converted into the color of the ferment, and becomes one with them."

...so that you can keep your finger inserted in the sand <note>The "sand" refers to a sand bath, a common alchemical method for providing even, indirect heat</note>, and let the vessel stand open to draw out the moisture; in the morning you find the material hard. Then put it into an iron mortar again and add another 4 lothons <note>original: "lothones"; a historical unit of weight, roughly half an ounce</note> of Mercury <term>Mercury: quicksilver, used here to create an amalgam with the base metal</term>, or at least as much as is needed until the material becomes soft again. <image-desc>A drawing of a conical or tear-drop shaped vessel, possibly a retort or a similar piece of alchemical apparatus, with horizontal striations on its upper part.</image-desc>

And when the eight days have passed, empty the material into a glass vessel of this kind, and seal the mouth of the glass on a stone with a round glass lid, which you shall place over the mouth of the glass, with a weight of Saturn <note>original: "Saturni pondere"; Saturn is the alchemical name for lead</note> placed on top. Place it on a tripod, and add a fire of such a kind that you can keep your hand between the walls of the furnace and the chamber. Keep it in that heat for six weeks, day and night; afterwards increase the fire a little, so that only molten lead can be maintained, such that it does not congeal and truly remains dissolved: and keep it melted in that heat. 

And this is its putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: the stage in the Great Work where the matter is broken down, traditionally associated with the color black</term>, and meanwhile you will see its perfect blackness. When this is seen, rejoice: for under that blackness, whiteness lies hidden, and it is a certain sign that the material was rightly joined and united at the beginning. You shall also know that after three days have passed, you must remove the lid from the furnace and see whether any pearls <note>original: "margaritæ"; here referring to droplets of condensation or "beads" forming on the glass</note> have risen to the edges of the glass. When this is seen, shake the glass until they fall down, and if they will not fall, take off the lid and wipe around the glass with a feather until they fall upon the material at the bottom. Then indeed you shall block up the glass again, place the weight on top, and cover the furnace again: <margin>A small fire must be used.</margin> and you shall repeat this every three or four days. 

It is better, however, that you add such a small fire that it does not sublime <note>To "sublime" is to turn a solid directly into vapor, which would cause the material to rise to the top of the vessel</note> upwards; although the time may be longer, it matters nothing to you—prefer the certain to the uncertain. For by a great heat you can lose your work, but truly never by a small fire. And beware that you do not apply so much fire to it that you acquire a red color instead of white.

<margin>Though various colors may show themselves, account must be taken only of three: black, white, and red.</margin> Know, my son, that one color changes itself into another: there are many and various colors of which no account is to be taken. # MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC

...black, another white, the last red, and between each color, various colors show themselves—indeed, more than can be imagined. However, take no account of those colors; they are volatile spirits not yet fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixing" means turning a volatile, vaporous substance into a solid that can withstand heat.</note>, and these are poisonous. As long as you see those various colors, beware of their vapors, for they would kill you. Those two colors which first show themselves are raised by a small fire, by gradually increasing that same fire.

<margin>A small fire should be used.</margin> Believe me, my son, that in this art there is no danger except in managing the fire. But if you wish to be certain, use a small fire; in this way, you cannot err, even if a somewhat longer time is required for the work.

Therefore, I tell you and teach you, my son, do not increase the fire so much that you acquire a red color instead of a white one. For that redness would be your matter—the substance within the glass—becoming like pulverized brick, reduced into small clumps like grains of wheat, with part of it looking like a tiny brick-dust with small "living" beads of Mercury <note>original: "gemmis vivis Mercurii"; likely referring to visible droplets of quicksilver (mercury) separating out.</note>. It would stick everywhere to the glass so that it settles and enters into the glass <note>This suggests the chemicals might etch or fuse with the container if overheated.</note>, and then your work would be utterly ruined, and you would have to start over. But this will not happen to you except by a too-vehement fire. The perfect red color does not appear like crushed brick, but rather like a brilliant, dark purple, and it is seen as a "celestial" color <note>original: "color cæleftis"; while this can mean "sky blue," in this context it refers to a sublime, divine purple-red associated with the final stage of the work.</note>. This occurs through great governance of the fire, as will be taught below, God willing. But I mention this color to you now so that you may recognize whether you are acting rightly or otherwise, and so that you do not fall into errors.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Return to the work.</margin> Now we wish to return to our work. If, under a small fire, the matter should rise again to the edges or the lid of the glass—as I have seen happen several times—you should make it fall back down as described above. Maintain it in this state for one day and night, until your matter becomes entirely a powder. It will have a color between ash-grey and black, like earth that has lost its moisture—as if you were to grind turf and dry it in a pan over the fire; these appear in a color between ash and black. And before you reach that color, you will see many and various colors in the work, and after the colors, you will see many wonderful things: for from your matter will be born various shrub-like shapes <note>original: "arbufta figmenti"; a common alchemical description for dendritic crystal growth, often called the "Philosophical Tree."</note>. Indeed, all the painters or goldsmiths in the world could not represent them. And at each step, as the matter becomes stronger and more mature, a change occurs just as often. Before you reach the ash-colored powder, your matter [is] entirely...

->CHAPTER IX.<-

AND when you see that black <term>ashy powder</term> <note>This "blackness" is known to alchemists as the *nigredo*, the first major stage of the work representing the "death" of the material.</note>, rejoice: for under that blackness, whiteness is enclosed. ->CHAPTER X.<-

LET my son also know that this matter is to be understood as that which you now have here in the glass; it is now earth, which has lost its <margin>Various errors.</margin> humidity, and yet it will not yet produce anything good. Let my son hold to the fact that there are many errors in this art. There are many who set out to make the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term>, and by a good moderation of the fire they lead it to this very stage, and they labor to fix the stone into the white and the red; and when the matter has been led this far, they think they can perform the <term>projection</term> <note>The final act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note> with it. But then, throwing it into crude Mercury or into imperfect metals, they find no success, and they fall into despair, repeatedly saying that the art is impossible.

### CHAPTER 11

Know, my son, that I am about to reveal to you the greatest secret of this art, which has never been made public. Therefore I adjure you, my son, by the Son of the living God, that you do not make this secret public except to your own son—and only if he seems to you to have the fear of God—lest your soul and mine be condemned on that account, because of the danger that could arise from it.

<margin>The greatest secret of the entire art.</margin>

Now, my son, open your eyes and see, open your ears and hear the greatest secret in the nature of things. My beloved son will understand, concerning every Stone of the Philosophers, how and by what means it is made and composed—namely, that in the "Great Works" <note>The <term>Magnum Opus</term> or the process of creating the Stone.</note> of which we speak here, those two stones (for the <term>White</term><note>The "Albedo" stage which produces silver.</note> and the <term>Red</term><note>The "Rubedo" stage which produces gold.</note>) can be completed in a single vessel and a single furnace. I say to you: understand well what I am saying. Even if you use <term>Luna</term><note>The alchemical name for Silver.</note> and <term>Mercury</term><note>Quicksilver.</note> in this way without the addition of <term>Sol</term><note>The alchemical name for Gold.</note>, you will make both stones from them—both the White and the Red. You may ask, then, why the Sun and the Moon are placed together in the work. This is done because the Sun is "fixed" <note>Stable and resistant to the heat of the fire.</note>, and so that the work might be shorter by this means. For before the Moon becomes fixed in the work, the Stone for the White has already been produced. Indeed, the Moon is not naturally fixed, and before it becomes so, it is necessary for a long-lasting <term>coction</term><note>A process of slow heating or "cooking" used to mature the substance.</note> to take place. The Moon must be fixed before it can fix Mercury; and for this reason, the Sun and the Moon ought to be in the work together. You can also make both stones from the Sun and Mercury alone, and that would be done more easily than from the Sun and Moon joined together. Because the Sun is fixed, it fixes Mercury more easily. 

But you might ask: if the Moon alone is placed with Mercury, how could the Stone for the Red come from that? You should understand the matter rightly: the Moon is red on the inside, even though it is white on the outside. For under all white things in which the four elements are present, redness is hidden beneath the external whiteness. The Moon is cold and <term>volatile</term><note>Prone to evaporating or changing state when heated.</note> like Mercury; it is coagulated from Mercury and sulfur together, and it is still "raw" and not fixed. Therefore, it is white on the outside and red within. Thus, when the Moon is in the work with Mercury alone, it is cooked and fixed by the governance of the fire, and since it...

## CHAPTER XII.

There were some ignorant men who, when they had prepared the stone to the white and to the red stages, saw that it had no ingress <note>original: "ingressum" — the ability of the alchemical substance to penetrate and merge with a base metal</note>, nor did it flow. Because they could easily see that it lacked ingress, they dissolved the stone and congealed it again twenty or thirty times, thinking that by doing so they would make it fusible <note>able to melt like wax or metal</note> and that it would then have ingress. But they achieved nothing, and even if they had dissolved and congealed it much longer, it could not have helped.

There were some others who extracted oil from antimony, with which they soaked their stone upon a marble slab. They dried it again in a glass dish, repeating this until the stone became fusible in the manner of wax and gave ingress. Then they cast it into Mercury, and they thought it would make the Mercury white; but as the Mercury grew hot, it <note>the Mercury</note> flew off into the air, and the oil of antimony followed immediately. The powder of the stone remained dry, just as it had been before it had absorbed the oil. The cause is this: because the oil of antimony was not fixed <note>original: "fixum" — stable and resistant to evaporation by fire</note>, even though it had made the stone fusible, it was not fixed with the stone, and it cannot be fixed with the stone. The reason is this: if the stone so soaked is placed in glass over a slow fire, the oil along with the stone would penetrate through the glass into nothingness; but if you added a fierce fire, the oil would fly off into the air because of the heat. Thus it cannot be fixed with the stone; and in this way, the ignorant remained in error.

## CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>How the stone is to be made fusible.</margin>
Now I will teach my beloved son how to make our stone fusible and give it ingress, which until now has never been revealed. Therefore, I ask you to keep this secret, if you love God, your soul, and mine.

Now know, my son, your stone has now been made white by the good moderation of the fire, as taught above. If you wish to keep the stone white now, you may; and if you wish to wait for the time until it turns red, you may likewise do so. If you wish to lead it to the red, you must leave it in the furnace and significantly increase your fire for a long time, such as for 15 or 16 days; see if it wishes to change into a saffron color <note>original: "color croceus" — a deep yellow-orange, often indicating a transition between the white and red stages of the Great Work</note>...

...but if you see it still remaining white, significantly increase the fire. The Stone must be cooked in a fierce fire; otherwise its tincture <term>tincture: the concentrated essence or "spirit" capable of coloring and transforming base metals</term> and its hidden sulfur <term>sulfur: in alchemy, the active, combustible, and masculine principle of a substance</term> cannot come forth and appear. Truly, before the Stone puts on its perfect redness, it must boil unto a white heat <note>original: "candorem" – glowing heat</note> for a period of easily ninety days. And now my son will easily understand: if this stone were already fusible <note>fusible: capable of being melted like wax or metal</note>, how could its tincture and redness be brought out? For when it boils even to a white heat, the stone would dissolve and penetrate the glass and the furnace.

<margin>The Stone must be prepared before it is made fusible and subtle.</margin>

For at the very end, it must stand glowing in the glass for easily three days. By these reasons you can observe that the Stone must first be made before it is rendered fusible. The ignorant are unable to grasp this due to the weakness of their minds, for they do not understand the power of nature at all. So, my son, whether the stone is white or red, it must first be completed before you can make it fusible and subtle <note>original: "subtilem" – refined to a point where it can penetrate other materials</note>. 

Once both your stones—the white as well as the red—are completed and prepared as I have taught you and demonstrated by reasons, so that you can easily grasp with your own mind that it must be so: now I wish to teach you in what way you shall prepare both stones and render them fusible and subtle, for making high projections <term>projections: the final step of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon molten base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</term>.

## CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>He continues to teach how the stone is to be made fusible and subtle.</margin>

Now listen, dear son, to the greatest secret that is in this art, which has never been set down in writing except by me alone for your sake. You shall pour over your Stone the clear and pure water of Paradise <note>water of Paradise: a poetic name for a highly purified alchemical solvent or "mercury of the philosophers"</note>, and unite the Stone with the water, and place it in a prison <note>prison: an airtight, sealed glass vessel</note> and seal it up. That water will fly up into the heaven within the circle of the Moon <note>circle of the Moon: likely the upper part of the vessel where vapors condense</note>, and be converted into dew, and fall down again drop by drop by the mixing and the skill of the artist. It will moisten the earth—that is, the Stone—so that it produces flowers of all colors. Through these flowers, your Stone shall rise from the dead into life, and all its enemies [will find] peace...

### CHAPTER XV.

Take your Stone, my son, whether it be white or red, from the vessel and place it in a stone mortar, and pour over it a good quantity of clean Mercury <note>original: *Mercurii mundi*</note>, which I will teach you how to cleanse later; and taking a wooden pestle, grind it continuously for an entire day. Then place it again in the glass, and set it in the **furnace of the Philosophers** <term>Fornax Philosophorum: a specialized alchemical furnace designed to provide constant, precisely regulated heat over long periods</term>, or on a tripod, adding such a fire by which lead can be kept liquid so that it does not congeal, with an even melting. But you shall seal <note>original: *lutabis* - to seal a vessel with "lute," a specialized clay or cement used to make it airtight</note> a small glass over the mouth of the glass in which the stone is. You shall keep it in that heat until the Mercury is entirely **dead** <note>In alchemy, to "kill" mercury means to fix it, or change it from a liquid, volatile state into a stable solid.</note>, which will easily happen in the space of 40 or 50 days.

<margin>Like attracts its like, and like rejoices in like.</margin> For the stone attracts all spirits to its nature: *like attracts its like, and like rejoices in like.* And when it is entirely dead, you shall decrease the fire a little until your matter turns white. And if the stone was the white stone, take it out and place the weight of a grain upon a glowing metal plate: see if your stone wishes to flow and makes its **entry** <note>original: *ingressum* - the ability of the alchemical substance to penetrate and transform a base metal.</note>.

<margin>The Test.</margin> It can be known in this way: when you place the stone upon a glowing plate of copper, and it then penetrates the glowing plate just as oil penetrates dry leather, and the copper plate becomes entirely white like silver where the stone lay—if it performs this, it is ready. If not, pour over it again the **Water of Paradise** <term>Aqua Paradisi: a highly refined alchemical solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve and "feed" the stone.</term> in every way as above, and moderate the fire as before. And if the weight of your stone was one **mark** <note>A historical unit of weight, typically equaling about 8 ounces.</note>, add 4 marks of the Water of Paradise: and do this as often as you pour the Water of Paradise over it. 

Repeat this work until the stone has been dissolved according to your desire. And if it is the red stone, let it stand in the same heat in which it stood with the Water of Paradise—that is, such a heat by which it can henceforth be kept melted without glowing, until your stone becomes red. But it requires a longer time than the white, and you shall test the red in every way as you did the white.

Know, my son, if you wish to prepare the stone so that you may make a **projection** <term>Projection: the final step of alchemy where a small amount of the Stone is cast onto molten base metal to transmute it into silver or gold.</term> upon Mercury, you must make it as fusible as wax; and this must be done with great care, because the stone could penetrate through the glass. But I advise you, my son, make your stone so fusible that it almost begins to glow before it wishes to melt: and once this is done for the white stone, make the projection upon **Jupiter** <note>In alchemical code, "Jupiter" refers to the metal Tin.</note>.

You cannot make the Red Stone more meltable <term>fusible</term> <note>Capable of being melted by heat.</note> than is possible by heating it to a glowing heat without the use of bellows. For when the Water of Paradise <note>original: "aqua Paradisi"; a poetic term for a highly purified alchemical solvent or "mercurial water" believed to possess life-giving properties.</note> has been "killed" <note>An alchemical term meaning the substance has been fixed or deprived of its volatility.</note> and fixed together with the Stone, it must remain in that heat in the furnace until it reaches a glow—easily for twenty days—before the Water of Paradise can draw out its redness. And when its redness has finally emerged, that fire must be increased so that the Stone glows moderately, appearing just to glow and no more. Leave it to stand thus for three days; then allow it to cool, and give thanks to God, for your Stone is perfected.

## CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>The greatest mystery and secret.</margin>
Therefore, my son, you must maintain a balance in making the Stone meltable. For if you were to make the White Stone <note>The version of the Philosopher's Stone used for making silver.</note> too meltable, it would penetrate the glass vessel itself. Furthermore, the Red Stone <note>The version used for making gold.</note> ought to be even less meltable; otherwise, you cannot acquire the red tincture of the Water of Paradise on the outside, as has been taught.

Know, beloved son, that by the clear Water of Paradise all things in the world can be made meltable when it is raised <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects again as a solid.</note> through them until it clings to them.

<margin>Inceration.</margin>
Know, my son, that <term>Inceration</term> <note>From the Latin "incera," meaning to soften with wax. It refers to the process of turning a dry, brittle substance into a soft, wax-like state so it can "enter" or merge with other metals.</note>—which is to say, making a hard thing that cannot melt become liquid, and giving it the power to enter <note>original: "ingressum"; the ability of the Stone to penetrate and transform the interior of a base metal.</note>—was first discovered among the Ancients. For after they had labored long and hard, and had prepared and perfected the White and Red Stones, they wished to perform the "projection" <note>The final act of throwing the finished Stone onto molten base metal to transmute it.</note> with it, but they achieved nothing. The Stone refused to dissolve; it remained merely powder and earth. Then they easily realized that nothing was missing except Inceration, because the Stone had no "entry." They sought Inceration in many things, and having investigated every substance, they found it in nothing else but Sulphur, Arsenic, and Mercury.

<margin>Inceration was first discovered by the Ancients, and how.</margin>

## CHAPTER XVII.

Know, my son, that in all things in nature, except for mineral spirits and metals, the "oil" <note>In alchemy, "oil" refers to the flammable or soul-like principle of a substance (the Sulfur).</note> flies away from the "earth" <note>The solid, physical residue.</note>. But in mineral spirits and metals, the oil does not separate itself; it remains with its earth even in the fire. Even if they are driven up by the fire, the earth flies up together with the oil. Their oil cannot be separated from the earth as it is in other things. And so the Ancients realized that if they wished to follow nature, they must possess such an oil—the same oil from which metals take their own—if they were to make those spirits (which they had made dry and earthy through sublimation) meltable again. To do this, they required this specific oil with which to soften <gloss>incerate</gloss> them.

...they [the alchemists] found a way to make materials meltable again, and so they discovered **inceration** <term>Inceration: An alchemical process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, waxy consistency, making it easier to melt.</term> in sulfur, Arsenic, and ten times more so in Mercury. Thus they discovered the art of inceration, by which they could make their stone fusible <note>able to be melted</note> according to their heart's desire. Once they possessed the art of inceration, they could do whatever they pleased; for they could make anything they wished capable of melting. Through heat, they sublimated <note>converted a solid directly into vapor</note> the spirits, making them powerful and poisonous; they rendered them so burning and subtle <note>refined or volatile</note> that it was a marvel to behold. 

When they had made them sufficiently subtle through sublimation, and sufficiently burning through corrosive substances, and had impressed enough of the "tincture" into them, they would "incerate" them with properly purified Mercury. That is, they would drench them with a specific quantity of well-cleaned Mercury, place them on a tripod <note>an alchemical stand for heating vessels</note>, and allow the substance to "ascend and descend" <note>original: "ascendere & descendere"; this refers to the cycle of evaporation and condensation within a sealed vessel</note> until the Mercury remained fixed with them. In this way, they created liquid spirits whenever they wished. 

Sometimes they also took **Gold** <note>original: "Solem"</note> and **Silver** <note>original: "Lunam"</note> and burned them into a fine "lime" or powder. They drenched this powder with purified Mercury and placed it on a tripod in a glass vessel of that sort, repeatedly turning it. In this way, they allowed it to sublimate until the Mercury remained fixed with them, making those powders so easy to melt that they could use them for **projection** <term>Projection: The final stage of the Great Work, where the alchemical medicine is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</term>. They even calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> all the "perfected" metals and dissolved the powders in sharp distilled vinegar until they were rendered [clear], and thus they purged those powders of their impurity. They reduced those crystalline stones into a subtle powder, drenched them with Mercury, and placed them on a tripod (as was said of Gold and Silver), and from that, they fashioned their medicine.

<margin>How the water of the clouds <note>Original: "aqua nubium." This refers to the volatile, watery moisture or "phlegm" trapped within Mercury that alchemists believed hindered the transformation process.</note> is removed from Mercury.</margin>
They mixed the gum with water, grinding it so finely it could not be felt between the fingers. Then, taking common distilled water, they placed the ground material into a glass pot, pouring a good quantity of water over it, and placed it in those sifted ashes <note>A "sand bath" or "ash bath" used to provide even, indirect heat.</note>; they made that vessel boil with the material for an hour or more: then they allowed it to cool: and the salt and honey <note>In this context, "honey" may refer to a thick, yellowish chemical concentrate or literal honey used as a reagent.</note> dissolved in that water: but the Sun and the Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Sun" (Sol) refers to gold and the "Moon" (Luna) refers to silver.</note> remained at the bottom. Then they poured off that water from the top, and again pouring fresh common water over it, they allowed it to boil as before; they repeated this until all the water poured off was pure, as it was in excess. Then they dried that powder with a very small fire. 

Then they took Mercury which had been pressed five or six times through a hare’s skin <note>A common method for filtering liquid mercury to remove physical impurities.</note>; they washed it with salt and vinegar until the salt remained shining and white: then with clean common water, they washed away all the salt and vinegar entirely, and afterwards dried it with clean linen cloths. They placed it into a glass pot, with an alembic <term>Alembic: An early chemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling volatile substances.</term> placed on top, set it in the ashes, and having luted <term>Luted: Sealed with a specialized clay or paste to make the vessel airtight.</term> the receiver, they built a fire, just as if one wished to distill rose water. They allowed it to stand in this way for 12 or 15 days to draw out the superfluous humidity it contains, by which the work would be ruined. In this manner, all Mercury must be prepared that is to be used in the work, and such a fire must be applied to it so that it does not all sublime <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again; here, the author warns against using too much heat which would cause the Mercury to rise and harden at the top.</term> upward. However, if a little should sublime upward, so that small droplets drip through the alembic, it does not matter. But if you were to sublime it upward so that some of it became "dead" <note>Mercury that has been oxidized or turned into a dry powder through excessive heat.</note>, it would have to be revived again in boiling water, and then it would again take on that watery humidity which would ruin the entire work.

## CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>Every living Mercury has the water of the clouds within it.</margin>
You shall know, my son, that every living Mercury has within itself the water of the clouds; you will be able to see this yourself: for a large portion of clean common water will fall into the receiver. This, however, must be emptied; otherwise, it would dwell with the bodies of the Sun and Moon, and they would become powder and fixed: for if it retained that humidity within itself, it would never be possessed. The superfluous humidity must be drawn away from it by distillation, without sublimation, as has been shown; keep it in the fire until you see that no more dew rises into the alembic. Afterward, retain it still in that same heat for 10 or 12 days without sublimation: when this is done, let it cool, and keep it in a wooden box in a dry and warm place, lest it suck in any humidity from the damp <note>Original: "sugido," likely from "sucidus," meaning moist or sappy.</note> air.

### CHAPTER XX.

You shall know, my son, that in this manner all <term>Mercury</term><note>The author uses 'Mercury' both as the common metal and as a philosophical 'spirit' that must be purified.</note> must be prepared from which we wish to make amalgamations, if the Mercury is otherwise to "die" and be "fixed" in the work. <note>In alchemy, to 'die' or be 'fixed' means to lose its liquid, volatile state and become a solid that can withstand heat.</note> This is what deceives many who do not achieve their desires: it is caused by the superfluous humidity which it contains, and being ignorant of what they lack, they remain in error.

Likewise, you will now hold, my son, that the <term>Sun</term><note>Latin: Sol; refers to Gold.</note>, the <term>Moon</term><note>Latin: Luna; refers to Silver.</note>, and the Mercury are now prepared for the binding together of this work.

Likewise, you should know, my son, that you shall weigh your powders of the Sun and the Moon; and you shall take an equal weight of your prepared Mercury—that is, as much of the <term>spirit</term> as of the <term>body</term>. <note>The 'spirit' is the volatile mercury, and the 'body' is the solid metal (gold or silver).</note> Otherwise, if there were not enough of the body, it would have to remain in the fire much longer before the spirit would be willing to "die" with the body and become a powder. But when the weight is equal, the spirit easily dies with the body, etc.

Indeed, my son might ask: since that spirit is now dead within the body and fixed to it, and has been brought to a perfect color—either white or red—and is then drenched with a great quantity of Mercury to make it <term>waxy</term><note>Latin: 'incerandum,' a process of making a dry substance soft and meltable like wax.</note> and <term>fusible</term> and subtle, in order to complete the work: sometimes 10 or 12 parts of the spirit are poured over one part of the stone or the fixed powder for the <term>white</term><note>The 'White Work' or albedo, the stage of silver-making.</note>; and over the powder for the <term>red</term><note>The 'Red Work' or rubedo, the final stage of gold-making.</note>, sometimes 20 or 24, or even 30 parts of the spirit are poured over one part of the powder fixed for the red. For while the white stone is drenched with 12 parts, the red work or powder easily requires 30 parts before it is willing to become fusible. The reason is this: the white stone is crude, moist, cold, and white; it only needs half the amount of the <term>Water of Paradise</term><note>Latin: 'aqua paradisi,' a term for a highly refined, life-giving alchemical solvent or mercurial water.</note> or spirit to make it waxy and fusible: for it has not been cooked in the fire as long as the red stone or powder, nor is it so dry. The Red is by nature hot and dry; its interior stands on the outside—that is, its heat and dryness—and its whiteness is within—that is, its coldness. And before it can be made fusible, easily 30 parts of the Water of Paradise must be poured over one part of the red powder or stone.

### CHAPTER 21.

<margin>Two reasons why it must be held in the fire for a long time.</margin>
My son shall know and understand that the first addition of the spirit and the body are both raw. That is one reason why it must stand for a long time before they embrace each other radically <note>meaning: at their very root or fundamental essence</note>. The second reason is this: that the first addition is so tiny and light that it must not be driven too hard, lest nothing or very little rises in the vessels; thus it must stand for a long time before it can die and become powder. And when the stone or powder is made white or red, it is fixed, even if it is not yet subtle; and it is a radical medicine <term>radical medicine: a substance that acts on the fundamental "root" of a metal to transform it</term>, even if it does not yet have "entry" <note>meaning: the ability to penetrate or transmute other metals</note>. 

And Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "When Mercury is dissolved, it easily dissolves all other metals or spirits; and when it is congealed, it congeals them; and when fixed, it fixes them." Thus, although much Water of Paradise <term>Water of Paradise: a highly purified, powerful alchemic solvent</term> is poured over it—thirty parts to one part of Mercury—it is coagulated, wherefore it easily coagulates the Water of Paradise and fixes it easily, as said before. 

There is also another reason, partly medicinal: if the stone cannot flow, that is, so that it may easily draw the Water of Paradise into its own nature. There is also another reason: when the Water of Paradise is poured over the powder and placed on the furnace, a much greater heat is added to it than was given at the start of the work; for the start of the work must not sublimate <term>sublimate: to turn a solid directly into vapor via heat</term>. And to this Water of Paradise such heat is applied that it sublimates upward and falls back down, drop by drop, into the powder. 

And when it begins to "die" and becomes powder at the same time, you shall increase the fire so that it sublimates through it; and you shall invert the glass vessel again and again. And when it has sublimated upward, the bottom part of the glass is placed on the top part, and thus that fixed powder falls onto the sublimated part of the spirit; and this work is repeated so many times until both remain as one at the bottom. Then a slightly more vehement fire is built until it reaches its color, either white or red, as you desire. 

Thus, for the reasons mentioned, it should not stand as long in the work as it did at the beginning. Therefore, they took no more of the spirit than of the body. To what purpose is all this? So that it may lead you, my son, to a true understanding of the work; so that you may know, my son, how to discern between good and evil, and know what you are doing, lest you fall into error or despair. Therefore, my son, diligently reread this and similar lessons often, and strive to imprint them on your memory, to avoid all errors that might occur in the work before you apply your hands to the task.

### CHAPTER 22.

<margin>Return to the work.</margin>
Now let us approach the work again. You shall take your powder of Gold <note>Latin: *Solis*, literally "of the Sun"</note> and Silver <note>Latin: *Lunae*, literally "of the Moon"</note> and weigh it; then take as much prepared Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> as the weight of your powder. Heat an iron mortar and pestle, but not so much that the Mercury evaporates into the air. Then put your prepared powder into the mortar, along with a twentieth part of an ounce of sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to help metals bond</term>, or a fourth part of a loth <term>loth: a historical European unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams</term>. Pulverize the sal ammoniac before putting it into the mortar. Then grind them with that warm pestle in the mortar. Amalgamate the Mercury and the powder into an amalgam <term>amalgam: a soft, putty-like mixture created when mercury dissolves another metal</term>. The sal ammoniac causes the powders and the Mercury to embrace each other fundamentally. Grind indeed for a whole day without ceasing; help one another, and let another person take over when one is tired. Grind for at least 12 continuous hours. Plug your nostrils, mouth, and ears so that the odor does not harm you, which might rise invisibly <note>A vital warning, as heating mercury produces highly toxic, invisible vapors</note>. And after 12 hours have passed, put your material into a small glass vessel of this kind, covered with another; place a weight on top, then set it in the secret furnace, and do as previously taught, with the same regulation of the fire, until the work is entirely perfected.
