The first regulation of the fire teaches how to complete the works that are accomplished by amalgams; the regulation of the fire is one and the same. However, the first construction is done in various ways, all coming to one end and seeking a shortness of time.

There were also some who took the stone given to us freely by God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: *à Deo Optimo Maximo*</note>, and dissolved it nine or ten times, purged it of its dregs, and congealed it again, reducing it to a fine white powder, and kept it in a box; then the stone was ready. Then they sublimated the Mercury—well washed and prepared as was taught above—by means of vitriol <term>vitriol: a sulfate mineral, used here to help purify the mercury through heat</term>; that is, they took 1 pound of sublimated Mercury and 4 pounds of crude vitriol, mixed them together, and sublimated it through that. They ground it again with the dregs and sublimated it once more; they ground it again over the dregs and sublimated it yet again; when this was done, they threw away the dregs. Then they sublimated it again with 2 pounds of fresh vitriol, repeatedly throwing away the dregs, and kept only the sublimate <note>The solid substance produced by the cooling of the vapors</note> in a box. ### OF MASTER JOHN ISAAC

And they filed those materials down minutely: by pounding the filings into a powder, they reduced them in an iron mortar, and then they washed the powder with distilled water, as was taught in the preceding work. After that, they ground it upon marble with prepared common salt and gum water, and by pounding, they reduced it into an impalpable powder <note>Original: "intangibilem puluerem"; a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers.</note>. They washed this with common distilled water until the water flowed away clean and clear; then they dried it by a gentle fire and preserved it by itself in a small box.

Likewise, they then took 8 parts, or loths <note>A 'loth' was a unit of weight used in Central Europe, roughly equivalent to 14–15 grams or half an ounce.</note>, of the powder of the stone freely given to us by God, and 4 loths or parts of the powder of the Sun and Moon <note>In the symbolic language of alchemy, the "Sun" refers to Gold and the "Moon" to Silver.</note>. These make 12 parts in total. Then they took as many parts of Mercury as the weight of the other two combined—that is, they took 12 loths of sublimated Mercury <term>Mercury sublimate: A volatile, white crystalline powder (mercuric chloride) often used as a reagent in alchemical "fixation."</term>, or 12 parts. Together, these make 24 loths or parts.

They mixed these three together thoroughly by grinding them with distilled vinegar, making them impalpable. Afterward, they dried the ground material in a glass vessel over warm ashes so that it would turn back into a powder. Once this was done, they placed the powder into a round glass vessel made in this manner <note>Referring to the illustration below</note>, filling the vessel all the way to the top. Then they took the vessel and suspended it inside a tripod, or in a secret furnace, in a chamber. With the door closed, they allowed it to hang there for 89 days, applying such a fire that they could comfortably hold a hand there for half an hour between the walls of the furnace and the chamber where the vessel hung. They maintained the fire at that same heat using a lamp made with a resin wick and distilled oil, which does not blacken the lamp and produces very little smoke. During this time, the material is cooked into a single substance.

When the 89 days had passed, they broke the glass and took out the material. They would heat an iron or bronze plate until glowing and place the material upon it, putting it into the furnace in which goldsmiths paint with enamel to see if the powder would smoke. Alternatively, they would weigh out 2 drams of the powder, place it in a small crucible, and heat it in the fire for half an hour. When it had cooled, they weighed it again; if it had lost any weight, the powder was not yet "fixed" <term>Fixation: The alchemical process of making a substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates or "flies" from the fire.</term>. Then they would put it back into a glass as before and suspend it in the furnace again, increasing the fire so that in the space of time it takes to say an Ave Maria <note>The time taken to recite this prayer—roughly 15 to 20 seconds—was a common way for pre-modern scientists to measure short durations without a stopwatch.</note>...

Then, with the fire increased, they sublimed <term>sublimed: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again in the upper part of the vessel</term> it upwards, and turned the vessel upside down and back again. They repeated this work until the whole remained fixed together at the bottom of the vessel. Then they let it stand until the white color revealed itself, using the same moderation of the fire; and when everything had turned white, the entire Elixir was "at the white" <note>The "White Elixir" was believed to be capable of transmuting base metals into silver.</note>. And if they wished to have it "at the red" <note>The "Red Elixir" or Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting metals into gold.</note>, they let it stand and increased the fire, for under the heat regulated for the white stage, the red tincture <term>tincture: the concentrated essence or soul of a substance, capable of imparting its properties (like color and stability) to other bodies</term> is unable to show itself. For this reason, you must keep both one and the other in your mind if you wish to profit in this art. Therefore, do not be weary of reading your lessons often with a diligent mind. Once the redness has been drawn out, the Elixir is perfected: the stone for the red, to reduce all imperfect metals into the true Sun <note>original: "Solem"; the alchemical name for Gold</note>, which is more excellent than that which comes from the mines, passing all tests.

<margin>2. Dissolving</margin>
The process by which they amalgamate that imperfect body <note>In alchemy, "imperfect bodies" usually refer to base metals like lead or copper that the alchemist intends to transform.</note> with living **Mercury**, and lead it back into its original essence: that is the "dissolving" <term>Solutio: the alchemical process of turning a solid into a liquid state, often seen as a return to a primal, undifferentiated form.</term> of the Ancients. Their solution is not a melting by the water of the clouds <note>i.e., common rainwater</note>, but it is a "dry water," which is **Mercury**; it is the foundation of the art, about which **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis"; refers to the 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician Al-Razi.</note> says: **"Unless you dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain."** <note>original: "Nisi corpora soluas, operam ludis."</note> **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy.</note> speaks of these solutions in the books titled *The Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>. This shortest path in the art is "reduction," if the bodies are clarified and reduced into a shining water—which is that water from which they first took their origin. This water encompasses within itself spirit, soul, and body, and it is what "makes us shine," as **Geber** says. And when they have converted the substance into **Mercury**, so that they can press it through a cloth <note>A common alchemical test for the purity and liquidity of mercury.</note>, they said they possessed the element of **Water**. The Philosophers said that from the thickness of that water, **Earth** is formed, and then they claimed to possess the second element: namely, **Water** and **Earth**.

<margin>3. Purification</margin>
The third word of the Ancients is **Purification** <note>original: "Mundificatio"</note>, about which **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: **"This earth putrefies with the water, and then immediately purifies itself; and when it is clean, the entire medicine is prepared from it by the help of God."** The Philosophers treat this in the *Assembly*, saying: **"Join the dry with the moist."** The dry is **Earth**, and the moist is **Water**. Behold, you now have the water and earth purified.

<margin>4. Evaporation</margin>
The fourth word is **Evaporation** of the water; this occurs when the **"Water of Paradise"** <note>A symbolic term for a highly rectified or spiritualized alchemical solvent.</note> ascends into heaven and falls back to earth in drops. They then call this "sublimation," or "ascent and descent." In this way, that water becomes the earth which had previously been strained <note>original: "piftrata" / "pistrata", likely referring to being worked or kneaded like dough</note> in the earth; and they called the ascent **"Air."** Thus you have **Water**, **Air**, and **Earth**; and this is what the Philosophers say: **"When the white effect is achieved, pour over it the Water of Paradise, and immediately join the sublimation; from this may come forth the spirit,"** which in the writings of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> is called "the bird." Regarding this matter, **Morienus** says: **"In the end, there will remain for you calcined water, sand, or ashes."** And **Hermes**, **Geber**, and **Morienus** say: **"Do not despise the ashes which you find in the lowest state; the ashes are shining, and in them you will find precious diamonds."** <note>The "diamonds" or "adamants" refer to the crystalline essence of the Philosopher's Stone found at the bottom of the vessel.</note> Then it is said: **"Immediately add the ferment to it,"** that is, when you reduce that imperfect thing to a white powder, you should pour over it the **Water of Paradise** in which **Gold** <note>original: "Sol" (the Sun), the alchemical symbol for gold.</note> has been amalgamated. When they pour this over the powder, they call it the "ferment" <note>An agent that "leavens" the base matter, causing it to transform into gold.</note>, the same water of the Philoso-

...of the philosophers: then they said: now join the soul to it. And they have named the spirit "water," and they speak the truth. Certain Philosophers also say: "Unless you strip bodies from bodies, and also spirits, you have accomplished nothing in our art." From that body we first make water when it is amalgamated, and then that body is stripped of its body; and after continuous decoction <term>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its chemical state</term> that body is dried out and dies with the spirit, and then the spirit becomes the body.

### Master Johannes Isaac Hollandus

<margin>Follow nature truly.</margin>
...what you seek, you will find: and they speak the truth. For in our works, we first make moist things from dry, dry things from moist, subtle things from coarse, and coarse things from subtle; we establish spirits from bodies, and bodies from spirits; and we make the higher as the lower, and equal the lower to the higher <note>This is a reference to the famous Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, which states "That which is below is like that which is above."</note>. Thus we convert materials one into another, as was taught previously. So, from the reasons mentioned above, it is clear that the Ancients spoke the truth in all things, although they are obscure: this was done so that the ignorant, who are not of the number of the "Sons of Art" <note>original: "filiorum" — Alchemists referred to their initiated students as "Sons of the Doctrine" or "Sons of Art" to maintain a lineage of secret knowledge.</note>, would not understand us, and so that the knowledge of these things would remain unknown to them.

Thereafter, my son shall know that the Ancients established many chapters so that the ignorant might think our art is practiced with great difficulty: and in every chapter they placed many and various works, under many names, such as: **Reduction**, **Solution**, **Washing**, **Sublimation**, **Distillation**, **Coagulation**, **Increation**, **Calcination**, and **Fixation** <note>These are the traditional alchemical stages. Reduction returns a metal to its "prime" state; Calcination uses heat to reduce a substance to powder; Fixation makes a volatile substance stable under fire.</note>; and so on, as was commemorated above. And now I will reveal to my son how the Ancients and the Wise devised those names in the work.

### Chapter XXV.

<margin>How the work must be established in imitation of the Ancients.</margin>
Likewise, if you wish to perform the work in the same manner in which our ancestors did, take **Mercury** from the mines where silver or gold is dug out, but take none that is elicited by artifice <note>The author insists on "native" mercury found in nature rather than mercury processed from other minerals like cinnabar, believing it holds more "life."</note>. You shall squeeze it through a hare-skin, and if anything remains in the hare-skin, inspect whether it is some body of metal; put this in a small crucible with a portion of pulverized **borax** <note>Borax was used as a flux to help metals melt and to clean away impurities.</note>. Place it in the fire so that it may be dissolved, and when it has been liquefied, see what body of metal it is. If you find it to be of some imperfect metal, that Mercury is entirely useless for our work; but if you find **Sun** [Gold] and **Moon** [Silver] <note>original: "Solem ac Lunam" — In alchemical shorthand, the Sun always represents Gold and the Moon represents Silver.</note>, it is upright. Then take as much of that Mercury as you wish, put it in a glass vessel, and through an **alembic** <note>A cap or lid used in distillation to collect and redirect vapors.</note> draw off its superfluous humidity, which would corrupt your work and prevent the Mercury from being able to "die" into powder.

<margin>Superfluous humidity must not be withdrawn.</margin>
<margin>Humidity to be withdrawn from Mercury.</margin>
For if the superfluous humidity were not withdrawn from it, even if that material remained in the fire until Judgment Day, it would not be reduced to powder in the least. The cause is the humidity which Mercury has within itself: for you see a great part of the humidity in it through distillation, as was taught before. But when the Mercury has been stripped of all its superfluous humidity, then take that imperfect body, that is...

<margin>Mercury never dies alone.</margin>
...of its own kind, or its relatives, which are also of its nature; and therefore it joins itself with them, and immediately dies <note>In alchemy, "death" often refers to the loss of metallic form or the transition into a different state of matter, such as a powder or oxide.</note> together with them. My son, reread all these things often, so that you will be able to understand nature in all things. But enough of these: let us return to our work.

All three stand on a tripod: namely, the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> in a glass by itself, the work with the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note> in another glass, and the **water of paradise** in a third glass. And all three stood together on a tripod in a sealed chamber, so firmly that nothing could escape <note>original: "expirare", literally "breathe out" or evaporate.</note>, and they were governed by a tiny fire, so that a hand could be held without danger of burning between the walls and the chamber; that is, so that the heat and the sensation of the hand are as one. For the heat must be so governed that you can hold your hand there for a half-hour without burning: and if the heat and the sensation of the hand were the same, all things were going well. 

Then the Ancients and Sages deliberated by what special name they should mark each sign they saw in the work, so that they might hide the art from the ignorant who are not of this art; and so that those people might think the art is practiced with great difficulty, they imposed various names on the work, as will still be shown. They listed many operations which also follow below, such as **Solution**, **Reduction**, **Sublimation**, **Distillation**, **Congelation**, **Evaporation**, **Inceration** <note>The process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency.</note>, **Calcination**, and many more and various operations, to lead the ignorant into error. 

But all these are bastards; they shall not possess the inheritance of the Sages. For all the aforesaid operations are done in a single closed glass, in which the work stands in the furnace, as will be taught, and as has been sufficiently taught above. The unrefined, however, cannot grasp this because of the weakness of their minds: they think each operation is distinct, and each is done with distinct vessels and instruments, and distinct furnaces, and a distinct regulation of fire, and thus they think the art is practiced with great difficulty. They cannot grasp that all things happen at once in one closed vessel, and in one furnace, and with one regulation of fire, as will be taught. 

In the beginning, the Ancients saw the matter placed in the glass acquire a black fleece or skin in the upper part; then they called it the <term>Blackening of the sea</term> <note>original: "Nigrificatione maris". This refers to the 'Nigredo' or black stage, the first phase of the Great Work.</note>. For that water above was completely black, and because Salt and the Moon were in it, they said it was the <term>Eclipse of the Sun and the Moon</term> <note>original: "Eclipsin Solis atque Lunæ"</note>, and the <term>Blackening</term> of the sea; and the ignorant understood this not at all.

Finally, they saw the earth begin to sink again into the water down to the bottom of the vessel; because this earth was black, they chose to call it "corruption," <margin>Corruption</margin> and the "fetid menstrual fluid." <note>original: "fœtidum menstruale." And not even the ignorant understood this; they did not know that all of this happens in a closed glass vessel in our furnace. They are not numbered among our sons <note>A common alchemical phrase meaning "sons of the art" or true initiates.</note>.

Therefore the philosopher **Danthynus** says: "His sweat must be drawn from him, and he must afterward be made to drink it."

**Hermes** says: "The earth shall be saturated with water." And **Morienus**: "Give drink to the thirsty one until he is nourished by his own sweat, and for eternity..."

...will thirst no more. Even the unlearned did not understand this, being ignorant that this occurs in a closed vessel in our furnace. By long boiling and long, tempered heat, they saw all the water dried out, and all of it at once converted into earth. This earth will still be worked after our labor, as **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; likely referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of chemistry/alchemy</note> says: *When earth is made of our own, our art is for the most part completed.* Then they saw this earth establish itself into a solid substance and remain firm, no longer <margin>Congelation</margin> ascending. Then the Ancients perceived that by longer boiling and tempered heat, that solid earth gradually became whiter and whiter, and at last became so perfectly white and shining that its brightness surpassed all the whiteness of the World. Then it was agreed among them to call this whitening **Calcination**, and it is the true <margin>Calcination</margin> **Calcination** of the Ancients, and this is its true name. Therefore **Hermes** and **Morienus** say: *Do not despise the ashes remaining in the lower place, for in them is the most excellent diamond.* And from these ashes (says **Geber**) a splendid virgin shall be born; she will conceive fruit in her womb, and then she is to produce a son of life.

This will happen, my son, when the **ferment** <note>A substance added to the alchemical matter to trigger a transformation, much like yeast in bread</note> is mixed with this white earth; then the earth, or that imperfect body, receives the ferment, and then the Virgin conceives in her womb; and this is the intention of the Ancients in these matters. Then the Philosophers say: *Nourish that son or boy with his own milk until he has grown up*—that is, when this earth, which is white in this manner and mixed with the ferment, is drenched with the clear and bright **water of paradise** <note>A poetic term for the purified mercurial solvent</note>. And by that water in this white [substance], the matter is thus **waxed** <term>inceratur/inceration: the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency</term>. Their meaning is that this boy is nourished with milk...

->with its own milk: and truly it is its milk. The ignorant do not grasp this.<-

Furthermore, when the matter was white and fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a substance that can withstand high heat without evaporating.</note> in this way, they then removed it from the furnace and amalgamated <note>Combined or blended</note> it with glass in which Salt had been placed; they also took this from the furnace and ground them together in a stone mortar with a stone pestle until the amalgamated Sun <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> was thoroughly mixed with the white stone or powder; and then they applied the ferment to it. Concerning this, Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit.</note> says: *Make the union, and give it the soul from there, so that it may never be separated from the soul.* "Perform the marriage," says Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry," whose name was often used by later European alchemists.</note>, "and place the bride with her groom in the bed, and you shall sprinkle the bed with celestial dew <note>original: "rore cælefti"; a metaphor for a pure, distilled alchemical solvent.</note>, and the bride shall conceive a son; he will be King over all his tribes, and all his enemies shall enter into peace with him, and he shall be crowned with a red diadem, and shall remain a King for eternity, and never lose his dominion." The ignorant do not grasp these obscure words at all.

Then, taking the material, they put it into the vessel again, and then, having taken the Water of Paradise <note>original: "aqua Paradisi"; likely a highly rectified spirit or mercury used as a solvent.</note>, they poured it over that material—roughly 10 parts to 1 part of the material. This was what Geber meant when he said: *Sprinkle the bed with celestial dew: the bride shall conceive a son.* That was the meaning. And they sealed the glass with a seal and placed it back in the furnace, increasing the fire a little more vehemently, until the Water of Paradise rose upward through sublimation and fell back down drop by drop into the material; and that was why the son of the shining virgin was nourished by his own milk until he reached maturity.

My son, you shall know and understand: if you wish to prepare the Stone to the red stage <note>The "Rubedo," the final successful stage of the Great Work.</note>, you must bring the white and red earth together with its ferment by increasing the fire until it becomes saffron-colored. And when it has become entirely saffron-colored, like dried saffron, then the element of air has been turned outward. Then indeed, the fire must be significantly increased so that the element of fire may come forth. For by that regulation of fire by which the air presented itself in the likeness of saffron, the fire [of the red stage] and the red tincture <note>The pigment or "soul" that transmutes base metals.</note> cannot and have no power to present themselves at the same time. Thus, the fire must be significantly increased until its red tincture is brought forth. And when your material is red, then drench it with the Water of Paradise until your stone has drunk in all the Water of Paradise and becomes all one powder. Then rule that powder with a moderation of fire, so that it becomes white again like snow. Then increase the fire, as taught above, until the powder is perfectly saffron-colored. Then increase the fire until it is perfectly red, and your work will be completed.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>The four elements in the work individually.</margin>
Now you have seen all four <term>elements</term><note>The classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, which alchemists believed composed all matter.</note> in the work individually. First, you saw water and earth, which were previously visible on the outside, and then fire and air, which were within. For those things which were in the intellect <note>meaning they were present potentially or theoretically</note> you have now seen clearly with your eyes; that is, when you perceived the perfect saffron-yellow color. And now you see its red <term>tincture</term><note>A concentrated medicinal or alchemical essence capable of changing the color and nature of a substance.</note> and the fire, which are now openly displayed. For this reason, the Ancient Philosophers spoke truly when they said, "Our Stone is composed of the four elements," and yet is one, and from one; this becomes clear from the reasons given above.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

Now you shall know hereafter, my son, that you must act as I have taught you here, if you desire to have the stone for the red <note>The "Red Work" or *Rubedo*, the final stage to produce gold.</note>. But if you only wish to have it for the white <note>The "White Work" or *Albedo*, the stage for producing silver.</note>, apply the **water of paradise** to it when you have mixed it with the <term>ferment</term><note>An agent, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical base to "ripen" it into the final Stone.</note>, as described above. Then let it ascend and descend <note>a process of circulation or distillation</note> until it settles at the bottom, fixed with the white stone. Then follow the same regime of fire until the powder becomes perfectly white again. Then you have the stone for the white, for the purpose of bringing imperfect metals back into pure <term>Moon</term><note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver.</note>.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

You shall know further, my son, that all these kinds of operations are equally very good, and their **projection** <note>The act of casting the alchemical "medicine" onto a base metal to transmute it.</note> is so high <note>meaning powerful or effective</note> that it is a thing to be wondered at. You shall discover this yourself: for when you cast your medicine upon any metal, or upon **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver.</note>, as long as the medicine has strength, the metal into which you cast your medicine will be breakable and brittle, like glass that can be pulverized. Then, afterward, cast the powder of that same metal into other imperfect metals, and it will still be a medicine. Do this as long as the metal remains breakable and brittle; but when it becomes **malleable** <note>Capable of being hammered or shaped without breaking, indicating it has become a true metal.</note>, the medicine has reached the limit of its powers. At that point, that metal is either <term>Sun</term><note>original: *Sol*; the alchemical name for gold.</note> or Moon, according to what the medicine had been. Thus, my son, you will see it easily; experience will easily teach you.

### CHAPTER XXXI

My son should know that there were those who took nine parts of "water of paradise" <note>original: *aquae paradisi*; a highly purified alchemical solvent, often a multi-distilled spirit or acid</note> which had been rectified <note>purified and concentrated through distillation</note> from superfluous moisture, as was previously taught. They took nine vials and mixed a part into each, sealing them with clay <note>luting the glass to ensure an airtight seal during heating</note>, and placed them on a tripod in a chamber. There they left them until the stone was entirely ready and the water of paradise was poured through. Then they would take one vial with its one part and pour it over the stone, mixing them well together, and place it back on the tripod. They left the remaining eight vials in the furnace until that one part was fixed <term>Fixed: A state where a substance becomes solid and resistant to evaporation by fire</term> with the stone. Then they would give it another part, doing as before; and so on with the third and fourth, until the stone had absorbed all nine parts and they were fixed with it. 

This seems to me the best method, and better than if everything were poured in at once; it shortens the work and happens very quickly. For the stone is not overwhelmed as it would be if it received all nine parts at once. It saves time, though it involves a little more labor to repeatedly take the vessel from the furnace, open it, and close it again—nonetheless, it is the best method for the work. 

<margin>The words of the Ancients regarding the pouring of those nine parts over one part of the stone.</margin>Regarding the pouring of these nine parts over one part of the stone, as I taught you before, the Ancients spoke thus when teaching their sons who understood their words: "Let nine parts of May dew <note>original: *roris Maialis*; dew collected in May was believed to be impregnated with celestial or "astral" spirit</note> be taken, each part enclosed in a vial and kept in a fever-like heat <note>a gentle, consistent warmth similar to body temperature</note>, until the lowest world <note>original: *mundus infimus*; an alchemical metaphor for the base matter at the bottom of the vessel</note> is white and dry. Then sprinkle the lowest world with one part of the May dew, and then another part, until the world flows like oil."

Thus, my son, understand that the Ancients prepared their Stone in various ways, and in the end, all were proven effective. ### CHAPTER XXXII.

Thus it is also clear through the aforementioned reasoning that the first method is the best. 

For in the separation of the elements, a violent fire is sometimes applied—specifically when the elements of fire are to be distilled, the material must glow; and when the dross is burned away from the earth, that is, when the earth is <term>calcined</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or oxidize it</note> in a **reverberatory furnace**, the earth must glow and be burned before the earth will become white. In this way, the good is often burned along with the bad, and it becomes part of the glass, and one is lost with the other. Therefore, the first [method] is best because of the great uncertainty [of the latter]; for the dross ought to be digested gradually. For <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry," whose Latinized name represents a corpus of essential alchemical texts</note> says: *The dragon shall eat its own tail, and shall be nourished by its own poison.* <note>The Ouroboros symbol, representing the cyclical nature of the work where the matter is purified by its own inherent forces.</note> And <term>Danthyaus</term> says: *The black raven shall brood its eggs until the chicks become white through old age.* <note>The "Raven's Head" is a symbol for the black stage; its transition to white chicks represents the shift to the albedo stage.</note>

Indeed, my son, what are the dregs? <note>original: "fæces"</note> <margin>What the dregs are.</margin> The dregs are a moisture ordained by God, from which whatever exists beneath the celestial course <note>i.e., everything on Earth under the heavens</note> is nourished, and which keeps those things in their own essence. In all things, there is a perfect, elemental natural heat, or fire; <margin>A double fire exists in all things: one natural, the other non-natural.</margin> and there is also an imperfect, non-natural heat and fire, which is a consumable and combustible fire. These two are permitted to exist together: and as long as that imperfect fire does not acquire more "bad accidents," <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities or external conditions that can change.</note> it preserves the thing in its essence, and is necessarily present so that the thing may remain in its being. However, when that imperfect fire acquires any bad accidents alongside itself—which are also hot and imperfect—and they are secretly mixed together, they become so inflamed that they burn, destroy, and kill the thing in which they reside, whether they be men, cattle, herbs, trees, or whatever is contained beneath the celestial course. Likewise, there are also two kinds of waters <margin>This double nature exists in all things—namely, natural water and the water of the clouds.</margin> in all things composed of the four elements: one is called natural water and elemental water, and it is perfect, good, and eternal; and then there is another water, the water of the clouds, which is imperfect and mixed with the elemental water. This water is necessary for the thing to acquire nourishment and moisture: and it will easily keep the thing in its essence as long as no further water of the clouds is added to it. But when more is added, they mix together and dampen and submerge that thing, to the point that it is entirely destroyed and dies. And what has been said about fire and water <margin>The same is to be understood regarding air and earth.</margin> is also to be understood regarding air and earth. If these dregs were not in the elements, all things would be perfect, spiritual, and subtle—the state for which God first ordained them—and there would be no death, as is correctly taught in the *Work on Vegetation* <note>original: "opere vegetabili"</note>. If you require more on the dregs and the diseases of the elements, look for Chapter 16 of the *Work on Vegetation*; there you will be perfectly taught concerning these things.

Now my son may ask: when a thing is destroyed in this manner, where then does that perfection remain which was within the thing? You have much on this matter in Chapter 29 of the *Work on Vegetation*. Look for that, and there you will be perfectly and rightly taught in what way "like attracts its like"; but I will add a few things on this matter here. Know that when any thing has died—whether it be a sensing being or devoid of sense, whether man, beast, animal, herb, or tree—whatever is composed of the four elements, when it has been destroyed, then the spirit of life is separated from it <margin>In destruction, like returns to its like.</margin> and returns to its like, from which it first took its origin, as in the *Work on Vegetation*, etc. And also the elements return to their like, from where they first arose. Indeed, over an even longer span of time, they are made so subtle <note>refined or finely divided</note> by the air and the heat of the Sun that the bones become like a fine powder, which is imperceptible between the fingers. And Nature performs this, as we see daily before our eyes; where does the stinking matter remain, except that it is consumed and reduced to nothing? Thus the element of earth is purified and made white like snow, so subtle that it cannot be felt. Nature performs this by itself, and rectifies <note>purifies or refines</note> the elements by itself, as was taught before.

Thus it becomes clear that there is no need for any separation of the elements in our stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>, nor any washing or purification in the Mercury, except only that it should be tested to see if it is good, by passing it through rabbit skin <note>original: "leporinum corium"; a common alchemical method for straining mercury to remove physical impurities</note> or some other soft leather.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>All separation of the elements should be avoided as unnecessary.</margin>
Why then have I said these things to my son? Only so that he may know it is not necessary to separate the elements in our work, nor to <term>rectify</term> <note>original: "rectificare"; in alchemy, this refers to purifying a substance by repeated distillation or refinement</note> them, based on the reasons given previously. The dross is dried into nothingness. Furthermore, the rectification cannot be achieved by the force of fire, as has been demonstrated, because of the destruction of the elements. For they escape the craftsman by fire, either leaving the vessels or being lost during the pouring from one to another, so that some element is lost. Then, when he wishes to join them back together, he inevitably has too much of one or too little of another; or, a wicked moisture from the water creeps in, which entirely corrupts the work. Therefore, my son, flee from every separation of the elements as something unnecessary.

*On the Oil of Metals.*

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

<margin>Oil can be drawn from all metals without the separation of elements.</margin>
Next, let my son know that oil can be extracted from all metals without the separation of elements, and without any washing or purification. Instead, it must be done with <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; typically nitric acid or a mixture of acids used to dissolve metals</note>, and a ferment must be applied by he who wishes to prepare oil from the <term>imperfect bodies</term> <note>Base metals like lead, tin, copper, and iron, as opposed to "perfect" gold and silver</note>. But I would not advise you to make oil from any imperfect bodies except from <term>Saturn</term> <note>Lead</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin</note>—one for the red work and the other for the white. There are many and varied ways of making oil, and they were discovered for the sake of saving time, because men could not wait for the duration of the <term>Great Works</term> <note>The long, traditional process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> in their haste to gain a quick profit. However, there is more danger in this work than in the Great Work, and also more operations to perform. For here, strong waters must be distilled, and much <term>sublimation</term> <note>Heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note> must be done, and many various labors must be carried out. Thus, this oil must be prepared with great labor, care, and expense.

### CHAPTER XL.

<margin>The Elixir.</margin>
There were also others who took one mark of **Silver**, and amalgamated it with **Mercury**, pressing the silver-amalgam through a linen cloth. ### Chapter 41.

<margin>Oil for the white work</margin>
<margin>from strong water and from the calxes of Jupiter.</margin>
<margin>The dead heads.</margin>
There are also some who have taken one pound of Roman vitriol <note>original: "vitrioli Roma."; likely a high-quality iron or copper sulfate</note>, one pound of arsenic sublimated to white, and likewise one pound of Mercury sublimated to white—as is taught in the mineral work—one pound of the calxes of Jupiter <note>original: "calcium Iouis"; Jupiter is the alchemical name for Tin</note>, and as much saltpeter as all the rest combined. Crush all these together, then grind them with distilled vinegar upon a stone so finely that a painter could paint with them using a brush. Then you shall dry it in the Sun, or over ashes. 

When this is done, divide all the material into three equal parts. From the first part, prepare a strong water <term>aqua fortis; a corrosive mineral acid, typically nitric acid</term> as it is usually made. Put the second part into a glass vessel and pour that strong water over it; then distil the strong water as is appropriate. Then put the third part into a glass vessel and pour over it all the strong water that came from the two previous distillations: distil the strong water again, as before. 

Then you shall pulverize those three "dead heads" <note>original: "capita mortua"; the solid residues left in the retort after distillation</note> and pour that strong water over them into a large glass vessel, with the alembic <note>the top part of a still</note> firmly sealed with lute <note>original: "superlutato"; a paste used to make joints airtight</note>, and so tightly compressed that nothing can escape. Place this in a furnace in a pot with ashes, with the receiver well-sealed nearby. Let it sit in this way for 8 days and nights before you light the fire, so that it may be properly incorporated into its "earth" or dregs. 

Then light the fire and apply a gentle heat for 24 hours; then for 24 hours a slightly stronger heat; and for 24 hours an even stronger heat, so that after those 24 hours the material begins to glow faintly. Keep it at that moderate glow for 24 hours. When these are finished, increase the fire so that it glows as if you intended to work iron, and keep it at that heat continuously for 3 hours. It does not matter if your glass vessel melts or liquefies. Then let it cool, remove it from the fire, and open your receiver carefully. 

You now have a water more excellent than the Sun <note>The Sun refers to Gold; this "water" is claimed to be more powerful or valuable than gold itself</note>. But as for that "dead head" or the dregs that remained, pulverize them. Grind that powder on a stone with distilled vinegar as finely as if it were to be used for painting; put the ground material into a stone pitcher and pour a large quantity of distilled vinegar over it. Place it for 8 days and nights in a bath <note>a "balneum" or water-bath used for steady, gentle heat</note>, and stir it every day with a wooden spoon. Then let it settle and pour the clear liquid from the top into another clean stone pitcher. 

Distil the vinegar, and in the bottom there will remain for you a remarkable white salt. Crush this again into powder, put it in the pitcher, and pour distilled vinegar on it once more. Place it in a boiling bath as described above, and work in this manner until your "earth" <note>the solid matter</note> leaves no more dregs behind...

Then place it on the fire, first a small fire and gradually a stronger one, until your crucible glows slightly, yet in such a way that the salt or the Silver does not melt. Keep it in that glow for 24 hours. Then let it cool, break open the crucible, and place it in a vessel with clean water; all the salt will dissolve at once over the ashes, and the Silver plates will sink to the bottom. Gradually pour off the water. Take out the plates and dry them; for they are as fragile as glass and black. Pulverize them in an iron mortar (and not a brass one), sift them, and if anything remains that is not calcined <term>Calcined: Reduced to a dry powder through the action of heat.</term>, set it again to be calcined as above, until all of it allows itself to be reduced to powder. Then grind that powder with common water or honey and honeycomb until it is smooth to the touch. When the powder is ground, put it into glass dishes, basins, or jars, and having poured in clean hot water, shake and mix it well. Let it settle, and gradually pour off the warm water from the top. Pour in clean hot water again, shake, let it settle, and gradually pour off the clear water from the top. Or, pour clean cold water over it and let it heat over the ashes, doing as described above. Mix all the wash-waters together, and do this until the water flows off as clear as it was when poured in, and the Silver is clean, white, and bright like snow. Then let the dregs of all the poured-off water settle, and gradually pour the water off from the top...

<summary>This page concludes the purification of Mercury using Roman vitriol and distillation, then details the 'cementation' of Silver—a process of heating silver plates with salt for 24 hours to turn them into a brittle, black substance that is then ground and washed into a pure white powder.</summary>

## ON THE PERFECTION OF THE MASTERY

### A sharp lye made of *quicklime* and *potash*.

Take one part quicklime <note>original: "calcis vivae"</note>, two parts potash <note>original: "cineris clavellati"; literally "clubbed ashes"</note>, and pour over them four times their weight of strong, warm vinegar. Repeat this over the mixture until it can support a weight while being strained in a lye-basin <note>original: "concha lixivii"; this refers to testing the density of the caustic solution</note>. Some people add a little Yemen alum <note>original: "aluminis iameni"</note> to the lime and ashes, and ammonium salt <note>sal ammoniac</note> at half the weight of the Yemen alum. This also helps with fixation <note><term>fixation</term>: an alchemical process where a volatile substance is treated so it can withstand fire without evaporating</note>.

### *Water of litharge*.

Take one part of a piece of litharge <note><term>litharge</term>: lead monoxide, a secondary mineral formed from the oxidation of galena ores</note>, a fourth part each of alkali salt and Yemen alum (measured against the weight of the aforementioned litharge), and half a part of ammonium salt. Dissolve the alum and alkali salt in double or triple their amount of vinegar in the manner described above, and stir three times every day until the whole appears dissolved and clear in this vinegar. Then distill it through a filter and save it for your work.

### *A Piece of Litharge*.

Take as much litharge as you wish and grind it strongly; wash it by pouring water from one vessel to another <note>original: "de paropside in paropsidem"</note> until the coarser parts are separated from the finer ones. Once these finer parts are dried, add to them their own weight of arsenic that has been sublimated once, and sublimate it from them twice. Afterward, make the whole descend through a "bearded" vessel <note>original: "botum barbatum"; likely a specific type of crucible or flask used for downward distillation</note> with oil inside, until a white piece descends, and the work will be done.

**Addition.** The whitening of litharge. Take a pound of litharge and grind it well; afterward take 5 pounds of salt and grind it well with the litharge, and place it in water for 9 days, stirring twice daily. Afterward, wash it well to remove the salt and dry it; and you will have whitened litharge, if it is done correctly.

### *Avicenna’s red water for dyeing the 4 white sublimated spirits*.

### CHAPTER I.

Take one ounce each of Egyptian vitriol <note>original: "atramenti Aegyptiaci"; a metallic sulfate</note> and iron filings <note>original: "limaturae faulec"</note>, a third of an ounce of verdigris <note>original: "floris aeris"; literally "flower of copper"</note>, and a quarter ounce of white alum used for whitening clothes (I think this is rock alum or burnt wine lees). Also take half an ounce each of sulfur, yellow arsenic <note>orpiment</note> and red arsenic <note>realgar</note>, Armenian stone <note>likely azurite</note>, and lapis lazuli; a quarter pound of clarified white honey; ammonium salt, and rock salt...

And it is better that you distill the vinegar from iron until it distills reddish, and similarly distill vinegar from vitriol; then join both together, and color whatever you wish with them.

The waters that produce red without repeated distillation are: the water of sublimated <term>Tutty</term><note>Zinc oxide, often found as a crust in smelting furnaces.</note>, and the water of <term>hematite</term><note>original: "sedine lapidis siue hæmatitis." However, the "water of copper" alone is better than these, and the "water of iron" is stronger still when it is sublimated and turned red. If you place it in vinegar, it will become a red water like blood, and the color is fixed. Although these two waters involve a tedious process, they are nonetheless more effective than the shorter methods.

### CHAPTER VI.

Take four parts of quicklime <note>original: *calcis viuæ*; calcium oxide, a caustic substance</note>, three parts of native sulfur, and pour over them ten parts (elsewhere said to be four) of vinegar reddened with copper filings. Once this is done, take one ounce each of green vitriol <note>original: *chalcanthi viridis*; iron sulfate</note> and red sublimated arsenic, one pound of vinegar, and half an ounce of red ink-pigment—if you can find it. If you cannot find it, sublimate <note>To heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again.</note> green or yellow vitriol with pure water; for when the water is distilled, the red ink-pigment will remain at the bottom of the cucurbit <note>The bottom heating vessel of a distillation apparatus.</note>. ### CHAPTER VII.

Take one part of *faulec* <term>faulec: a medieval alchemical term, usually referring to iron filings</term> and pour over it twice its weight of strong vinegar. Let it sit inside until it is thoroughly reddened. Then, distill it through an alembic until the vinegar distills red, and color whatever you wish with it. Do the same with copper filings until the vinegar is thoroughly green. Soak whatever you wish in this, then roast it, and it will be perfectly reddened with a firm, permanent color.

**Addition.** Along with the filings of *faulec* (which I believe to be iron), add reddened vitriol, and you will distill a fixed, red, philosophical oil.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Take *duenec* <term>duenec: an Arabic-derived alchemical term often referring to antimony, or sometimes vitriol</term> and prepared sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride</note> in equal amounts, as much as you wish. Grind them with oil made from egg yolks until they have the consistency of marrow. Then, roast this with a light heat and store it. You may color whatever you wish with it for a permanent coloration.

## *Fixed White Philosophical Oil*

Take a piece of white <term>litharge</term> <note>original: "lithatgyrij albi" — lead monoxide, often used as a pigment or flux.</note>, and one pound of tin extracted with arsenic. File this into a fine powder and add to it two ounces each of sulfur and white separated arsenic, and four ounces of separated white Mercury. Grind all of these together forcefully with eight ounces of the water of prepared white <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "salis armoniaci" — ammonium chloride, used to clean metals or as a volatile agent.</note>. 

Then dry and roast it with a light heat, and powder it strongly. Place it in a sublimation vessel and <term>sublimate</term> <note>To heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then hardens again at the top of the vessel, leaving impurities behind.</note> it as many times as necessary until nothing more rises. Then "wax" <note>original: "cera" — to bring a substance to a soft, waxy consistency through the addition of liquid.</note> all of this which remains at the bottom of the sublimator with its own weight of the aforementioned water. 

Then throw the whole thing into twice its weight of vinegar (distilled three times) in which two pounds of white and "feathery" <term>Yemeni alum</term> <note>original: "aluminis iameni" — a specific high-quality alum, possibly from Yemen, known for its crystalline, hair-like structure.</note> have been placed. Every day you must stir it strongly three times until everything is dissolved in the said vinegar; or, place that vinegar with the substances in a "place of dissolution," which is better. 

Once these are dissolved, distill them through an <term>alembic</term> <note>A classic alchemical still consisting of two vessels and a tube for distilling liquids.</note> seven times over their own dregs. A very clear white water will come out or be distilled. Use this for the final "waxing" of the bodies and spirits that have been calcined to white; they will be waxed very quickly with God’s help and His power. 

For this is the **permanent white water**, the **clear water**, the **Virgin’s Milk**, the **Vinegar of the Philosophers**, the calming and penetrating water, and the water that separates and joins. Hide it, therefore, and work with it. If you quench plates of purified copper in it, they will become silver better than that which is extracted from mines.

### *Another way for the fixed white philosophical oil.*

Take white lead <term>ceruse: a white pigment, usually basic lead carbonate</term> made from a piece of the whitest litharge <term>litharge: a secondary mineral form of lead monoxide</term>, and white lead of Jupiter <term>Jupiter: the alchemical name for the metal tin</term> extracted with arsenic—one pound of each. Wax <term>ceration: an alchemical process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</term> them and dissolve them in double their weight of prepared water of sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux or reagent</term>. Then distill this through an alembic <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of two retorts and a tube</term>, and soak in it one or two pounds of white calcined and sublimated quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note>. Dissolve and distill through the alembic again and again until a very clear white water is distilled. Then use this for the final waxing of substances into the white stage <note>The "white stage" or albedo represents the purification of the material in the Great Work.</note>.

In many books, the conclusion of this fixed white oil is found as follows: after the very clear white water has been distilled, it coagulates with a good coagulation, and it will be formed into a very white plate. Wax this plate with a good and final waxing using sal ammoniac and animal oil (or oil of egg yolks) that has been previously rectified until white. Then cast this upon separated copper <term>separated copper: copper that has been purified of its impurities or "dross"</term>, and it will become silver better than that which is taken from the mines. And if you quench a plate of separated copper in the aforementioned water before it coagulates, it will become the finest silver. This fixed white philosophical oil is indeed the fixed white philosophical animal oil; it is an oil that clears, penetrates, sprouts, separates, and joins. With this oil, every volatile substance is held back from flight <note>In alchemy, "flight" refers to a substance vaporizing or escaping during heating.</note>.

### *Fixed red philosophical oil.*

Take one pound of yellow sulfur <note>original: "sulphure citrino"</note> and vaporize it with one pound of quicklime <term>quicklime: calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance</term> and four pounds of the strongest white vinegar. Then renew these same ingredients over this sulfur three times. Afterward, renew the sulfur and the lime and dry it until the vinegar itself is perfectly reddened. Then divide this vinegar in half. In one half, dissolve a fourth part; put in filings of iron and copper that have descended with arsenic, and let the whole thing stand in it for seven days. Stir it twice or thrice every day. On the eighth day, separate the vinegar from the filings. ### CONCERNING THE PERFECTION OF THE MAGISTERY

Then take six ounces of sal ammoniac, six ounces of **oil of eggs** <note>an oil extracted from egg yolks</note> that has been distilled seven times or well-purified, and six ounces of the aforementioned white stone. After it has all been well-kneaded into a mass, place it and leave it in a glass vessel for the space of four days. Then throw the whole mass into one pound of egg-white water and seal the vessel in **horse dung** <note>in fimo; alchemists used the natural heat of decomposing manure for long-term, gentle incubation</note>. Leave it to dissolve for fifteen days, and it will be dissolved into a water as clear and white as milk. And this is the complete White Oil of the Philosophers.

Water or oil is also made from blood, eggs, and hair, and other things, which is also called the "Oil of the Philosophers."

# ARISTOTLE
<note>This text is part of the "Pseudo-Aristotle" tradition, where medieval alchemical works were attributed to the Greek philosopher to grant them authority.</note>

### A red fixing oil.
Take 1 and a half pounds of Roman vitriol <term>Roman vitriol: usually refers to iron(II) sulfate or copper sulfate</term>, 1 pound each of sal ammoniac <term>ammonium chloride</term>, saltpeter, and good red cinnabar <term>mercury sulfide</term>. Let a "strong water" <term>aqua fortis: a corrosive mineral acid, typically nitric acid</term> be made from these: but discard the "wanton" part, that is, the phlegm <note>original: "phlegma"; refers to the watery, inactive first stage of distillation</note>. In this strong water, quench glowing pieces of old bricks, or fresh bricks that have never been touched by water, and let the vessel be closed until the material has cooled. Afterward, let the pieces of brick be extracted and pulverized, and placed in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel</note> with an <term>alembic</term> <note>a distillation cap</note> placed on top. Distill the water or oil until the dregs remain entirely dry. In this liquid, dissolve well-purified Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> over a slow fire, and it will be "fixed" <note>rendered non-volatile or solid</note> and turned red. The material will be liquid, like theriac <note>a thick medicinal paste</note> or butter. Of this, perform one "projection" <note>the act of casting an alchemical substance upon a base metal</note> upon ten parts of pure Moon <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for Silver</note>, and it will be converted into the fixed color of the Sun <note>original: "Solis," the alchemical name for Gold</note>, passing every judgment and test; however, it will be deficient in weight unless the Silver is first fixed.

### Red water or oil:
Take: black ink <note>or vitriol</note>, reddened vitriol, a little sal ammoniac, and an equal amount of iron filings. Put them together and pour vinegar over them. Leave them for 15 days, and distill ten or more times until the vinegar distills red as blood, and at each turn, renew the ink. Thus far the addition.

Likewise, if after the medicine has been roasted according to the last process and its weight is completed by roasting, if it is soaked with the water of white purified sal ammoniac and sublimated in an aludel <note>A pear-shaped pot or tube used in the sublimation process</note> until nothing more rises from it, and afterward it descends and is processed further as was said, the medicine itself will be better and stronger, whether it is for the white or for the red work. ### Rectification of the Hidden Stone.
Our hidden, blessed stone is from a living thing <note>original: *de re animata*</note>, just as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> said: "It is true without falsehood, certain and most sure." <note>This is a famous opening line from the Emerald Tablet, a foundation text of alchemy.</note> You shall gently sublime the subtle from the dense with great skill, and let it ascend from the earth to heaven, and again descend to the earth until it has been well rectified <note>purified through repeated distillation or sublimation</note>. Additions.

### Composition of Elixirs:
Take <note>original: *R.*, the abbreviation for *Recipe*</note> prepared orpiment <term>orpiment: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral once used as a pigment and in alchemy</term>, sublimated three times; and an equal amount of purified mercury, also sublimated three times; and an equal amount of purified calx of the Moon <term>calx of the Moon: silver that has been reduced to a fine powder or oxide through heat</term>; and an equal amount of purified sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used in alchemy as a flux and for cleaning metals</term>, sublimated three times. Mix these together upon a porphyry stone <note>a hard, purple-red stone used for grinding chemicals</note>, and grind them together and dry them in the sun. Then grind them again and add water of tartar <note>a solution made from the potassium bitartrate crystals found in wine barrels</note>, and grind well, and dry in the sun. Then grind again, and add water, and afterwards dry; and do this ten or twelve times, until you make it so that it is like an ointment, and so that the parts are made subtle with one another by grinding, imbibing <note>soaking or saturating with liquid</note>, and drying.

And if you wish, in place of the water of tartar you can use the water of egg whites, or rectified water of blood, or water of the Moon <note>likely a silver nitrate solution or silver-infused water</note>, or of tin. And after you have imbibed and dried your medicine ten or twelve times, as was said, grind it again, and add some of the water with which you previously soaked it, until it is softer than paste. Place it in a glass vial within an earthenware vessel called a "Dissolver" <note>original: *Solutorium*</note>, and seal it well with a linen cloth and earth or paste. Place it in very warm horse dung <note>a standard alchemical technique where the natural fermentation of manure provided a steady, gentle heat</note>, and cover it all around, and leave it in the dung until the whole is dissolved into water. From every seventh to seventh, or eighth or ninth day, renew it with warmer dung.

And if you wish to heat your dung, pour cold water over it and it will grow warm <note>the addition of water can re-trigger the biological decomposition and heat production in manure</note>. Do this for all things that are strong and hard to resolve and convert into water, whenever you wish to dissolve them. And if it should happen that within four days or more they do not wish to dissolve, place it upon marble and grind it again with water on top, and dry it well, and place it again in the sun; grind and add water and dry, doing as we said before. Then place it to dissolve in the dung, as we said. And if it should happen that your medicine becomes dried out, take it out and grind it, and add water, as was said above...

...[the matter] is finished, and dry it in the Sun, as has been said: and do this often until the matter is thoroughly oily. Then set it to dissolve <note>original: *resoluendum*; the process of breaking a solid down into a liquid state, often through gentle heat or moisture</note>, as was stated above. And when it has been dissolved into water, place the vial in a distiller filled with ashes up to the joint of the lid, and let the vial remain uncovered. Close the distiller and seal the joint with clay <note>original: *luta*; "luting" involved sealing vessel joints with a paste of clay, dung, or hair to prevent the escape of vapors</note>. Afterward, create a small fire beneath it, just as is done when making rose water.

Receive and save that which distills, and maintain the fire for 24 hours or more, until the medicine is dry and you no longer see any smoke exiting through the pipe of the distiller. Then remove the fire and let it cool.

It is beneficial for the vial containing the medicine to have a wide mouth, so that the smoke may exit more easily and the vial does not break. Then remove the medicine from the vial and grind it upon a marble slab, and add onto it the water which you previously distilled from it. Grind it well and dry it in the Sun, as before, and set it to dissolve in dung <note>original: *fimus*; horse dung was used by alchemists as a source of steady, gentle "digestive" heat</note>.

And if there is not enough of the water that was distilled from it, add some of the water with which you previously soaked it when you first set it to dissolve. Know that it will dissolve in much less time than it did the first time.

When it is dissolved, place it in the distiller, and congeal and dry it just as you did before, and save the water which you distill from it. Then grind it again, and add the water over it and dry it in the Sun as before, and set it to dissolve and afterward to congeal. Do this four, five, or six times, until the whole substance becomes fixed <term>fixed: a substance that has become non-volatile and can endure high heat without evaporating</term> and resistant to the fire. For you can dissolve and congeal it so many times that nothing more will distill from it when you attempt to congeal it, and then it is said to be "fixed."

Know that when you have dissolved your medicine four or five times, you should filter it through a cloth <note>original: *per filtrum*</note> and then place it in a glass vial. Place the vial in a pot full of ashes, and let the vial be closed lightly with a linen cloth, so that a small amount of smoke may exit. Maintain a slow fire beneath the pot for a day and a night or more, until your medicine is congealed into a white stone, clear as crystal; then keep it. But note that the method of congealing in a distiller is safer than the other.

When your medicine is congealed, grind it and pour over it rectified <note>purified or distilled</note> oil of blood, or oil of eggs, or common oil distilled seven times with sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, used to "open" metals and minerals</term> and quicklime <note>original: *calce viua*; calcium oxide</note>, or the "oil of the three species" (or spirits), or the "white oil of the Philosophers." Do not add too much of it. And afterward put...

Grind it well, bring it to a waxy state, and dry it in the sun many times, then set it to dissolve. Next, congeal it as before. Afterward, grind it and pour the distilled water over it, along with the "oil of three kinds" or the white <term>oil of the Philosophers</term> <note>A term used for a highly refined, secret liquid base used by master alchemists.</note>. *Another composition of the Elixir, which is said to be better.*
Take one pound of prepared <term>calx of Luna</term> (silver), three ounces of prepared and thrice-sublimated <term>sulfur</term>, three ounces of prepared and thrice-sublimated <term>orpiment</term>, and one pound of prepared and thrice-sublimated <term>Mercury</term>. Grind all these well together, add the water of prepared and thrice-sublimated <term>sal ammoniac</term>, and dry it over a small charcoal fire.

Having completed these things, take <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "salem armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, a vital salt in alchemy used for dissolving metals.</note> that has been <term>sublimated</term> <note>heated until it turns to vapor and solidifies again, a process used for purification.</note> three times, dissolved, distilled through the alembic, and coagulated. Repeat this process of dissolving, distilling, and coagulating a third time. If it is dissolved seven times with the "water of life," and distilled and coagulated each time, and finally resolved into water, it will dissolve all <term>calcined</term> bodies, filings, and even scorched materials. With God's help and His power, it will dissolve all calcined and sublimated spirits in a wonderful solution in a <term>crucible</term> over the fire within a single hour.

->The Composition of the Water of Life, Complete and Perfect.<-

Let us compose our "philosophical water" with God's help and His power. Take six ounces of the water of sal ammoniac (dissolved and distilled at least three times) and six (or seven) ounces of the aforementioned rectified oil. Mix these two, and then moisten six ounces of the aforementioned crystalline plate upon a porphyry stone or a glass slab, adding it little by little until it has "drunk" it all up. When it has absorbed everything, let it ferment in a similar glass vessel for three days. On the fourth day, cast this substance into two pounds of the aforementioned water of life placed in a dissolving vessel. Seal the mouth well so that it cannot breathe, and "bury" it <note>original: "inhuma"; likely referring to placing the vessel in a warm "philosopher's dung" or a sand bath to provide gentle, even heat.</note> for fifteen days. On the sixteenth day, you will find the plate dissolved into a water as white as milk. 

This is the complete Water of Life, the "Oil of the Philosophers," the "penetrating and clarifying water" that lights candles and illuminates the house, through which all Philosophers have been sustained. With this water, every volatile thing is restrained from flight <note>This means the solvent "fixes" the chemicals, preventing them from evaporating away when heated.</note>—namely Mercury, sulfur, arsenic, and the <term>eagle</term> <note>original: "aquila"; an alchemical code name for sal ammoniac.</note>. By this I mean Mercury, sulfur, and arsenic that have been sublimated and calcined, all of which were described above.

->ARISTOTLE<-

<page-num>116</page-num>

### Additions.

*The rectification of common oil for the waxing of spirits and for making an entrance.* <note>The "waxing" (ceration) refers to softening a substance to a wax-like state; "entrance" (ingressum) refers to the ability of a substance to penetrate or fuse with a metal.</note> Take as much common oil as you wish, and mix it thoroughly with quicklime <note>original: "calce viua"</note> until it has the consistency of flour. Some also add common salt and salt of tartar <term>salt of tartar: potassium carbonate, often used as a flux in alchemy</term>, and leave it for two days. Afterward, distill it through an alembic, and renew the quicklime over the distilled liquid. Distill it four times until it is no longer combustible.

Others first boil the oil with a large quantity of water, so that the impurities sink to the bottom. Then they strain the oil that floats on top and place it with quicklime in a distilling vessel. They distill it once and keep it in a closed container.

*Incombustible oil for the waxing of the White Elixir.*

Take Mercury that has been fixed by circulation <term>circulation: a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</term> with the "water of the hidden white stone" rectified from the lime of barks <note>original: "calce corticú"</note>. Place this in a dissolving furnace <note>original: "furno resolutorio"</note> with a third part of the Water of Mercury. On the fourth day, it will dissolve into a white, fixed, incombustible oil. It cannot be purified in any other way except by the separation of the water through distillation; the oil remains at the bottom of the vessel. It cannot be distilled further except with the greatest effort because of its "fixation" <note>In alchemy, "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, for it resists and persists against the fire. With this oil, any sublimated Mercury can be fixed, and it dissolves all bodies because it is of a metallic nature. The Great Elixirs are waxed with it. It should be kept well in a warm place near the fire because it is of a warm nature; if it were placed in a cold place, it would congeal into a hard, meltable stone similar to white marble, which could not afterwards be dissolved or brought back to a liquid state due to its cooling.

Note that there is a certain method of distilling oil using small, polished rods placed at the bottom of the cucurbit <term>cucurbit: the gourd-shaped lower vessel of a still</term>. These rods reach the top, and the oil ascends along them; otherwise, it would not rise. These rods must be very small and peeled. I believe Aristotle speaks of this distillation when he says: "Now you should know that the distillation of oil is performed in three ways," which is found in the chapter on the Great L. <note>Possibly referring to a specific book or section, such as the "Lumen" or Light</note>

But you should know that Razi <note>original: "Rafi" — a reference to the Persian alchemist Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi</note> certainly speaks of that distillation with myrtle rods in his *Books of the 70* and his *30 Words*. In the *Book of the 70*, he says: "Thus also the oil, while you follow the footsteps of another, will flow." <note>original: "Sic etiam oleum, dum aliena sequaris vestigia manabit."</note>

### *The Composition of the Blessed Elixir.*

Let us therefore compose our blessed Elixir with God’s help and His power. Take: 2 pounds of sublimated and calcined mercury <term>mercury</term> <note>original: Mercurij; here referring to chemically purified quicksilver</note>, 1 pound each of sublimated and calcined sulfur and arsenic <note>original: fulph. & arsenici; these minerals were considered the "parents" of all metals</note>, and 13 ounces of the previously mentioned "philosophical animal water" <note>original: aqua animalis philosophice; a specialized alchemical solvent, often distilled from organic matter</note>, which has been composed and rectified. With this water, drench the aforementioned spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" refers to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur that can be vaporized by heat</note> little by little upon a porphyry stone <term>porphyry</term> <note>original: porfidú; a very hard purple-red stone used as a flat surface for grinding pigments and chemicals</note> or in a glass bowl <term>paropside</term> <note>original: paropside vitrea; a shallow dish or side-plate</note>, which is better, using a glass pestle until it has drunk the whole amount. 

When this is done, place all of it into a sublimation vessel <term>aludel</term> <note>original: aludel; a pear-shaped pot used for the process of sublimation</note> with an alembic <term>alembic</term> <note>original: alembico; a still-head used for distilling and collecting vapors</note> placed on top, along with its receiver, well-sealed with the "lute of the mastery" <note>original: luto magisterij; an airtight sealant made of clay, hair, or dung to prevent vapors from escaping</note> so that it may in no way breathe. Then place the sublimation vessel upon the furnace <term>athanor</term> <note>original: athanor; a "philosopher's furnace" designed to provide steady, even heat over long periods</note>, and make a light fire from coals underneath, until all the moisture has fallen into the receiver. Afterward, strengthen it to a moderate fire for about six hours, and then let the vessel cool. 

When it has cooled, extract what is inside and place it in the glass bowl. If any of it has risen up <note>sublimated to the top of the vessel</note>, gently return it to its dregs <note>original: fæces; the solid remains or sediment at the bottom</note> using the glass pestle, returning to it all the water that was distilled from it. Afterward, give it another 13 ounces of the aforementioned philosophical water to drink, and when it has drunk it all, return it to be sublimated as before. 

If the substance should be slow to soak or "drink," roast it in a wide-mouthed sublimation vessel, always with the alembic on top and its receiver well-sealed so it does not breathe; do this with a slow fire until it drinks it all up, and then sublimate as you did before. For the third time, return any risen material to the bottom and give it another 13 ounces of the water to drink, and return its own water to it similarly as before by gently grinding until it has drunk it all, and then sublimate as before. 

On the fourth time, return only its own distilled water to it, and sublimate or distill. Do this from then on as many times as necessary, always returning the water that distills from it and returning what rises to the top back down to the bottom, until absolutely nothing more is distilled from it. 

When this is done, you will find at the bottom of the vessel a crystalline plate—fixed, penetrating, deep-reaching, staining, and permanent. One part of this, if projected upon 50 parts of Venus <note>original: Veneris; the alchemical name for copper</note>, will transmute it into the truest silver. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> said in his secret: "one over a thousand" <note>meaning one part of the elixir could potentially transform a thousand parts of base metal</note>. 

I entreat you by the covenant of the Lord not to show this secret to anyone except our "son" <note>In alchemical tradition, a "son" is a worthy student or initiate into the secret arts</note>; and whoever is worthy of this hidden mystery shall be our son. May God make the burden light for you. You, however, when you have been exalted above all...

# BOOK OF THE PERFECT MASTERY, WHICH IS CALLED THE LUMINOUS LIGHT, AND TRULY SO, BECAUSE IN IT THE OBSCURE SAYINGS
*of the Philosophers in the alchemical art are best revealed.*
*It is also called the Flower of Flowers by Arnaldus de Villanova, far more correct and better than those printed until now.*

<image-desc>Decorative initial capital 'S' with foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>KNOW, dearest friend, that in every created thing under heaven, there are <term>four elements</term> <note>The classic Greek elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, then believed to be the building blocks of all matter</note>, present not by sight, but by their power. Because of this, our philosophers have handed down this knowledge under the veil of the "science of elements." Some have worked by following the literal meaning, using blood, hair, eggs, urine, and other things, so that they might first extract the four elements from them and complete the work with these. They do this by separating through <term>distillation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to create vapor and then cooling that vapor to collect it as a liquid</note> first the clear water from the aforementioned materials, then a yellow oil on the surface—which is said to contain fire and air—while the black earth remains at the bottom. Afterward, they wash and whiten the earth with the water by <term>imbibing</term> <note>Gradually soaking a solid with liquid</note> it, boiling it, and distilling that water so many times until the earth is whitened. Then they return its oil to it, prepared by fire, by soaking and distilling until the aforementioned earth drinks it all—namely the water, the oil, and the <term>tincture</term> <note>A concentrated essence or spirit of a substance</note>—until their vision is fulfilled. Afterward, they take this earth or "stone" and cast it upon molten metal, specifically upon copper or another...
