...else, and in short, they find nothing, because the whole thing is imaginary. And yet they act according to what the <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: *philosophi*; in this context, the ancient and medieval authorities on alchemy</note> say in their books according to the letter, and so they have fallen into error, not finding the entrance. And the cause of those errors is that they worked in unsuitable material: because it is certain that nothing is generated from a man except a man, and from a horse except a horse. Since, therefore, those materials are utterly foreign to the nature of metals, it is impossible for generation to occur in metals from them: because metals are not generated except from their own specific <term>seeds</term> <note>original: *spermatibus*; the essential generative substance that gives rise to a specific substance</note>. Therefore, one must seek what the seed of metals is, and thus we will have the entire mastery: because nothing is found in a thing that is not already in it. Now, metals are not found in hair, or such things. 

It is said, however, that the seed of metals is <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurius*; alchemists believed mercury was the "mother" or fluid principle of all metals</note>, and their origin, and this is certain. All the philosophers have said this, and both practice and reason show it to be true, as I will explain below. But the aforementioned things—namely blood, hair, and the like—are not Mercury; therefore, metals or their <term>transmutation</term> <note>original: *transmutatio*; the changing of one metal into another, usually base metal into gold</note> cannot be made from them. Those things are not our <term>Stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the alchemist's work</note>, even though they are written about as examples. 

Certain others take the four <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *spiritus*; volatile substances that vaporize when heated</note>, because they are named so literally: namely sulfur, arsenic, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and mercury. They are called spirits because they flee from fire and fly away in smoke. And they take these in place of the four elements, seeing that the philosophers say in their books that the science is in the spirits. They <term>sublimate</term> <note>original: *sublimatione*; the process of heating a substance to a vapor and collecting the deposit</note> these with a common sublimation, not a philosophical one, and they make them rise so that they are of an airy nature. 

Afterward, they fix them by <term>boiling</term> <note>original: *decoquendo*</note> and <term>calcining</term> <note>original: *calcinando*; heating to a high temperature to reduce to a powder</note>, so that they are of an earthy nature; afterward they <term>dissolve</term> <note>original: *soluunt*</note> them, so they are of a watery nature; afterward they <term>distill</term> <note>original: *destillant*</note> them, so they are of a fiery nature. They compose these according to the books literally, believing they possess the knowledge of the elements. And they cast the composite onto an <term>imperfect body</term> <note>base metals like lead or tin</note>, and they found nothing. 

This is one cause of their errors: because these are not the seed of perfect or imperfect metals, except for Mercury and sulfur (which is its coagulant), but we cannot reach that coagulation ourselves. For nature performs it through its own power and through a great span of time, which a human life cannot last. Therefore, it is impossible for the generation or transmutation of metals to happen from them. There are others who expend labor on sulfur and arsenic, and likewise on the combination of both, through various operations...

->## ARNALDUS ##<-

...But when they came to the **projection** <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" is cast upon base metals to transform them.</note>, they saw those substances burn up and vanish; they did not linger long within the bodies, but instead left the bodies even more impure than they had been before. The reason for this is that **sulfur** and **arsenic** are quickly consumed in the fire and reduced to charcoal. Therefore, neither on their own, nor joined to other bodies—such as blood, urine, or similar things—are they our **Stone**, or our medicine. 

Just as in the generation of a human being nothing is permitted except the **seed** <note>original: *spermatis*</note>, and likewise for all other natural generations, so our **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*, referring to the alchemical process</note> requires no joining of anything foreign. Some believe they will find the science in **salts** and **alums**, and they dissolve, **calcine** <term>calcine|to reduce a substance to powder through intense heat</term>, coagulate, melt, and prepare them. Others cast these alone upon imperfect bodies, while still others mix them with spirits or prepared bodies, but in the projection, they find nothing. The cause of their failure is the same as those mentioned before. 

Some believe they can select the medicine from metals alone; they prepare them by calcining, dissolving, and congealing, and then cast them upon a body, but they are deceived. Their error lies in the fact that they did not take the **seed** of the metals from the start, but rather the **body** as it exists in its own nature. 

Those who looked more closely considered **Mercury** to be the principle of metals and their very origin, cooked by a sulfurous heat. They **sublimated** Mercury by itself; afterward, they fixed, dissolved, and congealed it. Yet, coming to the projection, they found nothing. The cause of their error is this: just as the seed of a man brings no fruit unless it is cast into the **womb** <note>original: *matricem*</note> of the woman, so Mercury—which is the seed—is of no use unless it is cast into the "womb" of the bodies, that is, into **fixed lime** <term>calce|the powdery ash or "dead" body of a metal after it has been burned</term>, so that it may be nourished there. 

Some mixed this Mercury by **amalgamating** it with the body and washed it with fresh water for so long that the body appeared clean to them because of the brightness and nature of the Mercury. They cooked it until the end, so that it became hard, believing that the Mercury was mixed into such a body. But they found nothing; indeed, the body was more impure than it had been before, and the Mercury vanished. The cause of their error is that the **spirit** is not joined to the **body** except by the mediation of the **soul**. 

For the **soul** is the medium between the body and the spirit, joining them together. The soul, however, is the **ferment** <term>fermentum|a substance, like yeast in bread, that transforms and "leavens" the alchemical matter</term>. For just as the soul gives life to the human body, so the ferment gives life to the body that is already dead and entirely altered from its nature. Hence, the soul holds the leadership, exerting its powers. Therefore, regarding what the ferment is...

## ON THE PERFECTION OF THE MASTERY
<note>original: "DE PERF. MAGIST." — This is an abbreviation for *De Perfectione Magisterii*, referring to the completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note>

...as will be discussed below. Certain people have mixed **imperfect bodies** <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to metals. "Imperfect" metals are base metals like lead or tin that are subject to corrosion.</note> with **perfect bodies** <note>Perfect metals are gold and silver.</note>, and placed them to cook over a slow fire so they might be better united with one another. Afterward, they gradually strengthened the fire so that they might fix the non-fixed body <note>To "fix" a substance means to make a volatile element stable and resistant to heat.</note> with the help of the fire. By keeping it in the heat in this way, they **calcined** it <note>Reduced it to a powder through high heat.</note>, then later dissolved, congealed, and reduced it. Yet, when they finally performed an examination, they found nothing except the same pure body they had originally put in.

The cause of their errors is this: the corrupting element and the defect of imperfect bodies—namely, a **burning sulfurous earth**—is joined at the most minute level with the imperfect body, having adhered to it from the very beginning of its origin, and this prevents it from being perfected. Therefore, for the good part within the imperfect body to be perfected alongside a perfect body, the agent performing this must possess a double power: one by which it separates the burning sulfurous earth from the mixture, and another which converts that which has been separated into its own nature. 

However, a metal body in its **gross** <note>Solid or unrefined.</note> state cannot possess this power. Many have tried, and as if despairing of the science, they abandoned the **mastery** <note>The "Mastery" or Magisterium refers to the secret process of transmutation.</note> due to a weakness of understanding. 

Now, however, I want you to know that the matter of all metals, and their "seed," is **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius". To alchemists, this often refers to a philosophical principle of fluidity and metallic essence rather than just common quicksilver.</note> cooked and thickened in the belly of the earth by the decocting heat of sulfur. According to the variety and quantity of that sulfur in the earth, different metals are generated; nevertheless, their matter is always essentially one and the same, differing only by "accidents"—that is, by more or less cooking, whether burning or temperate. In this, all philosophers agree. 

It is certain that every thing is made from and consists of that into which it can be resolved; just as ice or snow, which is resolved into water by means of heat, exists because it came from water. But all metals can be converted into Mercury, as I will teach you below; they were therefore made from Mercury. 

In this way, the opinion of those who say "The species of metals cannot be transmuted" is resolved. This is indeed true, as they claim, **unless they are reduced to their primary matter.** <note>Primary matter refers to the fundamental substance from which the metals first formed.</note> Since reducing them to their primary matter is easy, as I shall show you below, transmutation is therefore both easy and possible. 

**Multiplication** <note>The process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical medicine.</note> is also possible in metals. For everything that grows and is born is multiplied and increases, as is evident in plants and animals; from a single grain, a thousand are made. Since metals are born and grow in the earth, it is therefore possible for them to be augmented infinitely. Thus the theory is clear; it follows that we should speak of the practice.

# ARNALD OF VILLANOVA

<page-num>222</page-num>

If we wish to reach the perfect mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the completion of the alchemical process</note>, it is necessary first that we have the **Philosophers' Stone** pure and clean, taken just as it is in its own mineral state with nothing added or taken away. You must **sublimate** <note>To heat a substance until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again, used here for purification.</note> it so that you may extract from it that which is pure and clear. Afterward, we must make it descend, then **distill** it; fourth, **calcine** <note>To reduce a substance to a powder through high heat.</note> it; fifth, **dissolve** it; sixth, **congeal** it; seventh, **fix** it; and eighth, **wax** it <note>original: *incerare*; a process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency.</note>. This is the whole practice and the reduction to the **prime matter** <note>The base material from which all things are made; the goal of alchemical deconstruction.</note>, because otherwise no generation or multiplication can occur. Pay close attention to these things being written for you.

I tell you, most dearly beloved, that it is necessary first to reduce bodies to their **prime matter** so that generation or multiplication may occur within them. Therefore, take heed of these things described to you. Take 1 pound of copper and let clean filings be made from it; mix this with 4 pounds of **Mercury** <note>Commonly known as quicksilver.</note> by grinding them in a mortar with a little salt and vinegar until they are amalgamated together. When the copper has been perfectly joined, place it in a good quantity of **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; typically distilled alcohol or a potent solvent.</note>—that is, in 12 parts of the water of life for every 1 part of the amalgam. Place the whole mixture in a **flask** <note>original: *urinali*; a glass vessel shaped like a urinal used for digestion.</note> over a fire of weak ashes, using the slowest heat for one natural day <note>A 24-hour period.</note>. Then allow it to cool, etc.

It is done elsewhere in this way: Take as much of the **white stone** as you wish—for example, one part—and four parts of its "water" (which is Mercury). Mix them together, incorporating them well by grinding until they are fully combined. Afterward, place it in a glass vessel and put ten parts of **water of life** inside. Then place the said vessel on a fire by means of ashes, and ensure the fire is slow for a day and a night. Then allow the furnace to cool, and when the vessel is cold, strain your water along with everything in it through a linen cloth until it passes through. Whatever of the * stone is dissolved will come out through the cloth. If you know how to perform this separation more skillfully, it would be better. 

Take that which has been dissolved and place it in a glass vial well-sealed with wax, always keeping it over its own heat. Afterward, take what remained in the cloth to be dissolved and place it again with fresh **blessed water** <note>original: *aqua benedicta*; likely another name for the solvent or purified water used in the process.</note> over the fire, just as before in the aforementioned vessel, for a day and a night. Then allow it to cool and strain it as before. Place the part that is dissolved to the side, as you did before. Repeat this until the entire work is converted into water—that is, to the **prime matter**, which exists in a liquid state, that is, Mer— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Mercury."</note>

# On the Perfection of the Mastery
<note>original: *DE PERF. MAGIST.* refers to the *De Perfectione Magisterii*, the completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note>

Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> altogether. Once this is done, take all of this and place it in a glass vessel over a slow fire, simmering it: until you see a blackness on the surface, which you should remove as finely as you can. And so, repeat the cooking and the removal of the rising blackness until it emits no more blackness, and the water remains clear. Now you have earth and water, namely the two principal elements. Then take that earth and the blackness you collected, and place them in a glass vessel, and pour the aforementioned water over it until it floats upon it. Cook it over a light or slow fire for four days; then pour in water again and cook it; and so on successively, until the water becomes white, shining, and clear. 

And know that this is what the philosophers have said: "This earth putrefies and is purified with water." When it has been purified, the entire **mastery** <term>Mastery: The *Magisterium*, or the completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosopher's Stone.</term> will be directed. Once it is purified and whitened, as has been said, by means of the water—which has been coagulated and thickened with the said earth by means of heat—you shall cook this coagulated earth with its own water (or thickened without the water of another) over a strong fire in a glass **cucurbit** <term>Cucurbit: The lower, gourd-shaped part of a distillation apparatus, resembling a gourd.</term> with a glass **alembic** <term>Alembic: The "cap" or lid of a still that catches vapors and directs them into a cooling tube.</term> placed on top, so that whatever water is there may ascend into the alembic, and the earth remains **calcined** <term>Calcined: A substance reduced to a dry, fine powder through the application of intense heat.</term>. 

Then take a **ferment** <note>In alchemy, the "ferment" acts like yeast in bread, a small amount of a noble metal (gold or silver) used to "tilt" the entire mixture toward that metal's nature.</note> of whatever you wish—a fourth part of its weight—that is, if there were 1 pound of the "body," take 3 ounces of the ferment. Indeed, the ferment of gold is gold, and the ferment of silver is silver. And let that ferment also be dissolved and made into "earth" <note>meaning reduced to a powder</note>, just as the imperfect body was prepared in the same way and order. Join them together and soak them with the aforementioned water, and cook for 3 days or more. Then soak them again in the aforementioned water and cook as before; repeat this as many times as it takes for these two to be reduced into one body, which you will recognize when the color among them no longer varies. 

Then pour the aforementioned water over them part by part, little by little, until it "drinks" as much of it as it can, always giving it new water. For in this union of bodies, the **spirits** <term>Spirits: Volatile substances that can evaporate or "fly," often associated with the life-force or soul of the material.</term> are mixed with them, and they become one with them, and are incorporated and joined in their very nature. The **seed** <note>original: *germen*</note> is joined with the aforementioned purified bodies. Previously, this was impossible because of their impurity and coarseness; but now it is joined to them, and grows in them, and increases its number, and is multiplied within them by an infinite multiplication, according to what has been wrought through the **true art** <note>original: *verum artificium*</note>. Now let us explain the most obscure words of the philosophers.

### ARNALDUS

For the first step is the reduction of the body into <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium"; in alchemy, this refers to a primordial liquid state or the "philosophical" mercury rather than common quicksilver</note>. You should know that this is what the philosophers called <term>Solution</term> <note>original: "Solutionem"</note>, which is the foundation of the art and the beginning of this <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterij"; the Great Work of alchemy</note>.
Wherefore <term>Rosinus</term> <note>a Latinized name usually identifying the 3rd-century alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis</note> says in the book of the <term>Assembly</term> <note>original: "Turbæ," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical dialogue</note>: "Unless you dissolve the bodies with our solution, you labor in vain."
Concerning this solution, <term>Parmenides</term> says, treating the subject in the same book: "Some, hearing of the solution of bodies, think it is <term>cloud-water</term> <note>original: "aquam nubis"; i.e., common rainwater</note>; however, if they had read and understood our books, they would certainly know that the water is 'permanent' <note>a stable, non-evaporating alchemical solvent</note>, which cannot be permanent without its body, to which it is joined and made one."
For the philosophers' water is not cloud-water, but the conversion of the bodies themselves into the water from which they were first created—namely, into <term>Mercury</term>—just as ice is converted into clear water, from which it originally came.
Behold, you have one element, which is water, and its reduction into the primary matter.

The second word concerns that which becomes Earth; and this is what the philosophers said: that Earth is created from the <term>thickness of the water</term> <note>original: "craffitie aquæ"; the sediment or dense residue</note>. Or according to another understanding, which in my judgment approaches the truth: that Earth is generated from the thickness of the water because the dregs of the water, which remain at the bottom of the vessel, are what the philosophers called Earth. This is converted with the water—that is, it is <term>whitened</term> <note>original: "dealbatur"; the process of Albedo or whitening</note> through <term>distillation</term> and <term>inhumation</term> <note>original: "inhumationem"; the practice of burying the vessel in warm earth or dung to maintain a gentle, steady heat</note>. This is the <term>sifting</term> <note>original: "cribratio"</note> of the philosophers, their <term>grinding</term> <note>original: "contritio"</note>, or <term>combustion</term>.
Thus you have another element, which is Earth.

The third word is the <term>purification</term> <note>original: "mundificatio"</note> of the Earth, regarding which <term>Morienus</term> <note>a legendary hermit and alchemist</note> says: "This Earth putrefies with water and is purified; when it has been purified, the entire <term>Mastery</term> will be directed." Regarding which <term>Constans the Philosopher</term> also says in the book of the <term>Assembly</term>: "Join the dry to the moist, namely, Earth and Water; for the dry is Earth, and the moist is Water." Behold, you have Water and Earth by themselves, and Earth whitened with Water.

The fourth word is Water, which can <term>evaporate</term> by distilling or <term>subliming</term> <note>original: "sublimando"; the process of heating a substance until it vapors and then collects as a solid in the upper part of the vessel</note>. In this sublimation or <term>ascent</term>, the Earth itself is made <term>aerial</term> <note>original: "terra aerea"</note>, whereas before it was <term>thickened</term> and <term>coagulated</term> with the Earth. And thus you have Water, Earth, and Air; as <term>Theophilus the Philosopher</term> says in the book of the <term>Assembly</term>: "Whiten it, burn the dry with fire, until the <term>spirit</term> comes out of it which is found within, which is called the <term>bird</term> or the <term>ash of Hermes</term>."
<term>Mireris the Philosopher</term> said: "And the Earth remains <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcinata"; reduced to a fine powder by high heat</note> at the bottom of the vessel, which is of a fiery nature."
And thus we have the four <term>elements</term> in the aforementioned preparations. Therefore, this calcined earth is the <term>powder</term> <note>original: "puluis"</note>, about which <term>Mireris the Philosopher</term> speaks, saying:

...saying: Do not despise the ashes; remove them from the lower part of the vessel <note>original: "testæ"; likely referring to a crucible or earthen vessel.</note>: for in them is the diadem of the heart. Afterwards, place the ferment with the aforementioned earth, which the Philosophers call the **soul**: and therefore, just as the human body is worth nothing without the soul—indeed, it is like dross—so it is also in our purpose: For the **ferment** <note>In alchemy, a "ferment" is a substance (often gold or silver) added to a base material to "leaven" it or transform it into its own higher nature.</note> is a body prepared, as was said, and it converts others into its own nature. And know that there is no ferment except the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>original: "Sol & Luna"; these represent gold and silver, the "perfect" metals.</note>. For these bodies dominate others and convert them to their own nature; and therefore they are called "ferment" by the Philosophers.

It is necessary, therefore, that the ferment be introduced into the body, because it is its soul. And this is what Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary early medieval alchemist.</note> the philosopher says: *Unless you cleanse the unclean body, and restore it to a whitened state, and mix the soul into it, you have directed nothing in this magistery.* Therefore, let there be a conjunction of the ferment with the cleansed body: and then the **spirit** is joined with them, and rejoices with them: because they are cleansed from their coarse nature and have been made subtle.

And this is what Archelaus the philosopher says in the book of the *Assembly* <note>original: "libro Turbæ"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: *The spirit will not be joined with the bodies until the bodies have been perfectly stripped of their impurities, and in the hour of conjunction wonders will appear:* for all the colors of the world will appear in the working—every color that can be imagined. The imperfect body is colored with a weak coloration by means of the ferment, which ferment is the soul; and the spirit, by means of the soul, is joined and bound to the body, and is converted together with it into the color of the ferment, and becomes one with them.

From the aforesaid, it appears to the subtle observer that the philosophers have spoken the truth in their most obscure words: for the philosophers themselves say in their books that our **stone** is made of the four elements; and they compared it to the elements. And it was shown first how there are four elements here. They also said that our stone is composed of body, soul, and spirit, and they spoke truly: for they compared the imperfect body to a "body" because it is weak. They called the water "spirit," and truly: because it is spirit. They called the ferment "soul" because, as was said above, it grants life to the imperfect body which it did not have before, and produces a better form.

Certain philosophers also said: *Unless you make the bodies of truth incorporeal, and the non-bodies into bodies—that is, the spirit from the body, and vice versa—you have not yet found the rule of working.* And they speak truly: For first the body becomes water, that is, Philosophical...

The **Mercury of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Iofophorum Mercurius" - a likely scribal error for "Philosophorum Mercurius"</note>, and thus it becomes incorporeal; then, in the conversion of the spirit into water, it becomes a body. And therefore some have said: *Convert the natures, and you shall find what you seek:* this is true. For in our **great work** <term>magisterium: the complete alchemical process required to create the Philosopher's Stone</term> we first make the thick thin, and from the body, water; and afterwards from the moist, dry—that is, from water, earth. And thus we convert nature, and we make from the corporeal something spiritual, and from the spiritual something corporeal, as has been said. And we make that which is above like that which is below, and that which is below like that which is above <note>This is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet" of Hermes Trismegistus, a foundational text of alchemy</note>; namely, we turn spirit into body, and body into spirit, as is evident at the start of the operation. As in the process of solution, that which is below is like that which is above, and the whole is turned into earth. 

It is clear, then, from what has been said, that in our **Stone** there are four elements, as well as soul, body, and spirit. Our Stone, as certain philosophers say, is made from one thing, and with one thing. And certainly they speak the truth: for our whole work is done with our "water," from it, and through it. For they dissolve this water, as was said above—not by a solution such as the ignorant believe, where it would be converted into rainwater <note>original: "aqua nubis" - water of the clouds</note>, but by a true philosophical solution. This means it is converted into the "first water" from which it originated in the beginning. They calcine this same substance and reduce it to earth; through this same water, they transform bodies into ash. From this, they whiten and purify the ash, according to the saying of **Morienus** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit credited with bringing alchemical secrets to the Arabs</note> who says that **Azoth** <term>Azoth: the universal solvent or "Mercury of the Philosophers," considered the animating spirit of hidden matter</term> and fire wash and purify the **Laton** <term>Laton: a term for an impure metal or "dead" matter that must be cleansed before it can be turned into gold</term>, and utterly strip away its darkness. 

Now, **Laton** is an impure body, and **Azoth** is Mercury. They join together various bodies prepared in the manner described above, with such a union that neither the power of fire—nor any other trial or test—cannot separate them. It is defended against the burning of the fire, and one thing is sent into the other. They **sublimate** <term>sublimation: while in modern chemistry this means a solid turning to gas, in alchemy it refers to the purification and "ennobling" of a substance</term> the bodies, but not by the "vulgar" sublimation understood by the deluded <note>original: "phantastici" - those governed by fantasies or false imaginations rather than true philosophical understanding</note>. These people believe that to sublimate is simply to ascend or rise upward through fire. Therefore, they take calcined bodies and mix them with "elevated" spirits—namely, **Mercury**, **Sulphur**, **Arsenic**, and **Sal Ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>—and by means of a strong and sudden fire, they cause the bodies to rise with the spirits. They do this because the "unfixed" part separates the "fixed" part through the sheer quantity of the unfixed portion, and thus they lift the bodies up with the spirits. They claim that these are then "sublimated bodies," but such people are mistaken and deceived, for they afterwards find these substances to be even more impure than they were before. Wherefore you should know that this is not...

### ON THE PERFECTION OF THE MASTERY
127
i 2

To sublimate, for us, is not merely to raise something up, to ascend, or to elevate it; rather, for the philosophers <note>The term "philosophers" here refers specifically to alchemists, who were often called "natural philosophers."</note>, to **sublimate** is to make a precious thing out of a base thing. It is to take a lowly and mingled thing and make it high, great, and pure. Just as we might say: "This man has been sublimated," meaning he has been raised to a high rank or dignity. This is how we speak of **sublimated bodies**: they are refined and transformed into a high, pure, clean, and most noble nature.

For this reason, to "sublimate" among the philosophers means to refine, to cleanse, to dregs-clear, to whiten, and to make red—all of which is accomplished by our **blessed water** <note>original: "aqua nostra benedicta"; a common alchemical term for a universal solvent, often associated with prepared Mercury.</note>. Therefore, understand our **sublimation** and **descension**, **distillation** and **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance until it reduces to powder.</note>, **solution**, **congealing**, **fixation**, and **inceration** <note>The process of softening a substance by adding liquid until it has a wax-like consistency.</note> in this way: all of this happens through the benefit of the blessed water, and it is in this that everyone else is deceived.

Our water also kills and brings to life. It causes many colors to appear: first, **black** during the "death" (mortification) of the body, while it is being turned into earth. Afterward, many and varied colors appear before the whitening (*albedo*), the end result of which is total whiteness. In the joining (*conjunction*) of the prepared and fermented body, as many colors appear as can be imagined by man. It becomes apparent that our Mastery is one thing, made from one thing, and with one thing. Yet it is made from four elements (as has been said) and from three (as was also said above).

You should know, my dearest friend, that the philosophers have multiplied the names of our **Stone** for the purpose of hiding it. They said our Stone is both physical and spiritual, and in truth, they did not lie, as the wise are able to understand. For both body and spirit are present: the body is made spiritual during the "solution" phase (as was said), and the spirit is made physical during its "conjunction" with the imperfect body and the ferment.

Some philosophers call it **copper** <note>original: "aes"</note>. As Eximaeus <note>Likely a reference to Zosimos or another figure from the "Turba Philosophorum," an early alchemical assembly text.</note> said in the Book of the Assembly: "Know," he says, "all you who seek knowledge, that there is no true dye (*tinctura*) except from our copper." They give it infinite names so that it might not be understood by the foolish. Yet, by whatever name they call it, the work remains one and the same among them all.

And Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says that the preparation of our Mastery is compared, in its order, to the **creation of a human being**. For first there is intercourse (*coitus*), then follows conception, then pregnancy, fourth is the birth, and fifth follows the nourishment. This is understood as follows: first our "sperm"—that is, **Mercury**—is joined with the earth (that is, with the imperfect body). This earth is called the "mother" because the earth is the mother of all elements. According to the Philosophers, this is the intercourse.

<summary>This page defines alchemical sublimation as a process of spiritual and physical refinement rather than simple vaporization, and introduces the "blessed water" as the primary agent of change. It explains the stages of the Great Work through the metaphor of human biological development, from conception to birth.</summary>

### *The PRACTICE of MASTER ARNALDO of Villanova addressed to a certain Pope. From the book called, The Breviary of the Books of Alchemy.*

<term>S</term>anctissimo <note>original: "Sanctissimo in Christo patri" — a standard formal salutation for a Pope.</note> father in Christ, most devotedly, after the kissing of your blessed feet: the change of the Most High God. I say to you, nourishing father, etc., that first of all, it is necessary to reduce bodies into their "first matter." First, I wish you to know that the matter of all metals, and their seed, is a white smoke, cooked and thickened in the belly of the earth by a sulfurous heat. According to the variety of the sulfur and its quantity in the earth, different metals are procreated; nevertheless, the matter of most of them is always one and essentially the same, differing only by "accident" <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the core essence of a thing, such as color or hardness.</note>, etc. Indeed, since an operator can do nothing without salt—just as one who shoots with a bow without a string—and Morienus <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who allegedly taught the secrets of the philosopher's stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says this more clearly: Take the phlegmatic and the choleric, and grind the sanguine with them, until a sky is made, staining for the debt, etc., in its own fire. The phlegmatic is cold and moist, like Mercury; the choleric is truly hot and dry, like sal ammoniac <note>original: "sal armoniacum" — Ammonium chloride, a vital reagent in alchemy used to "cleanse" and "open" metals.</note>; the sanguine is hot and moist, like the Sun, or gold. Note that sal ammoniac does not give color, but it provides entry; it prepares and purges. Then the remaining spirits enter the mixed bodies, and it joins them together and then recedes. For this salt is an ointment coagulated by the dryness of fire, from a nature that is hot, dry, and subtle; penetrating from part to part, it dissolves bodies, and is the joiner of opposites, and of all spirits with bodies. For it is a flying spirit, a generating stone, and a helper to the elixir. And if it were not for this salt, the elixir would neither be dissolved nor enter, nor would one thing be placed with any other, nor would one thing enter into another. It is a flying thing, existing as a body together with other bodies, and in it is something hidden and concealed. Of this, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian polymath; alchemical works were frequently attributed to him in the Latin West.</note> says in his *Greater Work*: "If you have placed it in the stead of fire, air, and sulfur, or anything else, you have not erred in the work." For it inclines itself toward any nature; and Almizadir <note>The Arabic name for sal ammoniac.</note> (that is, sal ammoniac) alone shall serve you. In the *Book of Alums and Salts*, it is handed down: "That if God had not created it, the elixir would not be perfected, and the study of Alchemy would be in vain." Therefore, the operator who acts without salt—as the *Allegory of the Sages* says—does not thin the bodies of the dead in their tombs, and for that reason, etc.

## ON THE DECOCTION OF THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE, and on the management of fire in the various stages of cooking for the coagulation of the stone.

### Verses on Solution.

He who seeks the secrets of the philosophers in filth,
Wastes his own expenses and the time of his labors. <note>original: "Qui quaerit in merdis..." – A common alchemical warning against "charity seekers" who tried to extract the Stone from literal waste or organic matter.</note>
Everything that the wise seek is in Mercury:
From here the body, the soul, the spirit, and the <term>tincture</term> <note>The "tincture" is the concentrated essence or power of the Stone used to transform base metals into gold.</note> are drawn.
No Mercury is to be taken, except for the mineral kind.

### Degrees of the fire of coagulation.

Let the first be formed, and let the senses rule it. <note>The first degree of heat should be gentle enough to be measured by touch.</note>
Nature rejoices in the second, equal to the senses.
The third exceeds them, but hurts with tolerance. <note>A heat that is hot to the touch but still bearable.</note>
The fourth, destroyer of the senses, knows not how to proceed. <note>The highest heat, which would burn or destroy the touch.</note>

Therefore let us descend to the practical work; let us submit it clearly, openly, and intelligibly. Note therefore, that in our operation, which is divine rather than human, only one single matter is required and no other: because our water is pure and mineral, placed in no other work, nor even mixed with any body; this matter is the substance from which different colors and effects appear during the management of the fire. And know that this one matter also requires a single glass vessel, which is called the Vessel of Hermes: and that requires another earthen vessel with its own cover, likewise made of earth. And that one earthen vessel requires a single furnace, namely the Furnace of Hermes, and a furnace cover. First, therefore, let us describe the glass vessel. Let the Vessel of Hermes be made of glass, which should be round in the manner of the celestial half-moon; this vessel must have an opening [where] the full moon will be carried. <note>The "full moon" here likely refers to the appearance of the matter or the stopper within the flask's neck.</note> The description of the Vessel of Hermes is somewhat oblong, in the manner of an egg, or in the manner of a flask.

Let us now describe the earthen vessel in which the aforementioned glass vessel must be placed. Let an earthen vessel be made that can withstand a strong and continuous fire, even to the point of glowing red, just like the earth from which <term>crucibles</term> <note>Heat-resistant containers used for melting metals.</note> are made for melting gold; and let the said vessel be of such capacity and size that the aforementioned glass vessel can be well-received there. In such a way that beneath the glass vessel, and above the vessel, and around it, sifted ashes can be placed to a thickness of at least two fingers: furthermore, let a cover be made for the aforementioned vessel,

### ON THE PERFECTION OF THE MASTERING
<note>The header "DE PERE. MAGIST." is an abbreviation for *De Perfectione Magisterii*, a title often associated with the works of Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), focusing on the "mastery" or completion of alchemical transformations.</note>

[covering], which is joined with its vessel in such a way that the flame of the fire cannot strike the glass vessel polished within. Moreover, the aforementioned lid should have a handle on top so that it can be removed and handled, etc. Now let us place the glass vessel into that earthenware vessel thus: First, have a good quantity of very well-sifted ashes and place them in the aforementioned earthenware vessel to a thickness of at least two fingers, pressing the ashes down firmly. Then place the glass vessel there with its holder or cover; however, the mouth of the glass itself must first be very well closed with sealed clay (this is the <term>clay of wisdom</term><note>Latin: *lutum sapientia*. This was a specialized airtight sealant, often made of clay, horsehair, and dung, used to hermetically seal glass vessels so no vapors could escape.</note>). Then place the remaining ashes all around and above, etc., just as you know.

Now let us add some noteworthy points: Note that in our operation, and in any alchemical work, whether it concerns <term>sublimations</term><note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</note>, <term>distillations</term>, or any <term>decoctions</term><note>The process of boiling or heating a substance for a long period to extract its essence or change its state.</note> whatsoever, it is necessary for two parts of the glass to be left empty.

Furthermore, the heavier and more compact or dense the coals are, the better they are for our work: because the fire made from them lasts longer in its quality, and thus oak coals and the like are to be chosen. And note that although there are four principal colors appearing in the work—namely black, white, red, and yellow—they appear in different degrees according to their stage of boiling. For with one fire we make the body black, with another white, with another red, and with another yellow. There are, indeed, four degrees of fire, which are contained in the four verses written above. And note that the <term>Philosophers</term><note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to the ancient and medieval alchemists.</note> hid this science of fire; no philosopher has spoken clearly about these degrees, but all mention only a light fire obscurely.

The first degree, therefore, is contained in the first verse, which is:

> ->*Let the first be formed, so that the senses may master it.*<-
<note>original: "Primus formetur, vt sensus ei dominetur."</note>

And how will it be known when the heat is of the first degree? Certainly thus: if the hands touch the ashes, or the <term>cupel</term><note>A shallow, porous vessel or casing used in the furnace.</note>, or the furnace lid, they can remain there without any injury. And this is the first degree, which the Philosophers have hidden: and with that fire alone, or one similar to it, and with no other, our matter <term>putrefies</term><note>Putrefaction was considered the essential first stage of the work, where the substance "died" and turned black (the *nigredo* phase) before being reborn.</note> according to some philosophers in 40 days, which I do not believe; according to others in 50, which I also do not believe; according to others in 70, which I also do not believe. But he who has tested and experienced it completed true putrefaction in 97 or at most one hundred days, and that is the truth. And note,

# GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO
<note>Latin: IO. AVR. AV GUR. refers to Joannes Aurelius Augurellus (c. 1441–1524), an Italian humanist and alchemist famous for his poem *Chrysopoeia* (Gold-making).</note>

Furthermore, it will not be long before you perceive the rest
From yourself: for all things are held joined by a single
Bond; from here is derived the measure of the **slow fire**,
And the place, and the proper measure of the future **stone**,
And the heat spread variously under the desired **powder**,
And in what way it must be increased, if perhaps the powder,
Hidden before and lasting for a long time, should be lacking.
All these things will lie open to you everywhere as certain and joyful,
If you preserve the sequence of things through long practice,
And perhaps one day, being upright, you will not disdain
To pay worthy thanks for these merits to me,
Who, leaving far behind the mockeries of the ignorant masses,
Now enter the narrow path with us leading—
A path so narrow that it admits few, and returns few
Unharmed; rather, it brings back almost everyone torn
By frequent briars, unless it leaves them wandering
Beneath a high cliff in blind turnings, from where neither they
Nor any pitied mortal hand could ever bring them back.
But do not hesitate to wander through the winding caves;
You will guide your blind footsteps with the **thread**
<note>Original: *filo*. An allusion to Ariadne’s thread, used by Theseus to navigate the Labyrinth; here, it represents the author's chemical instructions.</note>
Which I recently showed you, so that you might safely advance
And safely retreat. If you, being blessed, should reach the desired
End, thanks should be given first to the Gods,
And then deservedly to me: who, with them present,
Consulted for you. But if the gods above should not grant
That you reach the goal, and it were necessary to stop
The course begun—a misfortune by which the human condition
Often labors—at least by driving out the lies of the false common folk,
You might be able to see others wandering.
I will also warn you often, first and again:
Do not—if this rare grace from heaven should befall you
(For no one could hope for it from elsewhere)—
Reveal this to any dear or faithful companion.
Lest while you report it to others, you boast that you know
What you have learned; rather, keeping it in your secret breast,
Dwell with yourself, and turn over these secrets with yourself alone:
For the <term>Art</term><note>The "Art" or "Great Art" (Ars Magna) is a standard term for alchemy.</note> itself, suspected by the upright and hated by many,
Makes even the practitioners of the Art hated;
So many liars wander everywhere,
Having promised many things in vain, which they themselves...

### CHYSOPOEIA, BOOK II.

They did not find out, nor is it easy for them to know these things,
Who wander entirely from the right path that leads us.
Indeed, I have seen many distinguished men, learned in other matters,
Who value and treat with great importance
Whatever the ignorant and ignoble crowd approves.
What of those who deride all **Artisans**—of whom there is a vast multitude—
<note>Original: *Artifices*. Here referring specifically to practitioners of alchemy.</note>
As if there were no difference between the true and the false,
And weigh them all equally in a single balance?
There are those who often ask: what is the cause that anywhere,
Or at any time among so many who occupy themselves with such things,
No one appears who proves such great miracles by the **deed** itself?
<note>The skeptics argue that if alchemy were real, we would see evidence of it through "miracles" (the creation of gold).</note>
They claim, therefore, that there is no "Art" such as we speak of,
But that it clearly seems to them to be massive nonsense,
And the empty inventions of an insane mind.
But who, even if his heart were fortified with only fragile strength,
Could not keep silent about things that must never be told to anyone?
For whom does the prudence of things not forbid to speak
Of matters which, once they are spoken, will immediately bring him harm?
Safe from snares, by what virtue could he protect himself,
Who displayed openly that he hid within a small casket
Vast riches, before which the kingdoms and wealth of kings
Everywhere rise up, and all opulent things yield,
As if every other thing were lesser than those riches alone?
If anyone, therefore, has been able to gather such great treasures,
He wonderfully keeps them under the cover of a friendly silence.
You shall do the same; nor should it move you to desist from your path
Because you have seen no one increased by such wealth,
Or showing themselves to the common people as blessed.
Nor should these heavy and troublesome times hold you back—
Times which we, in our misery, never expected before—
When a barbarian enemy—alas!—would invade these mild lands,
And would utterly destroy a peace preserved for so long,
Not merely disturbing it with his injustice.
Now one hears of invaded cities and towns plundered everywhere;
Now of base spoils, nefarious abductions,
And fires thrown into wretched villas.
From here, the sad Muse of **Bononius** weeps for his **Narvisia**.
<note>Narvisia refers to Nervesa della Battaglia. Girolamo Bologni (Bononius), a poet and friend of Augurello, lost his estate there during the War of the League of Cambrai (c. 1509–1517).</note>
Even forms of worship are defiled, and the temples of the Gods
Violated by the foul soldier, and wickedly burned besides,
While divine and human things are thrown into such great confusion.

<summary>Augurello defends alchemical secrecy by arguing that displaying wealth would invite danger from kings and thieves, then laments the destruction caused by invading armies in Italy, specifically the loss of his friend Girolamo Bologni's estate.</summary>

War, that great wickedness, and discord, the parent of crimes, weave their webs.
Moreover, one could see hearts moved by dire fear,
And the shaking of men only a few days ago,
As if driven by the whips of the **Furies**,
<note>Original: *dirarum*. Referring to the Dirae or Furies, the mythological personifications of vengeance and madness.</note>
So that each man trembled to seek a new home for himself,
And departed burdened with his gathered possessions,
Leaving his ancestral soil to bear himself toward the
**Queen City**, which is surrounded by the great sea,
<note>Original: *vrbem Reginam... amphitrite*. The "Queen City" refers to Venice, protected by its lagoon (Amphitrite was a sea goddess).</note>
As if all things were safe under that sky,
Where once the chosen people of Italy retreated in flight,
So that they might save themselves upon small rocks
And a modest wave, when an immense fire burned all of
**Italy**, kindled from almost every side by savage
**Barbarism**, and fostered to last for many years.
<note>Augurello compares the contemporary wars in Italy to the original barbarian invasions that led to the founding of Venice in the lagoons.</note>
Therefore, come now—seeing how much you perceive these things 
To be subject to fortune (those "goods" which mortals 
Boast of with a misleading name)—
Strive to fortify yourself with this stable protection
Against the violent strikes of that lightning bolt:
So that if a horrific fear should ever invade us
Trembling again—which the **just King** of men and gods 
<note>God or Jupiter.</note>
May turn instead against our unjust enemies—
You may be a source of help to yourself, your kin, and your friends.
For when you possess this divine gift in secret,
You will be wealthier than all rich men, carrying it under your wing,
More fitly than in any casket, and with no labor;
Wherever your feet take you, and at any time,
You will carry with you all the comforts of a secure life.
But if the longed-for **peace** visits us again,
<note>Original: *pax*.</note>
Which we believe is now near (if the mind **prophesies** anything of the truth)
<note>Original: *augurat*. A clever pun on the author's name, Augurellus.</note>
And will be sent to us from heaven,
In what better way could you exercise the gifts of tranquil peace?
Whether you handle serious matters,
Or if games and honest pleasure are dear to your heart,
In both cases you may act with profit and justice.
For neither **avarice**, nor the insane desire for honors,
<note>Original: *auaricies*.</note>
Nor the other passions that disturb mortal hearts,
Moving them in various ways and vexing them in vain,
Will be able to conquer you with any allurements—
Safe as you are with such a great defense and the fortification of a peaceful mind.
But neither the dire movements of war, nor the [temptations] of peace...

May nurturing peace only move you to seek the causes of things so obscure, and not the riches or comforts which will follow you in such abundance wherever you wish to go. But let this especially move you: that you yourself might emerge worthy of such a great gift, by which you might be able to know the greatest and most intimate **first beginnings of things** from deep within.
<note>Original: *intimaque ingentum penitus primordia rerum*. This refers to the fundamental seeds or elements of matter that alchemists sought to manipulate.</note>
**Nature** would hardly ever create these things easily, unless someone aided her through the use of an already known **Art**.
<note>Original: *arte*. In this context, "Art" specifically refers to the practice of alchemy, viewed as a method to assist and accelerate natural processes.</note>
He who is able to know these things might be no less happy, and perhaps he would leave nothing else to be desired; for compared to such discoveries, he would consider all other things secondary and gladly value them less. For the mind, the better part of us, rejoices only when content with the disclosure of secrets, once it has brought itself into the deep retreats of truth.

## BOOK III of the GOLD-MAKING by
## GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO

I shall immediately pursue the desired origins of the **wealthy powder**; 
<note>Original: *opulenti pulueris*. This refers to the "Powder of Projection," the substance alchemists believed could transmute base metals into gold.</note>
skilled **craftsmen**, take up this part also, and turn it over in a mind that has long been willing. I shall now tell you of the greatest miracles of heavy things, of great daring deeds, and of the highest order of the art: the **fires** and the **durations**, the **numbers** and the **weights**.
<note>Original: *Ignes & spacia, & numeros, & pondera*. These are the four pillars of practical laboratory alchemy: the intensity of heat, the time required, the proportions of ingredients, and their specific weights.</note>
There is labor in great things, but no less glory, if the present **Gods** look upon someone with a peaceful light, and if a burning will follows, as if kindled from that source. Let the difficult experience of things not disturb you, nor let the unwelcome novelty of my expression delay me. 

You also, **Nymph**, who have been my guardian of the sacred fountain and have so often been called upon in my prayers—if anything of what I have played at before has touched your nurturing heart—do not abandon this final care of such great works of ours. If you cherish those things which your **greatest Bard** once sang of, adorning the earth and all it encompasses, do not allow your mind to utterly despise the things we imitate. I now place my own footsteps in the very marks and signs left by him.
<note>Original: *maximus olim Ille tuus Vates*. A reference to the Roman poet Virgil. Augurello is signaling that his alchemical poem is modeled after Virgil’s *Georgics*, which dealt with agriculture; here, the "farming" is of metals.</note>

We set these things before you, having examined the very depths of the inner earth, so that you do not reject them as if they were seen only from a distance. See if we can perhaps fix these great things while walking with small steps. May the **Mincius** 
<note>The Mincius (modern Mincio) is a river in Northern Italy near Mantua. Augurello invokes it to channel the poetic spirit of Virgil, who was born nearby.</note>
flow forever gently for you with its pure waters, and may it fringe its banks with slender reeds.

First, let the man who takes such matters to heart be free of his own will, removed from all care, and lead a life through tranquil leisure, secluded and even hidden. Let him have a house that is not necessarily large, but suitable for handling many things, and set apart from the common crowd. 

In certain places, let it have secret chambers where no entrance is open, unless perhaps the master himself orders a servant to bring something in—a servant who knows neither what they carry nor for what purpose. 

Here, let there be a short portico for the summer breeze, and let halls received in the winter time keep him warm and contained at home. Let there be a small garden where he may exercise himself all year round in his spare time, and where he may appear busily devoted only to this: 
* Now let him pick out the seeds of vegetables with a quick hand; 
* Now let him commit those same seeds to the tilled earth;
* Soon, let him feed his mind and eyes with flowering herbs. 

To this place, he may even occasionally admit sweet friends, and disguise what he is doing at home, keeping his companions occupied with pleasant games and charming wit.

Meanwhile, however, he should not let the hidden heat cease, if by chance he has placed the **gold-bearing seed** 
<note>Original: *Aurigerum semen*. In alchemical theory, this is the "seed" or essence of gold that must be nurtured in a furnace to "grow" or transmute other metals.</note> 
where it may now complete its own cycles of time. Or if, with continuous fire and much labor, he attempts to seek out what is hidden in the veins of gold. 

And so, it would not be out of place to have sought a faithful companion for this excellent task and long labor, who might then hide himself in the inner part of the house and, having shared the burden, look after the things that need care in turn. 

There is also that final consideration for the blessed **artisan** 
<term>artifex: the alchemist as a skilled maker or craftsman of nature</term>, 
by which he should commend himself and the work itself to the eternal gods. For these things do not come about without the divine will of the gods, nor will it be permitted for anyone to aspire to these things who has not studied how to be present for the gods in the proper way through prayer.

I myself, who have grasped these things so well, now try through song
To reveal them; thrice I have made pious vows and prayers to the **Muses**
<note>The nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>
With hands outstretched in supplication and a pure heart,

I seem to be carried through high hills and through pathless

Mind to wherever the fates carry me, so that I may be the first to bring back

<note>A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; the author claims to be the first to write of alchemy in high Latin verse.</note>

Therefore, I shall pursue the arts I have begun and the labors of works 
Previously unmentioned, and I shall be carried around the smoking 
Houses of the gods, who catch the thin air with bellows 
And distend the furnaces with liquid bronze.
And now we seem to hear the clamor of the **Cyclopes**
<note>Mythological giants who labored in the forge of Vulcan; here used as a metaphor for metalworkers.</note>
Close at hand; the sky murmurs, struck by the anvils,
And Mount **Etna**
<note>A volcano in Sicily, mythologically described as the location of Vulcan's forge.</note>
Resounds for me with the long screeching of the melting **Chalybes**
<note>A term for iron-workers, named after an ancient people of Asia Minor famous for smithing.</note>
And with unusual bellows.
Whether one seeks the <term>seeding of gold</term>
<note>The alchemical belief that gold could be "planted" or fermented like a biological seed to grow more of itself.</note>
Or first rightly demands the beginnings of silver,
Let him not despise knowing the various **degrees of fire**;
For there are many through which the work must proceed.
But two especially: one is the rival of **tranquil nature**,
But the other is suited to **violent art**.
This latter one strives to push the seed with the immense force of the works
Out of the solid gold bound by wondrous joints,
When first—as I shall soon relate to you—you have dissolved the gold,
And rendered it moist, as well as decayed and subdued,
So that at last it may easily endure the powerful fire,
And, swelling, it may exhale and be carried into the heights.
The former fire fosters that which has been taken out, and does not burn
The work with the power of exceeding heat, nor permits it to cool
Before it wondrously composes itself, and before—

<note>The "Minister" or assistant was a standard figure in alchemical laboratory practice, often representing the student or the hands that carry out the philosopher's will.</note>
For I shall relate great things first, then by speaking much
I shall conveniently explain those things which the ancient and barbarian crowd
Kept silent, or which I believe they wished to hide even from themselves,
Or perhaps they did not know how to use words more powerfully.
Therefore, I have dared to illustrate these things now in the **Latin tongue**,
And I even strive to add **meter** to them,
<note>Augurello wrote in dactylic hexameter, the prestigious verse form of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, to give alchemy the dignity of classical epic poetry.</note>
So that they may reach learned ears as more pleasing offerings.

<margin>1</margin> In the beginning, taking thin plates of **gold**, or filings of the pure metal,
You shall crush them with frequent blows, and
Into the fashion of ground powder, or river sand,
You shall diminish them; and grind them for a long time, until finally,
By their own internal decaying moisture, they are resolved and melt.
<note>This describes "calcination" or "attrition"—the physical breaking down of gold into a state where its "inner nature" can be accessed.</note>
It will also be useful here to pour in copious dews
Of its own **seed** at times, lest by chance you labor
<term>seed (semen): In alchemy, the "seed" refers to the essential generative principle of a metal, believed to allow it to "grow" or transform.</term>
To mix in anything foreign, as I taught above.

<margin>bracketed section</margin> Unless it is something that can connect many things, or perhaps you add
What is also found scattered commonly among all things:
For consider that every "like" thing rejoices in its own "like,"
And is even aided from the outside by whatever is similar to it,
Especially since nature seeks after nature,
And, having embraced its equal, refuses all contrary things.
So too, a string—though not struck by fingers or a plectrum—
Moves by chance, as if it then harmonizes with the struck strings
To which it was tuned with a concordant voice:
<note>This is "sympathetic resonance." Augurello uses the physics of music to explain why alchemical substances must be "in harmony" to react.</note>
In all things, the concord of matters prevails so greatly.
Wherefore, let it not be a burden to seek its match, whatever it is,
Or wherever it lies hidden, whether it be concealed in the deepest mountains,
Or torn from the rocks of the sea, or clings in the midst of springs,
Or brings itself forth from high **Olympus**,
<note>High heaven or the atmosphere; alchemists often looked for "celestial" influences in rain or dew.</note>
Or wherever it lies open, or in whatever part it is hidden.

<margin>bracketed section</margin> Whatever it is, it mixes itself with the whole body of the world;
By its powerful force, you may resolve things so compact.
Therefore, when they are now becoming moist, in the deep bottom
Of a **narrow vessel** you shall arrange these things, and not without order,
For it is necessary that they remain spread out evenly for you,
So that a single heat, penetrating equally through everything,
May be carried along, and compel the vapor from every part.
Now, let us consider with what things you can compose the mixture—

He describes the initial grinding of gold and emphasizes the principle of "sympathy" or "concordance," using a musical metaphor to explain how substances must be naturally aligned to work together.</summary>

Here, he moves to the construction of the specialized equipment needed for the next stage of the work: the refractory vessel and the furnace.</meta>

<page-num>239</page-num>
<header>GOLD-MAKING, BOOK III.</header>

I shall begin: That **vessel**, where it is necessary to endure immense heat once the gold has been thus duly prepared, is made of a wondrous kind of untamed earth, which the **Iberian** <note>original: "Hiberus"; referring to Spanish miners who exported high-quality refractory clay.</note> miner sends across for the glass-making arts of the Italians. For with this clay, the glassmaker melts glowing glass in fashioned pots, and purifies that same liquid glass in a long-lasting fire for whole nights and days. Therefore, first compose this with tenacious clay, from which the potter, as his wheel spins, brings forth rising little vessels and proceeds to bestow pleasing shapes upon them.

There is also a black earth in the **Euganean hills**, <note>The Euganean Hills near Padua were well known in the Renaissance for their volcanic soil and thermal springs.</note> where the path leads to the sulfurous springs of **Aponus**. <note>Abano Terme, famous since antiquity for its hot springs and medicinal mud.</note> No less is it sometimes dug from excavated pits under white earth, often resembling ancient marble. It is your task to take care to join all these materials into one, and to mix them repeatedly with your hands, so that you may produce a single uniform mass. From this, fashion cups resembling the shape of an oblong chalice; you should also strive to encircle the top of the rim with a small band, so that **glass vessels** <note>The "alembic" or "still-head" used to catch vapors.</note> may be fitted deep upon them to capture the thin vapors.

Nor indeed should your care for the **Furnace** <note>The *Athanor*, or "philosophical furnace," designed to maintain a steady, prolonged heat.</note> be any less, in which you must kindle a powerful fire, and, being industrious, nourish the flame for a long time and with great skill. Strengthen this furnace, therefore, fortified with a double wall, and draw a layer of aptly composed mud all around it. I would not be displeased if it were girt with bands of bronze and covered with hard flint—which, being stronger than a covering of iron, may better endure the force of such a great fire. Fill this also with many continuous holes, where you may place as many little vessels as are sufficient for the work and the labor.

When these things have been thus arranged, as soon as you kindle the fire, it seethes rapidly within the closed furnace and strikes the **vessel** directly from below, forcing the whole thing to become white-hot. But once the **golden species** <note>The "essence" or "form" of the gold being transformed.</note> is moistened by its own liquid—who would believe it? Yet the experts have seen these things—it is dissolved, and gradually it adheres to the sides of the vessel; soon it is seen to move slowly from here toward the curved glass lid. And that which was once hard, dense, and heavy...

It has soft qualities, and flies light, and cracks apart thinly. Indeed, it even shines, disguised in a snowy whiteness at first; then, suddenly, it takes on a blue paleness, and finally, the whole thing is bathed in a lightly tinted violet—which previously, imitating the color of the stars and the sky, had shone and remained steadfast in the tawny aura of the **gold**. <note>The author is describing the "iridescence" or color changes (often called the *cauda pavonis* or peacock’s tail) that occur as the substance is heated and refined.</note>

However, these signs alone shall not suffice; meanwhile, one may observe its very flavor. If a bitterness—scarcely perceived—should cling about the mouth, it is a sign. Furthermore, there is a dull sound, not easily caught by the ear, and also a scent that is not heavy, even if it breathes out a little like the scent of **black sulfur**. <note>original: "Sulphuris... atri"; sulfur was considered one of the two primary principles of all metals in medieval alchemy.</note> 

What more? Because sometimes it even seems to pour itself out into a liquid wave, which has crept up the "bones" <note>The "bones" likely refer to the solid remains or the internal structure of the material in the vessel.</note> of the work; to such an extent that it is no great thing to see **Gold** changed for once, and its heavy weight carried up into the high airs.

This is the **liquor** <note>The "mercurial" spirit or condensate of the gold.</note> which, if collected at a certain time, will provide two services from itself in abundance. One is that you may eventually pour the liquor of its own **seed** <note>original: "Seminis"; the "seed of gold" was the generative essence alchemists sought to isolate to "grow" more gold.</note> into the gold from here, when you first begin to dissolve it and have ground it down with your primary art. 

The other service will be this: when this moisture is skillfully mixed, it will perhaps restore those **pearls** <note>original: "Baccas," literally "berries," but used here as a common alchemical term for pearls.</note> brought from the **Indian shore** to their former shining whiteness, even when they seem to grow somewhat pale, covered with the film of age. Or, if the desire to do so should ever seize you, you will find that you can even fashion new pearls from the art with that clear and pure liquor.

For if ever you, following Nature—the most beautiful of things—wished to meditate upon and compose some distinguished work, you could choose nothing equally beautiful nor so marvelous to imitate through human art. Nature plays so much around the creation of these things—whether when **shells** <note>original: "Conchæ"</note> open themselves upon the surface of the sea <note>original: "summo... marmore"; literally "topmost marble," a poetic Latinism for the glassy surface of the calm sea.</note> when the breeding hour of the year has stimulated them, and, gaping, they are filled by the light conception of the **dew**, and then, being pregnant, they bring forth their offspring at a certain time, and a shining **Union** <note>original: "Vnio"; a Roman term for a large, unique pearl of the highest quality.</note> becomes their ethereal birth. Or whether you observe why the dewy conception from a similar origin does not always clothe itself in one single appearance...

<page-num>241</page-num>
# CHRYSOPOIEA, BOOK III.
<header>CHRY S O P. LIB. III.</header>

For when the pure dew has flowed into those greedy shells, a brightness is seen spreading throughout the entire body. But a turbid dew forces the offspring to become utterly soiled; you might see it turn pale when the sky is threatening. Indeed, they are composed of that dew, and there is hardly more of the sky in them than of the sea. Hence they vary: instead of brightness, their color is cloudy, or it is clear instead of light, while the white dawn warms the bed of old **Tithonus**. <note>Tithonus was the mortal husband of Aurora, the Goddess of the Dawn.</note>

For we see them feed from this source, and when they timely satisfy themselves, the offspring grow large. However, if it lightnings, the fearing shell itself suddenly contracts, and remains smaller, fasting through fear. But if it thunders, likewise compressed and fearing, it gives birth to a shape inflated with wind and without a body. And these are truly called the "abortions" of the shells; for healthy ones are said to consist of multiple layers, and the offspring are filled with a completely solid body. And so, you might consider it to be the callus of the body, which the skilled are accustomed to purge with a great deal of salt.

It is a marvel that they rejoice so much in a clear sky, yet grow red in the sun and lose their brightness; for this reason, they keep themselves submerged deeper in the sea, so that the rays of **Phoebus** <note>The Sun</note> cannot touch them anywhere. Yet they turn yellow and acquire the wrinkles of old age; nor does that vigor we seek endure, except during youth. Thus, even for these, a long life is harmful.

Sometimes an old <term>Pearl</term> <note>original: "Vnio"; a large, singular pearl of great price.</note> clings to the hard shells, which you cannot tear away from them except with a strong file. Although every pearl is equally soft while in its own sea, once removed, that same pearl immediately hardens. But if by chance the shell foresees the hand of the catcher, it immediately closes and hides itself and its riches within, knowing it is sought violently because of them; and thus, anticipating the attack, it often cuts the hand with its sharp edge, taking its penalty from the deceived enemy.

Finally, that which the skillful wisdom of the Great Poet <note>A reference to Virgil, who described the organized society of bees in the *Georgics*.</note> marvels at concerning the "king" of the bees, the shells themselves are said to observe: so that one, greater in age, may command and, being highly cunning, lead the others to pasture. If this leader should happen to be caught—for this single shell is the one sought by the **divers** <note>original: "vrinantibus"; those who dive for pearls.</note>...

<summary>Augurello uses the natural history of pearls—formed from dew and sensitive to the weather—as an allegory for the alchemical process's sensitivity to external conditions. He describes how the "offspring" (the stone or elixir) can become "aborted" or stunted if the conditions are not serene.</summary>

### GOLDEN CHRYSPOEIA, BOOK III.

When gold blooms in the manner of a wondrous rust <note>original: *rubiginis*. Here referring to a metallic patina or pigment produced by chemical reaction.</note>, suspended over the mouth of a pot of glowing hot vinegar, and first filled with marble dust, then placed in rotting manure or constant moisture. With these and other colors—which it would be a long task to enumerate—painters represent all simulated things upon their panels, whatever happens to be seen from near or far; just as the Ancients expressed these wonders, so too the Moderns <note>original: *Minores*, literally "the lesser" or "the later ones," referring to the artists of the Renaissance.</note> have now painted the same things with no less marvel.

All of these my **Julius** <note>Julius is likely Giulio Campagnola (c. 1482–1515), a Venetian engraver and painter known for his "sfumato" style and landscape backgrounds.</note> has imitated with genius and art, depicting whatever nature has exposed to the eyes: whether you see airy mountains rise or deep valleys sink away, or if you look upon gaps extending deep into the hills, the mountains themselves settling into hollow cracks. Or perhaps you prefer to see wide fields and flowery countrysides captured within a narrow margin, and rivers running through immense lands, and seas, and lakes, and the fountain in the green grass where Nymphs, Satyrs, and mountain-dwelling Silvani <note>Deities of the woods and wild places in Roman mythology.</note> gather, enjoying their own sky and sun there, all intent on various games.

And there are many other things besides, which the other arts are not ashamed to use as if they were their own, if the hand proceeds to mix them rightly with metals; just as when **Myron** <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE, known for the "Discobolus."</note> once cast breathing bronzes, or as now **Crispus** <note>Possibly a contemporary goldsmith or bronze-caster known to Augurello.</note> strives to strike out the same, being excellent at both molding and casting, and learned in constructing many things and mixing many substances, and knowing how to supply his own fire to them. 

Nor would I believe that he meditated in vain on many things through the <term>secret art</term> <note>Alchemy, often called the "ars sacra" or "arcanum."</note>, who recently produced for wretched mortals that horrendous kind of <term>engine</term> <note>original: *tormenti*. Referring to a cannon or artillery piece.</note> made of bronze, with which he shakes the high tops of walls from a distance; the machine hurls a heavy weight into the air with a terrible boom, by which the earth trembles as it is struck, and the towns around it shudder at the dire sound from afar, as if at a thunderbolt. 

Such sounds we, stunned, perceived with astonished ears lately on the Venetian shore, while the **Great King** <note>Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, who besieged Padua in 1509 during the War of the League of Cambrai.</note> sits at the city of **Padua**, occupying the wide fields with a diverse soldiery; while against him, the Venetian army remains within...

if I seem to unlock the hidden enclosures of Nature 
too much, or if perhaps it seems useless—
