if it is to be a mediator between spirit and body. For this <term>salt</term> <note>In alchemy, Salt represents the principle of fixity, body, and the "earth" element of a substance</note> contains the soul within itself; indeed, the body cannot live without its soul, nor can the soul exist without the spirit. Thus, the salt must be one with the spirit, and the spirit one with the salt. For this reason, that salt is the intermediary between them, if they are to remain together. And *Arnold of Villanova* <note>original: "Arnoldus de Villa noua"; a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: this Salt is miraculous. By this reasoning, it is plain that no <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> in the nature of things can be achieved that will remain perfect to the end, unless this salt is drawn out from the body together with the spirit, as was said before.

## CHAPTER LXVI.

<margin>
All those err who make amalgams with the Sun and Mercury, or with the Moon and Mercury, and why.
</margin>

Therefore, all those are mistaken who make any <term>amalgamations</term> <note>the process of blending metals, typically using mercury as a solvent</note> with the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Mercury, or with the Moon <note>Silver</note> and Mercury, and set them to be fixed, wishing to fix one with the other. They shall by no means fix them, neither now nor ever. For that salt lies in the deepest part of the Gold and Silver, and it holds within itself the soul of the Gold and Silver. No matter that exists in the nature of things can be drawn out from the inner parts of the Gold and the Silver except by its own spirit, and not by alien spirits. And that cannot be done in Gold and Silver either now or at any time [by those false means]. For Gold and Silver must be so opened and unlocked that they emit their own spirit from themselves; and the spirit will attract the salt, carrying the soul within it, out from the inner parts of the Gold and Silver, and will carry it up into the heaven <note>referring to the top of the distilling vessel</note>, and it shall become one nature with it. When, therefore, the body is now clean and pure, and the spirit with the salt carries the soul within it—the soul likewise being clean and pure—and then they are melted together again with their own proper and clean body, a true conjunction occurs, and it turns black. <margin>Where there is no true conjunction, the blackness does not show itself.</margin> And where this matter is not present, no blackness will bring itself forward; and where there is no true conjunction, the blackness does not show itself. Thus it should be plain that all amalgams, all fixations of <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "cynabrij"; a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide</note>, or all other fabricated, insane works, are false and fraudulent, however plausible they may seem, for the reasons I have previously taught. Therefore, avoid all false opinions, and weigh carefully what I have taught you, so that you may be enlightened in philosophy and understand the speech which the ancients always use in their books.

## CHAPTER LXVI.

Our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work</note> is to be drawn out of one thing and not from many; nor should anything foreign be added to it, in neither small nor great quantity. Truly, you must extract the soul from it, and remove the superfluities, and cleanse it; and prepare the body, and immediately pour the soul back into it again, and it shall live for ages, etc.

## CHAPTER LXVII.

Therefore, once <term>blackness</term> <note>original: "nigredine"; this refers to the 'Nigredo' or 'Black Crow' stage, signaling the successful death and putrefaction of the initial matter</note> is seen, you may be certain that the true conjunction has been achieved. <margin>By the already mentioned solution of spirit and body, the work becomes much more subtle and stronger.</margin>
## CHAPTER LXVIII.

Know also as a secret that this solution of the <term>spirit and body</term> <note>in this context, the 'spirit' is the volatile agent and the 'body' is the metallic base</note> is not strictly necessary, but the work becomes much more <term>subtle</term> <note>refined, purified, or possessing greater penetrating power</note> and stronger through it. I say that the Stone, after its perfection, in every single solution and <term>coagulation</term> <note>returning a liquid to a solid state</note>, gains a hundredfold in its <term>projection</term> <note>the final stage where a small amount of the Stone transforms a large amount of base metal into gold or silver</note>. And it is also more certain that the ferment and the spirit should both be dissolved into a clear water than if they were mixed together while dry. For what mixture is better and more certain than water with water, as was said before?

<margin>By frequent calcination, the work becomes very subtle.</margin>
<margin>Why 8 parts of ferment and 1 of spirit are to be taken.</margin>
## CHAPTER LXIX.

Know furthermore that when the spirit is fixed with the <term>ferment</term> <note>the substance that 'leavens' the matter and directs it toward the nature of gold or silver</note>, it is not even necessary that you then calcine and dissolve it; however, by every calcination and solution, you will gain a thousandfold in the projection. For by frequent calcination and solution, the work becomes so subtle that it is incredible. And for this reason, I teach you to take 8 parts of ferment and 1 of spirit, because you will often fix the work, and often calcine, dissolve, and coagulate it. The work will become as subtle as possible at the bottom, so that it may later reach a higher power of projection. One could take 4 parts of ferment and a fifth part of spirit and mix them together. But then you could not calcine it so many times, nor dissolve it, nor coagulate it. For the work would become too <term>fusible</term> <note>easily melted</note>. Thus you could not often calcine, dissolve, and coagulate, because it would become too easily melted in your hands, so that it could bear no flame. Therefore, if you wish to achieve a high and subtle work, take many parts of ferment and few of spirit, so that you may often calcine, dissolve, and coagulate your work...

### CHAPTER LXX.

<margin>How the Stone is to be multiplied.</margin>
Likewise, concerning the **multiplication** of your Stone in its virtue and its strengths, rather than in its size. It shall exalt itself in its nobility and <term>subtletty</term> <note>the degree of refinement or "spirituality" of the physical matter</note>, so that it now effects 10,000 [parts] in its <term>projection</term> <note>the act of casting the Stone onto base metals to transform them</note>. And when it has been thus multiplied and made subtle, and is exalted to great strengths and power, it easily effects 100,000 in projection. And if you were to multiply this Stone three times and make it subtle in virtue and power, its projection would be infinite, because of the great subtlety the Stone would then possess. Indeed, you could multiply the Stone so many times that you would never reach the limit of its projection, owing to the great subtlety and virtue it would obtain. But you could easily multiply it so often that you could not contain it in any glass; it would withdraw and vanish, for the stone would become so subtle that when you wished to dissolve it, it would penetrate the glass invisibly while the glass remained whole; and the Stone would convert the glass into the appearance and color of a **Ruby**. For place glass to be melted once the Stone is finished, and cast as much weight of the Stone upon the glass as you would take if you wished to convert <term>Jupiter</term> <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note> into the **Sun**; the Stone will convert the melted glass into a color like its own—into the appearance and color, I say, of a precious **Ruby**. And keep it thus melted in that crucible for half an hour; in this way the matter will harden, so much so that it will not melt now nor at any future time. It will be of the same hardness and the same color as a precious **Ruby** without spots. And there was a great debate among the **Ancients**, who said that glass colored in this way by the aforementioned Stone is better and more natural...

Regarding natural rubies: as you find in the book on stones which <term>Hermes the Philosopher</term> <note>original: "Hermes Philosophus"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note> composed, for he says: Into whatever thing **our stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is projected that can be melted, which is not a metal, and provided that thing is of a single nature, the stone is going to convert that thing into itself as much as can be done: but not to the same degree in which the stone itself exists, but rather to that degree which is possible for nature. Just as the Lord God created man in his own likeness for eternity, and with the same freedom, and in many other ways which would be too long to write in this place—for they do not concern our material—so I say that the stone converts only those things into its likeness which are not metals and which are of a single nature. 

Now, nothing in the nature of things is found to be of a single nature except crystal, or glass, or precious stones. For these are not made from composite things, but from one thing. From glass or crystal nothing else can be made but glass from glass, and crystal from crystal; however, they can be imbued with any colors whatsoever. For white crystalline glass acts like an elegant smooth tablet on which you can write anything; in the same way, white crystalline glass can be imbued with any color. And the more noble, beautiful, and subtle the color is, the more noble and excellent the glass becomes. 

So it is also with the stone: when it has infused its most excellent color into crystalline glass or crystal, it makes it like itself in color and beauty, but not in the same degree of power in which the stone exists. For that glass has no power of converting any other thing, or of making a <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectionem"; the act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto a larger mass of base material to transform it</note>. Nevertheless, it is the most noble, most beautiful, and most clear thing that exists in the nature of things; indeed, it is better than gold, because the most noble nature that exists under the celestial circle has been infused into it. 

Therefore the ancients agree in this: that this glass is so transformed to such a degree that it can never be liquefied, nor burned by fire; and it is as noble and excellent—indeed more excellent—than Oriental rubies, for the reason mentioned before. Therefore, one should take the stone and place crystalline glass into a strong crucible; and when it has already melted, he should project some of the stone upon it until the color pleases him well. For the stone would be soaked into the melted glass like oil into dry leather. When the color delights you, you would throw in nothing more, but would then allow it to flow together with the stone until it settles into a <term>Regulus</term> <note>original: "Regulum"; here referring to a pure, solidified mass of glassy material at the bottom of the crucible</note>, and becomes hard and transparent. For that is one of the operations, powers, and virtues of our stone: that all things with which it mixes itself, [when] liquid...

<margin>Every stone must have the same properties within itself as the invincible heaven.</margin>
...it may convert them into non-liquid substances. It makes all hard things soft, and all soft bodies hard: and whatever is combustible, it makes incombustible. And if it did not have this power of projection, it would not deserve to receive the name of the **Stone**. Then it would only be a <term>medicine of the second order</term> <note>original: "medicina secundi ordinis"; in alchemy, a preparation that can change the appearance of a substance but lacks the full transformative power of the true Philosopher's Stone</note>, and nothing more. ### CHAPTER LXXI.

<margin>How such Rubies are to be melted.</margin>
Now if you should wish to melt <note>original: "conflandis"; meaning to cast or fuse through heat</note> such **Rubies**, do as has been said: and when they have cooled, take them out, and cut them, and sharpen them upon a <term>grindstone</term> <note>original: "mola"; a lapidary's wheel</note> on which precious stones are sharpened, large or small, as you please, and polish them beautifully. And you will have excellent rubies without flaws, gladdening the hearts of men and securing victory for the hero, etc. And they received that power from the virtue of the stone working within them. Therefore I say: You might multiply the stone so many times, until it became so subtle—when you dissolved it again in that **red burning water** <note>original: "aqua ardente"; likely a strong acid or alchemical solvent used in the final stages</note>—that it would penetrate the glass invisibly, and you would lose it. The glass would remain whole, but would become red and transparent in the manner of a ruby, and hard and incombustible, as was said; and you would be deprived of your noble stone. It would become so spiritual that in the end it could not be contained in any glass vessels whatsoever, even if they were ten feet thick; and it would penetrate them because of the great subtlety of its multiplication and its great power. Therefore, take the stone, and multiply it in this manner.

Do this in all ways as was taught before. Repeat this workmanship until the entire substance flies up together from the red-hot plate. Then it is sufficiently "opened." Now, set it to be <term>sublimated</term> <note>the process where a solid turns into vapor and then solidifies again at the top of the vessel</note> in every way as before. You shall repeat this sublimation three or four times, always without adding any dregs; then it is enough. Then take a small portion of that which has been sublimated upward and place it to be <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "fixandam"; the process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> in the furnace where the spirit is <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, in such a glass vessel as is shown here. Place a small, smooth glass over the mouth. At first, apply a little heat, and then increase the fire by degrees several times, as is taught in the work. When it is fixed, weigh how much the fixed portion weighs. Then, for every three parts of the fixed substance, take one part of the spirit, and set it to be fixed again as before.

And it will be easily fixed. For it was fixed in all its parts. And the other parts which are added to the first part are fixed more easily than the first: for one part fixes another. <margin>In multiplication, no colors reveal themselves.</margin> And in multiplication, no blackness intervenes: nor do any <term>shifting colors</term> <note>original: "colores orbis"; literally "colors of the circle," often referring to the 'peacock’s tail' stage where many colors appear</note> reveal themselves, nor any whiteness. Nor in sublimation does anything show itself except redness: nor in <term>fixation</term> does any color manifest itself besides its own, which is an excellent redness. For the Stone has no color other than redness. It is only one substance, a simple matter, like the invincible heaven. You shall also know that although it was sublimated, it was not deprived of its fixity; and when the Stone is finished and prepared in its extreme virtue, then the Stone again cannot be changed into another by crafting it from its essence. For if the Stone could be extracted from its essence into another essence or nature, or if it could be changed: it would not be the Philosophers' Stone, nor would it be simple: nor a <term>glorified body</term> <note>original: "corpus glorificatum"; a term borrowed from theology to describe a perfected, immortal substance</note>. No, no. Understand my speech correctly. The Stone cannot be changed into any other nature or essence after it is perfected. For it is only one thing: and understand this in its own degree.

### CHAPTER 73.

<margin>A question and its solution.</margin>
Now someone might ask: can the Stone be changed by no means? It was fixed before and endured the fire: and yet you teach me to make it <term>volatile</term> <note>capable of being vaporized by heat</note> again, so that I may sublimate it. Has it not, therefore, been led back from its fixed corporeal nature into a purely spiritual nature? You speak correctly: that it first endured the fire and was afterwards made volatile: both are true. Therefore, it has not been led back from its nature into another nature: so it must be: and if it were not so, it would perform no <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectionem"; the final act of casting the Stone upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver</note>. For that which performs projection must be spirit, soul, and body equally strong and powerful: and if it were not such—but the body were stronger than the spirit, or the spirit more powerful than the body—then there would be a contrary nature in it: then it would not be one thing. Our Stone is body, soul, and spirit, and these three are one in a simple essence inseparably: equal in magnitude, strength, and power: one is not separated from the other: for there is one essence, one simple nature, the one being just like the other. Nevertheless, there are three—spirit, soul, and body—they are in one as we understand. Understand my words thoroughly, and learn to know the Stone, and what kind of nature it ought to be.

<summary>This page describes the final qualities of the Philosophers' Stone, emphasizing its vibrant red color and its immutable nature as a "glorified body" composed of perfectly balanced body, soul, and spirit. It explains that while the Stone can be made volatile for refinement, its essential nature remains one and the same to enable the final act of projection.</summary>

## CHAPTER LXX.

<margin>
Our Stone is neither fixed nor volatile.
</margin>
You shall also know, as a great secret, that our stone is neither <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "fixum"; a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to intense heat.</note> nor <term>volatile</term> <note>original: "volatilem"; a substance that easily evaporates or "flies" away when heated.</note>. It is simultaneously spirit and body; both must possess spirit and body within their own nature, and both must be equally strong, as we have previously demonstrated to you through reasoning.

<margin>
Why it appears fixed and endures fire.
</margin>
As for the fact that it appears to be fixed and endures the fire, this occurs because of its <term>solidity</term> <note>original: "soliditatem"; here referring to the density and lack of porosity in the perfected material.</note>, so that the parts of the stone are so compacted into one that nothing in the nature of things is as tightly compressed into one as our stone is. For in the world there is no thing as <term>subtle</term> <note>original: "subtilis"; in alchemy, "subtle" describes matter that is exceptionally fine, pure, and capable of penetrating other bodies.</note> or as clean as our stone. And the more subtle and pure a thing is, the more firmly its subtle and pure parts come together and are compressed into one, and the heavier they are in weight. For they "love" one another, to such an extent that they are squeezed into one and can only be separated with difficulty. See how its excellence waits for the fire: the fire cannot separate its parts because it is so firmly compacted into one. And yet, it is pure spirit: for it "flies" (evaporates) much more easily once it has been "opened" than any other spirits. And this is due to the great subtlety and purity it possesses in its nature. Will our stone not, therefore, resist the fire better and more strongly? For it is made of both body and spirit at once; and the body is so subtle—indeed, it was subtler than the spirit. And now the body and spirit are one in a single essence and a single nature. How much more strongly will our stone be able to resist the fire than gold, which is still as it was formed by nature and is "pure spirit" and resists fire? Therefore, the stone ought to resist the fire ten thousand times more strongly than gold. And when our stone is now opened and unlocked by our <term>burning water</term> <note>original: "aqua nostra ardenti"; likely a reference to a strong solvent or distilled alcohol used to dissolve the Stone's components.</note>, which separates its compacted parts and causes them to be raised up and inflated in the manner of a sponge: if gold ascends (sublimes) with a tiny fire more easily than any spirit because of the subtlety nature granted it, how much more easily and swiftly will our stone ascend from a fire of small heat than gold? For our stone possesses all the extreme subtlety that nature can give it. Moreover, the artist has infused into it the extreme virtue and subtlety, with that subtlety which can be given to it, so that it is a hundred thousand times more subtle than gold. Therefore, our stone must ascend more easily than gold because it is much more subtle. And when its parts are joined to it again in a lesser proportion, so that the parts are compressed together and forced into one again—which we call <term>fixation</term>—the stone will again endure the fire as it did before: and a thousand times more strongly...

For the more often the stone is opened and <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: "sublimatur"; the process of vaporizing a solid and recollecting it in a purified form.</note>, and again gathered together so that it is once more compressed into one—which we call <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixationem"; making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>—the more firmly it sticks together. Thus, the subtle parts, because of their great fineness, are gathered so firmly into one that it resists fire a hundred thousand times better than before, etc.

### CHAPTER LXXV.

<margin>The stone is not changed, but remains in its own essence, and why.</margin>
You shall also know that when you multiply the stone and raise it in height and power, it does not change in its nature: it does not turn black, nor does it release any variety of colors from itself; rather, it remains in its own essence and in its own nature, in which it had been before. For it has been brought to its ultimate state, so that it has become a <term>simple essence</term> <note>original: "simplex essentia"; a substance that is no longer a mixture of conflicting elements but has become a unified, incorruptible whole.</note> and a simple nature. And nature cannot change it by any means, nor by any art that exists in the world. Truly, you can make it more subtle than it is, but it remains in its own essence and in its own nature in which it exists, etc.

### CHAPTER LXXVI.

<margin>Condensation of the stone, which is improperly called fixation.</margin>
Therefore, you can open and unlock the stone as often as was said before, and afterwards sublimate it, and then pack it together again from its tiny parts, so that its parts cohere once more into one—which we call fixation. Indeed, we name it "fixing," but it is not truly fixation: it is merely <term>condensation</term> <note>original: "condensatio"; the packing together of particles into a denser, more solid state.</note>, so that all its subtle parts are gathered together again, tightly packed as they were before, so that it may again endure the fire. In this way, we can perform <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectionem"; the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note> with it just as we did before.

Thus, you will easily be able to multiply your stone three or four times, but no more. For it would become too subtle, so much so that it would slip away from you invisibly once it had been reduced to a liquid <note>original: "in aquam perductus"; literally "led into water," referring to the stone dissolving into a liquid elixir.</note>, because of its great subtlety, as I taught you above. Therefore, you can raise your stone to its highest degree, so that here below the <term>circle of the Moon</term> <note>original: "circulum Lunae"; a traditional term for the earthly realm, which was believed to be everything below the orbit of the moon.</note>, no matter so noble and subtle as this stone can be found. For when it has been raised so high that it cannot be raised further, nor made more subtle, no earthly matter can surpass the stone in nobility, nor in subtlety, nor in beauty, nor in power, nor in strength, nor in the wondrous influences and virtues that are enclosed within it when it is brought to its highest degree, as will be demonstrated in the section on projection, etc.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.

<margin>How the ancients made their stone before the discovery of strong waters.</margin>
You should know that the ancient Philosophers were accustomed to making their stone in the manner taught previously, before the art of strong waters <note>original: "aquarum fortium"; usually refers to nitric acid, a powerful solvent unknown to the earliest alchemists.</note> was discovered. For up until that time, the bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the base or precious metals being used in the work.</note> had to be opened slowly—namely, by calcining <note>heating to a high temperature to reduce a substance to powder</note>, reverberating, dissolving in our sharp vinegar <note>original: "acri nostro aceto"; likely distilled vinegar or a specific alchemical solvent</note>, and congealing, until our stone became spiritual <note>original: "spiritualis"; meaning refined into a non-solid or volatile state</note>. And then they worked further, as was taught before. 

And when the stone was entirely perfected, they did not yet have the true art of multiplying their stone in its own power. Instead, they tried to make it subtle little by little for its perfection by dissolving it in our sharpest vinegar and congealing it until it remained as a clear oil. And when they desired to turn that oil into a hard mass once more, they took prepared <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Solem præparatum"; alchemical code for purified gold</note>—namely, stripped of its body and red like blood—and mixed their oil with it, dissolving and congealing it once. Then they placed it in a secret furnace with a temperate heat until it was turned into a dark red mass like <term>dragon's blood</term> <note>original: "sanguinis draconis"; a deep red resin or, in alchemy, a specific stage of the "Great Work" characterized by a deep red color</note>, which, because of the frequent dissolving and congealing, was much more subtle than before.

<margin>Their successors discovered strong waters.</margin>
Noting this, their successors sharpened the edge of their minds and discovered <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aquam fortem"; nitric acid</note>, which greatly shortened the path for them. For they made strong water, as was said before, in which they could grind and wear down both bodies, taking one part of each after they had been cleansed. Then they mixed the waters and governed them so that the mixture was transparent and clear, without dregs. And then they easily made their stone spiritual. From there, they led their stone to extreme perfection. They could then make it subtle and multiply it in its own power as they pleased, using that same strong water mentioned before, properly <term>rectified</term> <note>original: "rectificatum"; purified through distillation</note>. And this they did in all the ways as was rightly taught before. Thus, strong water is a great aid for shortening the work and for leading the stone to a higher perfection.

It is a noble and delightful work, or a path in the art, as you shall hear. Therefore, first take <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Lunam"; alchemical code for silver</note> purified by fire on a shard or <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cupellam"; a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead or other impurities</note>, and properly refined from lead; dissolve...

### On the projection of the stone.

## CHAPTER LXXX.

<margin>How the projection is to be performed. The metal must be prepared before the projection can be made into it.</margin>
<margin>The white stone should only be projected upon Jupiter, and the reason why.</margin>
Next, I will teach you how and in what manner you shall use your stone and join it with metals to transmute them into <term>the Sun</term> <note>Gold</note> or <term>the Moon</term> <note>Silver</note>. You shall know this as a great secret: you can make no projection upon any metal unless it has first been prepared for it in this manner. If you wish to make a projection upon <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Iouem"; the alchemical name for Tin</note>, you shall melt it in a <term>crucible</term> <note>a ceramic melting pot</note>, and to every pound of Tin you shall add one ounce of pure Silver, melting them together. Then, cast your white stone upon it, and the Tin will be transmuted into true Silver—more or less, depending on how subtle your stone was made, as will be better explained. And if you wish to work with your red stone, you shall project it upon Silver; you need do nothing to the Silver except melt it, and then cast your red stone upon it. Your Silver will then become true Gold, better than that which is brought from the mines. Above all, you must know that when you wish to perform a projection, you should project your white stone only upon Tin, and upon no other metal. For Tin is the metal closest to Silver. Tin is a raw and "undercooked" body, and the stone needs to do nothing other than "ripen" the Tin, as has been taught elsewhere. It could easily transmute other metals into Silver as well, but they are filthier than Tin, and thus the projection would not be as "high" <note>meaning the ratio of transmutation would be lower</note>. Furthermore, the stone would have to flow in the fire with those impure metals much longer than with Tin before they could settle into a <term>regulus</term> <note>original: "Regulum"; a button or lump of pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible</note>.

<margin>Projection with the red stone must be made upon the moon, and the reason why.</margin>
## CHAPTER LXXXI.

Furthermore, you shall perform your projection with the red stone upon <term>the Moon</term> <note>Silver</note>, which is the purest of all metals upon which a projection can be made. Indeed, no projection can be made with the red stone except upon Silver. For if you were to project it upon <term>Saturn</term> <note>Lead</note> or the other metals, it would perform no projection upon them. For the red stone produces nothing except Gold. And you must know that one cannot arrive from the first degree to the third except by passing through the second. Thus, the imperfect metals would first have to be reduced to Silver, and only then to Gold. For no metal can reach the state of Gold unless it is first Silver. Indeed, Gold was Silver before it became Gold. Nature had to generate Silver from the matter first, before she could lead it to become Gold. Just so, one cannot reach a place 100 miles distant unless he first crosses the middle of the journey: from one

As Morienus says:

### CHAPTER LXXXII.

<margin>
The method of projection to be observed.
</margin>
Furthermore, you shall know the method of projecting. For if you were to project the Stone upon the Moon or <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin</note> while it is as "raw" as when it was first made or taken from the vessel: the matter of the Stone would not want to enter the metal, even if you had instilled a soul into that metal, or even if it were a living body such as the Moon is. The Stone would not want to mix itself with it because it is so subtle and compacted into one, even if it were a powder. For metal is thick and molten, and if you projected the Stone upon it, the Stone would melt and settle upon the metal, spreading itself over it. It would hold the metal back so that it could not flow; it would even protect the metal so that its <term>combustible sulfur</term> <note>In alchemical theory, sulfur was the principle of "combustibility" and change; the Stone was thought to stabilize it.</note> could not fly away, nor could fire burn that metal with the help of its combustible sulfur. Thus the Stone would protect the metal. For it would lie upon it just as molten oil floats upon water. But the Stone would refuse to mix itself with the metal, just as oil refuses to mix with water; no matter how much oil and water are shaken together, when they rest again, the oil floats on top once more, and the oil guards the water so that no foreign moisture can reach it.
<margin>
A more subtle spirit exists in all waters, which, if lost, causes the waters to stink.
</margin>
And the oil also preserves the water so that no air can breathe out from it, nor any subtle spirit. For a certain more subtle spirit exists in all waters. For if you let water stand uncovered for four or five days, that water will immediately stink once it has lost its spirit. But when it is covered with oil, even if the water stood under the oil for ten years, it would not stink; thus the oil would protect that water from all corruptions and preserve the spirit of the water so that it would not fly away. Which happens...

<sig>bb 4</sig>

<margin>The question and its solution.</margin>
...you might ask, why does oil not mix with water, and always float on top? For oil is heavier than water: how then does it float? For daily we see that it is always the light thing that floats.

---

->CHAPTER LXXXIII.<-

<margin>Why oil, although it is heavier than water, nevertheless floats.</margin>
First and before all things you shall know, that oil has no common part with water; even though it <note>the substance from which the oil came</note> might once have been one body with water, yet now the water has no part with the oil. For the <term>quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth essence," or the purest, most spiritual part of a substance</note>, which oil retains in the seed or in whatever other thing from which the oil is pressed out or distilled, has departed. For when the quintessence has withdrawn from any thing in which water, fire, air, earth, oil, and salt are held together: once that quintessence has departed, it is necessary that all those parts be separated from one another. Nor will they ever wish to come together again afterwards until they have been "glorified" <note>refined or brought to a higher, more perfect state</note>.

Therefore, oil refuses to be mixed with water, even though it was once a single body bound together by the quintessence. And oil always floats, yet it is heavier than water. Do you know how this happens? Oil is much more <term>subtle</term> <note>meaning refined, thin, or spirit-like in consistency</note> than water, even though oil contains many thick parts within itself, and even <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>a salt used in alchemy, known for its ability to sublimate or turn into vapor</note>. Furthermore, the parts of the oil are firmly compressed into one, so that it refuses to be pulled apart. Water is a solid element and is very "open" <note>porous or loose in its structure</note> because of the thickness within it; but oil is subtle and fiery, and is firmly compressed into a single unit. Because all heat tends to move upward, and all subtlety tends upward, and because those firm parts of the oil refuse to be separated from each other, the oil will not penetrate the dense waters to sink. 

Thus it is that oil must necessarily float. The same is true of our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>; it also floats upon metals just as oil floats upon water. For the Stone does not yet have a part with the metals, even though it may have been a metal once. It is heavier than the metal, and that is because it is more subtle and more firmly compacted. The metal stands liquefied and is very solid, like water; but the Stone is not of the nature of metal, for it is already the quintessence. Therefore it does not want to mix with the metal, nor enter into it. It floats because of those firm parts which refuse to be separated; the Stone simply does not want to enter the metal, and so it must necessarily float on the surface. Know that Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says:

> *Our Stone must have a part with the body, the spirit, and the soul, before it will perform projection.* <note>original Latin: "Lapis noster partem habere debet cum corpore & spiritu, atq; cum anima, antequam proiectionem faciet."</note>

### CHAPTER LXXXIV.
<note>original: "CAP. LXXXIV."</note>

<margin>No joining of contrary things can be made, except through a medium. <note>original: "Nulla coniunctio rerum cōtrariarum fieri potest, nisi per medium."</note></margin>
You shall further know that our stone has part with body, soul, and spirit. But the parts in the stone are united with such perfection, and by such a spiritual substance, and driven into one, that they refuse to mix themselves with any thick, imperfect, or impure parts, except through a medium; which medium must be joined to the spiritual substance, whether it be white or red <note>referring to the White Elixir for silver or the Red Elixir for gold</note>. For no gathering can happen in any things that are mutually contrary to each other, except through an intermediary, which makes the contrary things enter one into the other, and embrace each other, and remain together; concerning which matter I have taught you in many places.

So it is also here in the <term>projection</term> <note>the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transform it</note>. The stone does not wish to enter into black, dirty, foul, and imperfect metals without a medium. For black, impure metals are especially contrary to the stone. How then would those two contrary things come together, one into the other, without a medium? Truly, not at all, neither now nor at any time. A medium must be present, through which medium the one will penetrate the other. 

Now, what shall that medium be, through which those two dissimilar things shall come together? That medium must be alive and one with the dead, impure, and stinking body <note>the base metal</note>. And that same living body must be one in a single body with the stone, whether white or red. And when these two dead, stinking metals have within themselves that pure living body which is one with them—just as soul and body are—and the stone (whether white or red) is projected into them, also having within itself that same living body, then they meet; and each draws its own into its nature, so that a joining occurs there, and the one enters into the other. Thus the stone, gathered in that manner, expels all corruption along with itself, and produces a perfect living body—either better or more perfect than that which comes from the mines.

### CHAPTER LXXXV.
<note>original: "CAP. LXXXV."</note>

<margin>In what way the stone, both white and red, is to be prepared for joining with metals. <note>original: "Quo pacto lapis tam albus quā ruber separandus ad coniungēdum cum metallis."</note></margin>
Now I wish to teach you in what way you shall prepare and test your stone, whether it be white or red, for coupling it with metals and entering into them. Take, therefore, one part of your red stone and add to it a thousand parts of pure <term>Sol</term> <note>original: "Solis"; alchemical name for Gold</note>, and beat that into thin plates. Then take <term>quick sulphur</term> <note>original: "viuum sulphur"; native or "living" sulfur</note> and grind it upon a stone into a thick paste with oil, and with that smear your plates, and let them dry; then smear them again, and a third time, letting them dry each time. Then, with live coal—

<meta>This page continues the instructions for preparing an alchemical "medium" to facilitate the transformation of metals. Having previously discussed the necessity of an intermediary substance, the author now provides the specific laboratory procedure for preparing "Sol" (gold) and combining it with the "Stone" through a three-day heating process.</meta>

<page-num>389</page-num>

Place [it] upon the coals and allow it to be <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcinari"; the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder</note>. Then crush it into a powder, and wash the powder with common distilled water until your water flows off clear from the powder. Then grind the powder on a stone with honey from the comb or gum water, and grind it so finely as if it were to be used for painting. Then put it again into glass vessels and wash it with common warm distilled water; let the powder settle, then pour off the water from above. Stir it and let it settle, pour it off again, and repeat this until the water flows off as clear from the powder as when you first poured it on. Then dry your powder over a small fire or in the sun. Then your <term>Sol</term> <note>Latin for "Sun," the alchemical name for gold</note> is prepared, etc.

Then take a thousand parts of this powder of Sol, and one part of its "first stone," and pulverize the stone finely, and mix it with the powder of your prepared Sol. And then have a <term>crucible</term> <note>a ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at high temperatures</note> that can withstand a great and vehement fire; and fit another crucible to this one, and smooth it on a stone so that one fits the other exactly, or one is enclosed by the other like a lid. Then put your powder into this, and seal the crucibles one over the other firmly with <term>lute</term> <note>original: "luta"; a clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels and make them airtight</note>, and surround the outside with a strong lute to the thickness of three or four fingers, and let the lute dry thoroughly.

Then place the crucible in a wind furnace, and first apply a small fire; several times make it hotter and hotter, until your crucible is thoroughly white-hot. Then you shall greatly increase your fire until you are certain your material is melting in the crucible. Then keep the crucible for three days at a single temperature, so that your material remains molten; and afterwards allow it to cool of its own accord. Then break open your crucible, and you will find a remarkable hard mass; and it is brittle, as if it were glass, so that you are able to pulverize it.

And when you wish to perform the <term>projection</term> <note>the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note>, cast one part of this finely pulverized mass into a thousand parts of the nearest metal having a soul and life <note>likely referring to mercury or a "living" metallic base</note>; and it will transform it into true <term>Sol</term> <note>gold</note> or <term>Luna</term> <note>silver</note> better than that which comes from the mines. And this is that "work of three days" of which the Ancients made mention in their books. It is a great work, rendering the body of Sol so subtle in the space of three days while it remains melted with the stone, so that the Sol becomes more medicinal than it had been before—indeed, more than can be believed. And hold this as a great secret, etc.

<margin>
A stone prepared in the manner previously described cannot make a projection onto Mercury.

Furthermore, you shall now know that a stone prepared in this way cannot make a <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectionem"; the act of casting a small amount of an alchemical catalyst onto a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</note> onto Mercury, because of its difficult fusion <note>meaning it does not melt easily enough to combine with liquid mercury</note>. For with the stone, projection is only made to the red upon <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical name for silver</note>, and to the white upon <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Iouem"; the alchemical name for tin</note>. Therefore, there is no need to make it so fusible; concerning which matter I have taught you abundantly in [the section on] multiplication: how you shall make an oil from this stone. Therefore, there is no need to treat Mercury here. But you shall remember when you wish to work with the oil and project upon Mercury: take 1 pound of Mercury, and a half-mark of pure cupelled Moon [silver]. And <term>amalgamate</term> <note>mix or blend the silver into the mercury to form a pasty alloy</note> it with that pound of Mercury in a glass crucible, which is placed within an earthen crucible. Place it on the fire; and when it begins to smoke, cast upon it the oil of your stone, which is prepared with the "body" <note>the metallic substance</note>, as I taught you in multiplication and will now also teach by other means.

Take the oil of the white or red stone, and take <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Solem"; the alchemical name for gold</note> for the oil of the red stone. Then, to one part of oil, add ten parts of <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a fine powder through heat</note> Sun, prepared as was said above. Soak this <term>calx</term> <note>the powdered remains of a metal after heating</note> of Sun with this oil, and place it in a glass ampoule on a tripod. First apply a small fire, and several times increase it more and more until you can hardly hold your hand in the inner part of the furnace. In this way, let it stand for five or six days. Afterward, increase the fire until the stone of the inner furnace hisses when you touch it with a wet finger; and keep it in that heat for three days. Then let it cool by itself. Take it out, and having broken the glass, you will find a hard, congealed mass.

Wishing, therefore, to make a projection upon Mercury, put Mercury in a crucible as was said before, and take a part of this mass and pulverize it, and cast it upon it when the Mercury begins to smoke. Then increase the fire until it begins to flow. Then let it flow until it settles itself into a <term>Regulus</term> <note>a button of pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible</note>. Then extinguish the fire and let it cool. Take it out and beat it with a hammer on an anvil, and see if it is soft. If it is soft, you have good Sun [gold]. And as long as it is breakable or fragile like glass, it is still the "medicine" <note>the concentrated alchemical agent, not yet a usable metal</note>. Then cast molten Moon [silver] upon it until it remains soft under the hammer. Then you have good Sun [gold]. And as long as it is breakable, you have not yet reached the end of your projection, whether of the red or white stone, or of the red or white oil. Furthermore, you must project into other metals for so long until it remains soft and of an excellent color, and passes every test. Then you have the end of your projection, etc. I say to you, my son,

once the stone is finished—as I have taught you—whether in the white or the red work, and during its <term>multiplication</term> <note>the process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical Stone</note>, its <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectio"; the act of casting the Stone onto base metal to transmute it</note> is so infinite that it is incredible to those who do not fundamentally understand the Art. ->CHAPTER 87.<-

<margin>From what both stones are first coagulated.</margin>
Understand my words well, which I am about to say. The White and Red Stone first arose and were <term>coagulated</term> <note>turned from a liquid or vaporous state into a solid</note> from Mercury and from white <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, combustible principle, while Mercury represents the passive, fluid principle</note>; thus coagulated, they are a poison. For the stone coagulated from pure and white Sulphur, and from pure Mercury, is white <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: "arsenicum"; alchemists often identified arsenic as a "middle" substance that shared properties with both metals and non-metals</note>—pure and subtle—and it is a poison. <margin>The purer and more subtle a poison is, the more poisonous it becomes.</margin> For the purer and more subtle a poison is, the more poisonous it is. And when pure red Sulphur falls into pure Mercury, it coagulates the Mercury: and that becomes a shining yellow arsenic, which is also pure and subtle—indeed, much more subtle than white arsenic. If an ounce of arsenic were given to a great horse, it would undoubtedly die. For that poison would seek the heart and then spread through all the limbs, so that all the flesh and whatever is in the horse would be infected by the poison, such that it must die. And if dogs, or cats, or all birds were to eat of this horse, they would all die from it at once. Now, if an ounce of our poison can kill such a large horse, which weighs so many hundreds of pounds, and furthermore kills whatever eats of it—if, therefore, a single poison in such a small quantity can exert such great power upon such a large weight—then consider our Stone, which is refined from that same white or red arsenic. Through the red [Sulphur], over a long time, <term>Sol</term> <note>original: "Sol" (the Sun); the alchemical name for gold</note> was produced, and nature cooked it thus by the heat of the sun with continual digestion in the earth; it led the poison into its interior and brought the interior qualities outward. And from the matter which had previously been poisonous, Nature has produced a "Great Medicine." For gold is beneficial when combined with all medicines in all diseases. Our Stone is refined from those two aforementioned metals: namely, from Gold and Silver, as is apparent in the work, etc.

->CHAPTER 88.<-

<margin>Gold and Silver must be taken and unraveled by the artisan.</margin>
Therefore, you must take this Gold and Silver, and once again <term>unravel</term> <note>original: "retexe"; to decompose or break down a substance into its primary components</note> what nature worked upon them for so many years. Then the artisan un-weaves them backward until he arrives at that matter in which they were when nature first began to work in them: and he has reduced them again to "arsenic": and that poison once again [is brought] forth...

<margin>
Why the ancients compared the material to a poisonous dragon and called it a serpent.

...brought it out by the subtlety of the art. Thus, that material is a thousand times more poisonous than it was before nature first began to work within it. If two <term>drachms</term> <note>a small unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 1/8th of an ounce</note> of this material were given to a large horse, it would die immediately, as would anyone who ate from it. For the material is now so subtle, and has become so poisonous and hot, that it cannot be described. Furthermore, the material is often <term>sublimated</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note> many times; and in this sublimation, the material becomes so subtle, so hot, and so poisonous that its smoke would kill a man instantly without delay. Indeed, if it were placed under a seat upon which a man sat, and he remained there for the space of four or five <term>Lord’s Prayers</term> <note>a common historical way to measure time; four or five recitations would take about two minutes</note>, the material would invade his body so that he would surely die. For there is no beast so strong—even if it were a poisonous dragon—that it would not die if this smoke entered its body. For this reason, the Ancients compared the material to a poisonous Dragon, and said: *The Dragon devoured its own tail* <note>original: "Draco suam ipsius caudam voravit"; a reference to the Ouroboros, symbolizing the cyclical nature of the alchemical work</note>. They also called the material *the serpent impregnating itself* <note>original: "serpentem seipsum impraegnantem"</note>, and so on. Therefore, there is no greater or stronger poison to be found in the world than the material of the Stone, on account of its great subtlety and the immense heat that is within it when it is sublimated.

### CHAPTER 89.

<margin>
An extremely good thing can perform infinitely more good than an extremely bad thing can perform evil.
</margin>
But then, the artist—by his philosophical art and medicine—causes the poison, which had been on the outside, to station itself in the innermost part of the material. By his great medical art, he brings out the great medicinal virtue that lay hidden in its interior. It is then tempered with such a <term>temperament</term> <note>the balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, dry, and moist</note> of heat, cold, dryness, and moisture, that it becomes a celestial nature. And just as great as the poison was before, so great a medicine has it now become, once its interior parts have been brought to the surface. In this way, you will understand regarding that large horse—which could have been killed by an ounce of the stone before nature began to work in it (which we call <term>arsenic</term>)—if it had such great power then, do not wonder that the Stone can perform an infinite <term>projection</term> <note>the act of casting the Stone onto base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note> when it is brought to a celestial nature. For an extremely good thing can produce 100,000 times more good than an extremely evil thing can produce evil. For example: God is extremely good, and the devil is extremely evil; which has the greater power? God or the devil? It is the same with our Stone. When it was a poison, it could have killed such a great beast; and now that it has been made good, how much good will it do even in a tiny weight? Indeed, a thousand times more.

### CHAPTER 90.

<margin>Everything created by God has redness either on the outside or the inside.</margin>
Now you may ask how one part of the stone could <term>tinge</term> <note>to transform or dye a base metal into a precious one</note> 10,000 or 100,000 parts, or even more parts than the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for Silver</note>; this seems difficult to understand. You must know that under all greenness lies blackness, and under all blackness lies whiteness. And under all whiteness, redness is hidden. Indeed, whatever God has created possesses a perfect redness, either on the outside or the inside. For everything that is red within is white without; and between these are various intermediate colors. Likewise, whatever is white within is red without; and between the whiteness and the redness are colors of every kind, as was said before. 

The closer a thing approaches to perfection, the fewer colors it holds within itself; it becomes simpler the nearer it reaches its ultimate end. And when it has reached that highest and final end for which God ordained it, it possesses only one color, neither different inside nor outside. Instead, it holds within itself the power of all the colors that previously manifested in it. For a thing in which there are many colors, and many distinct, varied colors, contains just as many diverse <term>complexions</term> <note>the combination of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determine a substance's nature</note> and virtues. 

But when that thing is led into a simple, perfect essence, to its highest virtue for which God ordained it, all those virtues operate together in that work, in a short time, and miraculously. Yet there is only one simple essence in this thing; its color is red both inside and out. Between its interior and exterior—that is, in its middle—there is no difference; as it is on the outside, so it is on the inside and in the middle. Because of this, it performs its work all at once without delay, in a moment or the <term>blink of an eye</term> <note>original: "nictu oculi"</note>. For there is no contrary nature within it to oppose itself; therefore, they work together as one.

### CHAPTER 91.

<margin>He applies the preceding points to his Stone.</margin>
So it is with our Stone: into whatever it is cast, it performs a perfect work there. It turns that very thing inside out; it places the interior on the outside, and the exterior on the inside. For the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> is, in its interior, good **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical name for Gold</note>, bright and red. And when the White Stone is cast into **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, it draws its interior outward, and it becomes white and clear **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, while placing its redness inside. Thus, every thing has its own <term>tincture</term> <note>the soul or essence that gives a metal its specific properties and color</note> within itself, whether in white or red, even if the white and red Stone had no tincture of its own to give off—though it certainly does. Metals [receive] the tincture of the stone...

# MINERAL WORKS
### OF MASTER JOHN ISAAC

...they have no need [for help], whether in the white or in the red <note>referring to the "White Stone" used to create silver or the "Red Stone" used for gold</note>. For every thing contains within itself what is necessary for it; and every thing has enough <term>tincture</term> <note>the transforming principle or "dye" in alchemy that changes the nature of a substance</note> in itself, without the support of any other thing. Every thing created by God possesses its own medicine, without the addition of any foreign medicine, whether in the vegetable, animal, or mineral kingdom, to heal all the diseases that come upon it. If it were not so, the works of God would not be perfect. For whatever God ever made, it was all without fault, and needed no help from other foreign things; it holds within itself everything it needs, even if we do not fundamentally understand it. God did nothing in vain, not even the smallest leaf growing from the earth, as will be shown in the section on vegetables. Even though we do not see perfection in all things, they nevertheless have it enclosed within themselves. For through the medicine of the <term>art</term> <note>the "Art" refers to the practice of Alchemy</note>, we can extract from all things their hidden nature; and we can make its secret manifest, and its manifest secret <note>original: "secretum eius manifestum, ac manifestum secretum efficere." A common alchemical goal: to reveal the hidden essence and internalize the physical appearance</note>. 

And this is what our **Stone** accomplishes in metals. You should know that the white and red **Stone** emits no tincture from itself into the metals during <term>projection</term> <note>the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon molten base metal to transform it into silver or gold</note>. For the tincture that is in the **Stone** is so unified with the elements and with the living spirits—becoming one body and one substance—that they cannot be separated. For its nature is celestial, just as the heaven is invincible, from which the **Sun**, **Moon**, **Planets**, **Stars**, and whatever is and stands in the <term>firmament</term> <note>the heavens or the sky</note> takes its influence, which it shows to these lower things, as we see daily before our eyes.

<margin>
By the power and heat of the **Sun**, flowers of various colors are born, and the reason why this happens.
</margin>

By the power and heat of the **Sun**, flowers of various colors and various scents are born here. And all this is done by the heat of the **Sun**. Do you think the **Sun** pours colors and scents into the flowers or herbs from its own body? Not at all. Rather, it is a celestial nature; it has such power and influence within itself that it elicits colors, scents, and tastes from the seed from which the herbs or flowers are born. Even if the **Sun** were to shine for a thousand years, the **Sun** would infuse neither color, nor scent, nor taste. But **GOD** infused them, and all of that is enclosed within the seed. But unless the **Sun** shone upon them, never would colors, or tastes, or scents, or fruits be born, nor would they arise from the seed. The **Sun** is a celestial body, and it holds influence within itself, so that by its heat it elicits everything internal that is in the seed, and leads out the scent, and taste, and color to the outside; and this from the seed, so that through it, it may grow to its own perfection. And it brings it about that further other seeds...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical explanation of how the Alchemical Stone acts as a catalyst to bring out the inherent "perfection" or "tincture" already present in metals, rather than adding something entirely foreign to them. It transitions from this theory into a practical recipe for purifying copper.</meta>

...seeds may be born in abundance perpetually until the very end of the world: yet it does not distribute from its own body. This is exactly how it is with our **white and red stone** <note>The "White Stone" was believed to transmute base metals into silver, while the "Red Stone" produced gold</note>; it does not divide its own <term>tincture</term> <note>the transforming essence or "dye" that changes the nature of a metal</note> or body into the metals. Rather, it is a celestial body—as has been said of the Sun—which draws the tincture out of the metals themselves and leads it to its ultimate perfection, so that they may become seeds for making the Stone from them. 

But if God had not established any perfection within the metals, no change would occur even if the Stone were cast into the metals a thousand times. For the Stone could not possibly confer upon a thing what it did not already possess. I wrote to you regarding <term>multiplication</term> <note>the process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical agent</note> that the Stone makes a crystal take on the likeness of a Ruby, yet it is not a Ruby. It is nothing other than a stone which is one with the crystal glass, shining through it so that it resembles a Ruby in color. And if the Stone could be separated from the glass by the **Art** <note>the "Art" refers to the practice of alchemy</note>, the glass would be glass once again, just as it was before. Thus, the Stone cannot confer what it does not have. It truly transfers from bad to good, from the impure to the pure, whatever is similar to itself—and not in all things, but specifically in metals.

Then place all your crucibles into the furnace for <term>calcining</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or drive off volatile matter</note>: and first apply a small fire, and then several times more and more intense by degrees, continuing this until it glows white-hot. And this pouring off and pouring on again shall be repeated until the water flows out as clear as that which you pour over it.

And then cover the bag everywhere with good lute <note>sealing clay</note> that can withstand fire, to a thickness of two fingers. Then let it dry: and when it is dry, place the bag upon one or two iron supports: and place a crucible beneath the end of the bag in which that wooden quill is located. Then build a fierce fire around it, and it will easily melt and flow into the crucible: and maintain it thus until you have all your powder gathered into one body. 

And when you have it all together in one body, weigh how heavy it is, and to every <term>mark</term> <note>a historical unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 8 ounces</note>, you shall add an ounce <note>indicated by the symbol $\tilde{\text{z}}$</note> of pure, cupelled **Luna** <note>the alchemical name for Silver</note>: and you shall melt them together in a large crucible, and cast it into rods: and thus your "body" is prepared and <term>vivified</term> <note>brought to an active or "living" state, ready for further transformation</note> for the medicine of the second order to be cast upon it: according to the doctrine of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition</note> and **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century alchemist whose works influenced European chemistry</note>.

### CHAPTER XCIII.

<margin>How Silver is prepared for this second order.</margin>
Now I wish to teach you in what manner you shall prepare your **Silver** <note>original: *Lunam*; alchemists used the names of celestial bodies for metals: Luna is Silver</note>. Take **Roman vitriol** <note>likely copper sulfate or iron sulfate</note> and **saltpeter** in equal parts, and from these produce **strong water** <note>original: *aquam fortem*; nitric acid, used for dissolving metals</note> through distillations with an **alembic** <note>a chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling</note> according to the art, etc.

### CHAPTER XCIV.

<margin>Silver to be dissolved in white water.</margin>
<margin>Dissolved Silver to be precipitated.</margin>
<margin>The saltiness of the Silver is to be washed away, four or five times.</margin>
<margin>The Silver is to be reverberated until it swells like a sponge.</margin>
Likewise, dissolve the **Silver** in that white water; namely, for every **Mark** <note>a traditional unit of weight for precious metals</note> of Silver, take 2 Marks of strong water, and dissolve your Silver in it as is usually done. Then, when it is all dissolved together, **precipitate** your Silver; pour off that water from the top of the **lime** <note>original: *calce*; the powdery residue or "calx" left after a metal has been dissolved or burned</note>; and clean the lime of your Silver with common water, washing it to remove the saltiness four or five times. Then dry the lime by a small fire: and then place the lime of your Silver into 5 or 6 earthenware pans in a **reverberatory furnace** <note>a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material, rather than applying flame directly</note>: and reverberate your Silver with such heat that it does not melt, until your Silver swells up spongily in the manner of an open sponge. This will happen within eight days at most, or even sooner. Then let it cool on its own. 

Then take it out, and grind it upon a stone with **distilled vinegar** to dissolve it in a **Mary’s bath** <note>original: *balneo Mariæ*; a double boiler or water bath used for gentle, even heating</note>. Fill two parts of the receiving vessel and leave the third part empty: and cover it with a small smooth shingle or a small piece of glass, and let it stand thus for one night in tempered heat: so that you can hardly keep your hand in the water of your bath. Throughout the day and night, take the upper glass and stir it a little, so that the lime mixes with the vinegar: or use a long rod, and insert it into the vessel from above: and lift it up and let it down, just as women make butter; and in this way mix the lime of the Silver thoroughly with the vinegar. Do this five or six times throughout the day and night. 

Finally, let it stand undisturbed for one day, so that the lime can settle well. Then the vinegar will be a greenish-blue color. Let it cool on its own; then take it out, and pour off your colored vinegar from the top into another glass: and pour fresh distilled vinegar over the lime again, as before. Place it again to dissolve in the bath in every way, just as was taught before. Do this until all the lime of your Silver has been dissolved. Some dregs may remain at the bottom; treat them as nothing, for they remain from the Silver and its combustible sulfur, and its blackness, and the ash-dust collected during the reverberation. You may then pour a little more vinegar over the dregs to see if the vinegar is no longer colored.

### CHAPTER XCV.

<margin>Preparation of the spirit for the same medicine.</margin>
<margin>*Commonly called rock alum.</margin>
Now I will teach you how to prepare your spirit for making your medicine of the second order. Therefore, take pure, white, transparent **arsenic**, in which there are no sulfurous fibers: and crush it into powder, and with salt and * **rock alum** <note>original: *alumine rupeo*; a naturally occurring sulfate mineral used as a mordant and astringent</note>, grind it together, after it has been calcined: use 2 parts of alum to 1 of salt. When it is enough: put the matter of this kind into a pot, and smooth the mouth over an even stone. Then take a large glass **alembic** <note>a distillation cap with a beak</note>, and likewise smooth it so that the alembic fits the pot perfectly, as this figure demonstrates to you. Place it upon the **sublimation furnace**, first applying a tiny fire, so that the moisture flies into the receiver.

With a small fire, a certain more subtle spirit will ascend, which is called the **wild spirit** <note>original: *spiritus sylvestris*; an early term for volatile gases that could not be easily condensed</note>. It is so volatile and subtle that wherever it remains, the matter can never be fixed <note>made solid or stable</note> at any time. And therefore, in our art, it is entirely useless. ### CHAPTER XCVII.

<margin>How the same medicine can be made more subtle.</margin>
Likewise, if you then wish to make your medicine more **subtle** <note>refined or concentrated</note>, so that the **projection** <term>proiectio; the act of casting a small amount of alchemical medicine onto base metal to transform it</term> may be higher: take very strong distilled vinegar. Grind the aforementioned powder upon a stone with said vinegar, and empty it into a vessel, and place it in a **water bath** <term>balneum Mariae; a gentle heating method using hot water</term>. Everything will be resolved at once into clear water. Then congeal it over warm ashes; then dissolve it again as before. And in each solution and coagulation, your medicine is made so much more subtle that it gains ten-fold in projection, as the Philosopher **Geber** <note>an influential 8th-century alchemist, often cited as the father of Islamic chemistry</note> says. And if you were to dissolve and congeal that medicine so many times, it would stay in the manner of an oil. This oil, when dripped over warm **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> in a crucible, would convert the Mercury into pure Silver, better than that taken from the mines. And so, when the medicine has been brought thus far, it would no longer be a medicine of the **second order**, but of the **third order** <note>in alchemy, the third order is the highest degree of medicine, capable of instant and perfect transmutation</note>, and a perfect medicine for transmuting metals into true Silver. And if you then wished to make a perfect **Elixir** from the oil, you would take some of its **middle spirit** <note>the refined essence</note> or the matter which I taught you before to sublimate from pure **arsenic**. You shall weigh the oil and take twice as much of its middle spirit, and when you grind the oil upon a stone, and place it into a glass of this kind, and put it in a secret furnace for 10 days with a heat that does not reach glowing. Take out your matter, and it is changed and congealed into a stone; it is a perfect Elixir, transforming all metals into true Silver, better than that taken from the mines.

### CHAPTER XCIX.

You shall know and understand each work along with that which ought to be done within that work, and the other following works: the second, third, fourth, and fifth work, until the work reaches its end—that work which is carried out in the whole of Alchemy. And whichever Alchemist does not understand all these things before he begins to operate, he will produce nothing in the entire art of Alchemy, neither now nor at any time, even if he were to work forever. By a stroke of luck <note>original: *Forte fortuna*</note> he might arrive at some result in the art, just as a blind man hits a sparrow with an arrow: but otherwise he could not reach it. As often happens to the ignorant, who by luck arrived at some part of the art; but when they set about it again, they could not perform it a second time. Thus they wasted their effort and fell into despair. For what they should have done first, they frequently do last; and they even leave off the work exactly where it should have been started. They reach such a state of delusion that they become altogether foolish in the art.

### CHAPTER C.

Therefore, to avoid this wandering into error, I will teach you what **sublimation** <term>sublimatio; the process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and collects as a solid in the upper part of a vessel, used for purification</term> is, and why it was invented, and how one must sublimate in each work. Then I will teach how one must perform **calcination** <term>calcinatio; the reduction of a solid—often a metal—to a fine powder through prolonged heating</term>, and why calcination is done; and about **distillation** <term>destillatio; the process of vaporizing a liquid and condensing it back into a pure form</term>, and why it must be employed; and so on for many other methods regarding what must be done in each work that occurs in the art. You shall read this lesson again and again, and press it into your memory, lest you fall into error.

### CHAPTER CI.

<margin>
What the Ancients did once they understood the generation and growth of metals.
</margin>

<margin>
The reverberatory furnace.

Now that the calcination, sublimation, and dissolution of spirits has been discussed, I shall now teach you about the **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state, often to make it more brittle or powdery.</note> and **reverberation** <note>A process of heating where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof of a furnace onto the material, providing intense but indirect heat.</note> of bodies <note>In this context, "bodies" refers to the solid metallic or mineral bases used in alchemy.</note>. Furthermore, they discovered vessels baked from clay that were suitable for this purpose, so that bodies could be calcined or reverberated within them. Thus, they were to be guided gently over a fire in such a way that they would become accustomed to the heat. ### CHAPTER 107.

<margin>
How the method for reducing spirits to the **Sun** and **Moon** was discovered by the Ancients.
</margin>
When the wise men had proven all these aforementioned things and saw that they could lead all "dead" and "unclean" bodies <note>base metals like lead or tin</note> to the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, and furthermore achieve a high projection, they then inquired even further through reason whether it would be possible, through art and medicine, to also reduce **spirits** <note>original: "spiritus"; volatile substances such as mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that usually evaporate in fire</note> to the **Sun** and **Moon**. Concerning this matter they consulted together; and since they perceived the whole nature of the medicine, they understood that the medicine was composed and united by the art from spirits and bodies, and fixed together into one.

Then they also easily understood in their wisdom that if they were to reduce spirits to the **Sun** and **Moon**, the spirits must also possess the nature of the medicine; otherwise, the medicine would not want to mix with them, nor enter into them, for spirits [on their own] cannot create bodies: they have no proportion to one another. Medicine consists of spirits and bodies: and these are so fixed by fire that fire cannot separate them; yet the other is a pure spirit that ascends from the fire.

Thus, from this aforementioned reasoning, they easily comprehended two things. One was that if they were to succeed, they must first prepare the spirits so that they were of the same nature as the medicine, so that the medicine might contract a friendship with them, or wish to enter into them; for "like loves its like" <note>a fundamental alchemical principle suggesting that substances must be refined to a similar state to bond successfully</note>. Next, they also easily understood that if they were to bring "corporeal spirits" to the **Sun** and **Moon**, they would have to craft a medicine so liquid, so subtle, and so penetrating that when they projected it upon the corporeal spirits, it would immediately melt and penetrate before the fire became so hot that the spirit [would fly] from the body not...
