Moreover, these two spirits contain within themselves an excessively subtle spirit; this spirit must be separated with great skill. For if any of this subtle spirit were to remain within these two stones, that spirit would strip the work of its "fixation" <note>Fixation refers to the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note>, such that the work could never be completed. Furthermore, they contain a combustible sulfur <note>original: "sulphur combustibile." Alchemists believed sulfur was the principle of combustion and impurity that caused metals to rust or burn away.</note>, which would burn and destroy the entire work simultaneously as soon as it was brought to the fire.

---

### CHAPTER CXIII.

<margin>Coarse dross and dry earthiness must be removed from the stone, and how.</margin>
In addition to this, these two stones still contain a material that must likewise be taken from them, for it too would corrupt the work: this is their coarse dross <note>original: "fæces." This refers to the solid, impure residue left after a substance is dissolved or distilled.</note> and earthiness. If any of these remained in the stones—whether dross or dry earthiness—it would prevent the "medicine" <note>The "medicine" is another term for the Alchemical Elixir or the Stone in its potent, transformative state.</note> from being able to penetrate. Therefore, to remove all these things, it is necessary that these two stones be mixed with a **fixed dross** <note>original: "fixa fæce." A stable, non-volatile solid used as a medium during purification.</note> which attracts, and which does not itself become a spirit. Why must it be fixed? Because a fixed thing only with great difficulty lets go of a volatile thing once it has been mixed with it. This is because the fixed dross can retain the "middle spirit"—which is necessary for us in the work—until the subtle spirit has departed, and before the middle spirit separates itself from the dross. 

For this reason, the fixed dross must also be "attracting" or styptic <note>original: "stiptica." In early chemistry, this refers to a substance that contracts or binds other materials together.</note>, because it will not allow the spirit to rise too high in the vessel; rather, it keeps the most refined part just above the dross, or ensures it remains upon the dross, etc. And why must the fixed dross release nothing of itself? Because then it will not carry any impurity along with the middle spirit, so that the result will be pure and clean, and so it brings nothing foreign into the work. For nothing foreign can be present in the work. 

Furthermore, the dross must be of a cold and dry nature, through which these two stones are to be sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid in a cooler part of the apparatus, leaving impurities behind.</note>. Why cold? To restrain the heat which the combustible sulfur contains, so that it does not destroy the spirit during sublimation, but rather separates itself from the spirit. Why dry? So that the dross, by its dryness, may temper the heat of the combustible sulfur and retain it, so that it does not separate itself along with the middle spirit nor rise out of the dross. For this, one requires a tall and long vessel in which these two stones may be sublimated. Why a tall vessel? So that the subtle, volatile spirit, which can endure no heat, may rise into the upper part of that long vessel.

### CHAPTER CXIV.

<margin>The subtle spirit must be removed before you increase the fire in sublimation, and why.</margin>
Now you shall know that before you increase the fire in sublimation, you must remove the alembic <note>The alembic is the cap or "hood" of the distilling apparatus that collects and cools the vapors.</note> and take out the subtle spirit. And this is for this reason: lest when you apply a violent fire, the subtle spirit should fall back down; or when everything has been sublimated, the subtle volatile spirit might fall back again upon the dross, and not upon the middle spirit, so that they do not mix together again. Once the spirit is taken from the alembic, put the alembic back on: and then add fire, so the middle spirit can come out of the dross. And when it has been sublimated from the dross, take it out, and mix it again with your dross, and do in all ways as was taught before. Repeat that sublimation for as long and as many times until nothing more of the subtle spirit ascends. Then you shall set the middle spirit to be sublimated by itself, to see if any volatile spirit is joined to it. And if any is joined, take it out repeatedly, and also look to see if any combustible sulfur <note>original: "sulphure combustibili." Sulfur was viewed as the "fat of the earth" that caused metals to be reactive or "burnt" by fire.</note> and dross remains, etc. And you shall repeat the sublimation for as long as you find nothing more of the subtle volatile spirit ascending, and it leaves nothing in the bottom of the vessel. Then you are certain that you have the middle spirit clean and pure, and it is ready to be placed in the work.

->*For sublimating Mercury.*<-

### CHAPTER CXV.

<margin>The manner of sublimating Mercury.</margin>
You shall take Mercury <note>Quicksilver.</note> and clean it well, grinding it well with salt and vinegar in a wooden mortar with a wooden pestle. And when you have ground it for a long time with salt and vinegar, wash the salt from the Mercury with clean boiling water until the water runs off pure. Then dry the Mercury with a clean linen cloth. And then again add fresh clean salt and fresh vinegar, and grind again in the wooden mortar for 4 or 5 hours continuously. Then wash again with clean boiling water as before. And then again apply fresh vinegar and salt, and grind until such time as the Mercury [shows] no blackness...

<margin>This water of Mercury dissolves nothing except what is like itself.</margin>
For this water of Mercury dissolves nothing except what is like itself <note>A common alchemical principle: "like dissolves like."</note>, and lets whatever is not of its nature seek the bottom. And then you can slowly pour off the clear liquid, or filter it, and remove the dross, and put the clear water into a glass jar, and with an alembic placed on top and a receiver added to the beak, distill the humidity: and then increase your fire, and then sublimate the Mercury upwards into the alembic, and so you have your Mercury again, but made somewhat lighter. And then take the metal from the jar and reduce it into a body, and you have your metal clear, pure...

->The Stone made only from Gold.<-

## CHAPTER CXVI.

<margin>
The Stone made from Gold alone surpasses all others.
</margin>

<margin>
Although Gold is a single substance, it can nonetheless be divided into two parts that seem contrary to each other.
</margin>

<margin>
It can neither be destroyed by fire, nor rot in the earth, nor be corrupted in the air.
</margin>

Now I wish to describe to you the stone which is prepared from Gold <note>original: "Sole" (the Sun), the alchemical name for Gold</note> alone: which stone surpasses all stones that can be made by the hands of men. And you shall hold it as a secret that Gold is by its nature a species of metal in which no [disparate] parts exist. It is simple and pure, yet a dreg <note>original: "fæx," referring to a base or sediment</note> of one kind is within it, and that is hidden inside it. And although Gold is a simple body without separate parts, nonetheless by art its color can be drawn out, both the red and the white, but without art this cannot be done. Although I assert it to be one substance, nonetheless Gold can be divided into two parts which seem to be mutually contrary to one another. Gold is a species which is brought about by the power of nature. For nature has so worked within it that nature has shown its extreme powers in it. Indeed, nature has so worked in Gold that in the whole world nothing is more excellent than Gold. For Gold is clean and pure, and nature has brought it as close to a simple nature as it was able. So much so that in the whole world nothing approaches so closely to the "simple" <term>Simple: in alchemy, a "simple" refers to a pure, uncompounded substance consisting of only one element or essence</term> as Gold does. For Gold cannot be destroyed by fire, nor rot in the earth, nor become filthy, nor be corrupted in the air.

## CHAPTER CXVII.

<margin>
Nature produces nothing fixed nor simple.
</margin>

You shall know that in the whole world, nothing that nature has wrought is "fixed" <term>Fixed: a "fixed" substance is one that remains stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to intense heat</term>. But by art, Gold can be made fixed, along with many other things. But it is not granted to nature by God to produce anything fixed, or of a simple nature. For that which is fixed is eternal; it can neither now nor at any time be changed for better or worse.

For this reason, Gold all rises at once, or all remains fixed below at the bottom. Thus, by art we can make the Gold rise entirely, or by art fix it, so that the whole remains below forever, so that it can never be made to rise, but stays fixed eternally. From Gold you cannot separate the four elements as they are separated from all other things: because between the elements there is no contrariety <note>conflict between opposing qualities like hot/cold or wet/dry</note> which divides its parts, as shown above, etc.

### CHAPTER CXVIII.

<margin>The method of preparing the stone from Gold alone.</margin>
Now, when you wish to make the true stone of the philosophers, which is the most noble and highest stone: you shall know—you who wish to prepare the true stone from Gold <note>original: "Sole"</note> alone—that you should take 2 marks <note>a unit of weight, roughly 8 ounces each</note> of pure Gold, and beat it into thin plates, and cut it into pieces, great or small as you please, and place it in the <term>Royal Cement</term> <note>Cementum Regale: a corrosive mixture used to purify gold by removing base metals</note>, and add a certain amount of sulfur and <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and cement it for 24 continuous hours. Remove it, and melt it, and again beat it into thin plates as you did before, and place it once more to be cemented as previously described. Melt it again, and once more beat it into thin plates, and again place it to be cemented, in all the ways as said before. Repeat this at least three or four times, until you know for certain that your Gold is clean and pure. Then, prepare a <term>strong water</term> <note>aqua fortis: typically nitric acid</note> from <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate</note>, <term>vitriol</term> <note>iron or copper sulfate</note>, and sal ammoniac. The saltpeter shall equal the other two in quantity—that is, you will take 2 parts of saltpeter, and one part each of vitriol and sal ammoniac. And from these, prepare a strong water just as it is usually made according to the art. Or

### CHAPTER CXIX.

<margin>
Two works to be performed, contrary to each other.
</margin>
Now you shall know that two works are to be performed by you which will be contrary to each other: one part of the powder you shall make spiritual and volatile; but the other part of that powder you shall make corporeal and fixed. And you shall make both parts of the powder subtle, each in its own degree, so that nothing more subtle can be produced. You must bring the interior of both parts of the powder to the outside <note>a process of "turning the inside out" to reveal the hidden essence</note> before it becomes subtle. Its interior must be brought outside so that the stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> can be made from it. For in its interior part there is a certain kind of thick dregs, and these cannot be drawn out unless the interior is brought to the outside. And then a subtle stone can be made, etc.

### CHAPTER CXX.

<margin>
The first powder must be made spiritual, and how.
</margin>
Likewise, that work by which the spiritual powder is to be made will be the first work we undertake. That which Nature has closed must be opened, and everything which Nature has made or worked must be unraveled; and the powder must be prepared in that state in which it was when Nature began to work upon it. Then at last the powder or matter is ready for making the stone.

### CHAPTER CXXI.

<margin>
What must be done with the other part of the powder, which is to be made corporeal and fixed.
</margin>
In the other part of the powder which is to be made corporeal or fixed, the first task is to perfect where Nature left off. Therefore this work is direct <note>aligned with nature's goal</note>, while the other is contrary <note>reversing nature's process</note>. For in that former work, everything Nature worked must be unraveled at once; but in this work, one must begin where Nature left off. What Nature was not able to accomplish, that must furthermore be perfected by art <note>the alchemist's skill</note>.

<margin>The Sun is the Moon on the inside, and the Moon is the Sun on the inside.</margin>
For Nature does not move further to operate than until it has brought a thing into that state to which God, according to His will, has ordained it, etc. And so, we must begin where Nature left off, and lead the work toward perfection and the supreme virtue; that is, we shall lead its exterior to the inside, and place its interior on the outside, and then we shall strip away the exterior and interior dross, and we shall make it subtle and fixed. Thus, it is prepared for making the Stone <note>the Philosophers' Stone</note> from it. And whoever seeks other ways will err, and does not grasp the mind of the Sages. You shall know that the Sun cannot be separated except into two: that is, into whiteness and redness. When the Sun is in its thickness <note>its crude, metallic state</note>, you can take away its redness by art, so that the Sun shall be entirely white. And when the interior of the Sun is turned outward, you can draw away its whiteness, so that it shall remain entirely red. For the Sun is red on the outside in its tincture <term>the color-giving essence</term> and color, but on the inside it is truly white. For the Sun is the Moon on the inside, and the Moon is the Sun on the inside. But the Moon <note>Silver</note> is sickly, weak, and imperfect. Therefore, the Stone cannot easily be made from the Moon so as to be perfect. Concerning which nothing is to be written here, for that would lead us away from our purpose. For in this work, the discourse is only concerning the Sun, and not the Moon, etc.

### CHAPTER CXXII.

<margin>How the work is to be started.</margin>
Likewise, I now wish to teach you how and by what method you shall start the work. At the beginning, you shall make a strong water <term>aqua fortis, usually nitric acid</term> from sal ammoniac <term>ammonium chloride</term> and saltpeter <term>potassium nitrate</term> in equal parts. First, grind the saltpeter into a dry powder. Then mix the sal ammoniac well into the powder of the saltpeter, so that they are well mixed together and incorporated one into the other. Then place them to be distilled; but do not seal the receiver <note>the vessel that collects the distillate</note> tightly to the beak <note>the spout of the distilling lid</note> with luting <term>an airtight sealant paste</term> before it begins to distill. For if you seal the receiver to the beak of the alembic <term>the top part of the still</term> at the start, there are wild, windy spirits <note>original: "spiritus syluestres ventosi"; likely referring to the rapid release of gases like chlorine or nitrogen oxides</note> within the matter which would burst the receiver. But when it has distilled for a little while, seal it fearlessly to the beak, and distill the water according to the art.

### CHAPTER 123.

<margin>The Philosopher's Stone cannot be brought forth from the Moon.</margin>
You may therefore ask: can no stone then be produced from the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver</note>? Indeed: a stone can certainly be produced from the Moon; and likewise even from all things created in the world, a stone can indeed be produced by art. But it will not be the **Philosopher's Stone**, which transforms all imperfect metals into true Sun and Moon, nor which would perform that infinite projection <note>The "projection" is the final stage of alchemy, where a tiny amount of the Stone is thrown onto molten base metal to transform it into gold</note>, which cannot be described in writing because of the infinity of the projection. Over a long time and with great labor, a medicine or Elixir could indeed be produced from the Moon, which would perform a projection upon **Venus** <note>original: "Venerem"; the alchemical name for copper</note> properly cleansed by calcinations <note>heating a substance until it reduces to powder</note>, washings, and meltings. But never will a medicine, or Elixir, or anything similar in rank be produced from the Moon that performs a projection upon raw, imperfect metals; in the end it will be, or will become, adulterated and fraudulent. But **Venus** <note>copper</note> can be so prepared that it is transformed into true Moon <note>silver</note> by a medicine made from the Moon. And if you are to produce a medicine from the Moon, first and above all you must remove all the "sicknesses" of the Moon. For the Moon, just like all other metals, is subject to two diseases <note>Alchemists viewed base metals as "diseased" versions of gold; silver was considered closer to perfection than most, but still "ill" due to its impurities and lack of "fixity" or color</note>; you must remove them, along with all its blackness.

### CHAPTER 125.

<margin>The method for calcining the aforementioned material.</margin>
You shall take the sublimated material and grind it into an impalpable powder upon a marble slab. Then, have a glass vessel with a flat bottom, made of good glass that can withstand the fire. Put your material into it and spread it widely across the bottom of the glass, smoothing it with a feather or a rabbit's foot. Place the vessel with the material of the **stone** <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" in its developmental stage</note> into a secret furnace in which spirits are **calcined** <note>Reduced to a fine powder through prolonged heating</note>. Place the inner lid, which fits the vessel, upon it, and seal it firmly with good **lute** <note>original: "luto"; a clay-based cement used to airtightly seal alchemical apparatus</note> so that it neither splits nor breaks from the fire, and let it dry well. Then place that second lid over this one, which fits the furnace, and seal that one also firmly and let it dry. And when it is dry, put on the lid that fits the rim of the furnace, which covers all the other lids; seal it also firmly and let it dry.

When it is dry enough, light the fire under the furnace; first a lukewarm fire for 6 continuous hours. Once those are finished, increase your fire for another 6 hours. Once those are finished, increase your fire again for 6 hours. When those are finished, increase your fire so strongly that if you were to thrust your hand through that square opening on the side of the furnace and moisten the tip of your finger to touch the vessel hanging in the furnace, it would hiss and sound. Just as if a stone were very hot and you threw spit upon it and it hissed, so must this vessel hanging in the furnace hiss when moisture is sprinkled on it. It must be kept in such heat for a day and a night.

Indeed, you shall prepare a thin rod for yourself, and at its end tie a linen cloth folded six or seven times, and sew it firmly around. Dip and moisten the end in water. Remove the stone from the square hole in the middle of the furnace, and through it, thrust that rod as far as the vessel with the moistened tip. Listen carefully to whether the vessel hisses; if it emits a hissing sound when the rod touches the vessel, then it is correct enough. And if it does not hiss clearly or loudly, just as if you were dripping cold water on a hot stone, increase the fire until it hisses in that manner. And so you must keep it in that heat day and night. Often during the day and night you can test with that moist rod through that hole in the middle of the furnace whether your fire is suitably hot; but when you have tested it, always put the stone back into the square hole in the middle of the furnace.

You must keep it in such heat for 40 continuous days and nights. Once these are finished, let it cool down naturally for 3 or 4 days. Then take it out, and you will find the material of the stone properly calcined and prepared for **dissolving** <note>original: "solvendum"; the process of turning the solid calcined matter into a liquid state</note>.

### CHAPTER 126.

<margin>The calcined material is to be dissolved in distilled common water, or spread upon a table, etc.</margin>
Now take the calcined material of the stone and dissolve it in distilled **common water** <note>original: "aqua communi"; likely referring to pure rainwater or regular water that has been purified through repeated distillation</note>: or if you were to spread the material upon a glass table or marble, and place it in a cold and humid cellar, and place a glass vessel under the stone, and tilt the stone slightly so that the dissolved liquid could drip into the vessel—the material of the stone would easily dissolve into clear water within 8 or 10 days, so that nothing would remain. But this method is not to be approved because of dust and other filth rising in it, and even coming from the air; and also the humidity that is drawn from the cellar into the material of the stone to dissolve it is likewise not clean, etc. Therefore, to keep the material of the stone pure and clean, put the material of the stone into a **receptacle** <note>A specialized alchemical container</note> manufactured in this manner: smooth the mouth of the receptacle upon a stone, and also smooth a small piece of glass that fits the mouth of the receptacle, which you can firmly **lute** <note>To seal with alchemical cement or clay</note> over the mouth of the receptacle when it pleases you. And while the material of the stone is in the glass, have common water distilled again and again so many times that nothing remains after distillation; and from time to time pour a little of that water over the material of the stone, and it will be dissolved by a very small amount of water because of its subtlety. For subtle material is dissolved much more easily and with a smaller quantity of moisture.

Indeed, perform this pouring over, and the repeated dissolving of the material of the stone, and then distilling anew, so frequently until the material of the stone no longer wishes to congeal, but remains in the manner of a remarkable **white oil**: for its whiteness is on the outside, and its redness is in its interior, etc. <note>This refers to the alchemical transition where the substance appears white (the "Albedo" stage) but contains the potential for the final red stage (the "Rubedo")</note>. Thus the material of the stone must be changed often and many times; it must be now earth, now spirit, now lime, now water, now oil: and it must frequently be transferred from one nature into another. For unless it had been resolved and opened at the beginning, how could you have **sublimated** <note>The process of turning a solid into vapor and back into solid to purify it</note> it? And unless you had calcined it, how could you have dissolved it into simple water? And unless you had already converted the material of the stone into oil, how could you distill it and make it **subtle** <note>Refined, penetrating, and highly active</note>? so that it might acquire the power of transforming all metals into **the Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **the Moon** <note>Silver</note>? Therefore the matter must be converted so many times from one nature into another, to do all things that are in its **regimen** <note>The governed stages of the alchemical process</note>, to lead it to perfection.

### CHAPTER 127.

<margin>*What must be done with the matter when it now refuses to be congealed, and remains in the manner of a clear white oil.*</margin>
Therefore, the matter of the stone being in such a state, and now refusing to be congealed any further, and remaining in the manner of a clear white oil: take your glass from the bath, and place it upon the furnace in a pot with ashes <note>An ash bath provides gentle, even heat to prevent the glass from cracking</note>; and **lute** <note>original: "luta"; to seal with an airtight paste or clay</note> the receiver to the **beak** <note>original: "rostrum"; the spout or delivery tube of the distilling vessel</note> of the glass very tightly, and lute a small glass over the mouth of the glass. And the receiver which is at the beak of the glass shall also have a beak in its "belly": just as the glass in which the matter of the stone resides has; and stop up the beak of the receiver at its end thoroughly, lest any air escape through it. You will no longer be able to distill with **alembics** <note>A traditional distillation cap with a downward-sloping tube</note>, but all distillations which are now done must be carried out through large receivers having beaks in their bellies, so that the matter does not have to be poured back and forth too often. But when it has been drawn off from one glass into another, that glass shall be taken from the ashes, and that glass into which it was drawn off shall be placed upon the furnace in a pot with ashes, and lute that round glass over the mouth; and apply that other glass to the beak: and stop up the end of the beak with lute, and lute firmly near the beak that is joined to the glass standing upon the furnace. Distillation must be done entirely in glass receivers of this kind, to which a beak has been added in the belly, so that it is only necessary to draw it from one glass into another; in this way, it is not necessary to pour the matter out too often. And when the lute is thoroughly dry, apply fire to the furnace, first a little, and gradually increase your fire little by little by degrees: and you will see a most white spirit ascend, and it will pass over, and distill into the receiver. Seeing this, keep the fire at that heat until you see it no longer distills. Then still increase the fire significantly, and watch carefully whether any white spirits ascend, and when no longer through...

Then place it in the cellar again, and let it crystallize again, and take what has crystallized; repeat this until all your matter of the stone has been entirely turned into these small stones.

Then take at once all that has been turned into stone: and take all of it together from the dish, and place it upon hot ashes on the furnace: and immediately it will become water again as soon as it begins to grow warm; then evaporate it again into a dry powder, and you will have a white powder. ### CHAPTER CXXX.

Now I have taught you to prepare both materials for making the stone: one part spiritual and subtle, the other corporeal and fixed. This is because **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical name for Gold</note> leaves no earth behind, as was taught before in the work. Anyone who operates otherwise, or seeks other ways to create the true **Philosophers' Stone**, will err and sweat in vain; such a person understands neither himself nor the mind of the Philosophers. From the **Sun**, many medicines can be fashioned by which **projection** <term>projection: the process of casting a small amount of an alchemical agent onto a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</term> is performed, in which there is much utility and profit. However, to create the true Stone—that Great Work of the Philosophers—it must be instituted in this manner, and no other. Indeed, an oil could be made from the **Sun** prepared in this way, bodily and fixed, and then placed to be **calcinated** <term>calcination: the reduction of a metal to a fine powder through prolonged heating</term> for 40 days in a furnace where spirits are calcinated. If it were then removed and dissolved in distilled vinegar, and frozen again, and if this were repeated until the matter remained as a white and shining oil, it would have great power. If a plate of **Venus** <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for Copper</note> were heated to glowing, and that oil were sprinkled upon it, the oil would separate and penetrate through it, just as oil penetrates dry leather. It would render the plate of **Venus** entirely into fixed **Moon** <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical name for Silver</note> as far as the oil had spread. And if the oil were dripped upon heated **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, it would convert it into fixed **Moon**; and similarly **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, and so on, if it were dripped upon them while they stood melted. Furthermore, if the oil were placed in a glass vessel tempered for that purpose, made of strong glass, and placed in **digestion** <term>digestion: a process of slow, gentle heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance</term> in a moderate dry heat—if that oil were kept in it long enough—it would finally be converted into a red oil. Its interior would finally be led outward and its exterior inward through long digestion. Then it would transform all metals into true **Sun**, just as it previously transformed them into fixed **Moon**. But this would not be the **Stone**; it would be the fixed oil of the **Sun**, and a certain medicine and **Elixir**. Truly, to make the Stone, the **Sun** must be divided into two parts: one part is to be made spiritual and subtle, and the other corporeal and fixed and subtle, as was said before. Then those two opposites must be joined, as you will be taught. Although they are now contrary to one another, they are nevertheless fashioned from one thing and one material; and now they shall come together again into one thing, and become one material; and thereafter one material for

### CHAP. CXXXIII.

<margin>Silver is gold on the inside, just as gold is silver on the inside.</margin>
It might be asked: how can it be that 1 part of that color is able to convert a thousand parts into gold? Know this: silver is gold on the inside, just as gold is silver on the inside. <note>This reflects the alchemical theory that all metals are essentially the same substance at different stages of "maturity." Silver was seen as "unripe" gold.</note> And when our Stone is perfected, it places the interior of all metals on the outside, and the exterior on the inside, and leads all metals to their highest degree; so much so that they can reach no higher degree unless the Philosophers' Stone <note>original: "lapis Philosophorum"</note> were made from them. Thus it happens that one part of it transforms a thousand parts of silver into the Sun <note>original: "Solem" — The Sun is the standard alchemical symbol and name for gold.</note>, even if that one part had no tincture or color of its own. If it had no other power in its nature than merely to place the interior of silver on the outside and the exterior on the inside, that silver would be converted into its own gold, and its tincture would remain. And when the interior of the metal is placed on the outside, and the exterior is turned inward, it is finished and perfect.

### CHAPTER CXXXIV.

Now we wish to speak again of those thousand parts of silver. When converted in this manner by one part of the fixed stone, the silver will perhaps be breakable and brittle; and if you find it breakable, that one part of the stone is too effective and requires more silver. Therefore, melt those thousand parts again and add more silver, until it becomes malleable and soft. Perhaps that one part will easily convert two or three thousand parts of silver into pure gold. And when it is soft, that one part has completed its work. Experience will easily teach you this, as was said before.

### CHAP. CXXXV.

Now when you have those two or three thousand parts, you have enough gold to ferment your entire stone. And know that when your stone is perfected, as we have taught in this place, you can make no projection <term>projection: the final step of alchemy where a tiny amount of the Stone is cast onto molten base metal to transform the whole mass</term> with it, unless you first ferment it with gold, as I have taught you. For unless you ferment the stone, it would make no projection. For it no longer possesses the power of generation...

<margin>A perfected thing has no generation within itself.</margin>
...nothing more; for it has already reached its end. For the Stone is brought to its highest degree, so that the Stone at no time—not even after the Last Day <note>A reference to the end of the world/Judgment Day, implying eternal stability.</note>—can reach a higher state or degree. Thus it is clear that a perfected thing has no [further] generation <note>In alchemy, "generation" refers to the natural process of growth and change. Once a metal becomes gold or the Stone, it is "perfect" and stops changing.</note> within itself. Therefore, it is certain that our Stone will transform no metal from its own nature into another nature unless a power is present within it through which it might possess that capability. Thus, it is necessary—if the Stone is to have the power of vivifying <note>Bringing "life" or metallic perfection to.</note> all dead, impure metals, and is to free them from all impurity and make them like unto itself in every part—that the Stone be fermented with the most pure body that exists in the whole world <note>This refers to gold.</note>, and be glued together with it. This must be done so that the body becomes the Stone, and the Stone becomes that body: so that they shall remain as one together in one substance forever, and never be separated.

### CHAPTER CXXXVI.

<margin>On the conjunction which the Philosophers called fermentation, and the work of 3 days.</margin>
Likewise, the Philosophers called this conjunction "fermentation," and this is that "work of three days." The foolish <note>original: "stolidi" — Isaac often uses harsh language for those who misunderstand alchemical theory.</note> do not understand this fermentation; they think the ferment of a crude body <note>A "crude" body refers to an unrefined or base metal.</note> should be brought to the work of the Stone while the Stone is still being processed. These are insane heads; they do not understand the words of the Philosophers, but rather twist the Philosophers' words to suit their own foolish opinions. For instance, they put imperfect bodies and crude Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> together, and while they are in that insane labor, they add some perfected body and call it "ferment." For ferment cannot be added to the Stone until it is entirely perfected; and then it is added in the manner taught here, and as shall yet be taught. They also speak of "multiplying" the Stone once it has been perfected; that is what is meant by "fermenting." They want to ferment the Stone while it is still in the middle of the work; but the Stone cannot be fermented unless it is finished. The Stone is to be multiplied while it is in the work through sublimations and distillations, and by making the Stone subtle. Thus you can clearly understand that their entire opinion is false and fraudulent.

# THE MINERAL WORKS of Master John Isaac
# *Hollandus, or concerning the Philosophers' Stone,*

## BOOK TWO.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>In this preface, it is taught which work each person should beware of. There is much error in Alchemy, especially in the vegetable work, and much more in the animal work.</margin>
My son shall know that in this art there is much error, especially in the vegetable work <note>The "vegetable work" refers to alchemical processes using plants or wine-based spirits as the starting material.</note>, and even more so in the animal work <note>The "animal work" involves substances derived from living creatures, such as blood, hair, or urine.</note>. This is the reason.

### CHAPTER II.

IN the vegetable work, there is much to be distilled, dissolved, congealed, and rectified: and spirits must be accurately preserved lest they fly away into the air. Various strong waters <term>strong waters: *aquae fortes*, typically corrosive acids like nitric acid used to dissolve metals</term> must be prepared, and many humid spirits must be fixed <term>fixed: making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term>. There is need for much regulation and care, lest your spirits burst your fixation glass <note>A specialized glass vessel designed to withstand long periods of heating while the substance inside is "fixed."</note>, should a more abundant or violent fire be applied before they are nearly fixed. For then they lift themselves up, and being held enclosed within the fixation glass, they burst the glass through their rising, and then everything that was inside is lost. Therefore, one must watch diligently, for great danger lies in this, as those who have done it know; and much labor and time must be spent in rectifying wines, just as also in preparing strong waters and properly preserving spirits, lest they vanish.

### CHAPTER III.

THEN also in digestion <note>The process of slow, gentle heating, similar to incubation.</note> and putrefaction <note>The intentional "rotting" or breakdown of a substance, considered a vital stage for its transformation.</note>, there is need for great sharp-wittedness, and wonderful regimes of fires must be applied. Therefore, it is always necessary to stay awake, and great care must be taken, as those know who experience this very thing daily, etc. Furthermore, great care must be applied to the calcining <term>calcining: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> and reverberating of bodies and earth, lest by burning they be reduced into glass <note>Overheating could cause the material to vitrify (turn into slag or glass), rendering it useless for further alchemical work.</note> and made too dry: wherefore great account must be taken of the fire, and great caution applied. To these things, the earths must be clarified, and waters distilled, and moreover all the works necessary for this must be performed. Furthermore, in the conjunction <note>The chemical marriage or joining of two different substances.</note>, if you apply either too much of one or too little of the other, or if you poorly preserved your humidity in the beginning, your medicines do not have entry <note>original: "ingressum." In alchemy, "entry" or "penetration" refers to the medicine's ability to permeate and transform the base metal.</note>, and it is to be feared lest your work be ruined. Therefore, much care, burden, time, and huge expense must be applied; and just when we think we have properly performed all things, if the glass breaks for us, or anything [else goes wrong]...

<summary>In this opening of Book Two, Isaac Hollandus warns the reader about the extreme difficulties and physical risks of the "vegetable" and "animal" paths of alchemy, emphasizing the danger of exploding glassware and the precision required in fire regulation.</summary>

<margin>The separation of elements is to be avoided.</margin> Therefore, the separation of the elements is too dangerous: for it is far too easy for some part of any element to be lost, and then the labor, time, and expense are all perished at once. So if you listen to me, you will avoid the separation of the elements, whether in the Mercury of the mineral or vegetable work, or in the stone <note>original: "lapide"</note> which God gives us freely. Wherever there is talk of this matter and it is said that the elements must be separated, avoid all such works because of their uncertainty. For it is too easy for some of its moisture to be lost, in the beginning, middle, or end; and when any of its moisture is lost, the whole work is ruined and corrupted. For in the composition the work cannot be joined together, and its power of penetration is taken away and completely lost. Yet sometimes they are so long that one cannot reach the end because of the faults that fall into the work. For in the beginning, middle, or end, they do not preserve the genuine moisture, so that it becomes too dry:

So, my son, avoid those amalgamations <note>The process of combining mercury with another metal.</note>, or multiplications and fixations <term>fixation: the process of turning a volatile substance into a solid that can resist fire</term>, for however impressive and honest they may seem, they are of such a nature that the end cannot be reached. For this reason, my son, do not hurry too much to do or begin any of these works; for six hundred other faults besides these can happen, which we do not mention here.

<margin>
A commendation of the Great Work for its ease, safety, and simplicity.
</margin>
Therefore, hold fast to the Great Art, or the Great Elixir, as your ancestors did. By doing this, you will be able to investigate all of nature; but if you do otherwise, you are not following my advice. Above all, labor in the Great Work, for in it there is no [excessive] care, nor distillation, nor freezing, nor purification, nor foreign works, nor foreign things, nor filthy things containing dregs. You do not calcine, for there is no need; you do not separate the elements, for they are already pure. It needs nothing else: it is one single kind, one thing, and one vessel, one furnace, and one work for both the "white" <note>The stage of making silver.</note> and the "red" <note>The final stage of making gold.</note>, and no danger can befall the work. Hence the Ancients say: the work is nothing but "women's work and children's play" <note>A famous alchemical maxim suggesting that once the "seed" is found, the process is as easy as washing laundry or playing a game.</note>. The ignorant cannot perceive this because the work is so simple. For the Great Work dissolves itself, sublimes itself, fixes itself, makes itself liquid like wax, and perfects itself, etc.

And these things, my son, I have made known to you in open words; therefore, do not begin any "foreign" works <note>Processes using materials not native to the specific alchemical path.</note> before you have finished that **Great Work**. Then, begin whatever you please; for then no expense can harm you, nor time, for in all things you have become the master of your desire, etc.

<meta>This page continues the instructional dialogue between the master alchemist and his "son" (student), building on the principle that the "stone" must come from a single source. # MASTER JOHN ISAAC

...perfect medicine in itself, but unprepared; and if you know how to prepare it, you have no need to seek or ask for medicine from elsewhere, each for its own use: this has another meaning. No disease can happen to a man, but that he has the perfect medicine within him, to surely heal himself, if he can prepare it; and he can take and prepare it from himself without diminution of himself, or harm to the body. This is to be understood in the same way about all living things, birds, all plants, and all things which God created. And it is so: but the unskilled do not grasp the works of the Ancients, and they think to make medicine for metals from all things. Thus they take hair, eggs, blood, snails, and similar things, and think they can prepare medicine from them to reduce imperfect metals into perfect ones: and when they have already sweated egregiously <note>In this context, "sweated egregiously" refers to the literal heat of the furnace and the intense, exhausting labor of the laboratory.</note>, they have achieved nothing, remaining in error.

<margin>Like begets like.</margin>
My son shall know, moreover, that man begets man, horse begets horse, fox begets fox, and from fish comes fish; so like begets its like. It would be contrary to all reason and even to nature that metal could be made from any foreign species—blood, hair, eggs, or snails—for nothing of the sort is in them. How much less can a medicine be prepared from such things that would reduce imperfect metals into the Sun or the Moon <note>original: "Solem aut Lunam"; in alchemy, these are the standard symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>? Indeed, it is entirely contrary to reason, and even impossible; and I marvel that anyone could arrive at such errors. If they understood the power of nature, they would certainly not fall into such errors. Therefore, my son, you shall know and recognize what kind of thing a substance is, or what is within it, before you prepare it; in this way, you will not err.

<margin>Every oil of metals, as also their Salt, is an elixir.</margin>
My son shall know that every oil of metals is an Elixir, and likewise every salt; and if every oil of metals is an Elixir, let it be clear that all perfect metals have their own medicine within themselves. How much better, therefore, is the oil of the Sun and the Moon, which are both perfect, etc.

It dissolves itself, it purifies itself, it coagulates itself, it distills and sublimates itself, it fixes and perfects itself, it waxes <term>incerate: the process of softening a dry substance until it has the consistency of wax</term> itself, it makes itself liquid, etc.

# THE MINERAL WORKS

Furthermore, you can make an oil from all metals without the separation of the elements, and likewise you can make a salt from them all without the separation of the elements; these aforementioned things are done in various ways, and thus they belong to the Great Work <note>original: "opus magnum"; the ultimate goal of alchemy, usually the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. In addition to this, you can make a perfect medicine from the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold and the Moon (Luna) represents Silver.</note> without the separation of the elements, and without any labor, fear, or danger. Furthermore, you can make a perfect medicine from two stones freely given to us by God, without the separation of the elements and even without great apparatus.

Therefore, my son should understand that all the things mentioned above belong to the Great Work without much apparatus, great expense, or the addition of any foreign things; they do indeed require a long time, but they are safe. Moreover, my son, when you wish to prepare that Great Work, you must know it and all its kinds, and especially the father, mother, sister, and brother <note>These family members are allegories for the different chemical components or states of the primary matter.</note>, and place it naked in a clear and pure body like crystal, and cleanse it from all sins. Do the same for the father, mother, sister, and brother. Then you shall place them in a bed with the father, mother, sister, and brother, joining arms to arms and mouths to mouths in a chamber; then, at that same moment, they shall die. Then, drench those dead bodies with the clear water of paradise <note>Likely referring to a purified solvent or "mercury of the philosophers."</note>, and join them well with this water; this water shall ascend to heaven within the circle of the Moon, and it shall be turned into dew, and again it shall fall drop by drop according to the plan of the craftsman, and it shall moisten the earth so that flowers of various colors spring up. By the power of these flowers, the son of the lineage shall rise again with a red crown <note>The "red crown" (rubro diademate) signifies the *Rubedo* or reddening, the final stage of the alchemical process indicating success.</note>, and he shall be Emperor over all the tribes of the earth, and he shall never lose his dominion for eternity, and all his enemies shall enter into peace with him.

Some sweated for a long time before they produced the stone; others, by the sharpness of their intellect, shortened the time, as is done now daily with much sweat and labor. # MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC

<margin>The work can be easily shortened, and in what manner.</margin>
...they used nothing but distilled vinegar. Now their successors have discovered strong waters <note>original: "aquas fortes"; typically nitric acid, used to dissolve metals more quickly than vinegar.</note>, which has greatly shortened the work. And you shall understand, my son, that the work can be easily shortened; in the first preparation, let the matter be made subtle, so that the species is thoroughly united, so that nature alone does not have the task of digesting it; and let the moist be mixed with the dry so subtly that it becomes a single thing, just as the soul is joined to the body and spirit so that they are one. For this reason, our philosopher Hermes says: *In the beginning of your works, do not be slow in properly cleansing, clarifying, and subtly joining all things together, so that you may rejoice afterward.* Geber, Dantynus, and Morienus <note>Famous figures in the alchemical tradition; Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) and Morienus were considered foundational authorities.</note> also say: *Join the water properly with the earth, and the moist with the dry, so that afterward you may see the blackness of the sea*, that is, its dark color, which you will behold during its putrefaction <note>The "nigredo" or black stage of alchemy, signifying the death and decomposition of the matter before its rebirth.</note>, which will occur in the space of 29 days over a small fire; this is a perfect sign of a proper union.
<margin>A perfect sign of a proper union</margin>

So, my son, be diligent at the beginning, so that you prepare all your materials rightly and carefully: for once these are placed in the fire, you have finished all the labor, and you only need to manage the heat.

<margin>On the amalgamations of the Sun and Moon among the Ancients.</margin>
Know also, my son, that I shall hereafter mention various crafts, all of which are perfected at once. In the beginning, our ancestors labored over the amalgamations of the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical terms, the Sun is Gold and the Moon is Silver.</note>, which is a most perfect work, although it is long: truly it is the safest, and requires the least care. They also set down these amalgamations in various ways, and yet all reached one certain end, though not to an equally great height of projection <note>The "projection" is the final stage where the alchemical medicine is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note>. Others also, through the sharpness of their wit, shortened the work greatly, as we shall teach hereafter in the work.

and so that the body may be properly united to the spirit. And when the eight days have passed, empty the matter into a glass vessel of this kind. This is its putrefaction <note>the process of decay and chemical breakdown</note>, and meanwhile you will see its perfect blackness; when you see this, rejoice; for under that blackness the whiteness lies hidden, and it is a certain sign that the matter was properly joined and united at the beginning. Then you shall seal the glass again, place the weight on top, and cover the furnace once more: and you shall repeat this every three or four days. It is better, however, that you apply such a small fire that it does not sublimate <note>turn from solid to vapor</note> upwards; though the time may be longer, it matters nothing to you—prefer the certain to the uncertain. For you can lose your work with great heat, but never with a small fire. And beware that you do not apply so much fire that you acquire a red color instead of white.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>The rule of building the fire handed down must be kept.</margin>
<margin>Once whiteness is seen, one should rejoice.</margin>
AND when you see that ash-black powder, rejoice: for under that blackness, whiteness is enclosed. Then leave it in that regime of fire for a long time, until it becomes a little paler or whiter; and if it becomes whiter, keep the same regime of fire. But if it remains in the same state and you make no progress, you shall increase the fire a little, until you see the matter become a little brighter. And when you make some progress, then leave it in that same regime of fire in this manner; and if even then you make no progress, you shall increase the fire a little more. And when you see the matter becoming whiter and whiter, leave it in that regime of fire in this manner, and see that you do not increase your fire too much. And my son, keep this rule of building the fire, pursuing it by increasing it little by little, at least until the matter has become white, indeed whiter than snow. Then exult, my son, and be certain that under that whiteness perfect redness lies hidden; and under that whiteness, says Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist often quoted in medieval texts as a teacher of King Khalid</note>, it is hidden, as Christ lay in the tomb, and there shall be a resurrection, and after the resurrection there becomes a glorified body, which body shall live forever, and it shall be crowned with a red diadem, and shall be King over all its kind, all enemies shall make peace with him, and the King shall remain forever.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>Various errors.</margin>
My son shall likewise know that here the matter to be understood is that which you have here in the glass; it is now earth, which has lost its humidity <note>moisture or "spiritual" fluidity</note>, and as yet will produce nothing good. My son shall hold that in this art there are many errors. There are many who set out to make the Philosopher's Stone, and by good moderation of the fire they lead it to this stage, and they apply their labor to fixing the stone to the white and red; and when the matter has been brought thus far, they think they can make a <term>projection</term> <note>the final act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note> with it. But then, casting it upon crude Mercury or upon imperfect metals, they find no success, and they fall into despair, repeatedly saying that the art is impossible; and so it is, for the art is impossible for them: for they possess earth which has lost its humidity. Just as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry," whose Latinized works were the foundation of European alchemy</note> says: "Spirits which through much fixation and sublimation have lost their humidity produce nothing good as long as they are earth, or so dry." And such is this matter: the ignorant indeed cannot grasp this: when they have perfected the stone, that is the stone duly...

### CHAPTER XI.

Know, my son, that I shall manifest to you the greatest secret of this art, which has never been made public. Therefore I adjure you, my son, by the Son of the living God, that you do not make this secret public except to your own son, if he seems to you to have the fear of God, lest your soul and mine be condemned on that account, because of the danger that could arise from it.

<margin>The greatest secret of the whole art.</margin>
Now, my son, open your eyes and see, open your ears and hear the greatest secret that exists in the nature of things. My beloved son shall hold, from every Philosophers' Stone, how and in what way it is made and composed—namely, that in the great works of which we speak here, those two stones can be prepared for the <term>White</term> <note>the grade of the stone that transmutates metals into silver</note> and the <term>Red</term> <note>the highest grade of the stone that transmutates metals into gold</note> in one vessel and one furnace: I tell you, understand well what I say. Although you might place <term>Luna</term> <note>Alchemical silver</note> and <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver</note> in this manner without the addition of <term>Sol</term> <note>Alchemical gold</note>, you could make both stones from them, both for the white and for the red. 

<margin>Why Sun and Moon are placed together in the work, since both stones can be made from Moon and Mercury.</margin>
You may ask, then, why in the work the Sun and Moon are placed together. This is done because the Sun is <term>fixed</term> <note>stable and resistant to change by fire</note>, and so that the work might be shorter in this way. For before the Moon becomes fixed in the work, the stone is perfected for the White. For the Moon is not fixed, and before it becomes fixed, it is necessary for a long-lasting <term>coction</term> <note>a process of "cooking" or digestion by heat</note> to occur; and the Moon must be fixed before it can fix the Mercury; and for that reason, Sun and Moon must be in the work together. You can also produce both stones from Sun and Mercury alone, and that would happen more easily than from Sun and Moon joined together. Because the Sun is fixed, it fixes the Mercury more easily on that account. But you may ask, if the Moon alone is placed with Mercury, how could the stone for the Red come from it? Understand the matter rightly: the Moon is inwardly red, even though it is white on the outside. For under all white things in which the four elements are present, redness is hidden inside beneath the external whiteness. For the Moon is cold and <term>volatile</term> <note>tending to evaporate or change state easily when heated</note> like Mercury, for it is coagulated from Mercury and <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle</note> together, and it is still raw and not fixed. Therefore it is white without and red within. Thus, when the Moon is in the work with Mercury alone, it is cooked and fixed by the <term>regimen of fire</term> <note>the controlled stages of heating</note>, and with...

### CHAPTER XII.

There were some ignorant people who, when they had made the stone to the white and to the red, and then saw that it had no **entry** <note>original: "ingressum"; the capacity of the alchemical agent to penetrate and merge with a base metal.</note>, nor would it flow, from which they easily saw that entry was lacking in it. Therefore they dissolved the Stone, and congealed it again twenty or thirty times, thinking thus to make it fusible, and that it would have entry; but they profited nothing, and although they might have dissolved and congealed it much longer, it could help nothing.

There were some others who extracted oil from antimony, with which oil they saturated their stone upon a marble slab; they dried it again in a glass dish, repeating this until the stone became fusible like wax, and gave entry. Then they threw it into Mercury, and thought they were making the Mercury white; but when the Mercury began to boil, it flew off into the air, and the oil of antimony immediately followed it: the powder of the stone, however, remained dry, just as it had been before it had absorbed the oil. The cause is that the oil of antimony was not fixed, and although it had made the stone fusible, it was not fixed with the stone, and cannot be fixed with the stone. This is the reason: If the stone thus saturated were placed in glass over a slow fire, the oil together with the stone would penetrate through the glass into nothingness; but if you were to add a violent fire, the oil would fly off into the air because of the heat. Thus it cannot be fixed with the stone; and in this way the ignorant remained in error.

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>How the stone is to be made fusible.</margin>
Now I will teach my beloved son how to make our stone fusible, and to give it entry, which until now has never been manifested. Therefore I ask you to keep this secret, if you love God, your soul, and mine.

Now know, my son, your stone has now been made white by the good moderation of the fire, as was taught above; if you now wish to keep the white stone, you may; and if you wish to wait for the time until it becomes red, likewise you may. If you wish to lead it to the red, you must leave it in the furnace, and significantly increase your fire for a long time, such as for 15 or 16 days; see if it wishes to change into a saffron color:

With both of your stones, the white as well as the red, perfected and prepared as you have been taught by me and demonstrated by reasons—so that you can easily grasp with your own mind that it must be so—now I wish to teach you in what manner you shall prepare both stones and render them fusible and subtle, for the making of high **projections** <note>The final act of alchemy: casting the Stone onto a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</note>.

### CHAPTER XV.

Take your stone, my son, whether it be white or red, from the vessel and put it into a stone mortar. Pour over it a good quantity of **clean mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii mundi"</note>, which I will teach you how to cleanse later. Taking a wooden pestle, grind it continuously for an entire day. Then put it back into the glass vessel and place it in the **Philosophers' furnace** <note>A specialized furnace designed by alchemists to maintain precise, steady temperatures over many weeks or months.</note> or on a tripod, applying such a fire that liquid lead can be kept melted without congealing, in a steady liquefaction. But you must seal a small glass over the mouth of the vessel in which the stone is held. Keep it in that heat until the mercury is entirely **killed** <note>In alchemy, to "kill" mercury means to fix it, stripping away its fluid, volatile nature so that it becomes a solid, stable substance.</note>, which will easily happen in the space of 40 or 50 days.
<margin>Like attracts its like, and like rejoices in like.</margin>
For the stone attracts all spirits to its own nature: like attracts its like, and like rejoices in like. And when it is entirely killed, decrease the fire slightly until your matter becomes white. And if the stone was white, take it out and, on a glowing-hot metal plate,
<margin>The Test.</margin>
place a grain's weight of it. See if your stone wants to flow and enter into the metal. This can be known in this way: when you place the stone on a glowing plate of copper and it then penetrates the glowing plate like oil into dry leather, and the copper plate is entirely white like silver where the stone lay—if it performs this, it is ready. If not, pour over it the **water of paradise** <note>original: "aqua paradisi"; a highly refined alchemical solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve and "nourish" the stone.</note> in every way as described above, and moderate the fire as before. And if the weight of your stone was one **mark** <note>A traditional European unit of weight for precious metals, roughly equivalent to 8 ounces.</note>, add 4 marks of the water of paradise; do this every time you pour on the water of paradise. Repeat this work until the stone is dissolved according to your heart's desire. And if it be red, let it stand in the same heat in which it stood with the water of paradise—that is, such a heat by which it can thereafter be kept liquefied without glowing—until your stone becomes red. But the red needs a longer time than the white, and you shall test the red in all the same ways as the white.

Know, my son, if you wish to prepare the stone so that you may perform the **projection** <note>The final act of the Great Work, where a tiny amount of the finished Stone is thrown onto molten base metal to transform it into silver or gold.</note> upon mercury, you must make it as fusible as wax. This must be done with great care, because the stone could penetrate through the glass. But I advise you, my son, to make your stone so fusible that it almost begins to glow before it wants to melt; and do this for the white stone: then perform the projection upon **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iouem"; the alchemical code name for the metal Tin.</note>.

Truly, you cannot make the **red stone** <note>original: "lapidem rubrum"; the final, most potent stage of the alchemical Great Work</note> more fusible than is possible for it to be heated to a glow without blowing <note>meaning without the use of bellows to intensify the heat</note>. ### CHAPTER XVI.

Wherefore, my son, you must maintain moderation in making the stone fusible. Inceration

Know, my son, that **Inceration** <note>original: "Incerationem"; from the Latin 'cera' (wax), this is the process of softening a dry substance until it has a waxy, meltable consistency</note>—that is, making a hard thing that cannot melt become liquid, and ensuring it has **ingress** <note>original: "ingressum"; the ability of the Stone to "enter" and penetrate the body of a base metal to transform it</note>—was first discovered among the Ancients. For after they had labored long and hard, and had prepared and perfected the white and red stones, they wished to perform a **projection** <note>The act of throwing the Stone onto molten base metal to effect transmutation</note> with them, but they accomplished nothing. For the stone refused to dissolve; it remained a powder and earth. Then they could easily perceive that it lacked nothing except Inceration, because it did not have ingress. They then sought Inceration in many things, and having investigated all things, they found Inceration in nothing else but in **Sulfur, Arsenic, and Mercury**.

### CHAPTER XVII.

Know, my son, that in all things that exist in the nature of things, except for mineral spirits and metals, the oil flies away from the earth. But in mineral spirits and metals, the oil does not separate itself; they remain with their earth in the fire. And if they fly up from the fire, the earth flies together with the oil. Their oil cannot be separated from the earth as it is in other things. And thus they easily knew that if they wished to follow nature, they must have such an oil from which metals took their own oil. If they were to make those spirits—which they had made dry and earthy by sublimating them so that they could not be melted—fusible again, they had need of such an oil with which they might **incerate** them...

...they mixed gum water, grinding it until it was smooth to the touch. <margin>How the "water of clouds" is removed from Mercury.</margin>
Then they took **Mercury** and pressed it five or six times through a hare-skin <note>the skin of a hare was used as a fine filter; the liquid mercury is forced through the pores, leaving impurities behind</note>. They washed it with salt and vinegar until the salt remained shining and white. With clean common water, they washed away every trace of salt and vinegar, and afterwards dried it with clean linen cloths. They put it into a glass jar with an **alembic** <note>the "hood" or "cap" of a still used for distillation</note> placed on top, set it in the ashes, and after sealing the receiver with **lute** <note>an airtight clay or paste used to seal laboratory apparatus</note>, they built a fire, just as if one intended to distill rose water. They let it stand in this way for 12 or 15 days to draw out the superfluous humidity it contains, by which the work would otherwise be ruined. All Mercury to be used in the work must be prepared in this way, and such a fire must be applied to it so that it does not all **sublimate** <note>turn directly from a solid or liquid into a vapor and reform at the top</note> upward. Even if a little should sublimate upward, so that tiny droplets drip through the alembic, it does not matter. If, however, you were to sublimate it upward so that some of it became "dead" <note>rendered inert or chemically altered by too much heat</note>, it would have to be revived again in boiling water; but then it would again take on that watery humidity which would ruin the entire work.

### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>All living Mercury has "water of clouds" within it.</margin>
Know, my son, that all living Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium viuentem"; raw, liquid quicksilver</note> has within itself the **water of clouds** <note>a term for the internal, volatile moisture of the metal</note>. You will be able to see this for yourself: for a large portion of clean, common water will fall into the receiver. This must be emptied; otherwise, the Mercury would "die" when in the presence of the body of Gold and Silver and would become a powder and fixed <note>stable and resistant to heat</note>. If it retained that humidity within itself, it would never die, nor would it ever become powder or fixed, no matter how long it was kept. Its superfluous humidity must be removed by distillation without sublimation, as has been shown. You shall keep it in the fire until you see that no more dew rises into the alembic. Afterward, keep it in that same heat for 10 or 12 more days without sublimation. When this is done, let it cool and keep it in a wooden box in a dry and warm place, so that it does not [absorb] any humidity from the cold air...

### CHAPTER 20.

Know, my son, that in this way all **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"; quicksilver</note> must be prepared from which we wish to make amalgams, if otherwise the Mercury is to "die" <note>in alchemy, "death" refers to the loss of metallic volatility and the transformation of a substance into a fixed state</note> and be fixed in the work. This is the point where many fail and do not achieve their desires; it is caused by the superfluous moisture the Mercury contains, and those who are ignorant of what they lack remain in error.

Likewise, you shall now understand, my son, that **Gold** <note>original: "Solem"; the Sun</note>, **Silver** <note>original: "Lunam"; the Moon</note>, and **Mercury** are now prepared for the binding together of this work.

Furthermore, know, my son, that you must weigh your powders of Gold and Silver: and you shall take an equal weight of your prepared Mercury, that is, as much *spirit* as *body* <note>the "spirit" refers to the volatile Mercury, while the "body" refers to the fixed Gold or Silver</note>. Otherwise, if there were not enough body, it would have to stand in the fire much longer before the spirit would "die" together with the body and become a powder; but when the weight is equal, the spirit easily dies with the body, etc.

Truly, my son might ask—since that spirit has now "died" with the body and is fixed with it, and has been led to the perfect color, whether **White** <note>the "White Work" or *Albedo*, the stage of the work producing silver</note> or **Red** <note>the "Red Work" or *Rubedo*, the final stage producing gold</note>—about the point where it is drenched with a large quantity of Mercury to make it wax-like <note>original: "incerandum"; the process of *inceration*, making a dry substance soft and fusible like wax</note>, fusible, and subtle, for the completion of the work. Sometimes 10 or 12 parts of spirit are poured over one part of the stone or fixed powder for the **White**; and over the powder for the **Red**, sometimes 20, 24, or even 30 parts of spirit are poured over one part of the fixed red powder.

For while the White Stone is drenched with 12 parts, the Red requires—or rather the powder easily needs—30 parts before it will become fusible. The reason is this: the **White Stone** is raw and moist, cold and white; it needs only half as much of the **Water of Paradise** <note>original: "aquæ paradisi"; a specialized alchemical solvent or highly purified Mercury</note> or spirit to make it wax-like and fusible, for it has not been cooked in the fire as long as the Red Stone or powder, nor is it so dry. The **Red Stone** is hot and dry by nature; its interior stands on the outside—that is, its heat and dryness—and its whiteness is within—that is, its coldness. And before it can be made fusible, easily 30 parts of the Water of Paradise must be poured over one part of the red powder or stone.

Now, however, my son might ask whether such a large amount of the Water of Paradise must be poured over both stones before they become fusible and subti- [subtle]...

### CHAPTER 21.

<margin>Two reasons why it must be kept in the fire for a long time.</margin>
My son shall know and understand that the first addition of the spirit and the body are both raw. That is one reason why it must stand for a long time before they embrace each other fundamentally <note>original: "radicaliter"; meaning at their very roots or essence</note>. The other reason is this: the first addition must be pursued with such a small and slow fire that nothing, or very little, rises in the vessels; thus it must stand for a long time before it can die and become powder. And when the stone or powder has become white or red, it is fixed, even though it may not yet be meltable; and it is fundamentally a medicine, even if it does not yet have "ingress" <term>ingress: the alchemical ability of a substance to penetrate and transform the "pores" of a base metal</term>.

And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy to whom many foundational texts were attributed</note> says thus: "When Mercury is dissolved, it easily dissolves all other metals or spirits; and when it is congealed, it further congeals; and once fixed, it further fixes." Thus, although much **Water of Paradise** <term>Water of Paradise: a potent alchemical solvent or elixir, often a highly distilled "mercurial water" used to nourish the stone</term> has been poured over it—thirty parts to one part of Mercury—the Mercury is coagulated; therefore, it easily coagulates the Water of Paradise and fixes it easily, as said before. 

There is also another reason, which is partly medicinal: if the stone cannot flow <note>original: "fluere"; referring to the stone's ability to melt like wax on a hot plate</note>, it is so that it may easily draw the Water of Paradise into its own nature. There is likewise another reason: when the Water of Paradise is poured over the powder and placed upon the furnace, a much greater heat is applied to it than was given at the beginning of the work. For the beginning of the work must not "sublime" <note>original: "sublimare"; the process where a solid is heated into vapor and then condenses back into a solid in the upper part of the vessel</note>; but to this Water of Paradise such heat is applied that it sublimes upward and falls back down, drop by drop, onto the powder. 

And when it begins to die and simultaneously becomes powder, you shall increase the fire so that it sublimes by it; and you shall invert the glass again and again. When it has sublimed upward, the lower part of the glass is placed in the upper part; thus that fixed powder falls upon the sublimed part of the spirit. This work is repeated until one remains with the other at the bottom. Then a slightly more vehement fire is built until it reaches its color, either white or red, as you desire. 

Thus, for the reasons aforesaid, it ought not to stand as long in the work as it did in the beginning. For this reason, they took no more of the spirit than of the body. But to what purpose is all this? To lead you, my son, to a true understanding of the work, so that you may know how to discern between good and evil <note>meaning successful and failed alchemical results</note>, and so that you may know what you are doing, lest you fall into error or despair. Therefore, my son, diligently reread this and similar lessons often, and strive to imprint them on your memory to avoid all errors that could occur in the work, before you apply your hands to the labor.

<summary>This chapter explains why the alchemical process requires a slow, prolonged heat to ensure the "spirit" (Mercury) and "body" (Gold/Silver) properly combine and "die" into a fixed powder. It details the use of the "Water of Paradise" and the method of sublimation and circulation to achieve the final White or Red medicine.</summary>
