### CHAPTER 22.

<margin>Return to the work.</margin>
Now let us return to the work. You shall take your powder of **Gold** <note>original: "Solis"; literally "of the Sun," the alchemical name for gold</note> and **Silver** <note>original: "Lunæ"; literally "of the Moon," the alchemical name for silver</note>, and you shall weigh it; take as much prepared **Mercury** <term>Mercury: also known as quicksilver; in alchemy, it is the "spirit" that must be "fixed" or solidified</term> as the weight of your powder. Heat an iron mortar and pestle, but not so much that the Mercury evaporates into the air. Then put your prepared powder into the mortar, along with a twentieth part of an ounce of **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used here as a flux to help the metals bond</term>, or a quarter part of a **loth** <note>a loth was a historical unit of weight, roughly half an ounce or 10–15 grams</note>: grind the sal ammoniac before you put it in the mortar. Then grind it with that warm pestle in the mortar. Amalgamate the Mercury and the powder into an **amalgam** <note>a soft, putty-like mixture of mercury and other metals</note>. The sal ammoniac ensures that the powders and the Mercury embrace each other **fundamentally** <note>original: "radicaliter"; meaning at their very roots or essence</note>.

Indeed, grind for an entire day without ceasing; help one another, and let another person take over when one is tired; grind for at least 12 hours continuously. Plug your nostrils, mouth, and ears so that the odor—which can rise invisibly—does not harm you <note>The author is warning against mercury poisoning, though his method of plugging ears and nose would be insufficient against toxic vapors</note>. And when the 12 hours have passed, put your material into a small glass vessel like this:
<image-desc>A simple woodcut illustration of a chemical vessel, such as a retort or cucurbit, lying on its side with a rounded base and a long, tapering neck.</image-desc>
Cover it with another, place a weight on top, then set it in the **secret furnace** <note>a specialized alchemical furnace designed for long-term, steady heat</note>, and do as was previously taught, using the same regulation of the fire, until the work is entirely perfected.

The first regulation of the fire teaches how to complete works that are performed by amalgamations; the regulation of the fire is one and the same. However, the first construction is done in various ways, all coming to the same end and seeking to shorten the time.

There were also some who took the **stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> given freely to us by God the Best and Greatest, and they dissolved it nine or ten times, purged it of its **dregs** <note>original: "fæcibus"; the impurities or waste matter left after a reaction</note>, congealed it again, and reduced it into a subtle white powder, which they kept in a box: then the stone was ready. Then they took Mercury, well-washed and prepared as was taught above, and **sublimated** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the mercury</term> it by means of **vitriol** <term>vitriol: a sulfate mineral (like copper or iron sulfate), used here as a reactive agent</term>. That is, they took 1 pound of sublimated Mercury and 4 pounds of raw vitriol, mixed them together, and sublimated the Mercury through it. They would grind it again with the dregs and sublimate it once more; they ground it again over the dregs and sublimated it yet again; when this was done, they threw away the dregs. Then they sublimated it again through 2 pounds of fresh vitriol, repeatedly throwing away the dregs, and kept only the **sublimate** <note>the purified solid material resulting from sublimation</note> in a box. Then they took 3 **loths** of Silver and 1 of Gold, and melted them together,

And they filed these down bit by bit: they reduced the filings into a powder by pounding them in an iron mortar, and they washed the powder—as taught in the preceding work—with distilled water. After that, they ground it upon marble with prepared common salt and gum water, and by pounding, reduced it into an **intangible** <note>original: "intangibilem"; meaning a powder so fine it cannot be felt as individual grains</note> powder, and they washed it with common distilled water until the water flowed away clean and clear from it. These things being done, they put the powder into a round glass vessel made in this manner <note>referring to the illustration below</note>, filling the vessel to the very top. Then they took it and suspended it inside a tripod, or in a **secret furnace** <note>a furnace designed for long-term, steady heat, often hidden to protect the "Great Work"</note>, in a chamber; and with the door closed, they allowed it to hang there for 89 days, applying such a fire that they could comfortably hold a hand there for half an hour between the walls of the furnace and the chamber in which the vessel hung. They maintained the fire at that same heat with a lamp made with a wick of resin and with distilled oil, which does not blacken the lamp and produces little smoke; and during this time, the material is cooked into a single thing.

When the 89 days were finished, they broke the glass and removed the material. They would heat an iron or bronze plate until glowing, place the material upon it, and put it into the furnace in which goldsmiths paint with **enamel** <term>enamel: "encausto"; a glass-based decorative coating fused to metal at high temperatures</term>. They watched to see if the powder smoked. Or, they weighed 2 drachms of the powder, put it into a small crucible, and heated it in the fire for half an hour; and when it had cooled, they weighed it again. If they had lost anything in weight, the powder was not yet **fixed** <term>fixed: "fixus"; in alchemy, a substance is "fixed" when it becomes stable and no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to high heat</term>. Then they put it back into the glass as before, and suspended it again in the furnace, increasing the fire so that it was barely for the length of time of an **Ave Maria** <note>the "Hail Mary" prayer; in the pre-modern era, prayers were frequently used as standardized timers for laboratory processes</note>...

And if they wished to have it for red, they let it stand and increased the fire: for under the heat used for white, the red **tincture** <note>the coloring or transforming power of the Stone</note> cannot manifest itself. Therefore, you must keep both of these in your mind if you wish to profit in this art. For this reason, do not be weary of reading through your lessons often with a diligent mind. Once the redness has been drawn out, the Elixir was perfected: the **Stone for red** <note>original: "lapis ad rubrum"</note> for reducing all imperfect metals into the **true Sun** <note>original: "verum Solem"; Sun is the alchemical name for Gold</note>, which is more excellent than that from the mines, passing all tests.

### BY MASTER JOHANN ISAAC

<margin>2. Solution</margin>
They amalgamate that imperfect body with living mercury and lead it back into its original essence; this is the **solution** <note>original: "solutio"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note> of the Ancients. Their solution is not the melting of water from clouds, but is a "dry water"—that is, Mercury—and it is the foundation of the art, about which Rhazes <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD) was a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine and alchemy</note> says: "Unless you dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain." Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy</note> speaks of these solutions in the books titled *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between Greek philosophers</note>. This shortest way in the art is "reduction," if the bodies are clarified and reduced into a resplendent water, which is that water from which they first took their origin. This water encompasses spirit, soul, and body within itself, and it is what makes us shine, as Geber says. And when they had converted it into Mercury, so that they could squeeze it through a cloth, they said they possessed the element of Water; and the Philosophers said that from that thickness of water, Earth is formed, and then they claimed to possess the second element, namely Water and Earth.

<margin>3. Purification.</margin>
The third word of the Ancients is **Purification** <term>Purification: (Latin: mundificatio) the process of cleansing a substance of its "gross" or impure parts, often through repeated washing or heating</term>, about which Morienus <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who reportedly taught the secrets of the craft to the King of Egypt</note> says: "This earth putrefies with water, and then continuously purifies itself, and when it is pure, every medicine is prepared from it with God's help." The Philosophers discuss this in the *Assembly*, saying: "Join the dry with the moist." The dry is Earth, the moist is Water. Behold, you now have purified water and earth.

<margin>4. Evaporation.</margin>
The fourth word is the **Evaporation** of water; this occurs when the "water of Paradise" ascends into the sky and falls back to earth drop by drop. They call this "sublimation" <term>sublimation: in alchemy, the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collects as a solid or liquid higher up in the vessel</term>, or "ascent and descent." In this way, that water becomes the earth that had previously been crushed in the earth, and they called that ascent "Air." Thus you have Water, Air, and Earth; and this is what the Philosophers mean when they say: "When the white stage is achieved, pour over it the water of Paradise, and immediately join the sublimation, so that the spirit may come forth from it, which Hermes calls 'the bird'." Regarding this matter, Morienus says: "In the end, there will remain for you calcined water, sand, or ashes." And Hermes, Geber, and Morienus say: "Do not despise the ashes which you find in the lowest state; the ashes are shining, and in them you will find the precious adamant <note>original: "adamanta"; likely referring to a diamond-like, indestructible crystalline essence</note>." Then it is said: "Immediately add the ferment to it," that is, when they have reduced that imperfect thing to a white powder, so that you may pour over it the water of Paradise in which Gold <note>original: "Sol" (the Sun); the standard alchemical symbol for gold</note> has been amalgamated. When they pour this over the powder, they call it "ferment," with the same water of the Philo-

...of the philosophers. Then they said: "Now join the soul to it." Concerning this matter, **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; a reference to the 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician</note> says: "Next, we join the soul to our stone." For just as in a human being, the body does not live without a soul, so our stone does not live without a soul, no matter how pure the imperfect body might be. For it is the **ferment** <term>fermentum: an agent, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical matter to "leaven" it and direct it toward a specific metallic nature</term> itself that leads the matter to its proper nature. Therefore, they add the ferment—that is, **Gold** <note>original: "Solem" (the Sun)</note> amalgamated with the **water of paradise** <note>a poetic term for a highly purified mercurial solvent</note>. This is what **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the art to King Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: "Unless you cleanse the imperfect thing and whiten it into a powder, and then place the soul into it and mix it therewith, you have accomplished nothing in our art."

Therefore, the philosopher **Dastin** <note>original: "Dantynus"; likely referring to John Dastin, a prominent 14th-century English alchemist</note> says: "Perform the gathering of the soul with the purified body and the spirit." Then its spirit is added; and you should rejoice with them, for they have changed their nature, and coarse things have been made subtle. This is what the philosopher **Alanus** <note>Alanus ab Insulis, or Alain de Lille, to whom several alchemical works were attributed</note> says in the *Book of Assemblies* <note>original: "Libro Turbarum," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*</note>: "Spirits are not joined with bodies until they are perfectly stripped of all defilements." At the hour of mixing, truly wondrous things appear: all the colors of the world that can be imagined. At last, they all arrive at one color, which is **red**, and which they have called **Fire**. Then that imperfect body is colored with a firm color by the ferment, which is the soul; and the spirit is joined with the soul and bound with the body. Together with the body, it is converted into the color of the ferment, and they become one, so that fire, in all its strength and vehemence, cannot separate them.

From these aforementioned words, it is clear that the Philosophers spoke the truth. For they say: "Our stone consists of the four elements." Likewise: "Our stone is made of body, soul, and spirit." And truly: they compared that imperfect body to a dead body, because **Silver** <note>original: "Luna" (the Moon)</note> is weak and not at all "fixed" <term>fixed: a substance that is stable in fire and does not evaporate or change</term>. They named the spirit "water," and they speak truly, for that spirit is indeed a resplendent and flowing water. They called the ferment the "soul," and they spoke truly: for it gives life to that imperfect body which it did not have before, and leads it back into another form. Whatever they said in obscure words is true. Some philosophers also say: "Unless you strip bodies of their bodies, and also the spirits, you have accomplished nothing in our art." From that body, we first make water when it is amalgamated, and then that body is stripped of its "bodiliness" <note>original: "corpore exuitur"; meaning it loses its solid, metallic form</note>. Afterward, through continuous decoction <note>prolonged heating</note>, that body is dried out and dies with the spirit, and then the Spirit becomes the Body.

MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC.

<margin>Follow nature.</margin>
Whoever seeks, finds; and they speak the truth. For in our works, we first create moist things from dry, dry from moist, subtle from thick, and thick from subtle; we establish spirits from bodies, and bodies from spirits, and we make the higher so that it is as the lower, and we equate the lower to the higher <note>original: "superius, vt sit inferius... ac inferius superiori æquamus"; a reference to the famous Hermetic maxim from the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus</note>. Thus we convert one matter into another, as was previously taught. Therefore, from the aforementioned reasons, it is clear that the Ancients spoke the truth in all things, although they are obscure. This was done so that the ignorant, who are not of the number of the "sons of the art" <note>a common term for initiated alchemists</note>, would not understand us, and so that the knowledge of these things would remain unknown to them.

Next, my son <note>alchemical texts often addressed the reader as "son" to denote an apprentice or initiate</note> shall know that the Ancients set down many chapter headings so that the ignorant would think our art is practiced with great difficulty. In every chapter, they placed many and various operations under many names, such as **Reduction**, **Solution**, **Washing**, **Sublimation**, **Distillation**, **Coagulation**, **Inceration** <note>original: "Increatio," likely a typo for *inceratio*, the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, **Calcination**, **Fixation**, and so on, as was mentioned above. And now I will reveal to my son how the Ancients and Sages devised those names in the work.

### CHAPTER XXV.

<margin>How the work must be established in imitation of the Ancients.</margin>
Likewise, if you wish to perform the work in the same way our ancestors did, take **Mercury** <term>Quicksilver: the primary liquid metal used as a starting material</term> from the mines where silver or gold is dug out, but take none that is elicited by art <note>i.e., use natural native mercury rather than mercury refined from cinnabar by industrial means</note>. You shall squeeze it through a rabbit skin, and if anything remains in the rabbit skin, inspect whether it is a body of metal. Put this residue into a small crucible with a portion of powdered **borax** <term>a flux used to help metals melt and to clean their surfaces</term>. Place it in the fire and blow upon it so that it may be dissolved. When it has been melted, see what kind of metallic body it is. If you find it to be of some imperfect <note>base</note> metal, that Mercury is entirely useless for our work. But if you find **Gold** <note>original: "Solem" (the Sun)</note> and **Silver** <note>original: "Lunam" (the Moon)</note>, it is upright and good. Then take as much of that Mercury as you wish, put it in a glass vessel, and through an **alembic** <term>a lid or "helmet" used in distillation</term> draw off its superfluous moisture, which would corrupt your work and prevent the Mercury from being able to "die" into powder. For if the superfluous moisture were not drawn away from it, even if that matter remained in the fire until Judgment Day, it would never be reduced to powder. The cause is the moisture which the Mercury holds within itself; for you see a great part of its moisture through distillation, as was taught before. But when the Mercury is stripped of all its superfluous moisture, then take that imperfect body...

...it is cupelled Silver <note>original: "Lunam cupellatam"; silver purified in a cupel, a shallow porous cup used in assaying</note> which was afterwards remelted from lead in a crucible. The Ancients call this Silver an "imperfect body" because Silver is weak, white, raw, and not fixed. Moreover, they amalgamated this Silver with a large quantity of Mercury; and they always took 3 parts of Silver and 1 part of Gold, which Gold they called the "ferment" <note>original: "fermentum"; in alchemy, the ferment is a substance (like yeast) added to a larger mass to transform its nature</note>. Some amalgamated the Gold and Silver together, as the preceding work teaches, and some amalgamated them individually, and mixed the ferment—that is, the amalgamated Gold—into the Water of Paradise <note>a highly refined alchemical solvent or "mercurial water"</note>. Then they poured this over both powders and mixed them, as will be taught. And after they had amalgamated the Silver, they placed it into a glass...

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an alchemical vessel, specifically a pear-shaped glass flask (matrass or cucurbit) with a long neck, standing upright.</image-desc>

...as was previously taught in the work; I say into a glass of this kind, and they placed it on a tripod, as above, and with the same regulation of the fire. Thereafter they also amalgamated the Gold, and also placed it in the furnace in a glass, just like the Silver. They used the same governance of the fire as above, as well as the Water of Paradise and the water of the same Mercury, once its humidity had been drawn off, as has often been said. They also put it into a glass of the kind shown above, and placed it on a tripod next to the other three glasses, until the work reached the stage of inceration <note>original: "incerandum"; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency through the addition of liquid</note>. They did this so that the Water of Paradise might more easily "wax" and "die" <note>that is, lose its liquid form and become a fixed solid</note> within that work; for that water exists between the fixed and the non-fixed, for it had undergone decoction <note>prolonged heating</note> in the fire just as long as the work itself, although it had not yet "died" or been turned into powder.

Know, my son, that although the Water of Paradise (that is, your Mercury) were kept in the furnace for ten years, it would not die and turn into powder at once; something "living" <note>meaning liquid, volatile metallic mercury</note> would always remain, and when that part was moved, the whole would immediately become "alive" again. Wherefore Mercury says of himself: "As long as a part of my body as small as a lentil remains alive, I am no more dead than I ever was." This happens because no body is mixed with it or in it—neither father, nor mother, nor sister, nor brother, nor anyone from its closest kin or tribe is mixed with it or in it. But when "arms are joined to arms, and mouths to mouths," in that moment it dies <note>An allegorical description: Mercury only becomes a fixed solid when combined with its "kin," the other metals or spirits derived from them</note>. My son shall understand it in this way: that any of the metals be mixed with it, or the spirits that have arisen from the metals, or our White Stone or Red Stone; and all these are...

# OF MASTER JOHANNES ISAACUS

...of its own kind, or its relatives, which are also of its nature; and therefore it joins itself with them, and immediately dies <note>In alchemy, "death" or "mortification" refers to the breakdown of a substance's outward form so it can be transformed.</note> with them.
<margin>Mercury never dies alone.</margin>
But when it is alone, it does not die even in the space of ten years, no matter how tempered a fire you place beneath it.

My son, reread all these things quite often, for in this way you will be able to understand nature in all things. But enough of these matters; let us return to our work.

All three stand upon a tripod <note>original: "tripode"; a three-legged stand used to support a vessel over a heat source</note>: namely, the Sun <note>original: "Sol"; alchemical Gold</note> in a glass by itself, the work with the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; alchemical Silver</note> in another glass, and the Water of Paradise <note>A highly refined alchemical solvent or "mercurial water."</note> in a third glass. And all three stood together on the tripod in a sealed chamber, so firmly that nothing could escape, and they were governed by a very small fire, such that a hand could be held between the walls and the chamber without danger of burning. Indeed, the goal is that the heat and the sensation of the hand should be as one. For the heat must be so regulated that you can hold your hand there for a half-hour without being burned; and if the heat and the sensation of the hand were the same, all was going well.

Then the Ancients and the Sages would deliberate on what peculiar name they should give to each sign they observed in the work, so that they might hide the art from the ignorant who do not belong to this craft. To make such people believe the art is practiced with great difficulty, they gave the work various names, as will yet be shown. They listed many operations—which are also described below—such as <term>Solution</term> <note>dissolving a solid into liquid</note>, <term>Reduction</term> <note>restoring a substance to its former state</note>, <term>Sublimation</term> <note>heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again</note>, <term>Distillation</term>, <term>Congelation</term> <note>thickening or freezing</note>, <term>Evaporation</term>, <term>Inceration</term> <note>softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, <term>Calcination</term> <note>reducing a metal to powder through heat</note>, and many more varied operations, so that they might lead the ignorant into error. 

But all such men are pretenders and shall not possess the inheritance of the Sages. All the aforementioned operations actually take place within a closed glass in which the "work" stands in the furnace, as will be taught and has been sufficiently taught above. However, the unrefined are unable to grasp this due to the weakness of their minds; they think each operation is a distinct task, performed with unique vessels and instruments, in unique furnaces, and with unique regulation of the fire. Thus, thinking the art is practiced with great difficulty, they cannot grasp that all these things happen simultaneously in a single closed vessel, in a single furnace, and with a single governance of the fire, as will be taught.

In the beginning, the Ancients observed the matter placed in the glass acquire a black fleece or skin on the upper part;
<margin>The Blackening of the Sea.</margin>
then they called this the <term>Blackening of the Sea</term> <note>original: "Nigrificationē maris"; this refers to the "Nigredo" or black stage, the first major phase of the Great Work signifying decomposition.</note>. For that water was entirely black on top, and because the Sun and Moon were within it,
<margin>Eclipse of the Sun and Moon.</margin>
they said it was the <term>Eclipse of the Sun and Moon</term> <note>original: "Eclipsis Solis atque Lunæ"; a metaphor for the union and "death" of gold and silver in the mercurial solvent.</note>, as well as the Blackening of the Sea; and the ignorant did not understand this in the least.

It introduces the "Nigredo" stage, where the matter turns black, metaphorically described as an "Eclipse" or the "Blackening of the Sea."</summary>

# CHAPTER XXVI OF THE MINERAL WORKS

Then they saw that water—that is, Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"; alchemical quicksilver, representing the principle of volatility</note>—flying upward into the higher part of the glass from that matter, or from the bodies of the Sun <note>original: "Solis"; alchemical Gold</note> and the Moon <note>original: "Lunae"; alchemical Silver</note>. They said, "it carried the wind in its belly," because the Mercury from the matter or the body of the Sun and Moon flew through the air on account of the heat and fervor. Therefore a certain Philosopher said: "You shall offer air to it, in whose belly it will be carried through the production of the son who is its father." Then it shall be given a drink; that is, when it falls back again to the bottom or the matter, it will be given a drink from the moisture of the earth, which is its nurse. <note>These phrases are allegorical references to the "Emerald Tablet" (Tabula Smaragdina), a foundational cryptic text of alchemy.</note>

And concerning this matter, Hermes, the father of Philosophers, speaks: "That which is above seems to me to be as that which is below; and that which is below is as that which is above." <note>The most famous axiom in alchemy, suggesting a correspondence between the spiritual and material worlds, or between the vapors at the top of a vessel and the solids at the bottom.</note> And Danthynus says: "He who wishes to perform the miracle of the thing of which our stone is the father, and the earth the nurse, and the Moon the mother, it carries the wind in its belly, and its nurse is in the earth." Moreover, Danthynus says: "When it ascends from the earth upward into heaven, and again falls down to the earth, then it shall take strength from that which is above and that which is below." And he speaks the truth: when it begins to bud <note>original: "gemmare"; used here to describe the appearance of crystals or "spiritual" growths at the top of the glass</note> above, then the "buds" begin to fall back to the ground, and it dies into dust. When it is in such a state, it must be drenched with the clear water of paradise, and its mother the Moon must be offered to it, until that water is mixed with the dust. And then offer it the Sun—that is, the fire—until that which is more excellent than any thing in the world is perfected, <margin>Sublimation.</margin> which the ignorant do not grasp, etc.

When they looked more closely at the matter, they saw it ascend and descend even more within the glass: then they gave it the name "sublimation," <term>Sublimation: the process where a solid turns into vapor and then back into a solid, used here to describe the purification of the matter.</term> for it was true sublimation. Therefore Geber <note>A Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, a prolific 8th-century chemist/alchemist.</note> says in the *Assembly of Philosophers*: "When the work or the stone has been gathered together, immediately apply sublimation to it." But the ignorant did not understand that sublimation takes place in closed vessels, and so they erred. They also saw that when the drops fell back down, water still remained; then they thought it should be called distillation, and it was perfect distillation. <margin>Distillation.</margin> Therefore Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says in the *Assembly*: "After sublimation, apply distillation to it." Even this the ignorant did not understand. Finally, they saw the matter thicken and turn into earth, and a thick earth remain, finally standing above the water; and this happened because Mercury ascended and descended, stripping away the earth or the body. And when Mercury dripped downward, it was unwilling...

### BY MASTER JOHANN ISAAC.

...it mingled itself again with the body, and that body flowed over the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"; here referring to the volatile "water" or quicksilver within the vessel</note>; for the Mercury lay below, because it was heavier than that body was. And so the Ancients saw that everything, at the very end, flowed in the upper part over the water, and that was the Mercury; the earth sat or flowed upon it, and it grew thicker and thicker, and blacker and blacker. Finally, they saw the earth begin to sink again into the water to the bottom of the vessel; because this earth was black, they chose to call it **Corruption**, <margin>Corruption.</margin> and the "foul menstrual substance." <note>Alchemists often used biological metaphors; the "menstruum" refers to a primary solvent or base matter from which the "son" (the Stone) is born.</note> Concerning this matter, *Morienus* says in his booklet: *Our stone is found in the foul, corrupted menstrual substance; from it, our stone is reduced into a mass.* The ignorant, not understanding this, sought the stone in stables, in sewers, in dung, and in manure, and they were deceived. <note>The author clarifies that alchemical "filth" is a chemical state, not literal waste.</note> Then these Ancients perceived that this foul earth, by continuous cooking and the good management of a tempered and slow fire, lost its stench under that water, and its color changed. Then the Philosophers called this very thing the **Washing**. <margin>Washing.</margin>

Regarding this, the philosopher *Origines* says: *Perform the Washing; cleanse and purge this body with water, so that a binding together <term>conglutinatio: the joining of substances</term> can happen between body, soul, and spirit.* Yet it was not the intention of the Philosophers that bodies should be washed and purged with rainwater. Therefore, the ignorant calcined the bodies with salt, and ground those powders <term>calces: the fine powder remaining after a metal is burned</term> upon a stone, and drenched and washed them with clean water, doing so until the water flowed pure and clear. But then they had progressed no more than before; their time, expense, and labor were lost, as they remained in error. *Hermes* and *Geber* moreover say: *Know that our art is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the spreading of that water back over the earth until it is putrefied and purified, and washed with the earth.* Yet the ignorant did not even understand this: they did not know that all of this happens in a closed glass within our furnace. They are not among the number of our sons.

In addition, the Philosophers perceived over a long time and by continuous boiling, under the same management of fire, that the earth grew and thickened, while the water decreased and diminished because of the tempered cooking. Then they likewise said: *This is the perfect **Inceration*** <margin>Inceration.</margin>—and that was its proper name. <note>Inceration is the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency.</note> Therefore the philosopher *Danthynus* says: *Its sweat must be drawn from it, and it must afterwards be made to drink it.*

*Hermes* says: *The earth shall be imbued with water.* And *Morienus*: *Give a drink to the thirsty one until he is nourished by his own sweat, and for eternity...*

# WORKS ON MINERALS

...it shall thirst no more. Even the unlearned did not understand this, not knowing that this happens in a closed vessel in our furnace. By long-lasting boiling and by a long-lasting, tempered heat, they saw all the water dried out, and all of it converted at once into earth. This earth will still be worked upon after our operation, as **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose Latinized works were central to European science.</note> says: *When our earth has been made, our art is for the greatest part completed.* Then they saw that this earth established itself into a solid substance and stood firm, and did not ascend <margin>Congelation.</margin> any further. Then they almost always said: "This is perfect **Congelation**," <note>The process where a liquid substance is transformed into a solid state, often interpreted as the fixing of the volatile spirit.</note> and that was its proper name. Those who were ignorant, not understanding these words, knew nothing, as stated above.

**Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of the Hermetic tradition.</note> says: *Dissolve our stone, and then with great skill congeal it and reduce it to earth; afterwards make it white, and then living, and finally red: then you shall have finished the work in our art.* The philosopher **Danthynus** says: *Know that our art is nothing other than to perfectly dissolve, and perfectly congeal again, without any loss of substance, and without addition or removal; then you possess the whole art—close your books and seek nothing more.* Therefore **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit often cited as a teacher of alchemical secrets to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: *Our work is nothing other than the work of women and child’s play.* <note>A common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the "secret" is known, the work requires only patience and gentle heat, like cooking or simple games.</note> And the ignorant do not know in what sense these hidden words are to be taken. Then the Ancients perceived that by a longer boiling and tempered heat, that solid earth gradually became more and more white, until finally it became so perfectly white and shining that its brightness surpassed every brightness in the World. Then it was agreed among them to call this <margin>Calcination.</margin> whitening **Calcination**, <note>In alchemy, calcination usually refers to reducing a substance to a fine powder through heat, but here it specifically describes the purification into the white stage.</note> and this is the true Calcination of the Ancients, and this is its true name. Therefore **Hermes** and **Morienus** say: *Do not despise the ashes remaining in the lower place, for in them is the most excellent diamond.* And from these ashes, says **Geber**, *a splendid virgin shall be born; she shall conceive fruit in her womb, and then she shall bring forth the son of life.* This will happen, my son, when the **ferment** <note>A substance added to the base matter to trigger its transformation into the Stone, much like yeast in bread.</note> is mixed with this white earth. Then the earth, or that imperfect body, receives the ferment, and then the Virgin conceives in her womb; such is the mind of the Ancients in these matters. Then the Philosophers say: *Nourish that son or that boy with his own milk until he has grown up.* This means that when this earth, which has been made white in this manner and mixed with the ferment, is drenched with the clear and bright **water of paradise**, <note>Symbolic language for a highly purified solvent or "mercurial water" used to moisten the matter.</note> and that water is absorbed into this white and dry matter (which is called "waxing" <note>original: "inceratur"; Inceration is the process of softening a dry substance until it has the consistency of wax.</note>), their meaning is that this boy is nourished

...by its own milk <note>original: "lacte proprio"</note>; and truly it is its milk. The ignorant do not grasp this. Furthermore, when the material was white and fixed in that manner, they then took it out of the furnace, and they amalgamated glass in which there was Salt; they also took that from the furnace, and ground them together in a stone mortar with a stone pestle, until the **Sun** <note>In alchemical symbolism, "Sol" or the "Sun" usually represents gold or the perfected masculine principle.</note> was amalgamated and thoroughly mixed with the white stone or powder; and then they applied fermentation to it. Concerning which **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit often cited as a teacher of alchemical secrets.</note> says: *Make the conjunction, and then give it a soul, so that it is never separated from the soul for eternity.* *Perform the marriage,* says **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy; his "marriage" refers to the chemical union of opposites.</note>, *and place the bride with her groom in the bed, and you shall sprinkle his bed with celestial dew, and the bride shall conceive a son, who shall be King over all his tribes, and all his enemies shall enter into peace with him; he shall be crowned with a red diadem, and shall remain King of eternity, and shall never lose his dominion.* The ignorant by no means grasp these obscure words.

Then, taking up the material, they put it back into the vessel, and then, having received the **Water of Paradise** <note>A symbolic term for a highly purified solvent or "mercury" used to nourish the stone.</note>, they poured it over that material, easily ten parts to one part of material, and that was what **Geber** meant: *Sprinkle the bed with celestial dew: the Bride shall conceive a son.* That was the meaning. And they closed the glass with a seal <note>Likely the "Seal of Hermes," an airtight wax or glass closure to prevent the spirit from escaping.</note>, and placed it again in the furnace, increasing the fire a little more vehemently, until the water of paradise would sublimate upwards and fall back down drop by drop onto the material; and that was why the *son of the resplendent virgin was nourished by his own milk, until he had grown up.*

My son, you shall know and understand: if you wish to prepare the stone for the **Red Work**, you must lead the white and red earth through with its fermentation by increasing the fire, until it becomes saffron-colored. And when it is entirely saffron, like dried saffron, then the element of Air has been turned outward. Then indeed the fire must be significantly increased, so that the element of Fire may come forth. For in that regime of fire where the Air brought itself forth in the likeness of saffron, the Fire and the red tincture cannot bring themselves forth at the same time. Thus the fire must be significantly increased until its red tincture stands forth on the outside. And when your material is red, then pour over it the water of paradise, until your stone has drunk all the water of paradise, and all becomes one powder. Then govern that powder with a moderation of fire, so that it becomes white again like snow; then increase the fire, as taught above, until the powder is perfectly saffron; then increase the fire until it is perfectly red, and your work will be finished.

# MINERAL WORKS

### CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>The four elements in the work individually.</margin>
You have now seen all four elements appear individually in the work. First, you saw **water** and **earth**, which were manifest at the beginning; then you saw **fire** and **air**, which were hidden within. For those were previously only grasped by the intellect, but now you have seen them manifested to your eyes: specifically when you perceived the perfect saffron color. And now you see its **red tincture**, and the fire, which are now openly displayed. Therefore, when the Ancients said that "Our Stone is forged from the four elements," and yet is one thing and from one source, they spoke the truth. This becomes clear from the reasons given above.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

Now you shall know hereafter, my son, that you must act as I have taught you here if you desire to have the Stone for the **Red** <note>The "Rubedo" or Red Stage, the final goal of alchemy signifying the creation of gold.</note>. But if you only wish to have it for the **White** <note>The "Albedo" or White Stage, which produces silver.</note>, apply the **water of paradise** <note>A symbolic term for a highly purified mercurial solvent.</note> to it when you mix it with the ferment, as described above; and let it ascend and descend until it settles at the bottom, fixed with the white stone. Then follow the same regime of fire until the powder once again becomes perfectly white. Then you possess the stone for the White, for the purpose of transforming imperfect metals into pure **Silver** <note>original: "Lunam," literally "the Moon," the alchemical symbol for silver.</note>.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

Furthermore, my son, you shall know that all these kinds of works are equally excellent, and their **projection** <note>The act of casting a small amount of the "Medicine" or Stone onto a large mass of molten base metal to transform it.</note> is so great that it is a thing of wonder. You will discover this yourself: for when you project your **medicine** <note>The Alchemical Stone was often called a "medicine" for metals, "healing" them of their impurities to become gold.</note> upon any metal, or upon **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note>, as long as the medicine has strength, the metal into which you projected it will be breakable and fragile, like glass that can be powdered. Then, subsequently, cast that same powder into other imperfect metals, and it will still be a medicine. Do this as long as the metal remains breakable and fragile; but when it becomes **malleable** <note>Able to be hammered or shaped without breaking; a characteristic of pure gold and silver.</note>, the medicine has reached the limit of its strength. At that point, the metal is either **Gold** <note>original: "Sol," literally "the Sun."</note> or **Silver**, depending on what the medicine was. Thus, my son, you will see it easily, and experience will easily teach you.

<margin>Concerning the multiplication of the stone.</margin>

once it has been completed, the burden of a ship could easily be finished with it; indeed, a hundred vessels might be filled. My son shall know that he must take 10 or 12 lbs of **Mercury**, and shall sublimate them by means of **Roman vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolū Romanum," likely copper sulfate or iron sulfate used as a reagent</note>, using three parts vitriol to one part Mercury, and likewise sublimated again with fresh vitriol; and this you may do six or seven times. Measuring time by the recitation of prayers was common in laboratories before precise clocks were available.</note> could be recited twice. Grind this powder even more finely upon a marble slab with rectified **water of life** <term>aqua vitæ: distilled alcohol or "spirit of wine," used here as a solvent or carrier</term>; and do so for this reason: for that powder dries easily at a small fire, because that water of life flies away as soon as it feels heat. 

Then take that ground Gold (or medicine) and an equal weight of your sublimated Mercury as there is of Gold, and mix them well together. Dry it upon a stone, then grind both together yet again with good rectified water of life, and then dry it in the Sun, or in a bath <note>A "balneum" or bain-marie (water bath) for gentle heating.</note> at a small fire, until no more moisture remains within.

Then place it into a glass of this sort, and pour over it 12 parts of the prepared Mercury (which has been

stripped of its moisture, as was taught) for every one part of this powder. Then, with the glass properly sealed, move it between your hands, turning it over and over for an hour, so that all the Mercury is thoroughly mixed into "gemmules" <note>Small, bead-like droplets or grains.</note> with that powder. Then place it upon a tripod and apply fire, just as I taught you it must be given when the **water of paradise** <note>A symbolic term for a highly purified mercurial solvent mentioned in previous chapters.</note> was poured over it. And in this way, let it stand for 90 continuous days. And this whole mass is medicine, as good as—indeed, better than—the first medicine was. 

And if you then wish to make even more of the medicine, take a large glass of the same shape as the first in which you performed the multiplication, and weigh your medicine. If its weight is 10 marks, take 100 marks of the prepared Mercury (stripped of its moisture), and put it into that large glass with the medicine. Mix them thoroughly together, as I taught you above, by shaking it between your hands. Place it on the tripod for 90 days with the same regulation of fire as before; and the whole becomes medicine as good as the first was. And if still...

### CHAPTER XXXI

<margin>
The words of the Ancients regarding the pouring of those 9 parts over one part of the stone.
</margin>
My son shall know that there were those who took 9 parts of the **water of paradise** <note>original: "aquæ paradisi." In alchemy, this refers to a highly rectified, pure solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve and nourish the Stone.</note> rectified of its superfluous humidity, as was previously taught. They would take 9 vials and put one part into each, sealing them above with **lute** <note>original: "lutarunt." Lute was a clay-based cement used to hermetically seal glass vessels for heating.</note>. They placed them on a tripod in a chamber and left them there until the Stone was entirely prepared and until the water of paradise was poured over it. Then they would take one vial with one part and pour it over the Stone, mixing them thoroughly together, and place it on the tripod. They would leave the remaining 8 vials in the furnace until that one part was **fixed** <note>original: "fixa." Fixation is the process of turning a volatile liquid or vapor into a solid that can withstand heat.</note> with the Stone. Then they would give it another part, doing as before, and so on with the third and fourth, until the Stone had imbibed all 9 parts and these were fixed with it. This seems to me to be the best method, and better than if everything were poured in at once, for it shortens the work and happens very quickly. The Stone is not overwhelmed as it would be if it had to receive all nine parts at once, and it saves time; however, it requires a little more labor to repeatedly take the vessel from the furnace, open it, and close it again. But it is the best method for the work. And concerning these 9 parts to be poured over one part of the stone, as I taught you before, the Ancients spoke thus when they taught their sons who understood their words: "9 parts of **May dew** <note>original: "roris Maialis." Alchemists believed dew collected in May possessed special "vital spirits" from the stars, making it a powerful solvent.</note> shall be taken, each part enclosed in a vial and kept in a fever-heat or warmth, until the **lowest world** <note>original: "mundus infimus," a metaphorical term for the solid matter at the bottom of the flask.</note> becomes white and dry. Then sprinkle the lowest world with a part of the May dew, and then another part, until the lowest world flows like oil."

<margin>
Successors discovered many other methods for shortening the art.
</margin>
In this way, my son, understand that the Ancients prepared their Stone in various ways, and in the end, all were proven effective. My son shall know that while the Ancients operated as was previously taught (which is the best method), their successors discovered many other ways to shorten the art. These include making **aqua forti** <note>original: "aqua forti," literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid or similar mineral acids used to dissolve metals.</note> in various ways, as is recounted in many places regarding the mineral work, as well as in the animal work, and much more so in the vegetable work, in which wonderful things are held concerning **miraculous waters**—which seem miraculous because of the wonders performed by these waters, as is taught in the vegetable work. And also in the separation...

### CHAPTER XXXII

Therefore, I advise you, my son, to free yourself from works of this kind in which the separation of elements occurs, or the various methods of **strong waters** <note>original: "aquarum fortium." Aqua fortis (literally "strong water") usually refers to nitric acid, a powerful solvent used by alchemists to dissolve metals.</note>, as I have rightly taught in the preface to the **Great Work** <note>original: "magni operis." The Magnum Opus or Great Work is the alchemical term for the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. It is not without danger, even if one is skilled in the art. Instead, keep to these principal works which you were taught before, and will yet be taught; in them, there is no separation of elements, etc. We have taught above how our ancestors worked with **amalgamations** <note>original: "amalgamationibus." Amalgamation is the process of combining mercury with another metal, such as gold or silver, to form a soft paste.</note>, and they all reached one goal: and it is so good and certain that it could not be better. And below we shall teach how the Stone can be made with common aqua fortis, and an oil from metals, which will also be done without great labor and without the separation of elements, so that one may reach true and perfect works: and it is good and certain.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

My son shall know why the elements are separated: namely, so that what is imperfect may be made perfect, both for the purpose of removing all impurity through **rectification** <note>original: "rectificando." Rectification is the process of purifying a liquid, typically through repeated distillation, to reach its most potent or "right" state.</note> and for restoring it to purity; and for cleansing the bodies and the spirit from all filth. Once this is done, the same elements are to be joined together again.

Now my son shall know that fire purifies all things applied to it, no matter how impure they may be. Is this not true? Yes. Fire purifies all. Look at the works we taught above: when we first bring our Stone to the fire, the first sign is **perfect blackness** <note>original: "pfecta nigredo." Known as the *nigredo* stage, this represents the "putrefaction" or death of the old matter before it can be reborn as the Stone.</note>; we see it with our eyes, namely that the entire matter becomes black like pitch. How does this happen? The fire forces the corruption and dregs upward and expels them from the matter with a gentle and moderate heat. It is not done by force or the violence of fire; everything is conducted with a gentle and lukewarm heat. Because of this, the corruption or dregs within the matter float to the top in a moderate way until everything is black. Therefore **Morienus** <note>original: "Morie." Morienus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit, said to have taught the secrets of the art to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "See that you moderate the fire, lest you acquire whiteness in the place of blackness, otherwise your entire work would be corrupted..."

<summary>Isaac warns his son against dangerous and expensive elemental separations, advocating instead for the "Great Work" through certain amalgamations. He explains the necessity of the "nigredo" or blackness stage, where gentle heat purifies the matter by driving out corruption.</summary>

For in the separation of the elements, a violent fire is sometimes applied—namely, when the elements of fire are to be distilled, the matter must glow white-hot; and when the dross is burned out of the earth (that is, when the earth is calcined in a **reverberatory furnace** <term>fornace reuerberatoria: A furnace where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof onto the material, rather than the fire touching the material directly.</term>), the earth must glow and burn before it will become "white earth." And so, the good is often burned with the bad, and it becomes part of the glass, and one is lost with the other. Therefore, the first way is best because of the great uncertainty [of the second]; for the dross must be cooked away gradually. For Geber <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of Islamic alchemy.</note> says: "The dragon shall eat its own tail and be nourished by its own poison." <note>This refers to the Ouroboros, a symbol of the cyclical nature of the alchemical work.</note> And Danthynus says: "The black raven shall brood upon its eggs until the chicks become white from old age."

### CHAPTER XXXIV.

<margin>Everything was perfect in the beginning, and shall also be perfect in the end.</margin>
My son shall know, moreover, that the nature of all things under heaven—by the upright nature they received from their Creator—desires to rectify itself and to unload its dross, which is abundantly present within them. For nature is perfect in itself, without flaw; it was perfect in the beginning, and it shall be made perfect in the end by divine power. This applies not only to human nature, but also to whatever is forged and created from the four elements, and whatever is sentient or lacks sensation, with no exception. In the beginning and in the end, everything is perfect and complete in every part. Thus, everything under heaven seeks to be unburdened of its dross. Let [him] seek...

# MASTER JOHN ISAAC

<margin>What the dregs are.</margin>
Indeed, my son, what are the dregs <note>original: "fæces." In alchemy, this refers to the sediment or impure matter that remains after a process, but here Isaac defines it as a vital moisture.</note>? The dregs are a moisture ordained by God, from which whatever exists beneath the celestial course <note>The "celestial course" refers to the sublunary world—everything on Earth subject to change and decay, positioned below the rotating spheres of the stars and planets.</note> is nourished, and it is this which retains things in their essence. <margin>A twofold fire exists in all things, one natural, the other non-natural.</margin> Within all things there exists a perfect elemental natural heat or fire; and there also exists an imperfect, non-natural heat and fire, which is a fire that can be consumed and is combustible. These two are mixed together: as long as that imperfect fire does not acquire any more "bad accidents" <note>original: "mala accidentia." In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties of a thing (like color or temperature) that can change without changing the thing's core essence. "Bad accidents" here implies corruptive qualities.</note>, it preserves the thing in its essence, and it is necessarily within the thing so that the thing may remain in its essence. However, when that imperfect fire acquires any bad accidents alongside itself—which are also hot and imperfect—and they are secretly mixed together, they become so inflamed that they burn, destroy, and kill the thing in which they reside, whether it be humans, livestock, herbs, trees, or whatever is contained beneath the celestial course.

<margin>A twofold water also exists in all things: namely, natural water and the water of the clouds.</margin>
In the same way, there are two kinds of water in all things composed of the four elements. One is called natural water or elemental water, and it is perfect, good, and eternal. There is also another water, the water of the clouds, which is imperfect and mixed with the elemental water. This water is necessary to a thing for its nourishment and for acquiring moisture; it will easily keep a thing in its essence as long as no more water of the clouds is added to it. But when more is added, they mix together and dampen and drown that thing, so much so that the whole is destroyed and dies. <margin>The same is to be understood regarding air and earth.</margin> And what has been said of fire and water is also to be understood regarding air and earth. Unless these dregs were in the elements, all things would be perfect, spiritual, and subtle—which is what God first ordained—nor would there be death, as is rightly taught in the *Vegetable Work* <note>original: "opere vegetabili." This refers to Isaac’s specific alchemical treatise concerning the "vegetable" (living/growing) stone or kingdom.</note>. If you require more concerning the dregs and the diseases of the elements, look for Chapter 16 of the *Vegetable Work*; there you will be perfectly taught regarding these things.

Now my son might ask: when a thing is destroyed in that manner, where then does that perfection remain which was within the thing? You have much on this matter in Chapter 29 of the *Vegetable Work*. Seek that, and there you will be perfectly and rightly taught how "like attracts its like." But I will add a few words on this matter. You shall know that when any thing has died—whether it be a sensitive being or void of sense, whether human, beast, animal, herb, or tree—whatever was fashioned from the four elements, once it has been destroyed, then the spirit of life is separated from it. It returns to its like, from which it first took its origin, as in the *Vegetable Work*, etc. <margin>In destruction, like returns to its like.</margin> And the elements also return to their like, from whence they first arose. The flame of fire or...

...or look at coals: the flame is carried upward along with the heat; the smoke does the same, within which a sharp spirit <term>sharp spirit|original: spiritus acris. In alchemy, this refers to the volatile, acidic, or chemically active essence released during combustion or evaporation.</term> lies hidden, and it recedes toward its own like—just as all the other elements do, as seen in the work of plants.

<margin>The dregs are consumed by the air and the heat of the Sun, as proven by examples.</margin>
Now, my son might ask: where then do the dregs remain that were in the elements, after everything has returned to its own like? The air consumes them, as does the natural heat of the Sun over the course of time. For example: Place a glass basin filled with water in the Sun during the summer. The heat of the Sun will dry up all that water, and a black, slimy, and foul-smelling matter will remain at the bottom. However, if you keep the basin continually in the Sun—taking care that no wind blows into it—in the passage of time that black and slimy water will become as white as snow, and all the stench will vanish, leaving it pleasantly white. This is the work of the Sun’s heat and of Nature itself. Alternatively, take or cut a basin full of green herbs and place it in the Sun. The herbs will putrefy, stink, and wither; then every element departs toward its own like, as was said before, and that foul-smelling black earth will remain in the basin. In the passage of time, the air and the heat of the Sun will calcine <term>calcine|To heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter, often reducing it to a purified white powder.</term> that foul black earth until it is as white as snow. This is the way Nature operates. Consider a criminal placed upon the wheel <note>The "breaking wheel" was a form of capital punishment where the body was displayed publicly.</note>, or hanging from the gallows; the air and the heat of the sun consume all that filth and stench, so that nothing remains except white ashes. Through the long passage of time, even the hard bones—full of fat and marrow—are so consumed by the air and the sun’s heat that the bones become as clean and bright as snow. Indeed, over an even longer span of time, they are made so subtle <term>subtle|In this context, 'subtle' refers to matter that has been refined, purified, or broken down into extremely fine, almost spiritualized particles.</term> by the air and heat that the bones become like a fine dust, imperceptible between the fingers. Nature performs this work, as we see daily before our eyes. Where does the foul matter go, if not consumed and reduced to nothing? Thus the element of earth is purified and made white like snow, so refined that it cannot be felt. Nature performs this by itself, and rectifies <note>original: "rectificat." To rectify is to purify or refine a substance through natural or chemical processing until it reaches its proper state.</note> the elements on its own, as was taught before.

Thus it becomes clear that no separation of the elements is necessary in our Stone, nor is any washing or purification of the Mercury required, except to prove whether it is good by passing it through rabbit-skin or some other soft leather <note>A common alchemical method for filtering liquid mercury to remove physical impurities.</note>.

Isaac concludes that the alchemical Stone requires no manual separation of elements because Nature performs this purification itself.</summary>

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>Every separation of the elements should be avoided as unnecessary.</margin>
Now, why have I told these things to my son? So that he may know it is not necessary to separate the elements in our work, nor to rectify <term>rectify|To purify a substance, usually through repeated distillation or refinement, to reach its most potent state.</term> them, according to the previous arguments. The dregs are dried away into nothingness. Furthermore, rectification cannot be achieved by the power of fire, as has been demonstrated, because of the destruction of the elements. For they escape the craftsman—either fleeing from the fire, or through the vessels, or during the pouring from one container to another—so that some element is lost. Then, when he wishes to rejoin them, he surely has too much of one or too little of another; or perhaps a wicked watery humidity has crept in, which completely ruins the work. Therefore, my son, avoid every separation of the elements as something unnecessary.

->*On the Oil of Metals.*<-

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

<margin>Oil can be drawn from all metals without the separation of elements.</margin>
Next, let my son know that oil can be drawn from all metals without the separation of the elements, and without any washing or cleansing. However, this must be done with strong waters <term>strong waters|original: aquis fortibus. These are powerful mineral acids, like nitric acid, used to dissolve metals.</term>, and a ferment must be applied by anyone who wishes to make oil from imperfect bodies <term>imperfect bodies|A term for base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron, which alchemists believed could be "perfected" into gold or silver.</term>. But I would not advise you to make oil from any imperfect bodies except for Saturn <term>Saturn|The alchemical name for Lead.</term> and Jupiter <term>Jupiter|The alchemical name for Tin.</term>—one for the red work, the other for the white. There are many and varied ways of making oil, which were discovered for the sake of saving time; this was for those who could not wait for the long duration of the Great Works <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) refers to the full, lengthy process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> and wanted to gain profit quickly. Yet there is more danger in this work than in the Great Work, and also more manual labor. For here, strong waters must be distilled, much must be sublimated, and many various operations must be performed. Thus, this oil must be prepared with great labor, care, and expense.

In this context, it refers to highly concentrated alcohol or spirits of wine.</term>. This spirit must be so pure that a linen cloth soaked in it and set on fire will not be burned <note>This was a standard historical test for high-proof alcohol: if the alcohol is pure enough, it burns so quickly and at such a temperature that the cloth beneath remains uncharred.</note>.

And when it no longer drips, leave it yet for 3 days and nights in a boiling bath; for even then, invisible spirits will distill. Then remove it from the fire, seal it, and take that salt out from the pot below; make the pot clean and dry, and put the warm aqua fortis into the same, with the **alembic** <term>alembic|original: alembico. The upper part of a still used for cooling and collecting vapors.</term> properly sealed over it. Then distill through a water bath, first warm and then boiling, until everything has distilled. Then let it remain for a day and a night in a boiling bath, until all the spirits have distilled. Clean the pot again, put the water back in, and distill as above: repeat this until it has no more dregs, or until nothing remains in the glass

<margin>
Aqua fortis to be rectified.
</margin>

pot. Then your aqua fortis is **rectified** <term>rectified|original: rectificata. Purified or refined through repeated distillation.</term> and prepared for your works. And in this manner, rectify all your "strong waters" which you wish to use in the Art, even if it is not always taught specifically; thus your work does not become impure. This is one reason; the second reason is, when

Two reasons why strong waters must be rectified.
</margin>

aqua fortis is not rectified in a water bath, it cannot attract all the spirits of metals into itself, for the dregs of the strong waters hinder and corrupt them, and render the work impure. In this aqua fortis, dissolve 1 or 2 pounds of Mercury taken from ores and not from metals. <note>Hollandus specifies using "native" mercury rather than mercury recovered from an alloy or amalgam.</note> Then take clarified **vitriol** <term>vitriol|original: vitrioli. Metallic sulfates, usually iron or copper sulfate, used as a powerful reagent.</term>, so that it leaves no more dregs, and dry it to a powder with a small fire so that it retains its spirit. Over this powder, pour that dissolved Mercury together into a large glass pot, and stir it with a wooden spatula so that they are properly mixed together. Seal a large alembic and a large receiver, and distill through ashes first with a very small fire, and gradually with a larger one, until the aqua fortis has distilled, and you see the white Mercury to be **sublimated** <term>sublimation|original: sublimandū. The process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condenses back into a solid on a cooler surface, used for purification.</term> in the alembic. Then increase your fire a little more, and keep increasing the fire repeatedly during the sublimation until everything has been sublimated upward. Finally, let your pot glow below for one hour, then let it cool gradually—that is, allow your fire to die out on its own—and having removed the alembic and properly sealed the receiver, take the sublimated Mercury from the alembic. Dissolve that sublimated Mercury again in aqua fortis; it will be dissolved as easily as before. Then put the vitriol into the pot again...

# MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC
## MINERAL WORKS

recently clarified, powder and dry it so that it may be turned into a powder, yet in such a way that it retains its **spirits**, and after the aforementioned dissolved **Mercury** <term>Mercury|original: Mercurio. Quicksilver, considered by alchemists to be one of the three primary principles of all matter.</term> has been poured over it, agitated well and mixed, and immersed in the powder, distill and sublimate it again as described above. And repeat these distillations and sublimations four times, each time with fresh **Roman vitriol** <term>Roman vitriol|original: vitriolo Romano. Likely copper sulfate or iron sulfate, used as a powerful reagent in the purification of metals.</term>. Then, when the Mercury has been sublimated in this manner and placed in a clean glass jar, with the **alembic** <term>alembic|the hood or upper part of a still used to condense vapors.</term> and the receiver placed on top, sublimate it with ashes according to the custom. 

<margin>When Mercury is purely prepared.</margin>
Repeat those sublimations until it no longer leaves any dregs in the bottom: then it is purely prepared for our work; keep it in a closed glass box for use.

Take **Silver** <term>Silver|original: Luna (the Moon). In alchemical symbolic language, the Moon always represents the metal silver.</term> purified very dry in a cupel <note>original: testa. A shallow, porous vessel used in refining precious metals.</note>, and after it has been refined from **Lead** <term>Lead|original: Saturno (Saturn). The alchemical name for lead.</term> two or three times until the crucibles are no longer stained: reduce that Silver into thin plates the thickness of a gold crown, and cut them into square pieces. Then have a square **cementing crucible** made of strong earth that easily bears the fire: 

<margin>The cementation of Silver.</margin>
first place prepared common salt in the bottom to the thickness of a knife’s back, then a layer of Silver plates, then salt again, etc.; and place one above the other until the crucible is full. **Lute** <term>lute|a paste or cement used to seal alchemical vessels airtight.</term> the lid properly with the same strong material and let it dry thoroughly. Then place it in the fire, first with a small heat and gradually with a more vehement one, until your crucible glows slightly, yet in such a way that neither the salt nor the Silver melts. Maintain it in that glow for 24 hours. Then let it cool and break the crucible; place it in a vessel with clean water, and all the salt will be dissolved together over the ashes, and the Silver plates will sink to the bottom. Pour off the water gradually, take out the plates, and dry them. They are indeed as fragile as glass, and black. Powder them in an iron mortar, and not in one of bronze; sieve it, and if anything remains that is not **calcined** <term>calcined|original: calcinatum. The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to a brittle powder.</term>, place it again to be calcined as above, until it all allows itself to be reduced to powder. 

Then grind the powder with common water or honey with the honeycomb until it is impalpable; when ground, put the powder into glass dishes, basins, or jars, and having poured in clean warm water, agitate and mix it well. Allow it to settle; pour off the liquid from the top while warm, and pour in clean warm water again, agitate, let it settle, and gradually pour off the clear liquid from the top. Or pour cold clean water over it and let it be warmed over the ashes, doing as before. Mix all the waters together, and do this until the water flows off as clear as it was when poured in, and the Silver is clean, white, and clear like snow; then let all the dregs of the poured-off water settle, and gradually pour off the water from the top,
